(Above, the eighteenth fascicle) ○ The Seven Gates of the Place of Practice (Dōjō): 1.
Exhortation to Cultivate [the Path] During the Final Five Hundred Years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, amidst the Turbid and Evil World; for Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs.
Whether they be upāsakas or upāsikās who read, recite, and contemplate the definitive Mahāyāna sūtras of the sudden teaching;

those who wish to cultivate inconceivable, perfect, and penetrating wisdom and principle; those who wish to behold the bodies of the three sages—Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra—in their essential nature and marks;
or those who wish to attain purity of the six sense faculties, enter the realm of the Buddhas, and achieve unimpeded penetration.
If one wishes to hear the Dharma-gates taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and be able to receive, uphold, penetrate, and never forget them all in a single thought,
and to expound them without obstruction; if one wishes to dwell together with Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the twelve foremost leaders,
along with a hundred thousand great beings and all bodhisattvas, within the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma, and to become their companions and kin.

Those who wish, within a single thought-moment, to arise from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and travel everywhere to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas;
to behold the various form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of those Buddhas and perform manifold miraculous transformations;

to emit great radiance and preach the Dharma to universally deliver sentient beings, causing them to enter the inconceivable One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); and who wish to destroy the four Māras and purify all afflictions (*kleśa*).
To vex the afflictions, shatter fundamental ignorance, the three poisons, and the four inversions; to eliminate the obstacles of views, karma, and retribution;

and even to extinguish all transgressions that obstruct the Path—those who wish to see their own bodies enter the Bodhisattva’s stage of right determination and become endowed with all the sovereign merits of a Buddha should, in a secluded and tranquil place, rely upon the *Nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa-pariniṣpanna-artha-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment) for one hundred and twenty [days].

For a hundred days, or eighty days, or fifty days, one should practice with single-minded diligence the contemplation gate of the Universal Eye of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha-samantacakṣuḥ*),
as well as the three contemplation gates beginning with *śamatha*. First, during the initial twenty-one days,

one should fashion images of Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra, beholding them with the eyes and contemplating them with the mind, while performing prostrations with utmost sincerity and earnest devotion.
Confess your transgressions and deeply resolve upon vows, wishing to extinguish the karmic obstacles described above and wishing to attain the merits described above.
After twenty-one days, maintain focused mindfulness exclusively; when the allotted period is complete, you will certainly obtain these benefits.
Why is this? This *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* is the Mahāyāna of sudden teaching, the definitive meaning among all sūtras, and the king of secret [teachings].
This samādhi is the definitive realm of the Tathāgatas, expounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and serves as the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Therefore, practitioners should disregard their own bodies and lives and cultivate this Dharma until the end of the future, let alone for a period of three years.

"And yet, how can one not be indolent? He asked: "The path of the Buddha is long and distant; what ultimate benefit is there in practicing for only a hundred days? He replied: "This teaching is a sudden (or direct) teaching.

If one can practice according to this sudden method, within the course of contemplative practice, one will attain the non-duality of the beginning and the end—the 'beginning' being the initial arousal of the great mind, and the 'end' being the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood;

'non-duality' as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: 'At the very moment of first arousing the mind, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' and as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: 'The initial arousal of the mind and the final consummation are not two different things. [Thus, one is] with the Buddha..."

The single essence (as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein the Buddha-mind, sentient beings, and [the Dharma] are non-differentiated), the perfect and sudden great benefit (the text for which is in the "Universal Eye" chapter),
and the benefits of accomplishing the three kinds of contemplation (the text for which is in the "Majestic Virtue and Sovereignty" chapter) will be explained below.

II. Discerning the Vessels (If discerning the vessels for the three-month period of seated meditation, monks and nuns, as well as laymen and laywomen, do not intermingle; monks and men may sit together, as may nuns and women.

If discerning the vessels for the seven-day period of repentance through prostrations, then all four assemblies may participate. However, nuns and the laity must remain outside the altar area. Other matters regarding fitness and unfitness are described in the text itself).

There are, in brief, three types of persons capable of entering the ritual arena to perform repentance: first, those who practice and attain realization; second, those who eliminate karma and establish faith; and third, those who cultivate seeds and form karmic connections.
Regarding the conditions: those who wish to cultivate and realize [the truth] from the very beginning must first seek out a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Such a person should be one who has received the authentic transmission of correct realization through successive generations within the Dharma-Heart (Dharmaguptaka) school, or one who is thoroughly proficient in the Three Contemplations and Three Truths within the Tiantai school.

One should consult them regarding the secret and subtle [teachings], requesting instruction on the mind-dharma so that one may personally attain clear understanding and mastery of the nature of the mind. Thereafter...
Having heard and received this commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, one must first achieve thorough understanding so that no doubts remain.

Furthermore, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen should each maintain their respective precepts with purity; only then may they enter the practice hall with single-minded devotion to realize the goal. Why is this?
Each word and phrase of these liturgical verses for repentance is an object of contemplative wisdom and a text that accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*).

If one does not penetrate the sutras and awaken the mind, it will be difficult to grasp the meaning of the text; one will merely produce vocal rhythms that do not resonate with one's own mind, leaving no way for the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to be perfected.

If one is in the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), one may then receive the instructions of the Dharma Master; yet if one immediately craves to grasp the meaning, how will there be leisure to settle the mind?
Regarding *dhyāna*: if one violates the precepts and does not repent, the mind will harbor defiled thoughts; how can such a person be fit to practice meditative concentration?

One who seeks to realize the signs of attainment must first possess clear wisdom and understanding, with pure aspirations and conduct. Second, regarding those who have extinguished karma and established faith:

this refers to whether they be monastics or laypeople who, though they have not yet awakened to their own minds nor heard the commentaries on the sutras, nonetheless possess a general, pervasive faith in these teachings. This is...

This is the gateway for transcending the mundane and entering the sacred. Having encountered this site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one vows to cultivate together, severing all external conditions and resolving to rely upon the established schedule.
Regarding the various categories of precepts—whether already received or not yet received, whether maintained or violated—within the boundaries of this site of practice:
They vow never to commit what is unwholesome. Furthermore, they have an enlightened teacher who instructs them from beginning to end.

Should they incur the offense of breaking precepts or the offenses of the paths of karma, they shall specifically perform prostrations and recitations within the *dharmadhātu* (place of practice) to confess and purify these transgressions.

Such persons may also join the pure assembly to enter the path together. Although it is difficult to obtain such verified testimony as found in the sutras, they will nonetheless certainly attain the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Success is achieved. All sinful karma is extinguished, and the mind never regresses; this then becomes the foundation for cultivation throughout successive lifetimes.

If one has not yet made a vow, the mind will not refrain from creating karma; then, as sensory objects and conditions arise, latent tendencies will flow on secretly, making it difficult to achieve success in contemplative practice.

Third, regarding those who plant seeds and form karmic connections through perfuming: there are further those, whether monastics or laypeople, who have not yet given rise to [faith] within this teaching.
As for the mind, one merely has a general faith in the Triple Gem as that upon which to rely. Yet, one does not discern which gate is the deepest or which dharma is the most true.

Upon encountering a place of practice, one follows along with joy and wishes to enter; however, the intention is merely to perform the three-week repentance (*saptāha-pratikramaṇa*) to increase merit and eliminate calamities, unable to persevere until the end.
For those who sit in meditation and resolve to cultivate the Way, the Master of Dharma must explain this for them; this is the original intent.
This is dhyāna-contemplation. For those who perform prostrations and repentance at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*).

Since one is currently unable to practice according to the teachings, one must again make a vow that, whether on another day or in another life, one will certainly eliminate all external conditions and cultivate this practice.

Today, listen attentively to the words and phrases to perfume the seeds of wisdom; with utmost sincerity, perform prostrations and recollection to establish a virtuous connection. May I [be joined] with this...

Those who dwell at the site of enlightenment—throughout this life and in future lives—shall forever share in the practice of the Dharma. May those who first attain the Way vow to rescue and deliver one another.

May the many obstacles accumulated in past lives be eliminated. Thus, by recounting each of these sublime matters, may everyone clearly understand the great intent and receive the causal conditions for each.
Then, in future lives, they will surely [be joined] with those practicing at the site of enlightenment.

Because of their prior acquaintance, they may currently be permitted to enter the *dōjō*. For the twenty-one days of ritual repentance (*raigyō*), this is allowed; however, after the twenty-one days have passed, neither nuns nor women are permitted at all.

If it is a *dōjō* for the community of nuns (*nikushū*), then regardless of whether it involves ritual repentance or seated meditation (*zazen*), the monastic community (*sōshū*) is entirely ineligible to enter.

Since the rank of the nuns is lower than that of the monks, it is improper for them to follow the text in performing ritual repentance on behalf of the monks. They must receive [the instruction] themselves.
This is because of the instructions and precepts. Those belonging to the three aforementioned categories, if they enter the *maṇḍala*, will find no benefit.

The Master of the Dharma must by no means yield to personal sentiments or the pursuit of gain by admitting those who are merely casual. Since their arrogance has not been eliminated and their faith has not yet arisen, [they are unfit].

The three karmas become indolent; they delude and confuse the assembly; the sages and saints do not rejoice; the deities do not grant protection. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it—three times. (3) *Hā-yu* (Scold Desire). [Note:

These and the following sections—the "Requisites" (*jùyuán*), "Abandoning the Hindrances" (*qìgài*), and so forth, comprising three gates, as well as the seven gates such as "Harmonization" (*tiáohé*) within the subsequent method for seated meditation (*zuòchánfǎ*)—are all explained according to the *Tiantai Zhíguān*.

Here, because these are combined with the methods for establishing the altar (*zhì dàochǎng*) and performing repentance (*lǐchàn*), several additional gates have been added for practical application. While those [texts] first explain the requisites and subsequently clarify scolding, confession, and abandoning the hindrances, here, both scolding desire and abandoning the hindrances serve to cleanse the mind and make it pure, so that one is capable of entering the altar.]

The meaning is as follows: it is appropriate to first examine the capacity of the vessel; therefore, this is placed before the section on "Requisite Conditions. Although one may have been examined and found to possess the faculties suitable for practicing dhyāna, there are among them those who do not recognize the faults of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
They are frequently deluded by sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Here, "delusion" means that it causes people to harbor yearnings and feel a necessity to obtain these things.

For this reason, he rebukes them. There are five kinds of desire, namely: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. These five constantly deceive and delude ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), causing them...

Those who experience such [sensory] life lose their resolve for the Way. Therefore, those who wish to perform rites of repentance and cultivate meditative contemplation must reprove themselves, ensuring that the mind never again becomes attached to them.
As for "form" (rūpa): it refers to the seductive postures of men and women, precious objects such as gold and jewels, and brilliant, exquisite colors such as crimson and purple;
these cause fools to feel greed and attachment upon seeing them, leading them to commit various evils.
Regarding karma: King Bimbisāra, because of his lustful desire, entered an enemy kingdom and was alone in the chamber of the courtesan Ambapālī;
he was captured, humiliated, and died. King Udayana was defiled by wealth and beauty;
because of that defilement by beauty, he cut off the hands and feet of five hundred rishis. In the world today as well, there are many who act for the sake of wealth and beauty. Regarding sound:

This refers to various sounds such as the singing and chanting of men and women; for example, when five hundred sages dwelling in the Snowy Mountains heard the song of the maiden Kāñcanamālā, they immediately lost their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), becoming intoxicated, deluded, and deranged.

"Fragrance" refers to various fragrances such as those of food and drink, as well as all types of incense. "Flavor" likewise refers to various delicious tastes of food and drink, such as the novice monk’s craving for curd.
Upon the end of his life, he becomes an insect within curd. As for "contact": the bodies of men and women are soft, supple, and smooth;

in cold weather they provide warmth, and in hot weather they provide coolness. It is like the Ṛṣi Ekaśṛṅga, who, because of sensual contact, lost his supernatural powers and was mounted upon the neck by a courtesan.
Question: How does one rebuke them? Answer: As it is said in the Mahāyāna (Tiantai notes on each section: "In detail, as it is said in the Mahāyāna"): "Alas for sentient beings!
They are constantly tormented by the five desires, yet they still seek them without ceasing.

These five desires become more intense the more one obtains them, like adding fuel to a fire, which makes its flames grow fiercer. The five desires are of no benefit, like a dog gnawing on a dry bone. The five...
Desires increase contention, like crows competing for meat. The five desires burn people, like holding a torch against the wind. The five desires harm people, like treading upon a venomous snake.
The five desires lack reality, like what is obtained in a dream. The five desires are not enduring, like things borrowed on loan.
In an instant, it perishes and vanishes. The people of this world are deluded and ignorant; they are greedily attached to the five desires and do not abandon them even unto death.
Consequently, they undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives. If one craves these five desires, one is no different from the beasts.

All sentient beings are constantly driven by the five desires and are thus called slaves. Riding upon these wretched desires, they fall into the three miserable realms. I now cultivate dhyāna, and furthermore—
It acts as an obscuration; this is a great thief. One should quickly distance oneself from it. As a verse in the *Dhyāna-sūtra* says:
Because of craving for the taste of sensual desires, The cycle of birth and death is not severed. One nourishes an enemy and enters the grave, Vainly undergoing all manner of suffering and toil.
The body stinks like a corpse, With its nine apertures flowing with impurities.
Just as a worm in a latrine delights in excrement, so too is the fool’s craving for the body no different.
The wise person should contemplate the mind and not be stained by worldly things; being without entanglements and without desire, this is called true nirvana.
As all the Buddhas have taught, practice with a single mind and intention, counting the breaths within tranquil concentration.

This is called the fourth dhūta practice: Abandoning the Hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). (The preceding five desires are external objects; originally they have no connection [to the mind]. However, because deluded beings forcibly pursue them, their faults and afflictions are censured so that the mind will not seek them;

thus, it is simply said "censure" and not "abandon. Now, these five hindrances have already been formed into seeds through the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of many lifetimes; therefore, one is made to give rise to a fierce and sharp mind to resolutely cut them off and cast them away). There are five kinds of hindrances: first, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); second, [ill-will]...

Anger; third, drowsiness; fourth, restlessness and regret; fifth, doubt. When these five arise, they shroud the mind and wisdom, causing it to become naturally turbid so that one does not perceive right from wrong or good from evil;
therefore, they must be abandoned forever and not allowed to remain in the mind.

First, regarding desire: previously, desire was said to arise from the five external sense objects; now, it is discussed in terms of desire arising from the internal, perfect faculty of the mind (*manas*). That is to say:
When a practitioner sits upright to cultivate dhyāna, if thoughts of desire arise and continue in succession from moment to moment, they will shroud the wholesome mind and prevent it from growing.
Upon becoming aware of this, one should discard them. Why is this? Just as when the fire of desire arises within the body of Śūrpāraka, it was able to burn his very person;
how much more so when the fire of desire arises in the mind—how could it fail to burn all wholesome dharmas? A person possessed by craving and desire is far removed from the Way.
It is extremely remote. Why is this? Desire is a dwelling place of manifold afflictions and disturbances; it does not allow the mind to settle.
Following desire, there is no way to draw near to the Path. As a verse says:
Having already abandoned the pleasures of the five senses, having cast them aside and no longer desiring them—how could one wish to obtain them again?
It is like a fool eating his own vomit. All sensual desires involve suffering when sought, much terror when obtained, and burning affliction when lost;
there is not a single place therein that is joyful.
Question: Greed and the like are seeds perfumed over many eons; they spontaneously give rise to a mind of attachment toward objects.
How can one abandon them? Therefore, the answer below states: "Only when one completely severs all desire and need for worldly things is it called 'abandoning greed.
Second, as for anger: it is the root that destroys all wholesome dharmas and causes one to fall into the various evil realms.
These causal conditions are the enemies of the joy of the Dharma and the great thieves of the wholesome mind;
they are a treasury of various evils and sufferings (the remainder is as explained below in the section on repenting for anger). When a practitioner sits in meditation, they contemplate:
"A certain person is currently provoking me, harming my kin, or praising my enemies. They contemplate the past and the future in the same way. These constitute the nine grounds of resentment.
Due to vexation, anger arises; due to anger, resentment arises; due to resentment, enmity arises. Once enmity has arisen, one then gives rise to the intention to cause harm to that person.
Because such perceptions of anger shroud the mind, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*); one should swiftly abandon them so that greed does not increase.
This is like Śakra Devānām Indra, who questioned the Buddha with a verse:

What, when killed, brings peace? What, when killed, brings freedom from sorrow? What is the root of poison? The Buddha answered with this verse: "Hatred, when killed, brings peace; hatred, when killed, brings freedom from sorrow; hatred is the root of poison."
By slaying anger one finds peace; by slaying anger one is free from sorrow. Anger is the root of poison;
knowing that it thus destroys all virtue, one should cultivate loving-kindness and patience to eliminate it, so as to purify the mind. Third, regarding sleep:
It can destroy the happiness of this life and future lives, as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa, and is the greatest obstacle to wholesome dharmas. Why is this?

While other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) can be removed through conscious awareness, the hindrance of torpor (*middha-nīvaraṇa*) is like a dead person; because there is no perception or cognition, it is difficult to eliminate.
As a verse in the Sūtra says:
"Arise! Do not lie embracing a stinking corpse... (as detailed in the following verses).

One should be startled awake by impermanence and diminish sleep. One may rise to contemplate the stars and moon, wash the eyes with cold water, or even use meditative observation and the meditation staff to suppress it.
Regarding the four types of restlessness (*uddhacca*): the body delights in play, and one does not sit [steadily].
For a time he finds peace; yet his mouth delights in chanting and recitation, engaging in contentious disputes over right and wrong and profitless frivolous talk.

His mind and emotions run wild, following its own inclinations toward sensory objects, contemplating worldly arts and even various unwholesome thoughts—like a mad elephant without a hook or a camel with a pierced nose.
It cannot be restrained. As a verse says:
"You have already shaved your head and donned the dyed robes; Holding an earthen alms-bowl, you go about begging for food.
Why do you delight in and cling to frivolous play? Through negligence and indulgence of the passions, you lose the benefits of the Dharma."
Having realized that one has neither gained the benefit of the Dharma nor lost worldly pleasure, one should swiftly abandon [such agitation]. As for "regret":
because the mind is wavering amidst its objects, when one subsequently wishes to enter meditative concentration, one regrets what was previously done; this anxiety and distress then shroud the mind.
Therefore, it is called a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of remorse (*kaukṛtya*): first, that which arises after agitation (*auddhatya*), as previously described;
second, that which is like a person who has committed a grave and heavy offense and constantly harbors fear, with the arrow of remorse piercing the heart so firmly that it cannot be extracted.
As a verse says:
Doing what should not be done, and failing to do what should be done—one is consumed by the fire of remorse and falls into evil realms in the next world.
If a person can repent for their transgressions, once repented, they need no longer grieve;
thus the mind is peaceful and happy. One should not dwell constantly on it, nor because of mental regret.
That which was not done can be done, and those various evil deeds already committed cannot be made undone;
through such various causes and conditions, he censures restlessness and remorse to make the mind pure and free from obscurations. Regarding the five hindrances of doubt:
because the mind is obscured by doubt, one does not attain confidence in all dharmas. Because confidence is absent, [one does not attain... in the various dharmas.
Within the teachings of all Buddhas, emptiness yields nothing to be grasped. It is like a person entering a mountain of jewels; if they have no hands, they are unable to take anything.

Furthermore, while pervasive doubt is very common, it does not necessarily obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That which currently constitutes an obstruction to concentration refers to three kinds of doubt. First:
First is doubt regarding oneself; second is doubt regarding the teacher; third is doubt regarding the Dharma. Regarding doubt regarding oneself:

for instance, one might think, "I am dull-witted and ignorant, my defilements and impurities are deep and heavy, and I am not a practitioner of dhyāna. Having such self-doubt, the meditative states will ultimately fail to arise.
If you wish to abandon them, do not disparage yourself, for the roots of goodness from past lives are difficult to fathom. Second, regarding doubting the teacher:
one might harbor such doubt and arrogance as to think, "That person’s deportment and appearance are like this; they themselves lack the Way, so how could they benefit me?"
This constitutes an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The method for removing it is as explained in the Mahāyāna: it is like gold within a stinking leather bag;
because of the greed for the gold, one cannot discard the stinking bag. The practitioner is likewise:
even if the teacher is not pure, one should still give rise to a mind that regards them as a Buddha. This matter is fully elucidated in that treatise and should be explained in detail herein. (3)

Regarding those who doubt the Dharma: worldly people often cling to their own preconceived notions; thus, toward the teachings they cherish, they are unable to immediately accept and practice them with a mind of faith and reverence.
If hesitation arises in the mind, the Dharma will not permeate the heart. Why is this? As stated in the *Verses on the Removal of Doubt*:
If you harbor doubt and suspicion, you will be bound by the jailers of birth and death;

like a lion pouncing upon a deer, you shall not attain liberation within the Buddha-dharma. Faith is that which enables entry. If one lacks faith, though they remain within the Buddha-dharma, they will ultimately gain nothing.
Through such various causes and conditions, one should recognize the fault of doubt and swiftly abandon it. Question: Unwholesome dharmas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and immeasurable;
for what reason does one only abandon these five dharmas? Answer: Within these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the three poisons (*trivisa*)—equally divided—are present as the root.
Furthermore, they encompass the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). Specifically, the first is greed (*lobha*).
Poisons: first, the poison of anger; sleep and doubt are the poison of delusion; restlessness and regret are the "equal-share" [poison].
These four categories together comprise twenty-one thousand [types of afflictions]; these four combined total eighty-four thousand.
Therefore, to eliminate these five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is to eliminate all unwholesome dharmas. Through such various causes and conditions, the practitioner abandons them.
Regarding the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*): it is like being released from debt; like recovering from an illness;
like a person suffering from famine reaching a land of abundance; or like escaping safely and without harm from among wicked bandits.
When a practitioner removes these five hindrances, their mind becomes secure, pure, and blissful in exactly the same way. It is, for example, as the sun and moon [are obscured] by five things...
Obscuration refers to clouds, smoke, dust, mist, and the hand of the asura Rāhu. When obscured by these five hindrances, the sun cannot shine;
likewise, when the human mind is obstructed by the five hindrances, it is the same.

5. Having already recognized the faults and afflictions of the five desires through the fulfillment of the requisite conditions, and having internally abandoned the obstacles of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), one’s body and mind become tranquil and one is fit to enter the place of practice (*maṇḍala*).
One should rely exclusively on the sūtras to repent of karmic offenses and prepare for contemplation; however, the ordinary mind lacks a fixed standard.

One’s movements and stillness follow conditions; if conditions are not favorable, the mind likewise scatters accordingly. Therefore, one who wishes to practice contemplation must possess five conditions:
first, purity of precepts; second, sufficiency of clothing and food; third, obtaining a secluded and quiet place;
fourth, ceasing all worldly affairs; and fifth, finding virtuous friends. Regarding the first, purity of precepts, the Sūtra says: "Depending upon and because of these precepts, one attains birth..."

Regarding the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering: as for the precepts (*śīla*), these include the five precepts for laypeople, the ten precepts for those who have left home (śrāmaṇeras), the full ordination precepts (bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs), or the bodhisattva precepts.
If one maintains them with purity, as explained previously in the section on "Discerning the Vessel," such a person is of superior capacity.
Should they commit any transgressions, they must immediately perform repentance, as detailed below in the section on "The Gate of Repentance through Prostration."

Explanation: To state the essentials, if one has not yet resolved not to commit transgressions, then sensory objects and discursive thoughts will flow on secretly and incessantly, making it difficult to achieve success in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, the mind that upholds the precepts (*śīla*) is the second superior causal condition for wisdom. Regarding the second point, "having food and clothing in abundance":
this means that regardless of whether they are coarse or fine, much or little, one should first calculate and ensure they are sufficient so as to avoid [distress].
The thought of seeking after [possessions] obstructs contemplative practice; this is what is meant by "being fully provided. It is not by means of abundance that one is considered "fully provided.

As various sutras frequently observe regarding contentment, how could one be satisfied by mere opulence? Nevertheless, according to the renunciant who has abandoned worldly garments, there are three types, each termed "fully provided":
first, like the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains, who accepts whatever single garment he happens to obtain, even down to a blade of grass.
First, when leaves shield one’s form, it means one does not wander among human beings, as the power of endurance (*kṣānti*) has been perfected.
Second, like Kāśyapa and others, they constantly practice the *dhūta* austerities, possessing only the three robes of refuse-rag cloth and requiring no other surplus garments.

Third, in cold countries or for those whose power of endurance is not yet perfected, the Tathāgata also permits the possession of items such as the hundred-and-one articles in addition to the three robes.

Regarding food, one must necessarily perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), know the proper measure, and practice contentment. However, this applies only when there is a donor who has definitively committed to providing it;
if one seeks it for oneself, it does not fall under this restriction. Next, as for the methods of eating, there are four types:

first, for great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*) and noble ones (*mahāsattva*) dwelling in deep mountains far removed from the world, they eat medicinal herbs, fruits, and the like, sustaining their bodies with whatever they happen to obtain. Second, those who constantly practice the *dhūta* austerities...
The Dharma of Begging for Alms: It can destroy the four kinds of wrong livelihoods and sustain oneself through right livelihood, thereby producing the seeds of the Noble Path.

(The four wrong livelihoods are: first, downward-facing food—compounding medicines and engaging in planting; second, upward-facing food—observing the stars and constellations; third, sideways-facing food—flattering those of high status and acting as a messenger between the four quarters; fourth, crosswise-facing food—using incantations and divination to calculate good and bad fortune.)

All four of these involve sustaining one's life through impure means; therefore, they are called "wrong" (*mithyā*). Furthermore, there are five types of wrong livelihood (*pañca-mithyājīva*): first, feigning extraordinary or marvelous signs for the sake of gain and offerings; second, speaking of one's own virtues for the sake of gain; third, divining good or bad fortune through physiognomy;

fourth, maintaining a loud voice and a majestic appearance to inspire reverence in others; fifth, praising the gains one has received to stir the hearts of people. Third, the *araṇya-sthāna* (translated here as "place of tranquility"):

when a donor sends food, it refers to a situation where a disciple’s patron has granted permission, saying: "Simply settle your mind in practice; I shall provide you with meals for as long as you need."
One must not allow these to be interrupted. Regarding the designation of pure food within the fourfold Saṃgha, this requires prior permission from the monastic community;

once granted, one is exempted from the various administrative duties of the Saṃgha. However, if because of communal meals there are miscellaneous assignments, or if one interrupts the affairs of the community, thereby hindering spiritual practice, then one is not subject to this exemption.
Furthermore, regarding robes and food, if they enter the place of practice (the *dojō*), they must both have been previously offered as alms.
The Master decreed that one must provide for one's needs through fixed allotments and must not beg from place to place, nor seek them through improper means.
Once the *bodhimaṇḍa* has been established, even if there are external offerings of food, one must not accept them, for fear that they will attract external conditions and hinder meditative practice.

Third, regarding "attaining a secluded and quiet place": to refrain from performing various worldly affairs is called "seclusion" (*khan*); to be free from all distractions is called "quiet" (*ching*).
What is called "noise" is termed "stillness. There are three locations where one may practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): first, deep mountains in places remote from people;
second, *dhūta* hermitages (*araṇya*) situated away from villages, at least three li distant, where the sounds of cattle-herding have ceased and all clamor is absent;
third, within pure monasteries far removed from the dwellings of laypeople. All these are termed [places for practice].
Regarding "The Quiet Place: The Fourth—Cessation of All Mundane Affairs," there are four points herein: First, the cessation of affairs related to livelihood:
one does not engage in conditioned worldly activities. Second, the cessation of affairs related to human relations:

one does not pursue the company of worldly friends or acquaintances, severing all social interactions and exchanges; even toward devoted lay or ordained disciples, one maintains purity of body and mind.

For those who wish to participate in the sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodanā*), it is permissible during the time of prostration and repentance to remain outside the altar as one finds seclusion and convenience.

However, upon reaching the period of concentrated mindfulness after the twenty-one days have passed, one must not allow for even three types of activities: first, the cessation of crafts, technical skills, and worldly affairs;

second, the cessation of engaging in worldly craftsmanship, technical arts, medical prescriptions, incantations, divination, writing, mathematics, and accounting; third, the cessation of [worldly] learning.
One abandons all worldly affairs, such as reading, reciting, and formal study; this is for the purpose of ceasing all activities. Why is this?
If one has many worldly affairs, then the practice of the Path will be neglected, and the mind will be distracted and difficult to restrain. Fifth is drawing near to virtuous friends.

There are three kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): first, the spiritual friend as external protector, who manages offerings and is well able to guard the practitioner, ensuring that no other disturbances arise;
second, the spiritual friend as fellow practitioner, who cultivates the same path together, mutually encouraging and inspiring one another without mutual interference;
third, the spiritual friend as instructor, who [teaches] through internal and external skillful means of meditation...

He taught the dharma-gates of meditative concentration, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them. Whenever they presented their minds with questions or doubts, he was immediately able to resolve them thoroughly;
even in matters such as discerning demons and treating illnesses, he provided instruction on each and every point.
6. Regarding the "Adorned Places": the altar, the robes, and the physical form are all the bases upon which the practitioner’s mind relies.

Now, one who wishes to cultivate this Great Practice of the Perfect and Sudden must first perform prostrations and repentance (*li-chan*). As for the method of prostrations and repentance, it is essential that the mind be pure.
The mind does not arise in isolation; it must rely upon pure conditions and objects for support, whereby the mind itself becomes pure. Therefore, one must strictly purify these three matters.

Furthermore, if one wishes to invoke the worthy sages, the altar site must be solemnly adorned. If the altar site is not solemn and clean, the aspiration for the Way will not be aroused, and there will be nothing to move their descent.
For this reason, one should adorn the altar and purify one's robes, desiring that the body be free from all worldly affairs.
Within the thirty-seven days, one should discipline the body and mind, make offerings to the Triple Gem, and maintain single-minded mindfulness.
One should personally recall all evil karma committed since obtaining this present body, as well as throughout past lives, and give rise once more to a sense of shame and remorse.

By prostrating to the Buddha, repenting, practicing the Way, and reciting the sutras with focused and earnest resolve, when one cultivates contemplative practice, the body and mind will be pure and free from hindrances.

Because it is unimpeded, all that the mind aspires to shall be successfully attained. Regarding the method for the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), one must first select a location that is free from clamor, distraction, impurity, evil, and all obstacles and difficulties, as described in detail in the section on the requisite conditions mentioned previously.
If one finds a deep mountain ravine or a secluded forest spring, it is most excellent. If one must remain among humans, one should remove at least one or two feet of the old [ground].
On the ground, smear the earth with fragrant mud and suspend various banners and flowers. In the center, place an image of Vairocana;
on both sides, place images of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī—these constitute the Three Holy Ones. Light lotus lamps and burn the hundred-fold blended incense.

As for the various articles of adornment, they must only be pure and clean; they need not be precious. Each should act according to their means; however, when one’s strength is exhausted, that itself constitutes the ultimate.
Venerable sir, offerings are originally presented to the worthy and holy ones solely to manifest one's own devotion; how could the worthy and holy have likes or dislikes?

(The two characters for "like" and "dislike" are both pronounced in the departing tone. As for the method of arrangement, it may be done according to one’s convenience, as there are no restrictive or fixed rituals.
Next, regarding the purification of clothing: the two assemblies of monks and nuns ought naturally to maintain purity; if one seeks to manage this oneself...
Always guard against carelessness. When about to enter the *maṇḍala*, one must wash both the upper and lower parts, as well as the inner and outer surfaces of the body.

Next, one must bathe the entire body; for if the body is defiled by impurities, how could it be fit to approach the worthy sages? Although the Buddhas are without [discriminative] thought, [they respond to purity].
The deities and spirits will not provide protection. When the deities and spirits do not protect, malevolent spirits will cause confusion and turmoil, and obstacles and difficulties will arise.

For the two groups of lay followers, it is best to wear new clothes; if these are unavailable, they should follow the same standard as the monastics regarding purification, as well as for the laity’s own bodies.

It is not merely a matter of purifying the body; one must especially purify the mind. This refers to the section on establishing the resolve below: to single-mindedly vow in the heart and sever all external conditions.

This refers to such practices as maintaining mindfulness and not retreating when encountering difficulties. From the purification of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) up to the purification of the mind, there is a fourfold progression from the exterior toward the interior, each stage becoming increasingly intimate:
the ritual site is the most external; clothing comes next; and the body is even closer still.

The mind is the most internal [of all]. The Buddha resides within the mind; when the mind is pure, one immediately perceives the Buddha. Therefore, one must proceed from the coarse to the subtle, purifying them through successive stages.
Such is the appropriate method for the practice of ritual means. Only when the three karmas are thus purified may one enter the *maṇḍala*.

When first entering, one should use the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa-dina*). On these days, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings and various celestial benevolent deities descend to the human realm.
In the meantime, they inspect good and evil; seeing those who practice, they comfort and protect them.
To manifest auspicious signs, they cause the practitioner’s mind to give rise to joy, thereby increasing their roots of goodness.
7. Regarding the practitioner who has resolved their aspiration: upon first entering the *dōjō*, one should make this vow within one's own mind:

"From this moment until [the completion of] one hundred and twenty days (or whichever period of days—middle or lower—is appropriate), I shall focus my mind with single-minded concentration. During the first three periods of seven days, I shall direct my resolve exclusively toward the sacred realm."

As well as one's own body and mind. One should reflect upon the suffering of being bound by the karma of delusion throughout successive kalpas. After twenty-one days, focus single-mindedly on the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*).
Why is this? If the mind harbors divergent thoughts, it will naturally become entangled with various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Being called impure, how could one possibly be in accord with samādhi? Therefore, with a resolute mind, he did not begrudge his body or life;
he practiced single-mindedly and diligently for one hundred and twenty days, never retreating or becoming indolent even when it came close to the point of death.

(This refers to those of superior faculties who vow to achieve realization. Except for the causal conditions of death or the observance of mourning, they will certainly not regress. Even if they fall ill, except when bedridden and exhausted, they shall not leave the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*).
Question: The mental states of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) differ from morning to evening; how can one stabilize them so that they do not change for a hundred days? Answer:
Even if the body experiences suffering, one should contemplate the sentient beings of the evil realms (*apāya*); how much more so when practicing the causes for transcending suffering!
Regarding this: how could one not entrust one’s life to it? Su Wu held his mission; though his body suffered, his mind remained firm.

How could he, a great man who had realized the Way, be considered inferior to a worldly scholar? In the lower section of the *Sūtra on Repentance*, every passage cites the scriptures; these are all the fastenings and locks that secure the practice.
One should simply establish a great resolve; how can one first allow doubt to arise? Question: The mental states of sentient beings naturally drift toward diverse conditions;
how can they be made single-minded? Answer: There are two expedient means by which one may achieve single-mindedness.

The first is cultivation within phenomena (*dharma*), such as the methods of repentance and prostration over a period of twenty-one days, as well as the five types of remedial methods for stabilizing the mind according to specific ailments. The second is cultivation within principle (*tattva*).

As previously stated: after twenty-one days, one should single-mindedly collect the mind and contemplate all phenomena as empty and illusory, perceiving only the luminous nature of the spiritual essence (*lingxing*).
When contemplating in this manner, one abides within the state of equality between ordinary beings and sages; with the mind having something upon which to rely, no divergent thoughts arise.
Furthermore, there are various skillful means to prevent the mind from scattering, which shall be explained below in the section on seated meditation (*zazen*).

Confession, and Chan Contemplation.* *The Second Scroll, Concluding the Extensive Text for Cultivation and Realization through Confession in the *Complete Enlightenment* Sanctuary.* Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cudang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
The Eight Gates of the Ritual of Repentance, Part One:
Invoking the Sages to Inspire the Aspiration for Enlightenment, Purify the Defilements of Sin, Exert Effort in Practice, and Realize Entry into the Sublime Realm.
One must request all the worthy ones and sages of the ten directions to serve as witnesses. Although the Buddhas and worthy sages are omnipresent, they do not manifest before those who lack devotion.
Therefore, one must rely on wisdom and remain detached from consciousness, constantly maintaining the perception of the Buddha.

When the mind is pure and wisdom is clear, and principle accords with the transformations of phenomena, one will see the Buddha at all times; this is called "pure dependent origination" and constitutes the invitation to the Buddha. Thus...

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "For example, when the sun rises, it shines universally upon the world, and its reflection appears without exception within all vessels of pure water. The Buddha-sun is likewise;
it manifests universally throughout the Dharma-realm, neither before nor after, appearing without exception within the vessels of the pure minds of all sentient beings.
Question: In the liturgical repentances of various schools, everyone first kneels with their right knee on the ground (huku) and reverently holds incense and flowers as an offering. Why is this?

[The questioner asks: "Regarding the section on 'Nurturing' (*yǎng*), what is the purpose of this passage? Is it not for the preliminary invocation? [The respondent] answers: "The various [standard] texts involve long-term practice, such as daily morning and evening worship and recitation.

The present occasion, however, is for establishing a ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) and applying diligent effort to seek realization; therefore, one proceeds directly with the preliminary invocation. [The questioner] asks: "Why not simply follow the conventional path:

first perform the half-kneeling prostration (*huqù*), offer worship, circumambulate, and conclude with hymns of praise (*fànzàn*), and only then proceed with the invocation? [The respondent] answers: "If one does not first invoke [the deity], [the subsequent rites will lack efficacy]."
When wishing to make offerings and circumambulate whom, one should first request their presence and subsequently perform offerings, praises, prostrations, and so forth.
Now, you should burn incense and scatter flowers, maintaining single-minded right mindfulness, vocally reciting the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and making individual petitions to each;
you must not be disrespectful or distracted.
With incense and flowers, we most sincerely invite the Honored One—
the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya— who enters the Great Radiant Treasury within the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta Sūtra, who pervades the ten directions,
who manifests in all pure lands from the fundamental source of both ordinary beings and sages, and whose wisdom and phenomena are non-dual.
Vairocana Buddha (Vairocana and Śākyamuni are variations in the Sanskrit pronunciation; both signify "Universal Radiance").
I pray that you will not forsake your compassion, descend to this site of practice, and accept my offerings.

With incense and flowers, I reverently invite all Buddhas who have entered the Great Radiant Treasury (*mahā-prabhāsa-garbha*) within the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*), abiding in the ground of awakening for all sentient beings and maintaining them with radiant adornment (*prabhā-vyūha*).
(As stated above... [and so forth]. From "I pray that you will not abandon us" onwards, until after the invitation with incense and flowers, each instance follows the preceding pattern.)

With a sincere heart, we reverently invite the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, whose physical forms are interfused and whose speech is unimpeded, who have heard and expounded the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (and so forth).
With a sincere heart, we reverently invite those who possess great compassion and great vows, who shall protect *Complete Enlightenment* until the end of the future.
The Sūtra states: "I, with a sincere heart, entreat all the Buddhas of the three periods of time...

[and so forth]... my original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, who possesses great kindness and great compassion, manifests thousands of millions of billions of reflected forms and physical bodies in response to the capacities of beings in the Sahā world. By means of wisdom that is like an illusion, he brings forth..."
The sound of an echo in the valley proclaims the teaching that exhausts all words like the wind in empty space;
it rescues and gathers sentient beings who suffer from dreams and delusions, causing them to awaken and enter into the nature of phenomena (as extensively described).

(As stated above) With a sincere heart,

and I also invoke the profound and vast treasury of Dharma consisting of all the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras—both sudden and gradual—in those worlds. I pray that they all [come to me].

With a sincere heart, we reverently entreat the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who manifests in various forms to save suffering sentient beings (and so forth).
With a sincere heart, I reverently entreat the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, foremost among the virtuous, within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiant Treasury (and so forth).
With a sincere heart,
I reverently entreat those of great kindness and great compassion who constantly abide in the realm of the Yama-māra, employing skillful means according to conditions to rescue and deliver [beings].

In this path, [I] wholeheartedly invoke the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Three Times and the Ten Directions throughout the entire realm of empty space, in all lands as numerous as motes of dust—namely, the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Dedications, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices, and the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths. As... [and so forth].
These fifty-one honored Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas (and so forth),

I most sincerely entreat as the fundamental masters for those of superior capacity in the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; may they serve as the model for cultivation and realization through the sudden gate for the final age,
whereby the bodhisattva practices are perfected within a single lifetime through the quest for the Dharma across one hundred cities.

The Bodhisattva Sudhana (and so forth) with a sincere heart reverently invites all the Sangha of worthy and holy ones— those in training and those beyond training, the four stages of approach and the three fruits,
as well as Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas— dwelling within the dust-mote lands throughout the entirety of space in the ten directions of the three periods of time (and so forth).
With a sincere heart, we invoke the twenty-eight celestial kings from the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra*,

the Great Brahmā King, Śakra, Lord of the Heaven atop Mount Sumeru, and the Four Celestial Kings who Protect the Nation— all of whom once addressed the Buddha and made vows to protect those who uphold this sutra,
constantly ensuring their peace and security so that their resolve never regresses. We now entreat you not to abandon these vows, but to lead [these practitioners].
All these attendants followed behind the Tathāgata when he descended to this site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* to accept my offerings (and so forth).
With a sincere heart, I now extend this invitation to the Vajrapāṇi deities within the *Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta*:
Agniśikha-vajra, Praṇāśana-vajra, Nīlambā-vajrī, and others, numbering eighty thousand, together with their retinues. They once addressed the Buddha themselves, saying:
He made this vow: "For those sentient beings of the final age who uphold this sutra, I shall protect them as I would my own eyes.
Furthermore, wherever they practice on the path to enlightenment, we Vajras, leading our own retinues, shall protect them morning and night so that they do not regress.
Their homes shall be forever free from calamities and afflictions; epidemics shall be extinguished, and their wealth and treasures [shall increase]."

Abundant and sufficient, they shall never lack for anything. Now I entreat you not to abandon this vow, but to lead your respective retinues and attend upon the Tathāgata from behind, descending to this site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* to accept my offerings (and so forth).
With a sincere heart, I reverently invite the powerful *kumbhāṇḍa* king Jīvaṃjīvaka and other *kumbhāṇḍa* kings of the ten directions from within the assembly of the *Pūrṇabodhi-sūtra*.
He also addressed the Buddha, saying: "I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra.
Within a radius of one yojana of their dwelling, if there are spirits or ghosts who invade their domain, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust. I now entreat you not to abandon this vow;
when the future Tathāgata arrives at this site of enlightenment, may my realm be included among his attendants, and may he accept my offerings."
[Recite] "Nurturing... and so forth, with a sincere heart,
we respectfully invoke all the great Dragon Kings and the eight classes of beings, as well as the local spirits and deities of this place,

the Spirit King of Mount Guifeng, and the Spirit of Mount Zigai (if these are not located on the mountain itself, omit the first two phrases), along with the benevolent deities who protect the Dharma.
The guardian deities of the monastery, the presiding deities of the site, the lords of the directions, the lord of the earth, the lord of fire, the lord of wind,
the lord of water, the lord of mountains, the lord of space, and the various hosts of medicinal deities: we pray that, in accordance with the Buddha’s entrustment,
you will descend to protect this site of practice and accept our offerings (and so forth).
[Offering incense and flowers] (Kneeling with the right knee on the ground):
May we, [Name] and others, with single-minded devotion, pray that our own Honored One, Vairocana Buddha, and our teacher,
Śākyamuni World-Honored One, not forsaking their compassion, accept this invitation and descend to this site of practice to sit upon the lion throne within the Lotus Treasury.

The seat. Within the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, may the hundreds, thousands, millions, and billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River who protect this *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, and all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, together with compassion, come to this site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and sit upon lotus seats.
May this Mahāyāna of the sudden teaching, the definitive meaning of the *Vaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, appear within my mind and perfect my contemplative practice. Mañjuśrī...
May Samantabhadra and the twelve great bodhisattvas, together with their retinues and the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, likewise surround the Tathāgata, each sitting upon a lotus seat.
May the Great Brahmā King, the Sumeru King, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings vow to protect [the Buddha] before him.
May the kings of the *kumbhāṇḍas* and other spirits of the ten directions likewise vow to protect those who uphold this sutra, through the power of their vows.

Come to this site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). May the local deities and spirits of this place, the various thrones, the great nāga kings, the protective deities who guard the Dharma, the presiding deity of the site of practice, all those who preside over water, mountains, fire, wind, lands, and forests and crops, and even the deities who preside over medicinal herbs, together with their retinues, come to this place and protect this foremost site of practice. These Tathāgatas...
I pray that all Bodhisattvas and worthy sages will come and bear witness.

Today, for the sake of sentient beings within the six realms across the lands of the ten directions, I wish to cultivate the wondrous gate of the three contemplations of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* according to the definitive sutras of the sudden teaching.

Because I desire to shatter all obstacles and bring my contemplative practice to fulfillment, I shall, for twenty-one days, apply myself with single-minded diligence in accordance with what is taught in the sutras.
Practicing in accordance with the Dharma, I pray that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, who understand the practitioner, will, by the power of their original vows, accept my repentance.
May all that I practice be decisively accomplished; may all karmic obstacles be destroyed; may the Dharma gates manifest before me;
and through this, may I deliver sentient beings so that they all attain realization and entry.
Having completed the invocation, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
The invocation being finished, it is known that all Buddhas and Great Bodhisattvas do not disregard this request.

Subsequently, within the non-dual realm of the Great Luminous Treasury, the pure land manifested therein—the assembly of the Dharma of equality—remains in the samādhi of non-arising, responding through compassion.
Moved by this, my karmic conditions were awakened. It was like the moon falling into the river of realization, appearing without moving.

Although our physical eyes cannot behold it, when we collect the mind in contemplation, it becomes perfectly clear. We see Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all the worthy sages filling the site of enlightenment and pervading the realm of empty space.
They know and perceive our sincere and earnest entreaty that we shall practice according to the teachings. This is...
