If one wishes to accomplish these merits, one should cultivate the ten kinds of vast vows and practices (*praṇidhāna*). Therefore, the practitioners of the fundamental lineage in the Western Regions have extracted [this text] from the sūtras to circulate it separately, chanting, recollecting, and practicing it. There are three translations in total: first, that by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of the Jin dynasty;

second, that by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of the Tang dynasty; and third, that by the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others during the Zhenguan era. These ten practices and vows are precisely these eight [sections], beginning with "Offerings" and so forth, with the exception of the section on "Exhortation."

The opening [of the sūtra] establishes two gates: turning the wheel of Dharma and its long endurance in the world. Furthermore, within the section on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), two gates are distinguished: learning in accordance with the Buddha and complying with sentient beings. Thus, ten gates are formed. Although these eight layers are all gates for entering the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*), each possesses its own distinct characteristics and merits: Through prostration, one removes the obstacles of pride accumulated over immeasurable kalpas and attains a body of nobility.

Through praise, one removes the obstacles of harsh speech and so forth accumulated over immeasurable kalpas and attains the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*). Through making offerings, one removes the obstacles of jealousy accumulated over many kalpas and attains great wealth and prosperity in every birth.

Through repentance (*deśanā*), one removes the three obstacles throughout the limits of existence and attains the perfection of both the primary and secondary rewards (*sambhoga* and *nirmāṇa*). Through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one removes the obstacles of stinginess and greed accumulated over many kalpas and attains vast assemblies of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in every birth. Through requesting [the Buddhas to teach], one removes...

"May the obstacles of slandering the Dharma throughout many kalpas be removed; may I attain great learning and eloquence in every birth; may this be dedicated toward removing the obstacle of narrowness and inferiority, so that I may obtain vast and immeasurable merit and goodness; may I resolve to remove the obstacle of despondency and retreat, so as to maintain all practices and swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Then all these people knelt on their right knees, reverently holding incense and flowers, making offerings according to the Dharma, and made this vow:
"May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the worlds of the ten directions and make offerings to all Buddhas."
The manifested Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, along with the assemblies of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, receive these clouds of incense and flowers, which they transform into luminous platforms.

Vast as boundless realms, they perform immeasurable Buddha-works throughout the entire Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and all Buddha-fields of the ten directions and the three periods of time. (As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All within the entirety of the Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and all Buddha-fields of the ten directions and the three periods of time...")
There are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the atoms of the ultimate dust. At each and every Buddha’s abode, there is an ocean-like assembly surrounding them.

I now offer all manner of supreme and exquisite offerings to them—namely, clouds of flowers, clouds of garlands, clouds of celestial music, and even clouds of robes and various incenses—each of which is as vast as Mount Sumeru or the great ocean. Question: This text states that in that sutra it says, "Fragrant flowers fill the worlds of the ten directions," and so forth regarding making offerings.

How can one procure such a multitude of offering implements, and how can one encounter such a multitude of Buddhas? Answer: According to the third chapter, the "Gate of Offerings," in the *Huayan Yuanqi Zhang* (Chapter on the Dependent Origination of the Avatamsaka), it says: "Whatever a Bodhisattva provides—even a single flower, a single incense, a single robe, or a single canopy..."

The articles of offering are none that do not accord with ultimate truth and are equal to the realm of empty space. Thus, by means of a body that is the entirety of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one travels through all Buddha-fields and offers these objects that accord with truth to the Buddhas.

For this reason, the bodhisattva’s practice is not in vain; regarding those sages encountered during their cultivation, they never miss the proper time. All offerings are constantly accomplished in accordance with principle. Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma to the Buddhas accords with ultimate truth. The commentary states: based on this, it is said that "a single incense stick, a single flower," and so forth; it further says, "constantly in accordance with principle."

As for "accomplishment," it means knowing that everything listed in the sutra accords with principle—that the one is many, and so forth. Therefore, the practitioner need only settle the mind in contemplative practice; then, object by object, they will naturally become manifold, all becoming the various Buddhas. Thus it is said:

"May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas. The subsequent passage in the sutra states that compared to this offering of contemplative practice, an offering made from a deluded mind does not equal even a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-kalā*—not even a single *śata* (fraction) of it.

The term "all" (*jie*) signifies the sense of spontaneity (*ziran*); it expresses that within the Dharma-realm there exists such inconceivable power and function as a natural law (*dharmatā*). The term "clouds" (*yun*) signifies the sense of following conditions (*suiyuan*); it expresses that [the manifestation] arises through the power of the force of practice and vows.

It is seen. This means that while these offerings appear as manifest forms, wisdom illuminates their lack of intrinsic nature. They arise from the dharma-nature of emptiness and the non-arising of phenomena. The seer and the seen are utterly without basis; they come forth through functional application, yet there is nowhere from which they come. When the function ceases, they depart.
Though it has no destination when it departs, it can contain compassion and moisten all with the rain of Dharma, benefiting all things in layers upon layers without end;
thus it possesses the likeness of a cloud). 3. Praising the Tathāgata (has two sections).

I. Praise in Sanskrit (This is a verse from the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra praising the wisdom of the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*). People of that time called it "Sanskrit" (*Brahman*), not realizing it was a praise of the Buddha performed using the Sanskrit language.)
The wondrous form of the Tathāgata is non-dual and not a transformation body;
there is nothing in the world equal to it. It is peerless and inconceivable;
therefore, I now pay homage. The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so.
All phenomena are eternally abiding; therefore, I take refuge in and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.

(2) Direct Praise: Having thus requested the Triple Gem, one should immediately prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground, bowing at the Buddha’s feet. Then, maintaining upright posture and dignified deportment, one stands with single-minded attention facing the Dharma seat, burning [incense].
Scattering incense and flowers, one contemplates in the mind the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem while gazing upon them with eyes that do not turn away. One recites these words:
"The true Dharma-nature is his body; ultimate awakening is his wisdom. Seated upon the lotus-flower pedestal of the treasury, he is named Vairocana.
Among the hundreds of thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, he alone is the sovereign, presiding over and dwelling in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
World-Honored One, yet while merging with True Suchness, you are not great; you are fully present within every single hair-tip. While dwelling within a minute speck of dust, you are not small;
you pervade the vast Dharma-realm. Throughout the ten directions you perform great spiritual transformations, and from the three subtle [bodies] you radiate great beams of light.
He manifests the marks of the ten bodies of ordinary and holy beings; his six sense faculties function interchangeably according to the stages of realization.

Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-lands, bow their heads and follow him constantly; a hundred million *akoṭis* of devas surround him with reverent hearts. (Next, praise the merit of the Dharma.)
The Vaipulya, definitive, and Perfect Enlightenment Dharma-gate is taught in unison by billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within their pure lands;
it is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and serves as the eye of all sūtras—a gate of the sudden and complete teaching. (Next, praise the Jewel of the Sangha.)
Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the Buddhas; he presides over faith, understanding, and realized wisdom. Samantabhadra represents the essence of the Dharma-realm;

he presides over compassion, vows, principle, and practice. Together with the twelve chief bodhisattvas and their followers throughout the ten directions, they dwell in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.

This is the assembly of the Three Jewels of the True Teaching at the lecture hall of the Pure Land—how majestic! How resplendent! It stands far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. Nevertheless...

Now, we, the disciples [Name] and others, at this time, having offered praise, worship, and repentance, take all the merit from our cultivation of the Mahāyāna and dedicate it as a blessing to those in the twenty-eight heavens of the upper realms:
to the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the rest; to the eight classes of nāgas and spirits;
to Yama and the five paths of rebirth; to the Six Jie, the Eight Kings, the ghost kings who inflict diseases, and their retinues. This...

May those dwelling as local deities of the land, those within monasteries who protect the True Dharma, as well as kings and sovereigns, the myriad people of the realm, teachers, monks, parents, all spiritual friends, donors from the ten directions, and all sentient beings of the dharma-realm—by means of these roots of goodness, may they equally cultivate and accumulate the two kinds of adornments:
merit and wisdom; and having become free from hindrances and emerged from the entanglements, may they achieve [enlightenment].

The Path of the Knowledge of All Modes (*Sarvajñatā-mārga*) (*Avataṃsaka Sūtra*): After citing buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, it continues: "I shall, with profound faith and understanding, perceive them all before me through my knowledge and vision; and I shall do so entirely by means of a subtle tongue-faculty surpassing that of the goddess Sarasvatī."

They produce inexhaustible sounds and words to praise the ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits. Regarding the phrase "profound faith" and so forth, this refers to the power of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). This is its own cause (*svahetu*), while the power of Samantabhadra’s Dharma serves as its condition (*pratyaya*). This meaning is explained in detail below in the section on prostrating to the Buddhas, where the relevant sūtra is cited;

it is fully set forth there because the text is complete. As for the goddess Sarasvatī, the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifestation) of that same sūtra states: "The Sovereign Heavenly King has a celestial maiden named Suvaktrā (Excellent Mouth). From her mouth issues a single sound, which accords with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music.

Within each of these musical performances, there are again hundreds of thousands of distinct tones. The commentary explains: While she merely harmonizes with music, this [wisdom] accords with the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it transcends her. One should know that it is only by clarifying contemplative wisdom that one can understand what is being praised.
All are like the ocean—deep, vast, and inexhaustible). IV.

Paying Homage to the Triple Gem (Having finished the eulogies, one should with single-mindedness and upright body maintain proper deportment and pay homage to the Buddhas in succession. Regarding the method for paying homage to the Buddhas: one must, with a sincere heart, call to mind the true body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha being honored as being like empty space;

yet it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon in water, clearly and distinctly as if facing one’s very eyes. When receiving precepts or performing prostrations, one should apply this same mental focus before each and every Buddha, invoking the essence by means of the name.)

One should perform this prostration without allowing the mind to become distracted. Furthermore, one must know for oneself that body and mind are empty and quiescent, such that no marks of prostration exist. Following conditions, one perceives the Dharma-realm; before each and every Buddha, this very body is present, bowing with head and face in reverent salutation.

According to the "Contemplation Gate of Prostrating to the Buddhas" by Tripitaka Master Ratnamati, there are seven grades of prostration, from inferior to superior: first, the prostration of pride; second, the prostration of chanting in response—these two are not proper rites. Third, the prostration of reverence, which arises from the heart and is manifested through body and speech, with the five wheels touching the ground. Fourth, the signless prostration, which enters deeply into the Dharma...

1. Nature-worship (*svabhāva-pūjā*): This is to be free from the characteristics of subject and object. 2. Worship of the arising of function (*vṛtti-pravṛtti-pūjā*): Contemplate that both one’s own body and the Buddha arise from conditions, like illusions and shadows; then universally employ body and mind to pay homage to all. 3. Internal contemplation worship (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā-pūjā*): Worship only the true Buddha of the Dharma-body within the gateway of the body, without taking other Buddhas as objects.

4. Ultimate reality worship (*dharmatā-pūjā*): Whether internal or external, whether ordinary beings or Buddhas, they share the same ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). To see a Buddha as an object to be worshipped is itself a false view. Contemplating the true reality of one’s own body, one sees that the Buddha is likewise so; this is called "equal worship. Thus Mañjuśrī said:

"Because it is neither born nor extinguished," "Homage to the Buddha who has nothing to observe," and so forth. Nevertheless, all four prostrations belong to the category of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Specifically: 1. The fourth prostration is the Contemplation of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), paying homage to the Buddha of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); for one enters the nature of the Dharma. 2. The fifth is the Contemplation of the Provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), paying homage to the Buddha of Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

for from the essence, function arises. 3. The sixth is the Contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*), paying homage to the Buddha of the Ultimate Truth; for one does not calculate emptiness, but directly perceives the true nature of the coming-and-going of awakening. 4. The seventh is the Three Contemplations in a Single Mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*), paying homage to the Buddha of the Single Realm of the Three Truths;

for one does not reject the provisional while clinging to the real, but brings them to a state of cessation where there is no dependence. However, since the scriptural text of these seven prostrations currently belongs to the gate of following appearances (*lakṣaṇānuyāyin*), they correspond for now to the third and fifth [contemplations]. This is because every thought is reverent, and in every moment one contemplates the body and the Buddha-nature as following conditions, like a phantom or a reflection. The rest...

The "markless prostration" and so forth represent the meaning of focusing the mind by distancing oneself from marks at a lower level. Thus, although the three contemplations are perfectly clear and luminous, one performs this contemplative wisdom precisely while showing reverence with body and speech; it does not mean that body and speech do not perform prostrations and praises at all.

Rather, one simply employs the contemplation of marklessness and so forth as the equivalent of worshipping the Buddha—one must reflect well upon this. If one were to claim that the contemplative wisdom alone constitutes worshipping the Buddha and no bodily prostration is required, then in the third [contemplation] one would likewise have to consider mere reverence sufficient for prostration, which would be inconsistent with the movement of body and speech.

The principles of this analogy are as such; how could they not be erroneous? Question: In the Mahāyāna school, if a transgression arises from the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is termed a violation of the precepts (*śīla-bheda*). May we apply this same principle to the case where bowing with the mind constitutes the generation of merit? Answer:

When one forms a thought within the mind specifically intending to employ body and speech to carry out acts such as killing or stealing, and that mental intention is fulfilled without any subsequent regret, it is termed a violation of the precepts. Now, in the present case, one merely intends to employ the karma of the body—such as bowing—and the karma of speech—such as praising—with a resolute will and without any hesitation.

Even if one has not yet succeeded in strictly purifying the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), during the act of bowing, merit is clearly and certainly generated. If there were no intention to employ body and speech, there would fundamentally be no merit; just as if one originally had no intention to kill and so forth, there would likewise fundamentally be no sin. However, once contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is perfected, the object of contemplation is constant...

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one’s prostrations are uninterrupted; yet, the mind that observes [this] does not regress, flowing naturally like a stream. It is like a person who has taken up an evil vow (*duṣaṇa-śīla*):

even without actually killing or stealing, the thought of such acts flows through every moment. One who takes up an evil vow performs the deeds of a butcher, hunter, bandit, and so forth. Question: In the fifth prostration, it is said that both subject and object are like reflections. Since reflections have no intention, how can they constitute a ritual of worship? Answer: It is precisely this very thought of reverence.

It is also like a shadow. In the world, mirrors and the like reflect only the shadows of forms; they cannot reflect the shadows of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or the mind. Yet this Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna), equal to the realm of empty space, perceives forms, sounds, and so forth, as well as the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta).

When performing this contemplation, one first contemplates that one’s own body and mind are portions of the power of ignorance, arising from defiled conditions. Now, by means of correct knowledge, one contemplates them as empty and devoid of self-nature, causing them to become immediately the Single True Dharma-realm (eka-dharmadhātu).

Thereafter, one contemplates that this Dharma-realm does not abide in its own nature, but constantly arises through the power of conditions. Thus, one pays homage and shows reverence, single-mindedly taking refuge and entrusting oneself to the Buddhas and the meaning of the Dharma. Through these pure conditions, one brings forth the body and mind as the Buddha; following these pure conditions, they arise as one's body and mind.

And as for the Buddha, he is seen like a reflection in a mirror. Since my own body and mind lack intrinsic nature, they are in union with the *dharmadhātu*. Because the *dharmadhātu* is all-pervasive, my body and mind, following that which they rely upon—the *dharmadhātu*—are likewise all-pervasive. There is nothing they do not pervade, and there is nothing they do not pay homage to;

thus it is said, "I universally prostrate to all. In the sixth [section], it says: "The True Buddha within the body" is like a great scripture contained within a speck of dust, like pure gold wrapped in cloth, like a Buddha image within a burnt mold, or like the sound of a bell within a vessel.

Since there is here a mutual relationship between the true and the false, the internal and the external, it is not a case of unilaterally negating all marks; thus, this practice also pertains to the "contemplation according to recollection" (*anusmṛti*). According to the Huayan school, there is furthermore a rite of worship that integrates self and other, which is fully expressed in four propositions:

First, worshipping many Buddhas with a single body. That sutra says: "With each and every body, one universally worships Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields. It further says: "A Bodhisattva should know that in every thought-moment of their own mind, a Buddha always attains perfect enlightenment;

all sentient beings are likewise so, for in every thought-moment they all possess a Buddha who attains perfect enlightenment. Second, worshipping a single Buddha with many bodies. The sutra says: "At the abode of each and every Buddha, one manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable fields. It further says: "The Tathāgata..."

When attaining perfect enlightenment, one universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment therein. Third, paying homage to one Buddha with one body; fourth, paying homage to many Buddhas with many bodies. That sutra states:

"When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he entered the Samādhi of the Wisdom of Excellent Awakening and saw bodies equal in number to all sentient beings dwelling within his own body, even within a single pore. Within a single pore, there are bodies equal in number to all sentient beings pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it is the same for every pore. There is not the slightest space that is empty and devoid of the Buddha-body. The commentary explains:

This is merely taking a single moment of mind to correspond with a Buddha, taking a single Buddha to correspond with one's body, and correlating the text with its meaning to form four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). However, in reality, the number of bodies is equal and inexhaustible. Question: Why?

Question: Is the body of a practitioner of the path, in each and every instance, identical to the inexhaustible [body] of the Buddha? Answer: Because the causes and conditions are complete. That sutra says: "By the power of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. This refers to the power of the Dharma, which is the condition (*pratyaya*). It further says: "Arouse deep faith and understanding as if [the Buddha] were before one's eyes.

This refers to one's own power, which is the cause (*hetu*). "Deep and supreme" refers to *adhimukti* (resolute belief). *Adhimukti* means to decisively grasp and maintain [the truth]. That is to say, by the power of Samantabhadra’s Dharma, one sees that all objects are the realm of the Buddha.

When the mind relies on wisdom rather than consciousness, then every moment of mind is a mind that beholds the Buddha. Therefore, the sutra says: "All phenomena are without arising; all phenomena are without cessation. If one can understand them thus, the Buddhas are ever present before one. Thus, that sutra concludes with a prostration.

The Buddha said: "As long as the realm of empty space is not exhausted, the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, the karma of sentient beings is not exhausted, and the afflictions of sentient beings are not exhausted, so too shall my prostrations continue—indeed, because the realms of empty space and sentient beings are inexhaustible, these prostrations and reverences of mine shall never come to an end.

Moment after moment they shall continue in succession without interruption; my actions of body, speech, and mind shall never grow weary. This applies to each of the ten types of praise and vows for making offerings and offering praise, exactly as described here. One should understand this by concluding [the practice] accordingly.

If one does not rely on the power of the Samantabhadra Contemplation Practice, how could one achieve such uninterrupted continuity from moment to moment? The wise should reflect carefully that one must not perform these acts of prostration, praise, and offering with a mind of arising and ceasing or with a focus on grasping at appearances."

V. Repentance of All Obstructions (Having finished prostrating to the Buddha, one stands before the Dharma seat. With body upright and dignified, kneeling reverently with the right knee touching the ground, one burns incense and scatters flowers while visualizing the Triple Gem filling the entirety of space.

The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, surrounded by an infinite retinue of magnificent adornments, acts as the presiding master of the repentance. Visualizing each of them as if they were right before one’s eyes, with single-minded focus and profound shame and remorse, one confesses and reveals all evil karma created throughout immeasurable kalpas by the six sense organs and the three types of action.

One severs the continuity of such thoughts and vows from this moment until the end of the future, never to commit them again. Why is this? Because the nature of karma is difficult to empty and its retribution is never lost; if one commits it, one will not cease.)

[Objection: These are the causes and conditions for false and inverted [states], and thus one will in turn receive false retributions. However, the phrases used in the confession are mostly drawn from the texts of the Great Buddha Sūtras, as well as the intent of the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sādhana-dhyāna-sūtra* (Fǔxián guān jīng), and the intent of the verses from the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Divyadundubhinirghoṣa*, and the *Suvarṇabherī*.
For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*, I vow to sever all hindrances and take refuge through repentance.
As for what is called "repentance" (*chànhuì*), its full term is *chànmó* (Sanskrit: *kṣamā*), which here means "to regret one's transgressions. To explain it in detail:

"confession" (*chàn*) refers to laying bare one's prior offenses, while "regret" (*huì*) refers to reforming one's future conduct. However, those who wish to repent must first understand the causes and conditions of their successive arising. By...

Since beginningless time, through non-awakening, one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; activating body, speech, and mind, one creates all karma—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable.
If one examines the mind, one should repent both the wholesome and the unwholesome, because at the time of delusion, these were produced by a heart of greedy attachment.
However, if one proceeds according to the specific nature of the offenses committed, one repents only the unwholesome karma, because from the time of awakening onwards...
Because one who has attained Buddhahood ultimately never abandons wholesome conduct; because wholesome deeds accord with principle;

and because, during delusion, seeking retribution by grasping at signs constitutes a fault, whereas after awakening, one is free from both [grasping and retribution] yet does not abandon wholesome dharmas, they are therefore not extinguished.

All evil karma inevitably brings about suffering; therefore, it must be severed entirely, which is why one performs universal repentance (*pāpa-deśanā*). Within this repentance, there are further two types.
First, if one has committed a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense), one must first perform the ritual repentance according to the teachings.

A prohibited offense is not inherently poisonous or evil, but is simply forbidden by the Buddha’s precepts as something not permitted to do. To do it is improper; to do it constitutes an offense. This is based on the Hīnayāna standard.

The principle is that the four *pārājika* offenses and the eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses do not admit of confession; it is only for the four categories from *saṃghāvaśeṇa* downward that confession is permitted.

Regarding the ritual procedure for the Hīnayāna confession: one must request a *mahā-bhikṣu* to serve as witness. When confessing before a senior monk, five formalities are required: first, baring the right shoulder; second, placing the right knee on the ground;
third, joining the palms; fourth, stating the name of the offense; and fifth, prostrating at his feet. If confessing before a junior monk (*kṣudra-varṣa*), the prostration at the feet is omitted.

One should simply practice four methods. In the case of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one must invite twenty pure monks to perform the *mānatva* penance for six nights, providing them with service and offerings.
When the seven days are complete, the offense is removed through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), and one's precepts are restored to purity as received from the Tathāgata.
For nuns, forty pure and virtuous elders must be assembled; in the case of a minor offense, one serves for one day.
Regarding these matters, it is not strictly necessary to assemble [the community]. However, if one commits a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offense), one must further undertake specific practices.

A *prakṛti-sāvadya* refers to the ten non-virtues, such as killing and stealing; their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is evil. Even before the Buddha appeared in the world, when there were no formal precepts or prohibitions, committing such acts was inherently sinful, as they result in falling into the three miserable realms (*durgati*).
As for "undertaking practices," there are two types: first, ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*); second, rational repentance (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*), as described in the Vaipulya sutras.

The *Buddhanāmasūtra* and other such texts require that one both perform the ritual procedures and initiate spiritual practice. That is to say, according to those Vaipulya sūtras, one must first purify the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
One should smear the ground with fragrant mud and construct a circular altar within the hall, adorning it with colored paintings.

One should hang five-colored banners, burn "coastal incense" (*sāgara-gandha*), light lamps, and arrange a high seat. While twenty-four honored images are ideal, having many more is not prohibited. One should also provide various delicacies and meals.

Exert one's heart and mind to the utmost. Prepare new, clean clothing and footwear; do not use old items that have not been washed. When entering or exiting, when putting on or taking off, ensure they are kept separate and not mixed.
Observe a seven-day fast of abstinence. Bathe three times each day. On the first day, make offerings to the Sangha according to one’s means, whether much or little.

One should separately invite a master who is well-versed in both the internal and external Vinayas to serve as preceptor. Receive the twenty-four precepts and the dhāraṇīs, and confess one's transgressions before the master.
It is essential that this take place on either the eighth or fifteenth day; it should be scheduled for seven days, and this duration cannot be reduced.
If one can advance further, one may proceed as desired according to one's capacity; however, ten people is the limit and may not exceed this number. Lay followers may also participate.

One must prepare the three robes with single-layered seams and be fully equipped with the Buddha-dharma precepts. One circumambulates one hundred and twenty times, then returns to one’s seat for contemplation, and so forth, as extensively described in the sūtras.
Now, in this Maṇḍala of Perfect Enlightenment, the ritual path differs slightly: it possesses its own specific tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā).

The *Tiānshèng* [Sūtra] serves as a source of refuge; its contemplative wisdom accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Here, I shall merely cite its general intent, though the specific ritual procedures differ slightly.

As for the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, it is a minor work on ritual practice that primarily elucidates the arousal of conduct, and further states that one must first pay respect to the Triple Gem and so forth;
I have now extracted and utilized these points from that text. Moreover, that text instructs one to give rise to seven kinds of mind.
Taking these as skillful means, one should cultivate seven kinds of mental states: first, a sense of shame and remorse; second, fear and dread; third, weary detachment;

fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta; fifth, equanimity toward enemies and kin; sixth, mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s grace; and seventh, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of transgressions.
Having given rise to these seven mental states, one should visualize the Buddhas and holy sages of the ten directions, join the palms in respectful salutation, and present this petition.

This extends up to shame, remorse, reform, and so forth. According to the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, one must first recognize the ten types of minds that accord with birth and death as the objects to be remedied, thereby reversing those ten minds.
First, through false conceptualization of self and person, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises.

Second, with internal afflictions already present, one encounters adverse external conditions, causing the mind of self-centeredness to flourish. Third, with both internal and external factors present, one destroys virtuous deeds and takes no joy in the goodness of others.
Fourth, one gives rein to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, committing every kind of evil. Fifth, although these actions may not be extensive...

1. Malicious thoughts pervade everywhere. 2. Six types of malicious thoughts continue in succession, uninterrupted day and night. 3. One conceals and denies one's faults, unwilling to let others know of them.
4. One is obstinate and aggressive, showing no fear of the evil realms. 5. One lacks both shame and remorse, having no dread of ordinary people or sages.
Tenth, they deny cause and effect and become icchantikas. From beginningless time, whether for themselves or others, there has been no one who has not been thus.

Next, they give rise to a mind that rebels against birth and death, which must be overturned and destroyed from its roots. First, clearly believe in cause and effect. Second, feel shame and remorse, chastising oneself;
conceal one's offenses with shame before the heavens and manifest one's offenses with remorse before others. Third, fear the evil realms, overturning all obstinacy and aggression. Fourth, [do not...]

1. Concealing flaws: this is the opposite of exposing them. 2. Severing the continuity of the mind: this is like committing a crime against the king's law again after having already been punished, or like eating food again after having already vomited it up.

3. Generating the bodhicitta as vast as space: this is the opposite of the preceding evil pervasiveness. 4. Cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions: this is the opposite of the preceding indulgence in evil. 5. Guarding and protecting the True Dharma:
this is the opposite of the preceding destruction of goodness. 6. Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions: this is the opposite of... [text fragment]

This is an adverse condition. Tenth, one contemplates that the nature of sin is empty and perceives non-self. If one possesses these [ten contemplations], there is no sin that will not be extinguished;

if one does not understand them, even if one enters the Dharma hall, it will be nothing but toil and hardship. Disciple Bhikṣu [Name] and others, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, repent with a sincere heart.
Since beginningless kalpas, we have not known that our own substance is fundamentally true and eternal;
due to this fundamental delusion of ignorance, it perfumes the True Mind to produce false consciousness.
This transforms and gives rise to the sense organs and the physical body, which possess material obstruction; we then take them to be the mark of self, sharing in their safety and peril.
The sense organs and consciousnesses mutually support one another to perceive the six objects; these objects entice my craving, giving rise to the three poisons.
From these three poisons, actions of body, speech, and mind are provoked, creating various evil karmas as vast as the sands of the Ganges:
stealing, sexual misconduct, and killing sentient beings, as well as resorting to deceitful speech, lying, and harsh abuse.
Greedy and stingy, double-tongued, consuming pungent roots and greens; Drinking wine and eating meat, severing compassion and showing contempt for the Triple Gem;
Disdaining the honorable and the lowly, opposing one’s parents, and deceiving one’s kin;
Failing to guard the six sense faculties and being constantly dissolute; Merely destroying the three poisons and envying the virtuous and good.
With doubts regarding cause and effect, harboring the mind of a beast, they act openly without shame or remorse.
Regarding the property of the Buddha’s permanent *caitya*, they may borrow it or use it falsely without returning it.
Receiving the faithful offerings of others, they do not observe the fast; in both movement and stillness, their dignified deportment frequently violates the precepts.
Polluting monasteries and always dwelling in seclusion, using official power and influence to seize the wealth of others;
preaching the Dharma impurely while indulging in greed and anger, engaging in meaningless speech before the Buddha and the Sangha—
now I wander in saṃsāra, fallen into hell, where the sufferings of a thousand births and ten thousand deaths must be endured.
The bodies of hungry ghosts are but skin and bone joined together; when they encounter water or drink in their thirst, it turns into fierce fire.
Animals exhaust their strength to repay the debts of others; in their frantic flight, they fear slaughter and injury.
In this age of anger, they do not hear the name of the Triple Gem; when will they attain the fruit of Bodhi?
I now repent of my sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Baring my heart and showing my very soul without concealment.
I pray that the Buddha, not forsaking his great compassion, Will act as witness for me as I repent of all these transgressions.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart I take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
VI. Miscellaneous Matters (Exhortation, Rejoicing, and Aspiration; Recitation of Verses on Impermanence; Petitioning for Mindfulness of the Buddha, etc.
With a sincere heart, I observe and entreat all those throughout the ten directions who have newly attained enlightenment: I only pray that, out of compassion, you will turn the Wheel of Dharma.
All Tathāgatas who desire to enter parinirvāṇa, we pray that you remain in the world for the sake of sentient beings.
Having made this request, with a sincere heart, we take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem;
with a sincere heart, we rejoice.
All the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, by the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and ordinary beings—
I rejoice in them all with full accord. Having thus rejoiced,
I take refuge in the Three Jewels with a sincere heart and pay homage to them.
With a sincere heart,
we dedicate [this merit] to ourselves and all who have turned toward the Buddha; may all the roots of virtue, however small or great, cultivated through these causes and conditions,
be dedicated toward Great Bodhi, so that all sentient beings may together realize the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Having performed the dedication, we take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
We, the disciple bhikṣus, so-and-so and others, together with all sentient beings, make this vow with a sincere heart:
May I, after repenting and eliminating all obstacles, Open my mind and resolve to penetrate the true source;
May I always abide in silent illumination, acting spontaneously, And never allow the root-body to act as its own master.
May I forever take compassion and wisdom as the essence of my heart, And always perceive affliction and greed as mere adventitious dust.
When the six consciousnesses function, let right wisdom function; Where the six sense objects appear, contemplate them as empty and true.
Diligently distance yourself from the conditions of the ten evil karmas, And constantly practice the ten pāramitās.
Rely upon the Triple Gem without negligence, Bravely and vigorously striving to deliver all beings of the four modes of birth.
When delusive habits arise, they are all thoroughly understood; The awakened mind shines forth, its illumination ever-increasingly bright.
The power and function of Bodhi universally support and permeate; The gates of the Bodhisattva’s practice are never neglected or forgotten.
Furthermore, may the assembly of disciples at this site of enlightenment Be free from all calamities and each find peace and tranquility.

For all who see, hear, or rejoice in this, May they resolve to awaken the great Bodhicitta.
Relying upon these excellent causes and conditions of today, May we be together in the Dharma assembly in every life and every birth.
Having made this vow, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha. (From this point forward, the verses on impermanence are recited.

Do not remain embracing this corpse; This body is a mere conventional name, composed of various impurities.

Having contracted a grave illness with arrows piercing the body, amidst the gathering of all such agonies, how can one sleep?
Furthermore, a verse says (from the *Āgama Sūtra*):

Regarding the seven preceding sections on the methods of practice for the affairs [of cultivation], one should perceive the phenomena exactly as they appear in the text. One must not become mired in the words or lose sight of the meaning;

rather, one must ensure that the principles and the facts are clearly understood within one's own mind. Thereupon, one enters into contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and makes it a long-term endeavor.

This is the object of focus (*ālambana*). The first invocation is concluded. One must pay homage to the Buddhas, the Dharma, the Bodhisattvas, and the worthy sages (*ārya*), taking the original text as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
From the second offering upward, until the time of dispersing from the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), twenty-five offerings are made;

Regarding the days: at the conclusion of each chapter of the *Vajragarbha*, the *Viśuddhamati*, the *Ghoṣadatta*, and the *Pariniṣpanna-bodhi* chapters, one should pay homage to the fifty-three Buddhas, or to the various Buddhas listed in the preceding fascicle.

Add these to complete twenty-eight recitations. If, during the interval, a minor obstacle suddenly arises, or if one perceives that the assembly is weary and wishes to proceed with brevity, then follow the usual liturgy for the six periods of repentance.

After completing one or two recitations, return to the original sequence for the formal repentance; the order must not be bypassed. As for the act of repentance itself, each person must perform it individually.
Following this sequence, one must not allow discrepancies that would cause the loss of the meaning, intent, and the continuity of the lineage.

Revealing Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, "Manifesting Perfect Enlightenment" chapter): (The first five lines [of the verse] state that all phenomena are empty; the next line [the sixth] reveals the perfection of the essence of enlightenment; the seventh and eighth lines provide an inverse explanation of the character "enlightenment" (*bodhi*); the ninth and tenth lines explain the principle of "perfection"; and the final two lines provide a direct explanation of these two characters).
All phenomena are false and illusory, arising through the convergence of causes and conditions. Like the moon reflected in water, they are but shifting conceptions;
like forms in a dream, they have no substance. (The realm of superior wisdom) Deluded consciousness has no essence at all;
(the [real] mind is empty) The true mind is inherently numinous; (its nature is manifest) To be deluded regarding it is called "non-awakening."

Non-awakening is called ignorance (the opposite of awakening). After awakening, there are various thoughts of desire; one must still know that awakening is not yet perfected (perfection is "roundness";
this clarifies that simply severing thought is awakening, which is only then named "Perfect Awakening"—this refers to the following two lines).

For those whose every thought is Perfect Awakening, not a single thought should accord with emotional attachments (this is an exegesis of the two characters for "Perfect Awakening"). The *Treatise* says: "That which is called awakening refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought," which is precisely what the preceding line calls the "True Mind's Original State."
This is the Spirit itself.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Pure Land of the Treasury of Light.

Praise of the Buddha’s Dharma-body (The text and meaning are fully contained within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
My Buddha, the perfectly luminous awakening, Is entirely the body of the dharma-realm. Brilliantly manifest, it is not the removal of delusion;
Vast and open, it is the original truth. Radiant, the mind is the sovereign; Penetrating and harmonious, wisdom is the cause.
Lotus pedestals fill the expanse; lion thrones extend everywhere. Layer upon layer of radiant forms appear;

Compassion and wisdom have never been separated; he is no different from the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. His realization is identical to this very essence (the basis for the nirmāṇakāya);

out of pity for the ignorance of ordinary beings (the intent regarding the basis of vision), he wishes to respond to the three thousandfold world system by dividing his body into ten billion forms, all emerging from the land of radiant light.
Responding to conditions, he appeared in Jambudvīpa; all were named Muni Buddha.
All were called Great Men who, according to the capacities of beings, opened the gates of the Dharma-teaching.
The sudden and gradual approaches differ in their paths, yet they manifest the intent of the Buddha’s teaching. (To clarify this intent refers to the final phrase of the preceding passage.)
Wishing to reveal true knowledge and vision (appearing in the world solely for the sake of this one great causal matter), he first observed the delusions of the six realms of existence.
For seven days, he contemplated these matters. The "losing the head and crying out" illustrates the capacity for easy awakening; this metaphor appears in the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (Fo ding jing).

The "abandoning his father and urging [him] with only prostrations" illustrates the capacity for difficult awakening; this metaphor is found within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, he spoke of the distinctions of the Three Vehicles to entice [beings] toward renunciation.
Furthermore, discussing this single principle together: for those of superior faculties, the single principle is directly revealed;

for those of inferior capacity, they are gradually guided by means of the three vehicles. To cling to delusion requires the clearing away of filth—this clarifies the intent behind establishing the gradual teachings;
to ascend to truth, how could one rely on a ladder?—this clarifies the intent behind proclaiming the sudden teaching.
Now, following the Buddha’s direct pointing (to this sutra), the East is fundamentally without the West (a metaphor for the ordinary person being none other than the Buddha).
Praising the divergent paths of the sudden and gradual teachings— once one knows this, one simply rests (for this is not what is taken as the primary tenet here).
Within the Sudden Gate, the beginning and end are explained from this source; Having personally attained the awakening of the mind’s essence, it is now vast and all-pervading.
One should give rise to the Bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva;
The eighty-four thousand dharmas are subsumed within the single path of the Three Vehicles. If one can rely upon this teaching, [the goal will be realized].
How could the fruit of Buddhahood be difficult to seek?
To praise sudden enlightenment and desire to see the purity of the mind’s source, one must realize that the self-identity is empty; where, then, is the physical form truly real?
Thoughts have no trace from the start; suddenly, the numinous clarity awakens. Spontaneously, the world is pervaded by truth;
like pure gold, the hidden treasury is opened. The brilliant sun emerges from the clouds’ gloom; the delusions accumulated over many lifetimes vanish within a single thought.
If you try to compare the mind with the Buddha, it is identical to the Buddha from beginning to end.

(5. Repentance) Sincere Repentance (Repentance of the Five Precepts):
We, the assembly of disciples, prostrate ourselves before the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the ten directions and the three periods of time. May you bear witness, protect, and keep us in mind.
Since beginningless, vast kalpas past, our minds have been shrouded by ignorance; we have been deluded regarding our own Buddha-wisdom and have created karma through false confusion.

They revolve in the cycle of birth and death, turning their backs on the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to follow teachers and friends. Their faculty of sight clings to forms, making them slaves to affection and attachment;
they do not perceive the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body pervading all. Their ears crave the realm of sound, which brings endless harm;

they do not hear the Tathāgata’s perfect voice preaching the Dharma. Their noses crave fragrant scents, whereby the fetters arise; they cannot perceive the wondrous fragrance of merit. Their tongues...
Greedily craving various flavors, they devour sentient beings; they employ false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words; they slander the Triple Gem and insult their parents.
How could such persons consume the profound flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma? Their sense-faculty of the body clings to tactile sensations, indulging in them without end;

day and night they remain mired in delusion, ignorant of what is supreme. They fully commit all manner of evil deeds—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and thus the compassionate light of the Buddhas does not reach them.

They are able to illuminate [the truth], yet their mental faculty (*manas*) clings to phenomena; as they encounter objects and seize upon conditions, greed, anger, and false views arise in every thought-moment.

All manner of evils are born from the mental faculty. How could they know the Tathāgata’s profound *dharmadhātu*? With their six sense-faculties and three karmic actions, they commit every kind of transgression;
the three obstructions and ten entanglements pull one another along without ceasing. They give rise to the four inversions and become *icchantikas*. Not so.

Disrespecting one's parents and elders; lacking shame and remorse; committing the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the seven prohibitions—whether committed by oneself, taught to others, witnessed being committed, or rejoiced in—once a single delusion arises, a million obstacles open up. These proliferate endlessly, fully obstructing all manner of wholesome virtues.
One is unable to give rise to the great bodhicitta and unable to practice any wholesome dharmas, suffering through the long night without end.
There is a mind of weariness. Such transgressions as these are known only by the Buddha’s awakening; I now repent them all. I sever the mind of continuity.
Furthermore, these karmic obstacles arise solely from inversion and possess no fixed reality; they are originally empty and quiescent.

where the stages of awakening of sentient beings are equally pure, and all Tathāgatas together maintain it.
The bodies and minds of both ordinary beings and sages are utterly tranquil; throughout the ten directions, all is perfect and unconditioned.

The Chapter on Mañjuśrī is intended to cause faith and understanding to be authentic, thereby fulfilling the causal basis for practice. (5. Purifying one's own mind is the foundation for praising the practice.)

Mañjuśrī paid homage to the Buddha as his initial inquiry: "May the Sugata explain the original causes of the Tathāgata’s awakening, For he wishes to reveal the practices for cultivation and realization.
First, he sets forth the nature of Perfect Enlightenment as fundamentally true;
Yet we have long harbored false attachments, Taking the four elements entirely to be our bodies."
Recognizing these as empty flowers and a second moon, One thus remains forever a dreamer within a dream.
The Buddha knows that the nature of awareness is the true self; Originally devoid of a physical body, one undergoes sinking and delusion.
The wise are likewise empty and eternally unmoving; This is called the primary cause for practicing the Dharma.

The Chapter on Samantabhadra (Resolving the difficulties regarding the simultaneous awakening and gradual cultivation; it also demonstrates the skillful means of practice). Investigation and Explanation of the Application of Mind:
Samantabhadra Opens the Previous Gate of Dharma. Desiring to universally sever the doubts of sentient beings, the Buddha has already stated that "the awakened one is an illusion.
If this is so, I do not know what further purpose there is in cultivation and realization.
"How does one use illusion to further cultivate illusion? When illusion is exhausted and returns to emptiness, what remains to rely upon?
The Buddha said: "Illusion arises from true awakening; when illusion is exhausted, awakening is fulfilled—what deficiency could there be?
When distancing oneself from illusion, one is able to distance oneself from its dissolution. If the fire that produced it is not yet extinguished, the ashes will continue to fly."
Illusion is itself the realization of emptiness, and emptiness is itself awakening; because there is no gradual sequence, they are eliminated.

This is the initial section on the Contemplation of the Two Emptinesses in the "Universal Eye" chapter (investigating the four great elements to find no self, and seeing the five aggregates as entirely empty and non-existent, thereby destroying the two attachments. When attachment ceases and principle manifests, this is called the accomplishment of the Contemplation of the Two Emptinesses).
Having resolved and contemplated the difficulties of cultivation, the principle of the modes of practice during cultivation should now be proclaimed.
The Universal Eye, responding to the occasion, rose from his seat and asked about the gradual stages of meditation for oneself and others.
The Buddha said: "Sentient beings who seek awakening should maintain right mindfulness and remain detached from all conditions."
Whether moving or still, always contemplate these four elements: Fire, wind, earth, and water—what solidity is there?
Thus one knows that the illusory body and mind perish; Non-illusion is originally a nature of quiescence.
Like a mirror polished of dust, clarity appears immediately; The practice of the contemplation of the two emptinesses is perfected at this time.

The Subsequent Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (in which defilement and purity are obliterated, and even the images of ordinary and holy beings cease; the original, true, and perfect reality manifests, interpenetrating and unimpeded with all phenomena—this is called the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm).
When the illusory defilements of body and mind are forever extinguished, the ten directions are as pure as mani jewels.
As the speaker faces the elimination of reflected images, perfect awareness manifests throughout the entire realm of space.
Because this perfect luminosity is attained, the mind is pure; both the mundane and the supramundane are thus.
Because the eighty-four thousand [dharmas] are pure, they are all equally unmoving, pervasive without exception, filling one another without mutual destruction or confusion.
How could a thousand lights in a single room be contradictory?
Without weariness or [defilement], all are awakening; that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas—what further doubt can there be?

The Chapter on the Diamond-Cut (Investigating and Explaining the Beginning and End of Delusion and Enlightenment; Universally Resolving the Obstacles and Contradictions Regarding Sentient Beings Being Identical to the Buddha).
The principle that sentient beings are identical to the Buddha is profound and subtle; those of middling and inferior faculties still harbor doubts.
Vajragarbha desires to cause them to attain decisive faith, yet the threefold objections he raises appear to contradict the Buddha’s teachings.
The Sugata, responding to capacities, has opened the wondrous enlightenment; yet ordinary and holy beings cling to delusions that obscure their numinous awareness.
When all conditions arise from thought, they cause the mind to stir—this is like directly using a boat to make the shore appear to move.
Once the obscuration is cleared away, the flowers vanish; there is neither arising nor ceasing, just as when ore is smelted, the gold is revealed through refining.
Even with a body reduced to ashes and meager wisdom, realization remains difficult; how could the ordinary mind of a firefly possibly conceive of it?
(Maitreya Chapter: To deeply investigate the root of saṃsāra is to find it in craving. If craving persists, even if one practices through the five natures, one will not attain Buddhahood.)
Vimalamitra asked about the root of cutting off saṃsāra; The Buddha said that craving is the root.
Because of desire-objects, the conditions of attraction and aversion arise; From this, the gateway for creating karma first opens.
Once wholesome and unwholesome karma are established, the retributions of suffering and pleasure follow; Even reaching the realm of dhyāna, sensation still persists.
Affection and intense ignorance give rise to the five natures; These five natures must be discussed in relation to the two obstructions.
One should eliminate hatred and affection, diligently seeking awakening;

Entering the world with great compassion to transform sentient beings according to their conditions, And practicing for the dual benefit of self and others until all obstructions are exhausted— Then one ascends to the Dharma-treasury and realizes true perfection.

Chapter on Pure Wisdom (Briefly distinguishing the stages of cultivation and realization; clarifying the ten levels of faith, the three stages of worthiness, the ten bhūmis, and the stage of Buddhahood; the meaning of following and not following awakening, wherein the degrees of depth differ).
The two gates of cultivation and realization were already understood previously; now, when investigating what is realized by ordinary beings and sages, what is sought is Buddhahood.
Wishing to follow conditions and distinguish the stages of the path, one first discusses cultivation and realization, though the nature is fundamentally non-existent.
By relying on the discourse on the extinction of illusions, one distinguishes the differences; yet when illusory wisdom is exhausted, there is no divergent path.
The arising and ceasing have already manifested the purity of the *dharmadhātu*; this compliant awakening is the awakening of ordinary beings.
When prior purity and hindrances reach the stage of the worthy ones (*ārya*), one dwells constantly in non-abiding awakening and realizes *tathatā*.
When hindrance itself is awakening, it is called "Buddha. Furthermore, hearing, tranquility, mindfulness, and so forth are like a perfect pearl.

The Buddha, in this degenerate age, feels deep sorrow and suffering; Ever fearing that those of initial capacity may lack the strength to persevere, he commands the assembly:
"You must diligently protect them, Lest demons or heretics afflict their bodies and minds.
Having received these instructions, we increase our vigilance and guard.
Within the assembly, eighty thousand Vajradharas, together with the twenty-eight Heavenly Kings,
Great Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts who protect the lands— ten million of them, all formidable and worthy of respect—
rose from their seats and expressed their vows: "In the final age, we shall always be able to protect the site of enlightenment."
May practitioners never fall into despondency, And may those who cultivate never lack the provisions for the path.
We, leading our retinues, shall protect you morning and night, So that within ten days of your dwelling here, you shall be free from calamity.
When the Buddha finished speaking this sutra, the great assembly rejoiced; With faith and acceptance, they took it to heart and practiced in accordance with the teachings of the Buddha-King.
Namo to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (as above for the twelve prostrations).
With a sincere mind, I repent.
Now, regarding repentance, there are two kinds: first, repentance according to phenomena; second, repentance according to principle. As for repentance according to phenomena—

At that time, one must be utterly sincere. Paying homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and strictly maintaining the ritual precinct (*maṇḍala*), one should lay bare the manifestations of one's offenses before the Triple Gem.

With a heart of profound remorse and shame, one should reflect that, first of all, the merit of the Buddhas can cause offenses to be extinguished, severing their continuity forever so that one dares not commit them again.
For one who repents according to the principle, it is sufficient simply to give rise to the bodhicitta; naturally, the offenses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will be crushed.
Regarding afflictions: one knows that offenses are illusory and contemplates that the characteristics of offenses are empty. Thus, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sādhana-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "[Afflictions] do not abide within, without, or in between.

When performing repentance according to this principle, it is most essential that one's contemplative practice be clear and lucid. If a person has previously entered a ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) and undergone these two types of repentance, they should...

Know that the defilement of sin will certainly be extinguished; the essential requirement is a sincere heart. It is like a person who has previously violated the king’s law, yet encounters the king’s gracious pardon, whereby all previously committed offenses are entirely washed away.
The Dharma King has established this method of repentance fundamentally for the sake of saving sentient beings of evil karma.

Once the repentance has been performed, the Buddha says it will certainly be extinguished; do not dwell upon it further with thoughts or recollections. Birth and extinction arise from the mind; one must eliminate their root.
Fundamentally, if one has committed offenses and does not repent, their delusion is extreme; the calamities will afflict future lives, and they shall suffer for ten thousand kalpas.
For this reason, today we solemnly purify the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and take refuge in the Triple Gem. We repent of both principle and phenomena.

When wishing to repent of one's offenses, one realizes that the karmic obstacles created are difficult to extinguish. What are the causes and conditions by which repenting of these offenses makes them easy to extinguish? As the Buddha said in the sutras:
There are two kinds of vigorous children: first, those who do not commit offenses themselves; second, those who are able to repent after having committed them.

It is further said that there are two kinds of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) that can eliminate the various offenses of sentient beings: first, a sense of shame (*hrī*); second, a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Shame (*hrī*) means not committing evil oneself; remorse (*apatrāpya*) means not causing others to do so. One who possesses shame and remorse may be called a human being;
if one lacks shame and remorse, they are no different from the birds and beasts. Therefore, this disciple today, with shame and remorse, takes refuge in and relies upon the Buddha.

We, the disciples [Name] and others, from beginningless kalpas until this very day—according to the teachings of the *Sāṭhāgata-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*, there are fundamental grave offenses, each of which causes one to fall into the Avīci Hell;
we now repent of them all. These are: first, destroying stupas and monasteries, burning scriptures and images, and misappropriating all the property of the Triple Gem;

second, slandering the Dharma of the Three Vehicles by claiming it is not the holy teaching, creating obstacles and hindrances, and concealing or hiding its truth; third, striking, reviling, scolding, or rebuking any ordained person—whether they observe the precepts or violate them—and speaking of their faults, imprisoning them, or stripping away their *kāṣāya* robes and subjecting them to coercion.

They cause one to return to lay life; they subject one to forced labor and servitude; they sever the root of one's life-force; fourth, among the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, one commits any one of them; fifth, one gives rise to false views, denying cause and effect.

Having understood these characteristics, you must now disclose them all and repent with a sincere heart. Blinded by ignorance, you give rise to various afflictions; through the six sense organs and three karmas, you commit endless sins.
These obstruct the causes for the Buddha-dharma, open the path for icchantikas, contravene the intent of the Sages, follow along with evil conditions, abandon Bodhi, and become addicted to...
They dally with birth and death, lacking even a single thought of the Dharma of renunciation. For a long night, they have accumulated the causes of all bitter poisons:
destroying stupas and monasteries, burning images and sutras, stealing the wealth and offerings of the Sangha, giving rise to great false views, and repudiating cause and effect.

They act as icchantikas, slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; they kill their fathers and harm their mothers, break the harmony of the Sangha, damage the physical body of the Buddha, and commit murder.
Various noble ones (āryas) who have harmed their teachers and elders; who have defiled those beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as their own kin and strangers;
who have beaten, reviled, or scolded renunciants and forced them to return to lay life; who have cut off their life-force; who associate with those of evil dharma;

who defile stupas and monasteries; who violate the fasts and precepts; who indulge their bodies and minds in dissipation; and who commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, harsh speech, double-tongued speech, lying, and frivolous speech—[these are] the wrong views.
I behold greed and anger, craving and delusion, shamelessness and lack of remorse—such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.
Furthermore, disciples and others, from beginningless time until this day, due to wrong views, have wandered in successive delusions and remained attached to perverse matters.

They have taken the lives of living beings and offered sacrifices to malevolent spirits, *chi-mei*, *wang-liang*, ghosts, and deities, hoping thereby to prolong their years, yet they could never achieve this.
Or they falsely claimed to have seen ghosts and feigned divine utterances. Such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless.

[Up to] this point, I now repent with shame and remorse for all [my transgressions]. Furthermore, from beginningless time until today, I have sometimes acted with arrogance and haughtiness, being self-exalting and conceited;
or, relying on my lineage, I have looked down upon others, treating the lowly with contempt because of my own nobility.
Using strength to oppress the weak; indulging in alcohol and engaging in brawls and disturbances without distinguishing between kin and strangers;
remaining muddled and confused all day long, failing to recognize the honorable from the lowly—I now repent for all such transgressions.
Furthermore, I may have been greedily attached to food and drink without moderation; I may have eaten raw meat or consumed the five pungent herbs;
I may have defiled scriptures and images with foul odors or intruded upon the pure assembly; I may have indulged my thoughts and desires without restraint;
I may have distanced myself from virtuous people and befriended evil companions. All such transgressions, I now fully repent.

Furthermore, whatever offenses I have committed through arrogance and conceit, obstinacy and self-will, insolence and impudence, failing to recognize human feelings while asserting my own views as right and others' as wrong,
or through the pursuit of mere luck and chance— all such transgressions, I now fully repent.

Furthermore, there may have been times when, in the face of wealth, I showed no sense of renunciation; lacking integrity and unable to restrain myself, I butchered meat and sold liquor, living by means of deception.
Or, I engaged in lending at interest, calculating profits by the hour and selling my days for gain, amassing wealth through harsh exploitation and greedy pursuit without satiety.

Or, lacking the virtue of the precepts, I pointlessly accepted offerings and alms from the faithful, receiving the sustenance of others without shame or remorse. All such transgressions as these, I now fully repent.
Furthermore, I now repent of all such transgressions as beating slaves and striking maidservants, driving servants and subordinates without regard for their hunger, thirst, cold, or exhaustion;
or destroying and breaking bridges and blocking pathways. I now repent of all such sins.

Furthermore, some are negligent and self-indulgent, characterized by indeterminate mental distraction. They engage in gambling and chess, gather in large crowds, drink alcohol, eat meat, and toast one another.
They indulge in aimless chatter, discussing all manner of worldly affairs from year to year, thus wasting their days in vain.
From the first watch to the last of the night, they do not cultivate meditation or recitation; being indolent and lazy, they spend the entire day lying in a corpse-like slumber. Regarding the six...
The mind of mindfulness does not manage its affairs; seeing the superior achievements of others, it immediately gives rise to envy.

With a heart harboring malice and poison, it fully arouses afflictions, causing the fierce winds of all evils to blow upon the firewood of transgressions, keeping them constantly ablaze without respite.

All subtle virtues of the three karmas are utterly consumed by this fire. Once the roots of goodness are exhausted, one becomes an icchantika and falls into the great hells, with no prospect of escape.

Therefore, disciples, today we come before the Three Jewels of the ten directions with our heads bowed to the ground, repenting of all the various transgressions mentioned above—whether light or heavy, coarse or subtle—from ourselves.
Whether I committed them myself, caused others to commit them, or rejoiced in their commission;

whether I compelled others to do so by force or influence, or even praised those who practice unwholesome dharmas—I now, with utmost sincerity, confess and repent for all such acts. May they all be extinguished.
Furthermore, we disciples, relying on the teachings, have awakened to the principle; we have illuminated the truth and examined our delusions.

Reflecting inwardly upon the karmic offenses we have committed throughout many kalpas of birth, we realize that if we do not repent, we will surely fall into the three miserable realms and suffer calamities for successive kalpas, making it difficult for our roots of goodness to continue.
Alas, what a great peril! To have committed such transgressions and violations—how painful it is that, out of ignorance, one does not know to reform and repent.

If one continues to conceal and cover them over, they will become the cause for certainty; when the time of death arrives, the signs of hell will appear, and as the winds of karma dissolve the body, the mind will be filled with terror and agitation.
Dragged along by their evil karma, they undergo every form of bitter suffering. Blazing clouds of fire flash like lightning, and boiling cauldrons surge like thunder.

The hell-wardens display their ferocity as iron snakes unleash their venom; sharp blades rise in disarray and instruments of torment clash together. Their vision is lost and their souls are already departed; they know not where to find refuge or salvation.
In the profound darkness of the deep night, throughout accumulated kalpas and endless years, one experiences all the eight hot and eight cold hells without exception.

Emerging from the hells, one may fall among the animals, where one encounters every kind of creature, such as great pythons and venomous insects. Or one may receive the retribution of a hungry ghost, with the joints of one's bones burning with fire.

For kalpas on end, I have suffered boundless misery in the realm of hungry ghosts. I now take refuge in the Triple Gem and repent my transgressions. May the Great Compassion of all Buddhas deign to deliver me;
may deluded karma be instantly dispelled and transformed into pure causes. Let body and mind together become empty, and let both sin and merit abide nowhere.
Perceiving the true nature as identical to the Buddha-dharmakāya, the transgressions of the three karmas shall become the three gates of liberation. The six sense faculties...

Heavy obstructions are transformed into the six supernormal powers; the sword-trees and knife-mountains all become jeweled calyxes; the rivers of blood and boiling excrement are entirely turned into flower ponds;
and the defiled lands of the dharma-realm are purified all at once.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
With a sincere heart make this vow:
"May my disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of the offenses of ignorance, perversion, the five heinous crimes, and so forth, [attain...]".
In life after life, may I encounter the conditions for the True Dharma; may right faith arise, right view become clear, the Bodhicitta be awakened, and the practices of a Bodhisattva be perfected.
May I serve as a guardian of the city of the Dharma, propagate the Great Way, and vow to uphold both the Semblance Dharma and the period when the Dharma is not yet established.
Whether at home or in the monastic life, may they always be disciples of the Buddha.

Furthermore, by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of all evils, may they, in birth after birth and life after life, be compassionate and harmonious, loyal and filial, humble and patient, knowing integrity and possessing a sense of shame.

May they anticipate others' intentions to offer greetings, be compliant, virtuous, and prudent; be pure, righteous, and yielding, revering and honoring both the Sangha and the laity, even toward those who harbor enmity.

If one’s kin are not without affection and remembrance; if one stays far away from evil friends and constantly encounters virtuous conditions; if one restrains the six sense faculties and guards the three karmas;

if one endures toil and hardship with a mind that does not retreat or sink; if one establishes the vow for Bodhi and bears the burden of sentient beings, always acting as their refuge—[then this is true kinship].
Having made this vow, with a sincere heart, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Addressing the assembly, please listen as I recite the verses on impermanence from the sutras:
For all classes of sentient beings, The law of death is ever present; Even by means of every expedient,
Unable to ward off this dharma, though they have long enjoyed immeasurable pleasure, they will inevitably fall back into decline.
Therefore, O gods and humans, you should not indulge in craving. Amidst the swirling eddies of desire, one suffers constant distress in both the present and the future.
Why do foolish people give rise to love and delight for desire?
Like a flower of exquisite color that is poisonous, like touching the flames of a fierce fire— the pleasures of desire are just like this;

later one undergoes great suffering and distress. Just as adding more fuel to a fire makes its flames impossible to extinguish, and it can burn both oneself and others— the pleasures of desire are just like this.
