The body and mind of birth and death are said to be delusions; how can cognition be of the same category?
(This is the inquiry. What follows is the explanation. The first two lines of the explanation clarify the various phenomena previously negated; the remainder all reveal the single mind. First:

It is simply because they arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature (as with the aforementioned cognition and all other phenomena, which all arise from conditions and therefore have no self-essence).

Its nature is empty (because of the nature of space), it is immovable (because it is eternally unmoving), and it is entirely even (because of its emptiness and stillness; all things are equal). The following two lines manifest the single mind.
The first phrase indicates [the subject] as follows: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the one mind" (*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"That which is empty and quiescent is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha"). This is likewise stated in the *Treatise*. The "Garbha" (Womb/Treasury) has three meanings.
First, they are listed as follows: "The Real is contained within the False" (1. the sense of inclusion); "The False contains the Real" (2. the sense of concealment).
There remains the meaning of inexhaustible birth (the third meaning of birth).

These three sections of the doctrinal gate should all be set forth (this concludes the enumeration and indicates what will be explained. First, regarding the four lines of three phrases, the meaning of "concealment" is briefly explained):
All sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha* (they conceal the Tathāgata within; the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "All sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha*").

The Dharmakāya is present within the afflictions (*kleśa*). (As the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, which is not separate from the treasury of afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha.

Each of the nine similes in the scriptural text is analyzed [as follows]: (The *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* states: "Within all sentient beings, amidst the various afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, there exists the body and wisdom of the Tathāgata.")

"Up to and including being eternally undefiled and fully endowed with virtuous marks, no different from myself. He then illustrates this by means of nine similes: (1) the Buddha’s body within a withered flower; (2) honey between two cliffs; (3) pure rice amidst husks and chaff; (4) genuine gold amidst filth; (5) a treasure storehouse in a poor man’s house;

(6) the kernel within a mango; (7) a golden image wrapped in tattered rags; (8) a queen’s fetus in the womb of a poor woman; (9) a cast image within a scorched mold. "The Buddha’s virtues within the dust are not the same as the dust.
(The Sūtra says: "Eternally undefiled. The following two explanations encompass the meaning.)
It encompasses all ordinary and holy beings of the ten directions; what need is there to speak of lands and their inhabitants?

(The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states that all things—physical marks, lands, supernormal powers, and radiance—are the Tathāgata. Thus it is called a "treasury" because all sentient beings are within the wisdom of the Tathāgata. The following three explanations clarify the meaning of "producing"):
Upon awakening, one gives birth to pure and wholesome dharmas: The causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles, as well as gods and humans. (The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states...)

Wisdom gives rise to the cause of the untainted (*anāsrava*). It is also able to produce the practices that lead to the human and celestial realms. The preceding section explained the names and their definitive meaning; the following two lines explain the characteristics of its activity (*ākāra*):

"It possesses the virtue of remaining unchanging while following conditions; Within the midst of delusion, it accomplishes phenomena, yet its essence is empty and divine. (Being empty, it accomplishes phenomena.)"

Furthermore, phenomena are eternally empty; thus we know that they are divine and numinous. These two phrases explain the functional activity (*karmayoga*). First, it clarifies the functional activity of *tathatā* (suchness): "Capable of sustaining" (*neng chi*):

It sustains its own essence and the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues, which have not been lost or abandoned since beginningless time. "Capable of resisting" (*neng yu*): It resists the sands-of-dust adventitious afflictions, remaining undefiled from time immemorial.

"Ascending and sinking realms" (*shengchen jie*): "Ascending" refers to true virtues; it is capable of sustaining them without loss. "Sinking" refers to false afflictions; it is capable of resisting them without being defiled. Thus we know that [the mind] possesses both the real and the delusive.

[This] contemplates the boundaries of rising and sinking. (The following clarifies the functional operation of arising and ceasing. *Ability to Create*: (The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is able to universally bring about the creation of all realms of rebirth, whether they arise or cease.

*Ability to Cultivate*: (Being able to know the real and penetrate the false, one resolves to cultivate practice. The *Treatise* says: "One who is able to know names and meanings is taught true awakening," etc.
*Defilement*: (Creating good and evil. *Purity*: (Cultivating the six perfections. *Cause*: (Pervading the six and the two. As above, these are the many meanings concerning the real and the false.

"Because they exist in relation to causes and conditions, it is said... (This is the meaning within the section on the Dependent Origination of Defilement and Purity. Although True Suchness is spoken of, it is spoken of by way of contrast with conditions.
"If one considers the self-substance of the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no thought and no speech;

what is there to inquire about? (This summarizes the general purport of the scriptural passage. For this reason, the Sūtra states: "That which perceives is all like empty space. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no arising or ceasing of cognition or vision," up to "it is like the Dharma-realm. The following provides a detailed explanation.)

Within this, from the very beginning there is neither subject nor object (the wisdom that knows; as the Sūtra says, "because there is no knowing-seeing"). Nor is there the known (birth-and-death; as the Sūtra says, "because there is no arising or ceasing").

This is the meaning of emptiness that is not empty, which is neither adventitious nor newly produced (the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata-garbha is twofold, namely empty and non-empty. 'Empty' means it is not non-existent in terms of delusion; 'non-empty' means the virtues are inherently present.

Therefore, the merit is not something separate, adventitious, or newly produced). What was stated above regarding the absence of subject and object, along with the two subsequent phrases, all constitute the meaning of emptiness.
How could it belong to the sage or the ordinary, or to defilement or purity? Who can create karma or cultivate the truth?

(The terms "ordinary," "defiled," and "create karma" all pertain to the arising and ceasing of the known; the terms "sage," "pure," and "cultivate the truth" all pertain to the cognitive vision of the knower. Therefore, the Sūtra says they do not exist. The following four lines all concern the meaning of non-emptiness, explaining the latter three lines of the Sūtra.
Its essence is identical to the Dharma-realm, abiding in true suchness.
Sentient beings and their environment are interfused and indivisible (this explains the characteristics of the Dharma-realm).
Transversally pervasive (because it pervades the ten directions), vertically exhaustive and eternal (this is the meaning of "ultimate"). Ultimate (the original text).

Perfectly complete throughout the ten directions (these six characters are all from the original text, though they are not in their sequential order). Fully encompassing (the characteristic of perfection).
Chapter Fourteen, Section Two: This concluding summary of the inquiry in the fourth section is called the "Dharma-practice of the Ground.
By means of this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a pure mind within the Mahāyāna.
Sentient beings of the末法 (final age) who practice in reliance upon this will not fall into false views.

You have asked about the Tathāgata’s fundamental practice on the ground; such is the Tathāgata’s practice while on the causal ground—this is precisely what is called "the dharma-practice of the causal ground.
All Bodhisattvas (translated here as *pú tí sā tuó*) cultivate it in this way.

(Practicing in accordance with this) sentient beings of the final age (the main text) may likewise rely on (what has been described above as the state of abiding) within the Mahāyāna to generate a pure (the main text) intention (the mind),

seeking association with the assembly of the righteous and distancing themselves from false teachers (not following false views). You, the various members of the Dharma assembly within this assembly (referring to the preceding text).
The transmission of these Dharma verses varies (explanatory gloss):
"Homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One" (and so forth, twelve prostrations).
With a sincere heart, I repent.
Now, repentance (*chánghuì*) is the primary gateway for initiating practice and the essential path for spiritual progress. In ceasing evil and cultivating goodness, nothing precedes this.
"Repentance" (*chàn*) is a term meaning to offer thanks and apology; "repentance" (*huì*) takes the sense of remorse and self-reproach as its meaning.

When the preceding mind gives rise to delusions and pursues objects with emotional attachments, the subsequent consciousness awakens to awareness and, relying on the truth, performs purification. One must subdue oneself and examine one's affairs, rectify one's intentions, and punish one's errors, thereby tracing back [to the source].

One transforms the past mind and preempts the commission of future offenses. Yet, although we may understand the truth and awaken from delusion, having resolved to attain Bodhicitta, as long as we have not yet reached the stage of the fruits of sainthood, we all belong to the group of those with indeterminate nature.

If we do not carefully contemplate the root of transgression and investigate the source of delusion, but instead merely maintain a mediocre disposition and constantly harbor a nature easily defiled, then we are like light feathers [blown about by the wind].

As one travels along the road, drifting east and west with the wind, meeting the good may lead to immediate transcendence, yet encountering the evil cannot avoid sinking into the mire. With the six sense objects in constant turmoil, how can one know what state of mind has arisen?
With the six realms of existence vast and boundless, how can one know into which path one will fall? One must necessarily examine the beginning and the end in detail.
Having investigated and grasped the root source, one repents of karma and repents of the mind, according to principle and according to fact.

Furthermore, the retribution of birth-and-death suffering and pleasure arises from the causes of tainted wholesome and unwholesome deeds. The causes of wholesome and unwholesome deeds arise from thoughts of greed and anger.

Thoughts of greed and anger arise from the mind of right and wrong (which is delusion). The mind of right and wrong arises from being deluded regarding the truth and clinging to the false. Being deluded regarding the truth and clinging to the false is precisely...

Fundamental ignorance. Fundamental ignorance has already been repented according to principle as previously described; now we shall next repent the shifting and branching secondary afflictions of the mind.
These shifting and branching secondary afflictions are precisely the threefold obstacles of affliction, karma, and retribution explained in the preceding section.
Regarding the term "shifting" (*zhǎnzhuǎn*): these three types of obstacles mutually depend upon one another and revolve in succession.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Due to afflictions (*kleśa*), one gives rise to unwholesome karma; due to the causal conditions of unwholesome karma, one obtains bitter fruits.
These afflictions are precisely this greed, hatred, and delusion. If any one of these—greed, hatred, or delusion—is predominant, it each encompasses twenty-one thousand afflictions.
If they are in equal proportion, they collectively encompass twenty-one thousand afflictions. Thus, they constitute eighty thousand.
The four thousand afflictions do not depart from the mind of the three poisons; these arise from fundamental non-awakening.

This is truly because one is fundamentally deluded regarding the Truth and clings to the false, mistakenly identifying with the mark of self (*ātman*). Consequently, one craves those things that accord with one's emotions to nourish and benefit oneself;

one feels anger toward those that oppose one's emotions, fearing they will harm or distress oneself; and through the sentiment of ignorance, one engages in various calculations and deliberations. Thus, one should know the three poisons.
One must rely on delusion regarding the truth; therefore, the Sūtra says that ignorance is the seed.

Since the three poisons exist, one consequently experiences desire for form and wealth, thereby committing sexual misconduct, theft, lying, and frivolous speech, pursuing all manner of things. Furthermore, due to hatred, one harbors resentment toward others.
There are those who take life, harbor contentious intentions, engage in divisive speech, use harsh abuse, and inflict a hundred kinds of injury;

they cause harm in many ways because they do not understand causes and conditions and cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. How much more so for those who weary their minds with hypocrisy—their ignorance and clumsiness only increase.

Therefore, it is said that the three poisons give rise to evil karma (though the three poisons also give rise to tainted wholesome karma and immovable karma, here we cite only what ought to be repented). Indeed, the creation of karma is like a dream.
Retribution is like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound; though its substance is empty, it responds without error.

Due to the fulfillment of prior evil karma, one undergoes birth in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Even when one’s transgressions are exhausted and one is born as a human, there remain various sufferings of residual retribution.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Those who commit the ten unwholesome karmas, upon emerging from the three miserable paths and being born among humans, each [suffers such consequences]."
There are two kinds of residual retribution (as detailed below). Thus we know that the three obstacles are mutually dependent, with afflictions being the primary one;
these we shall now first repent of. Yet these afflictions have been censured in various ways by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the principle.
These afflictions are designated as "enemies," for they are able to sever the life-root of wisdom in sentient beings.

They are also called "thieves," for they are able to plunder the various roots of goodness in sentient beings. They are also called "torrential rivers," for they are able to sweep sentient beings away into the ocean of birth and death.
They are also called "fetters and shackles," for they are able to bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death, preventing them from escaping. Thus, [the six...]
The path is entangled; the four modes of birth are never-ending, evil karma is inexhaustible, and the fruits of suffering do not cease.
One should know that all these are the faults and afflictions of *kleśa*. Therefore, at this time, we first repent of the three poisons of affliction.

Regarding the enumeration of the three poisons, craving (*rāga*) is primary. To uproot it, we first repent of craving. However, the initial arousal of karma is driven by the moisture of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Karma leads to rebirth. Although one may understand its emptiness through the principle of repentance regarding craving and ignorance, the habitual tendencies of craving have been established for so long that they cannot be suddenly exhausted;
just as the scent remains in a garment even after the odorant has been removed, one must give rise to a fierce and sharp resolve to repent, eliminate, and sever them.
However, as for the objects of craving, who but a fool would desire them? A wise person reflects carefully and finds that they possess no real flavor at all.
It is like a dog gnawing on a dry bone: the bone pierces its teeth and wounds it, and blood flows out, staining its own mouth;
yet the dog says the bone has flavor and, unaware of the pain, does not stop gnawing. It only harms itself and gains nothing in the end. Craving is just the same: it binds one without ceasing.

Seeing that the world is weary and that suffering arises in great measure—[as Śāriputra asked: "Is it the sense-faculties that are bound to objects, or are the objects alone that bind the faculties?"]—the Buddha therefore said:
The faculties are not bound to their objects, nor are the objects bound to the faculties. It is solely due to craving that the faculties and their objects enter into one another and become entangled;
thus, the mental consciousness becomes clouded and fails to attain liberation. It is like the black ox and the white ox employed by a farmer:

when they plow the field, there is a yoke between them, making it difficult for both to escape (yet it is not the case that the black ox binds the white one, nor is it the case that the white ox binds the black).

The white ox tied to the black one is so bound together solely by the halter; thus they are linked to one another. This connection has been passed down through generations, and because the white ox remains within the halter, both are driven by craving.
Since the halter is no different [for either], this entanglement from time immemorial has been difficult to abandon.
Now, fearing that these thoughts may arise again even after awakening, one must establish a firm resolve and direct the mind to examine the folly of these transgressions.

Although I have already offered repentance and apology above, I still fear that my sincere devotion has not been fully expressed. Now, with a renewed heart of utmost sincerity, I shall again recite these verses:
Greed, craving, and ignorance give rise to and moisten karma; Ignorance I have already repented, yet greed remains unremoved.
The fragrance within the robes is still difficult to dispel; How can the ordinary mind avoid being embodied by the realm of desire?
The substance of emotion is corrupt, yet the mind of form and spirit is falsely delighted; the wild beast bites at withered skeletons, finding its own blood sweet.
Birth and death are endless because of this craving; bound and entangled without release, one is like the earth-moth or the white and black oxen constantly tethered to one another.
The two dharmas of sense-faculties and objects are perpetually intermingled.
If one does not repent and eliminate the sins of craving and attachment, Even if one cultivates ten thousand practices, they will be of no avail.
I now vow with steadfast resolve to constantly sever them;

Within the *ālayavijñāna*, there is nothing that does not contain the five sense organs and six sense objects, all like illusory reflections. When body and mind are pure, they are like a clear, still pond.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
The repentance for the transgression of greedy attachment is now complete. Next, repent of anger. The poison of anger causes even greater harm.

While the fetters of greedy attachment are still merely restrictive and oppressive, the mind of anger is sudden and violent; who would dare to speak with it? Its heart is like boiling fire, and its mouth is like—

Swords and blades [are needed for such tasks]. Thus, one knows that anger is difficult to suppress and eliminate suddenly; it must be addressed before it has arisen by observing the object of one's anger.

Furthermore, sound is like an echo in a valley, and form is like a flower in the sky. A flower in the sky makes no distinction between beauty and ugliness, and an echo in a valley makes no difference between high and low.
Likewise, the objects of love and hatred, and the sounds of praise and blame, are all nothing but emptiness. What is there to be angry at? What is there to be pleased with?

Joy! Having long been deluded and inverted, I have allowed emotions to arise in response to external conditions. Today I have awakened to this; how could I, as a guest of the Dharma, persist in attachment?
I vow to cultivate patience to block the source of anger, and to take up the practice of compassion to eliminate the root of resentment.

Although I have already offered repentance and apologies above, I still fear that my sincere devotion has not yet been fully expressed. Now, with a most earnest heart, I shall again recite these verses:
"Though all boundless afflictions are evil, Harmfulness is particularly prevalent, and anger is the worst of all.
A single thought can give rise to eighty thousand obstacles; A single word can kill hundreds of thousands of people."
Violent winds and sudden rains make progress difficult; Heaving breath and swollen cheeks make him hard to approach.
As the blade passes through life like cutting bamboo, Fire flares from the heart, as if to burn the body.
Knowing that echoes are equal whether praise or blame, One realizes that empty flowers are the same in accordance or opposition.
From now on, I repent for the sins of my angry mind; I shall cultivate loving-kindness and compassion as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Having finished this repentance, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
The confession of the offense of anger is now complete. Next is the confession of ignorance (*moha*). Ignorance is likewise a category of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);

it is merely divided into two types based on its sharpness or dullness. When encountering objects, one gives rise to emotional attachments, grasping at all such phenomena with distorted and erroneous understandings.
Collectively, these are termed "delusion" (*moha*). It is not necessary for one to be like cattle or sheep to be called "poisoned by delusion.

When this conduct of delusion is compared to ignorance (*avidyā*), there is a distinction between their general and specific meanings, and a distinction between their fundamental and derivative senses. Ignorance merely confuses the True [Self]; delusion, however, grasps at the internal body and external objects as being truly existent.
While the characteristics of ignorance have already been understood, delusion gives rise to various emotional attachments toward each individual phenomenon. This must be so.
You must reform and repent, returning to virtuous friends and training in the Mahāyāna (for even the two vehicles cannot avoid this).

Merely by drawing near to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, you will surely attain the three types of wisdom—listening, contemplation, and cultivation. Once the light of concentration and wisdom has emerged, how could deluded thoughts remain?
Resolutely direct this mind to repent for your former inferiority.

Although I have previously offered repentance and thanks, I still fear that my sincere devotion has not yet been fully expressed. Now, with a renewed heart of utmost sincerity, I shall again recite these verses:
"The three poisons have already been eliminated; of the first two, I have repented. Now I must likewise repent for ignorance (*moha*).
Ignorance need not be like that of birds or beasts; its manifestation in the mind arises precisely from clinging to right and wrong."
Mutually clinging to existence or emptiness, they frequently engage in strife;

With perverse theories on cause and effect, their deluded sentiments harbor doubts and they abandon the right conditions, slighting the True Dharma. The Honored One has come; leave heterodox teachings and serve heterodox teachers.
Quickly seek out their tenets and receive instruction from them; Diligently search for virtuous friends and swiftly take refuge in them.
Having repented through correct reflection upon the Buddha’s knowledge and vision— which extinguishes the many seeds of false views born during the kalpa of destruction—
I now take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.

(Regarding the two layers of ignorance, craving, and so forth, these have already been repented and extinguished as above. However, the two matters of karma and its retribution have not yet been repented and removed. Since the assembly is weary, we shall set them aside for another time; for now, let us first complete the remaining ritual services.)
With a sincere heart, we make this vow: may our disciples,
from this point after repenting for the three poisons, in life after life and age after age, dwell securely in the bodhicitta,
constantly cultivate the practices and vows of compassion and wisdom, swiftly enter the Bodhisattva stage of Freedom from Defilement, and possess a nature free from desire.
Regarding the wealth and resources of others, one should not give rise to covetous thoughts; one should neither desire nor seek them.

Furthermore, one should vow to be forever free from ill-will, constantly giving rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of harmonious moisture, and a mind of inclusive affection.
One should forever abandon greed, resentment, enmity, harm, and the feverish affliction of distress, always reflecting upon and practicing benevolence and kindness.
Zhaniyi: Furthermore, may they forever leave behind false views and abide in the Right Path; may they not practice divination, nor adopt evil precepts;
may their minds perceive what is correct and true, being without deception or flattery; and may they give rise to resolute faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, even in their mental actions.
I shall follow the practice of wisdom, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, rescuing and gathering all beings.
Although I have already made these vows above, I have not yet expressed my sincere devotion; therefore, I now once more speak these verses with a most earnest heart.
May I, after repenting for the remaining three poisons, transform them into the three types of bodhicitta:
great compassion, great wisdom, and great vows—may these not be diminished or endangered, and may greed, hatred, and delusion never arise again.

(This is according to the *Text for Receiving the Bodhicitta Precepts* of the Huayan School, which holds that the essence of bodhicitta consists of the three minds of great compassion, great wisdom, and great vows.)

May all thoughts of greed become the joy of great vows, delighting in the cultivation of all virtuous causes; may the mind of hatred transform into great compassion, pitying sentient beings and seeking to deliver them.
(The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Delighting in the cultivation of all virtuous practices. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* correlates this with the "mind of great vows" within the bodhicitta;
the wording and the meaning of "vow-joy" (*praṇidhāna-ruci*) are not different.)
The poison of delusion is transformed into great wisdom; One thoroughly realizes the boundless gates of the wondrous Dharma.
When these three thoughts are held in mind at all times, This is the manifestation of the bodhicitta.
Once these three types of thought have been aroused, The six pāramitās will naturally be induced.
The six pāramitās rely upon the three minds; the causes and conditions of the six realms reside within the three poisons.
Once the three poisons have ceased and the three minds are perfected, the causes of the six realms perish and the six perfections become complete.
From now until the realization of Bodhi, birth after birth shall continue without interruption.
Furthermore, may there be no obstacles or difficulties in this life, may I not lack the provisions for future lives,
and at the time of death, may I not fall into confusion, but instead take birth wherever my mind desires with full autonomy.
Having made this aspiration, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ Announce to the assembly that you should listen to these verses on impermanence from the sutras:
The fundamental nature of both ordinary beings and sages is equally eternal; Yet ordinary beings cling to appearances and thus fall into impermanence.
Their bodies are oppressed by the six realms and the three miserable paths; In birth after birth, they undergo aging, sickness, and death.
This old age, sickness, and death are universally loathed; their physical forms are so hideous they are utterly repulsive.
The youthful appearance of a guest lasts but a moment; before long, all shall see them withered and frail.
Even if one’s lifespan were to reach a full hundred years, in the end one cannot escape the pressure of impermanence.
The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death constantly follow in pursuit; they perpetually bring no benefit to sentient beings.
One should draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and, in every thought-moment, restrain oneself to cultivate the causes for the eternally abiding.
Abandoning impermanent form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Zhōngnān Mountain.
Part Six, Upper (The Chapter on Samantabhadra. Nine invocations, twenty-two verses; the third part of the three-part repentance for the body).
Praising the Buddha (Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Fascicle 50. The Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Manifestation).
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears through immeasurable dharmas; he does not appear through a single condition nor through a single matter.
Thus is the appearance of the Tathāgata accomplished (this is the general characterization). That is to say:

he provides the great cloud of Dharma and rains the great rain of Dharma, which can extinguish the afflictions of all sentient beings (the first); and it can give rise to the roots of goodness in all sentient beings (the second).
It can cease all the delusions of view among sentient beings (4). It can accomplish the jewel-treasure of all wisdom-dharmas (4).

It distinguishes the mental inclinations and joys of all sentient beings (5). It rains the single-flavored water of the Dharma of great compassion, manifesting infinite distinctions according to their teachings (6).
First it gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of bodhisattvas; next, it gives rise to the wisdom of the various practices of pratyekabuddhas; next, it gives rise to...
The wisdom regarding the various practices of the śrāvakas arises first; next arises the wisdom regarding the various practices of the conditioned roots of goodness of other sentient beings.
This rain of the Dharma of a single flavor accords with the differences in their capacities (the seventh).

The Samantabhadra Chapter consists of nine sections and twenty-two verses. This section investigates and explains the application of the mind (the Bodhisattva’s doubt regarding sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation;
because these two aspects appear contradictory, the Buddha provides a thorough explanation).

With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage. [Question: Regarding the skillful means of awakening and cultivation (and so forth). [There is one subsequent prostration; the rest is the same as this.
For Vairocana Buddha, follow the usual procedure.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Great Compassionate World-Treasure, sentient beings of the final age who cultivate the Mahāyāna..."

Those who possess the nature of the true cause and are able to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, upon hearing this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment—which transcends the hearing of the definitive meaning through ordinary conditions—how should they practice?

(Regarding those who possess the true cause and true conditions [as pointed out above]: this is the gateway for applying the mind. If one did not yet know that the nature of awakening is fundamentally perfect and that delusion is fundamentally illusory, such doubts would not arise. It is precisely because one already knows that all phenomena are empty that one instead harbors doubts regarding the meaning of cultivation.

"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings (referring to the people who have heard the preceding section of the sutra; for them, four gates are established) realize that they are like illusions, then their bodies and minds are likewise illusory."

"How does one use illusion to cultivate illusion? (This is the first question: "Since illusion is illusory, what is there to cultivate? If the nature of all illusions were entirely extinguished, then there would be no mind;
who then would perform cultivation? How, then, can it be said that cultivation is like an illusion? (This is the second question: "If [all is] annihilated, who cultivates?
If sentient beings fundamentally do not engage in cultivation, yet constantly dwell within the midst of birth and death as mere illusory transformations, they have never understood [the truth].
In this realm of illusion, how can the mind of discursive thought be liberated? (This is the third [point], which prevents the fault of not practicing.

I pray that for all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age, you will provide some skillful means so that they may practice gradually and successively, enabling all beings to forever leave behind all illusions. (This is the fourth [point], requesting the skillful means for practice.)
This section of the sutra contains two verses of praise. First:
The three [verses] correctly describe the sutra text, which reveals that what was previously taught is realized all at once;
from this point onward follows the gradual cultivation and purification.
When Samantabhadra questioned the Tathāgata, he raised a point where gradual cultivation and sudden enlightenment appear to be contradictory:
"If one knows that birth and death are all like an illusion, then the wisdom that knows this is likewise so;
how then can one use an illusion to cultivate an illusion? (The first line describes the question: why cultivate an illusion with an illusion?)
Who is it that practices the extinction of illusion? (2. Describing cessation; asking who practices.
If one does not practice at all, how can there be liberation? What difference is there between awakening and the former time of delusion?
(2. Prohibiting non-practice; practicing below. I pray that you give rise to compassion for the final age.
Section Two: Revealing the Expedient Means to Universally Enable Understanding (The Fourfold Request for the Expedient Means of Cultivation).

Section Three: Specific Explanation of the Meaning of Illusion (*māyā*). Regarding "illusion": it refers to the illusory phenomena existing in the world. Based on grasses, wood, and so forth, illusions are fashioned into humans and animals, appearing with all the marks of coming and going and active movement;

yet in an instant, when the phenomenon ceases, they revert to being mere grass and wood. However, among the various sūtras and teachings, metaphors of illusion are particularly numerous. This is truly because such arts were quite prevalent in the Five Indias; having been extensively seen and heard there, the principles of the Dharma were easy to clarify. When [these teachings] were translated here in this land [of China], however, they became difficult to understand. Now...

According to the ancient masters, in their interpretation of the *Avataṃsaka* passage on "illusory-like" (māyopama), both the phenomena (*dharma*) and the metaphors (*upamāna*) are each analyzed into five factors. Regarding the five factors within the metaphor: (1) a single cloth as the basis; (2) the magician’s artifice; (3) the illusory horse produced;

(4) the horse being non-existent even while appearing to exist; and (5) the deluded attachment to it as a horse. Regarding the five factors within the phenomenon: (1) true nature (*tathatā*); (2) mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*); (3) the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); (4) the fact that the self and phenomena are empty; and (5) the deluded attachment to self and phenomena. All subsequent metaphors of illusion should be understood by following this pattern.
Samantabhadra raises up illusion to manifest the Dharma; The student must know the efficacy of illusory arts.
(Illusory arts have five meanings previously explained; they are now fully correlated here: Illusory art (the first meaning, like the mind-consciousness) can turn a cloth into a horse;
(The second meaning, like the fundamental nature) It gallops away as if real, its eyes sparkling clear. (Third, like the dependent nature)
The arising of phenomena is like an illusory horse: it is empty in essence yet appears to exist (the fourth point, as in the principle of the original substance).
The real headband exists, yet its concealment results in emptiness (the fifth point, regarding conceptual attachment).
Originally, it is merely like the headband; this is difficult to believe.
All conditions resemble horses and easily follow one another; if illusory wisdom is cultivated, the illusory and false substance will appear.

One should seek the tracks of the front horse among the rear horses. Having cited these reasons to report to the Buddha, it is somewhat difficult for the principles of true conditions to be fully established.
Next follows the Tathāgata’s praise, his granting of the request for instruction, and the actual discourse, which consists of four sections; this is the first of those two initial sections.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you are indeed able to provide skillful means for all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age to cultivate the bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi."
Gradually, [the Buddha] causes all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. (Praise and inquiry. "Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you" (this is the promise to speak.
Following this, there are four sections of the main exposition; herein, there are two such sections).
Good son, the various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky appear from space.
(First point: that illusion arises from enlightenment is the fundamental principle. Although the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed.

The illusory minds of sentient beings are extinguished by relying on the illusory; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind is entirely unmoving. (The exhaustion of the two illusions and the fulfillment of awakening have already resolved the preceding doubts.)
This section of the sutra contains four verses of praise.
Regarding the third [verse]: Briefly explaining the text:
The Buddha said, "Since you are able to pose such inquiries, I shall now speak; you must listen with careful attention."

Beginningless ignorance (the verse says: "beginningless illusory ignorance"), all these illusory transformations (because one thoroughly understands them as illusions), arise entirely from the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment).
Illusory wisdom serves as the antidote to illusory deluded thoughts (the illusory minds of sentient beings are extinguished by relying on the illusory [antidote]).
When both illusions are removed, awakening becomes clear; (all illusions are extinguished, yet the awakened mind remains unmoving).

It is like flowers in the sky vanishing within the void; (just as wondrous illusory flowers arise from the empty space, though the illusory flowers vanish,) how could the empty space itself ever be diminished?
(The nature of emptiness is indestructible.)
The subsequent analysis and explanation begins with the doubt and difficulty regarding how illusion arises from awakening.
Fourth, second: "The doubt that illusory transformations and defilements arise from pure awakening" (two lines).
Therefore, the general characteristics are briefly explained (six lines).
How can false defilement arise within the pure? This statement is difficult to understand;
let us further investigate it through the method of "Mind-Only" (cittamātra). There are eight successive layers of mutual support: (1) the section on the Hīnayāna explaining the single mind;

(2) both the perceived and the perceiver existing together as the single mind; (3) subsuming the perceived into the perceiver as the single mind; (4) subsuming the objects of perception into the sovereign [mind] as the single mind; (5) subsuming the seven [consciousnesses] into the eighth as the single mind; (6) subsuming the storehouse [consciousness]...
1. Consciousness returns to the Tathāgatagarbha as the One Mind. 2. The seven layers of defilement and purity are but the One Mind.

3. Universally encompassing all phenomena is the One Mind. 4. The True Mind is eternally abiding and eternally pure; 5. From the beginningless past, ordinary beings and sages have equally possessed it.

6. It possesses the virtue of remaining unchanging while following conditions; 7. Its numinous clarity is unhindered even when seeing the cage of worldly existence. (Commentary on the eight successive points.)
The Meaning of the Weight [of the Title] (5) 3.
The Distinct Mutual Dependence of the Flowing [Phenomena] and the Universal Presence within the Minds of Sentient Beings:
This is True Suchness Buddha, Who is eternally one with the Buddha within the household of the Dharma-realm.
Because of delusion, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when mixed with falsehood, it is named the *ālayavijñāna*.

By its very nature, it can produce the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); seeing the various faculties and objects proliferate in profusion, one fails to know that these arise from the transformation of the mind.
Clinging to them as self and phenomena, one spreads all manner of heterodox views.
My own body immediately gives rise to greed, delusion, and anger; moment by moment it creates karma in pursuit of luxury.
When that karma ripens, one receives a physical form like a shadow or an echo, cycling through birth and death forever without respite.
(The two preceding chants both explain that those born of illusory transformation awaken the mind of enlightenment.)
Sixth, Part Three: Specific Explanation. Once the illusory mind and the consciousness of the mind have been extinguished by relying on illusory wisdom, one realizes that the mind is unmoving.
This concludes the explanation of how defiled phenomena arise from reality (concluding that illusion arises from awakening).

Next, the discussion on how the friend’s delusion returns to the truth (this indicates that when illusion is exhausted, awakening is fulfilled). Below, the explanation of the text consists of four layers, all of which are illusory phenomena:

first, the sense organs; second, fundamental ignorance and the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; third, all karmic actions; and fourth, the retributions received. To realize and awaken to one's original mind is to overturn non-awakening (the first layer).
This gives rise to the cause of the wondrous awakening of Bodhi; these causes are the three minds of compassion, wisdom, and the vow.
By means of this, one overturns the three poisons of craving, ignorance, and hatred (2). Diligently practicing the six perfections eliminates all karmic actions;
once the six perfections are perfected, karma naturally ceases (3).

When karma has thus been extinguished, one no longer receives retribution, completely transcending the realms of ghosts, animals, and hells, as well as those of devas and humans (4). Therefore it is said, "All illusions are utterly extinguished. "All" refers to these four [realms].
The initial awakening (shijue) accords with the original awakening (benjue); this is the body of the Unsurpassed Dharma King (the mind of awakening is unmoving).

Below this is the third section, which successively transcends illusion and correctly demonstrates the application of the mind. This section has two parts: first, the teaching (dharma), and second, the analogy (metaphor).
Good son, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they firmly maintain the mind that distances itself, even the mind that is like an illusion is likewise distanced.

One distances oneself from illusion, and again distances oneself from that distancing. One distances oneself even from the distancing from illusion; once there is nothing further to distance oneself from, all illusions are eliminated. (The following [passage] secretly reveals true awakening.)

Chapter Seven: Two Dharmas—The Superior Answer Explaining Awakening and Cultivation, and Resolving Obstacles and Difficulties. From the gate of detailed instruction on the application of the mind through loving-kindness:
One should remain far removed from all sensory objects; Even the mind that is able to remain detached should not be maintained.
Successively departing from deluded sentiments and leaving behind subtle thoughts, the mind has no place of attachment and is severed from all traces of dust.
Having attained that which is nothing to be departed from, one eliminates all illusions; only when thought is exhausted can one merge with the original source.

It is like drilling for fire: two pieces of wood act as causes, and fire emerges. When the wood is exhausted, the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished. Thus, one uses illusion to cultivate illusion.
It is also thus. Although all illusions may come to an end, they do not enter into total annihilation.
Chapter Eight, Part Two:
The Metaphor of Eliminating Illusions Through Successive Layers. Since the words and meaning were obscured, it is further clarified by means of the metaphor of drilling for fire.
All wood inherently contains the nature of fire; Through the power of friction and drilling, fire is born.
The fire emerging from the wood then consumes the wood itself; Knowing that the cause is manifested through emotion, one eliminates emotion.
When the wood is consumed and extinguished, the fire naturally ceases; In the void where emotion is destroyed, wisdom returns to its source.
Good son, to know illusion is to be free from it; no expedient means need be employed. To be free from illusion is awakening itself, and there is no gradual progression.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this will thus be able to forever leave behind all illusions.
Chapter Nine: Two When the fourth delusion of illusion does not arise, one speaks of "removing illusion" to eliminate attachment.
Since illusory phenomena are entirely empty, there is nothing not removed;
knowing that illusion is fundamentally non-existent is itself liberation. Why then should one need to apply expedient means or exert effort?
To seek to cure the illness of dreams is truly contrary to the Dharma; To diligently sweep away empty flowers is surely folly.
Awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa without gradual stages; The True Name is free from illusion, forever without remainder.

Namo to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (and so forth). (Twelfth Prostration) Universally for the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm.
Below this is the repentance for the ten evil deeds. Repent with a sincere heart.

Now, regarding what is called "repentance" (*pāpadeśanā*): its essence is to reform the past and cultivate the future, to extinguish evil and promote good. When human beings dwell in this world, who is without fault?

Even those who study the Way give rise to afflictions when their mindfulness lapses; even Arhats manifest residual habits through the movement of body, speech, and mind. How much less could this be otherwise?
How much more so for ordinary people who cannot possibly be without transgressions? It is only the wise who perceive them first; having perceived them, they immediately offer repentance.

The foolish conceal them, whereby they spread and entangle themselves. Thus, through long habituation throughout the night of ignorance, there is no prospect of awakening. If one can feel shame and remorse, and reveal these faults, [liberation is possible].
One who performs repentance does not merely extinguish transgressions; they also increase immeasurable merit and establish the sublime fruit of the Tathāgata’s flames.
Those who wish to practice this dharma should first externally solemnize their physical demeanor and reverently gaze upon the sacred image.
Internally, they give rise to a sense of earnest intent, revering the Dharma-gate with profound sincerity and reaching a state of utmost urgency. They generate two kinds of thoughts.
What are these two? First, they reflect to themselves: "This life of mine is difficult to preserve; it may perish in a single morning. I do not know when this body might be restored.
If I do not encounter the Buddhas and the worthy sages, and instead suddenly fall into the company of evil friends, I shall commit various transgressions."
Karma: One should fall into a deep and perilous pit. Second, one reflects to oneself:

"In this life, although I have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and become a disciple of the Buddha, as a disciple I ought to perpetuate the lineage of the Sages and purify the wholesome dharmas of body, speech, and mind.
Yet, dwelling therein, I think: 'We openly commit evil deeds and later conceal them,' claiming it was another."

To know [this] means that they do not see what is hidden. To harbor such thoughts in one's heart and remain defiant and shameless regarding this treasure is the height of folly and delusion in the world.
Now, there currently exist the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the devas and immortals;

when have they ever failed to behold the evil deeds we commit with their pure divine eyes? Furthermore, there are the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest, who distinguish between good and evil.
Child, the recording of sins and merits is precise to the smallest detail, without the slightest error.
Now, regarding those who commit evil deeds, after their lives have ended, the ox-headed jailers will record their spirits and bring them before King Yama to investigate right and wrong.
At that time, although none of one's enemies have yet provided evidence, each will say, "In the past, you slaughtered my body; you roasted, boiled, and steamed me."
They roast him. Or they say: "You have plundered my wealth and separated me from my kin; it is only now that I have attained this [retribution].
You have presented evidence right before my eyes; how dare you speak such words? You must simply accept your past calamities with a willing heart.
As clarified in the sutras, within the hells no one is punished unjustly. If one has committed various sins throughout one's life, the mind itself—
As for those who have forgotten [their transgressions], at the moment of their birth, all the signs of the places where they committed evil will appear before them.
Each will say, "You were once by my side committing such crimes; how can you now claim innocence? Thus one knows that there is no place of escape for those who commit sins.
Thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and consigns them to hell, where they shall endure through kalpas and throughout all years.
There is no way to escape this; it is not far off. It does not concern others alone—it is precisely my own body that shall undergo this suffering.
Though the bond between father and son is most intimate, once this moment arrives, there is no one who can take one’s place.

All of you, while your forms are still strong and your bodies free from various ailments, must each exert yourselves and strive as if competing with your very lives. When the time of great terror arrives, there will be nothing left for regret.

Cease. Therefore, we, the disciples, prostrate ourselves before all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space, as well as the Honored Dharma and the Holy Sangha.
We pray that the Triple Gem of the ten directions, the Primordial Honored One Vairocana Buddha, and the Lord of Repentance Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, may bear witness to our repentance.
Having completed the repentance for the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), we shall now proceed to repent for the obscuration of manifested karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). As for karma...
It is able to adorn the realms of existence. Thus, the retributions of the six paths differ, and their forms and types are each distinct;
one must know that these are all produced by the power of karma. Yet, among ordinary people, many frequently give rise to doubts and perplexities regarding this. Why is this?
Because one observes that among people in the present life, those who practice virtue encounter misfortune, while those who commit evil find success;
for this reason, the foolish claim that there is no distinction between good and evil. They do not know that karmic retribution is of three kinds:

first, retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*); second, retribution in the next life (*upapadyavipāka*); and third, retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavipāka*). Regarding retribution in the present life: what is created in this lifetime...

One may cultivate merit while still bearing the retribution for past offenses; thus, one experiences the rewards of suffering and pleasure in this very life. Regarding "retribution in the next life" (*upapadya-vedanīya*):
this refers to karma created in the present body that is experienced as retribution in the subsequent birth. Regarding "subsequent retribution" (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*):

this refers to karma created over many past lives that continues to yield retribution from the present life through the next, or the third, or even throughout hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of future births.

One then receives its retribution. Furthermore, there may be karma created in this life that is not received until a future life—perhaps in the second, third, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of lives before it is finally experienced;
all such cases are termed "retribution in a later life" (*paścātpāka*).

When one cultivates goodness in this life or encounters calamities and afflictions, these are the seeds of evil karma created in previous lives or over many kalpas and many births, which have now reached the time for their manifestation.
Manifestation. It is because the power of present goodness is weak that one cannot dispel [obstacles], and thus there is misfortune.

It is not that present goodness is being opened up to invite present suffering. As for those who commit transgressions while living their lives yet instead receive blessings and joy, this is also due to the manifestation of determined wholesome karma from many previous lives;
although they are evil in the present life, it cannot obstruct [that karma]. It is not that present [karma] is being opened up...

Though one has committed transgressions, one may still attract present blessings. Clearly and distinctly, this is the Buddha’s injunction; you must examine it with careful scrutiny. Do not allow base sentiments to give rise to doubt within yourself.
Having already explained the causes and conditions of karmic power, we shall next proceed to the formal repentance (*pratideśanā*). Now, those who create karma include both monastics and laypeople;

for now, I shall explain the path for both monastics and laity in general, and subsequently perform the specific repentances. Regarding the general repentance for monastics first: karma is of two kinds—wholesome and unwholesome.
There are three types of immovability (*āniñjya*). Now, we shall only repent of evil karma; evil karma itself consists of seven branches:
the three of body and the four of speech. We shall now repent of each one in successive order. Among the three types of bodily karma, the first concerns manifest forms which are coarse;

they are easy to prevent through restraint, yet the transgression carries heavy consequences. Since matters proceed from the coarse to the subtle, this repentance demonstrates that what is heavy becomes light. Now, regarding this—
At that time, first repent for the three transgressions of bodily action. Among these three, first repent for the sin of killing.
Disciple Bhikṣu [Name] and others, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from immeasurable kalpas past until this very day, have committed immeasurable and boundless sins of killing.
Encountering objects, we did not deliberate upon what constitutes sin or merit; driven by greed and hatred—

Fierce and violent, they show no mercy toward either benefactors or enemies; their minds are intoxicated by the poison of ignorance. How could they know how to advance or retreat? Relying on official rank and exploiting power, they falsely execute the innocent.
Boasting of their own martial prowess, they recklessly harm the virtuous and good. Greedy and accepting bribes, they cruelly deceive those within their ranks.

Arrogant in spirit and malevolent at heart, they beat and bury the weak and defenseless. During the four seasons and eight festivals, when their kinsmen gather in circles, they perform sacrifices to ghosts and spirits and celebrate the marriages of their sons.
They marry off their daughters; they fly hawks and run dogs; they spread nets and set snares; they drain ponds and pools; they burn mountains and fields;
they boil silkworm cocoons; they swat away mosquitoes and gadflies; they employ incantations and talismans for sorcery; they cause abortions; they kill at will; they are without shame or remorse;
they do these things themselves and teach others to do so; they rejoice when seeing them done; they destroy the conditions of life and sever the seeds of great compassion. Of those who are killed...
Those who do so all form great enmities; life after life, they will continue to kill and harm one another. Such offenses are immeasurable and boundless.
By these causes and conditions, they shall fall into hell, where for hundreds or thousands of kalpas it is difficult to calculate the time of their release.

They will undergo myriad forms of suffering that can never be fully recounted. After long kalpas and long periods as animals or hungry ghosts, they may eventually obtain a human body and receive [the results of] two...

They plant various remaining retributions: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness (from here on, each section describes two retributions, all of which are from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*). Enveloped by ignorance, they do not recognize the causes of karma.
Now, encountering this place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they finally awaken and turn toward Śākyamuni Bhagavat and all the worthy sages.
They burn incense and scatter flowers, proclaiming the sin of killing, confessing and repenting openly, and not daring to conceal it.
By these causes and conditions, may the grave offense of killing committed by me and all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* be ultimately purified.

Having performed this repentance, with a sincere heart I take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha. (Regarding karmic actions, hindrances, and retributions, their manifestations appear grossly in the body and speech;

therefore, one simply takes refuge in the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. By repenting according to the teachings, reproaching those hindrances, they are immediately eliminated. One then makes a vow to reverse them; thus, follow the method of this text.)

Next is the repentance for the sin of stealing. Furthermore, disciples and all beings of the Dharma-realm, from immeasurable kalpas past until this very day, have committed sins of theft that are infinite and boundless.
Greedful intent has not been eliminated; a thousand schemes have been plotted. The ordinary mind is difficult to satisfy, employing a hundred forms of deception and fraud.
Monks and nuns have been robbed, and the permanent property of the Sangha has been encroached upon and violated, whether by night or by day.
I prostrate myself. To bore through walls and break down fences is to turn wealth toward poverty; to deceive the honest into servitude is to employ light scales and small measures.

Always harboring a thieving heart, one’s every movement is utterly devoid of integrity, and one constantly maintains a mind like that of a robber. Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless.

By reason of these causes and conditions, one shall fall into hell, where for hundreds or thousands of kalpas it will be difficult to calculate the time of release. One shall undergo myriad forms of suffering that are ultimately impossible to describe in full.
It is said that after long kalpas and long periods as animals and hungry ghosts, they later obtain a human body and undergo two kinds of residual retribution: first, poverty;
second, the loss of wealth and lack of autonomy. Shrouded by ignorance, they do not recognize the causes of karma.
Now, having encountered the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they finally awaken and turn toward Śākyamuni Bhagavān and all the worthy sages, burning incense and scattering flowers.
I vow to repent for the offense of stealing. I openly confess and do not dare to conceal it.
By these causes and conditions, may I and all sentient beings of the dharma realm be forever purified of the grave offense of theft.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart, take refuge in and pay homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Next, repent for the transgression of lustful desire. Furthermore, disciples, from immeasurable kalpas ago until this very day:
They indulge in the debauchery of female forms, making no distinction between kin and stranger; as lust intensifies, their delusion deepens, such that they no longer consider beauty or ugliness.

Bound by attachment to the realm of form as if by ropes, and intoxicated by the craving for the sphere of sound, they give rein to their unruly impulses and commit transgressions even within the precincts of the saṃghārāma.

They openly commit karmic offenses against the pure monasteries of the four quarters, feeling neither shame nor disgrace; how are they any different from beasts? Lacking both moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), their appearance is like that of birds and wild animals.
Amidst theatrical performances and banquets, they indulge their hearts in theft and greed; yet when at the rows of the monastic hall, they look directly into the faces of others.

The ears follow sounds, so that when obstructed by the preaching of the Dharma, they do not hear; the eyes pursue forms, so that they are deluded regarding the Honored One’s countenance and fail to behold it.

They steal flowers and fruit from the Buddha to curry favor with worldly people. Since the laity are thus, the monastics are likewise sometimes so. Consequently, both their sleep and their food are cut off; their bones grow thin and their bodies waste away.

Although their form is that of humans, their conduct is like that of a mad antelope. Such sins as these are immeasurable and boundless; by reason of these causes and conditions, they shall fall into hell.
Men embrace glowing copper pillars, while women lie upon iron beds. Their sorrows and sufferings are of ten thousand kinds, which cannot be fully recounted here.
Having been among animals and hungry ghosts for long kalpas and long periods of time, they later obtain a human body; yet there remain two kinds of residual retribution:
first, their wives are not chaste and virtuous; second, they cannot have a retinue according to their wishes. Enveloped by ignorance, they do not recognize the causes of karma.
Now that I have encountered this site of enlightenment, I have finally attained awakening. I take refuge in Śākyamuni Bhagavān and all the worthy sages.
Burning incense and scattering flowers, I proclaim the transgression of sexual desire; I confess and repent openly, not daring to conceal it.
By these causes and conditions, may the grave offense of sexual desire for myself and all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm now be ultimately purified.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge in our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Above, we have already completed the repentance for the three types of offenses among bodily actions—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

Now, we shall proceed to repent for the four transgressions of verbal action. Among these four, the offense of lying is light in its sprout but heavy in its root, and it causes the most widespread harm.

These constitute offenses against the paths of action (*karmapatha*), as well as violations of the disciplinary regulations (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*). They destroy the bodhisattva precepts and constitute a *pārājika* offense, whether by nature (*prakṛtisāvadya*) or by prohibition (*prajñaptisāvadya*);

in all such cases, the gravity of the offense is established. (However, if one praises oneself out of humility, following conventional worldly speech—even if the matter does not correspond to reality—provided it does no harm to others, no offense is incurred.
Therefore, one must arouse a fierce and intense resolve to first repent of all words of deception and falsehood.
We, the disciples, from immeasurable kalpas past until this very day, have committed sins of false speech that are infinite and boundless.
The mouth serves as a medium for calamity; the tongue is the root of strife. Good and evil arise from three lifetimes; praise and blame stem from a single word.
For great offenses, they bring about the extinction of clans and the ruin of entire cities; for minor transgressions, they endanger their own persons and risk their very lives.

Their nature is not true, and the words they utter are mostly false. They deceive their close kin and elders, and they defraud their parents. Sometimes acting as practitioners of medicine, they employ every means of deception, manipulating the dosage of various prescriptions to prolong or shorten life.
Or they open up divinations and resolutions, recklessly proclaiming good or bad fortune. They employ ten thousand forms of clever trickery, yet—

There is not a single reality [to be found]. Talismans, scriptures, and incense offerings are empty paths for summoning souls; wine and dried meat are used to invoke spirits and falsely claim to redeem the *po* (soul).

Such transgressions are immeasurable and boundless. Due to these causes and conditions, one shall fall into hell for hundreds or thousands of kalpas, with the time of liberation difficult to calculate.

One will undergo ten thousand varieties of suffering that are ultimately impossible to describe in full. Following this, one will remain among animals and hungry ghosts for long kalpas and long periods of time. Afterward...
Having attained a human body, there are further two kinds of residual retribution: first, being frequently subjected to slander; second, being deceived by others.

Enveloped by ignorance, one fails to recognize the causes of karma. Only now, encountering the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), does one finally awaken and turn toward Śākyamuni Buddha and all the worthy sages.
One burns incense, scatters flowers, confesses the sin of false speech, and reveals it for repentance. Not...
I dare not conceal [these faults]. By these causes and conditions, may the grave offense of false speech for myself and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm be ultimately purified.
