It can give rise to greed and anger, causing one to create karma, and it can obstruct the sections of morality and meditative concentration from this point forward.
The physical form is entirely the dwelling place of the "it" (the "it" refers to the false self);

it is grasped as one's own body, sharing in its safety and peril. (The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains that the grasping of a self clings to the root-body as the self. The text states: "It is grasped as one's own body because they share the same safety and peril.
This means that when the body is at ease, the mind is joyful and happy; when the body is in peril, the mind is sorrowful and suffering. Therefore, it is said they are the same.)
Now, wishing to destroy the thief of self-grasping, one must begin the investigation with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
When investigating, do not sever [the inquiry] according to mere sentiment; where there is illumination, one must further contemplate according to principle.
First, examine this body for its many faults and afflictions, until one exhaustively probes those faults down to their most subtle essence.
At all times, maintain this reflection: fire, wind, earth, and water are each distinct from one another (earth is not wind, nor is fire water;

it is thus for each). Those that are joined and blended together appear as one (like four people from distant lands who happen to be in the same place, whether standing or sitting, appearing as a single entity). Within that which appears as one, the constituent parts are fundamentally fragmented.
Sentient beings have been constantly deluded since time immemorial; clinging to the "one" as a person, they falsely treasure it and uphold it throughout life after life.
They follow and acknowledge it, creating birth; hastening and striving in their schemes, they provide only for it.
It awakens and it receives; it seeks form and pursues form; in the end, desiring to deceive others, it deceives them.
Before one’s hunger has been relieved, one craves fine food; before one is fully chilled by the cold, one seeks fresh garments.
The orientation of halls and chambers must suit one's convenience; mats and bedding require warmth or coolness according to the season.
In every thought, one laments not having enough servants and concubines; in every heart, one is attached to a beloved wife and children.
One strives for official rank solely for the sake of others; for whom else does one accumulate wealth?
The whole world lets others constantly bear heavy burdens, yet one must first ensure that I may forever ride upon their fatness.
One plans for a thousand years through seeking and begging, yet how could a friend ever have expected a lifespan of a hundred years?

It is said that a ravine is easy to fill, yet this is not necessarily so; (though it is said to be easy to fill, in reality it is not, hence "not necessarily. If contrasted with the mind's difficulty in being satisfied, then it becomes "easy").
That the human heart is difficult to satisfy is indeed as such. (To say that the human heart is difficult to satisfy means that it is truly difficult to satisfy).
To provide for one’s body with food and clothing according to immediate necessity—doing so merely for the sake of sustaining oneself does not constitute an obstruction.
When material resources belong to oneself, one may exert oneself in their pursuit (from housing and bedding down to various implements for sustaining the body; seeking them may be excused).
In principle, one ought to be content with sufficient food and clothing (because they are sought only until one’s needs are exhausted, it is called "provisional").

Why then do you never cease your striving despite abundance? (While providing for the body, one should have enough for three hundred and twenty years; yet even when there is no end to what can be consumed, one’s activity does not stop—hence it is called "never ceasing.")

Rest! Such delusions are not particularly grave. (This does not concern the body. Fame and reputation are empty and false; (this does not open up the body. Why must one seek them? (Even if you see them, they do not concern the body.
Exhausting oneself in the pursuit of worldly gain—how could that be necessary? (Since it was said to be for the sake of the body,) [it is surely not so.]

To engage in ball games and hunting is improper; it only causes the body to become increasingly distressed and suffering, yet one does not know for whose sake one acts thus. Why do you so exclusively love fine silks? What warmth is there in them? (The body simply requires warmth;
why must one wear fine silks? The warmth of fine silks does not equal that of plain silk. Hoarding much gold and jade will not satisfy hunger. (This matter, moreover, does not open up the person.
Seeking and searching with a hundred heads, one never grows weary.

Exerting oneself over a thousand *li* never tires; (these two lines concern profit. The following six lines concern reputation; they do not even acknowledge one’s own person. This is to know the "foolish among fools.
Competing for victory and defeat through various arts and skills, vying for high and low status down to the smallest fraction;
though one may attain the leadership of ten thousand men, the world will resent it, while a single person who briefly speaks of what is wrong will be praised. (If one were to judge by principle...)

Having already gained the praise of ten thousand people, if suddenly one person disparages them, it would only be right to lose that one person’s praise; yet nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine people still remain praising them.

Why strive so bitterly for that single fraction among the ten thousand? Is this not utterly foolish? In every thought and calculation, they scheme only for themselves (even toward their own close brothers or those on the same path, they seek only their own advancement).
In every sight and hearing, they wish for others to decline. (As for wishing for others to decline...)
To seek one's own solitary exaltation;

to feel aversion and resentment at the slightest failure of one’s desires, yet to follow and comply with every thousandfold satisfaction—such are the conditions of conformity and opposition, the gates of calamity and fortune within the realm of heaven and earth. When you encounter even a single circumstance that accords with your will, you must prepare for it;

how can you evade or shirk when faced with a single thing that opposes your feelings? Time and again you receive blessings, and as soon as you have received one blessing, you immediately encounter a calamity. At this point, you wonder: to whom can you entrust the burden so that they alone may suffer it? Reflect thus upon the world.
Above, there are no people who have attained equanimity; not knowing the proper measure, they lack contentment—these "black-headed worms" are truly laughable and strange.
(That they are "laughable" refers to the extreme of their insatiable minds; it is an excess.
Suddenly, when one person approaches the end of their life, they realize that their consciousness must inevitably migrate. (Ten times ten, a hundred million...)
People do not realize their error until the very moment of death. Suddenly, among them, one person speaks thus with great distress:
"Reflecting back on how I have nurtured this body for so many years, Now it cannot avoid being separated from me.
Since you cannot go along with me, In an instant, it shall be my time to walk alone. Thus it is for every person at the end of life.
None could bear to let him go; they waited, intending to take him away. When morning came, he could not be taken, for it was simply that he himself was unable to go.
The merit of providing for him is beyond calculation. Questioner: Why did you wait for such a long time to come and serve you? [The Master:
You have never, even for a single thought-moment, treated me with slight or contempt. (Each and every one of you intended only this.)
How could one who transforms others be willing to transform oneself? Therefore, all sentient beings possess the seeds of the seven types of pride and the nine types of pride.

Regarding the various matters described above (as set forth in the preceding verses), you should now understand them all by reflecting upon and grasping them; today I shall explain them clearly to you.
You must listen attentively and not consort with folly; when the limit of death arrives, I shall part from you.
I shall cast off this shadow [of the body], and you will become a corpse.

Since you know these matters yet have never failed in your duties, and do not perceive even a fraction of your own deficiency, how can you disregard such vast and heavy heavenly grace? (The affairs of the body exceed...)
Regarding the service of one's parents: You ought to repay them and must not neglect them.
Now, as I am about to depart for the next life, I turn to ask you: Your allotted time ahead is limited and matters are difficult to manage;
you must quickly declare whether things are good or bad. Do not be distracted by busyness, but exert yourself so that there is no delay.
Who would have thought that this ungrateful and stubborn obstacle Would remain silent, failing to utter a single word from its pen?
(The "pen" refers to the tip; it straightens [the corpse, which is often bent, by stretching it out straight]).
It straightens both eyes, and as it reclines upon the measured bed, it spreads out its four companions. I pity you, for your anger is truly a cause for painful reproach and disgrace.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of shame or remorse. (Ordinary people, burdened by their debts of gratitude, have failed to repay them;
they ought also to offer thanks. Under a mulberry tree for a brief moment, one may still receive a reward; but throughout a lifetime in the human world, how can it be like this?

(A single meal still brings the reward of having one’s wheels supported; how much more so the kindness of life after life? Therefore, it says below: In a lifetime of ceaseless toil, what has been accomplished?
A lifetime of restless turmoil is truly pitiable (one may reflect upon and reproach oneself for this);
turning it over in thought, I know it was all wrong. For three nights and five days I regretted my lack of progress;
reflecting inwardly from youth until old age, I see that I have always been bound by the prison of the four elements.
Although they have heard that the Sovereign True Body is here preaching—something they have heard before—others do not hear it at all; those who do not hear it number in the tens of millions.

Even those who have heard it lack the leisure to cast even a momentary glance with the eye of wisdom; day after day, they fail to investigate or discern it, let alone those who have never heard the Dharma.
They are preoccupied with serving their parents and attending to evil friends (for "serving" them refers to the fact that evil friends entice people by catering to their physical desires).
When have I ever studied the Dharma? (The Dharma belongs to my own consciousness, yet I lack the leisure to study it.
Whenever there is a superior opportunity or a place where I ought to go, I push aside urgent matters and procrastinate;
because of this "snake-basket" of past transgressions, I am made to return empty-handed from the Mountain of Jewels.
To have wandered in vain without merit is already a grievance; how much more so to be dragged into the office of the banquet!

(The meaning below clarifies that when seeking retribution, if one cannot find it, one is nonetheless forced to endure dullness; yet one does not refuse to reflect sincerely upon where one’s journey through future lives will lead, and thus examines one’s own lifelong conduct, realizing that all was either right or wrong, compliant or contrary.)
This further stirs their alarm and doubt. Since birth, they have been driven by the demon of craving;
their actions lack the support of either meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*). Their karma is such that they need not merely lament;

who can guarantee that their spirits will avoid the Avīci Hell? (Once one has lost oneself, it cannot be recovered later. One should simply observe those who come after with a benevolent heart and urge them to change their course early.)
The preceding carriage has already overturned; one can only sigh in lamentation. When the rear horse stands at the edge of a pit, it is impossible to change course even with clear understanding;
it will only result in returning to dullness. One must seek advantage day and night. (6) Six:
Contemplating the Body up to the Previous Section merely clarifies that this body is not the self, and furthermore, that it is a source of suffering and affliction.
Regarding these objects: now, upon careful examination, they are not only sources of affliction, but moreover lack any inherent self-nature, because each and every one belongs to something else.
Having already described how this body possesses many afflictions, one must necessarily contemplate its disintegration until it reaches the state of emptiness within emptiness.
Earth, water, fire, and wind appear as if they were combined, though in principle each should consume its own;
one should investigate these four elements alone, which falsely constitute the self. Search for the master of this self within whom it resides:
since these four have distinct natures from the outset—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—how could they ever be compatible?
Heavy, stagnant, and having form; light, empty, and formless—these are called wind. When moisture and warmth conflict, they become water and fire;
these four elements, being mutually opposed, clash with one another. You all must certainly decide who shall be the master;
you must point it out clearly and not pretend to be deaf. If you say that from beginning to end, "I" am the source of it all, [then you have found it].

Thus, the four types of self are established, which directly contradicts your own tenet (for those who postulate a self all claim it to be one and eternal; now you say there are four, which is to contradict your own tenet).

When questioned, your words become increasingly crude and muddled (when the mind perceives each principle, yet you do not speak of it as such, but instead falsely dismiss it, calling it "crude and muddled").
As the inquiry into the principles is repeated, they become even more obscure and dim; shifting back and forth, they are pushed aside until they lack any definitive point of reference.
You must directly cause each one to pass through individually. The earth element has form and is pervasive, yet it possesses obstruction.
Now, first examine you yourself until your original traces are gone. Within this earth of yours there are many attendants;
Examine them from head to toe, do not look east or west.

Regarding what is stated in various sutras and treatises—most of which proceed from the crown of the head down to the feet—the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "First, one contemplates externally the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and so forth; subsequently, having removed the skin and flesh, one proceeds exclusively from these [parts] up to the crown.

This sutra thus moves externally to the flesh, taking that which is easily seen by the eye as the starting point, and gradually proceeding to the hidden parts that are difficult to see. Hair and body hair (the most external); nails (external to the four limbs); teeth (of the same category as nails, next in order, being the external bones visible therefrom);

skin (next to hair, body hair, and nails); flesh (beneath the skin); sinews and bones (sinews binding the bones); marrow (the marrow within the bones); brain (the flesh of the head); and filth (referring collectively to all of these). All are included.
Returning to the earth (briefly citing eleven items; taking two substances as examples, we now divide them into these two parts). Seventh and Eighth:

For now, we shall merely investigate earth and fire (continuing to briefly cite examples. The verses must be explained. Although many speak of the internal, external, and intermediate, even the thirty-six items do not exhaustively cover them;
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twelve, lists them extensively over two pages).
First one sees the hair, fur, nails, and teeth; next, the layers of skin, flesh, sinews, and bones (as noted above in the commentary, proceeding step by step until reaching the flesh).
Within each and every bone there is marrow, which is as foul-smelling and repulsive as pus. (Having finished collecting the sutra, the following section below lists these in detail.)
The heart is a mass of flesh situated below the lungs; the lungs act as a floral canopy, enshrouding the heart.
The liver and gallbladder lie adjacent to one another, while the spleen grinds the food. The kidneys connect to the navel, and the *mìnmén* (gate of life) communicates with the stomach.
There are two abdomens, large and small, with the ribs dividing both sides and connecting upward to the chest.

The eyes, ears, mouth, and nose serve as gateways; the fingers and palms of the hands each perform distinct functions (the fingers carry out tasks, while the feet are able to walk; thus they possess distinct merits).

The tongue and throat connect the interior and exterior, while the ankles, elbows, and arms each follow one another in sequence (from above the ankles up to the left elbow and arm, reaching even to the left shoulder blade; the right side is likewise so; hence it is said that they "each follow one another").
The cheeks and shoulders are truly extraordinary; the two cheeks and both shoulders appear distinct.

At the kneecaps (the points of flexion and extension), the thighs and hips (the opening joints of the body’s two legs in the postures of sitting, standing, bending, and stretching) form the opening joints.

The crown-lock and the waist-axle penetrate from beginning to end (this refers most particularly to the entire body extending straight down from above; hence it is said they "penetrate from beginning to end").
The vertebrae and spinal processes form the pillar of the body (supporting the body, hence called the "body-pillar");
the skull is the divine lid (people call the skull the "celestial spirit-lid"), resembling the azure firmament;
the three hundred and sixty-five segments of bone (as described in the *Wuzang lun*) are bound together between them by tendons and vessels to form the physical frame.
The joints of the sinews and the skin are lined with hard marrow; all together they form a semblance of shape.
Though there are many kinds of earth-snakes, they are not yet equal to water, fire, and wind.
If one says that every variety is entirely "I," then the ego-clinging of "I" becomes inexhaustible. (The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "O Bodhisattva...")

When he thus contemplates with single-minded attention: "Who is this that is 'I'? To whom does 'I' belong? Where does it abide? Is it the skin? Is it the bones? Is it the flesh?"—and when he examines each part individually and collectively, none are found to be the self.
(If the skin alone were the self, the other limbs and joints would not be; if every single part were the self, there would be multiple selves. Therefore, it is said that none are reasonable.
When the limbs are scattered in all directions, one loses the sense of where [the self] resides. Whether as a single path or many paths, [it is nowhere to be found].
Realization is not as one might expect; therefore, it is said that "one loses what one followed.

Having analyzed and refuted the elements of earth, self, and person, from now on I dare no longer deceive or delude myself (this is because the principle of self-awakening is eternally free of fixed attachments).
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the large and small excretions all return to water.
VIII. Three: Examining Only Water; Next, Examining the Element of Water to Refute the Self.
Still fearing that residual doubts have not been dispelled, one examines the nature of water:
The nature of water is entirely nothing but moisture; Throughout the body, names are assigned differently according to location.
Tears, saliva, nasal mucus, spittle, and froth; phlegm in the chest, bodily filth, and the essence and blood of the kidneys flowing through the channels;
the excretions of stool and urine—these are most abundant and overflowing.
If you take such things as "self" and "other," listen briefly as I examine two matters for you.

If one calls urine "the person" (if this were so, the person would be exhausted bit by bit), and if one regards saliva as "the self" (if this were so, one would be spitting out the self every day), then the evident principle becomes increasingly difficult to establish.
Since both urine and saliva consist of water and fire, if these are called the self, how do they differ from other fluids such as tears, mucus, and spittle?
Heat belongs to fire; movement belongs to wind. Ninth: A brief analysis of wind and fire.
The two serpents of wind and fire have not yet been distinguished; one must further investigate them to ensure impartiality.

(Earth and water have many attendants, so when people seek [the truth], they all say these are not "I. Wind and fire are easily subdued; if one does not contemplate this, I fear one will unfairly single out these two heads.

Therefore, I briefly investigate. Fire is characterized only by warmth, and wind only by movement; the transgressions committed by these two against people are the lightest. (People do not cling to them much.)
Therefore, it follows that [heat] is light. (Next, regarding heat: The nature of warmth is entirely identical to external fire;
the movement of form is no different from the movement of external wind-forms. (If wind can move trees, why does the moving form not manifest in the body?
Since there is no distinct principle for warmth and movement, by analogy with what precedes, it is clearly evident that [the self] is not the self.
Investigating words through the gate of contemplation, one examines the four great elements;
having thoroughly researched the principles until they are fully realized, the assembly sits for a long time and grows weary. To reach a definitive judgment, one must leave room for what follows.
[Recite] "Namo to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One" (and so forth) (Twelve Prostrations).
I repent with a sincere heart.
As for the karmic obstructions of the offenses being repented, they arise in succession from beginning to end; in total, there are four layers.

These are fundamental ignorance, along with the obstructions of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstructions of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and the obstructions of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). The ignorance, delusions, and karma of these have already been repented and eliminated. Next...

One should perform repentance. Regarding those who have yet to experience the retribution for karmic obstructions—those who, throughout many kalpas, have created karma that has accumulated within the *ālaya-vijñāna* and whose seeds of karma have been perfected through the habitual perfuming of ignorance and craving, such that they are destined to undergo karmic retribution upon seeking birth in this life—one should repent today so that the retribution need not be experienced.
As it is said in the sutras: "When the time for karmic retribution arrives, there is no place where one can escape it—not in the void, nor in the midst of the ocean."
It is not by entering among mountain rocks that one finds a place where one may escape and avoid receiving retribution; only through the power of repentance can it be eliminated.
How is this known? When the five signs of decline appeared for the Devaputra Sunirmita in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, his heart was filled with intense fear.
He took refuge in and exhorted himself toward the Triple Gem, and the five signs immediately vanished, allowing him to prolong his celestial lifespan. Such are the cases.
As clarified by the various scriptures and teachings, such instances are not limited to one; thus we know that repentance truly can extinguish calamity.
However, if ordinary people do not encounter the guidance of virtuous friends, there is no evil they will not commit.
Consequently, when their lives are about to end and they face the final moment, the terrifying manifestations of hell appear before them. At that time, remorse and fear assail them simultaneously.

Failing to cultivate goodness beforehand, one only regrets when facing the ultimate end. What can be achieved by regretting later? Calamities and misfortunes await in another place, prepared in advance;
one must enter alone and travel far to hell, where one can only proceed forward into the fiery cauldrons.
Body and mind are shattered; the spirit suffers in agony. At such a time, if one wishes to seek even a single prostration or a single confession, how could it ever be obtained later?
Do not rely on your own youth, wealth, power, or influence, nor indulge in indolence, laziness, negligence, or self-indulgence.
Once the enemy arrives, there is no distinction made between old and young, poor and rich, noble and humble—all shall be ground to dust and vanish in an instant.
Arrive there without letting anyone know. A person’s life is as impermanent as the morning dew; though the outgoing breath remains, the incoming breath is difficult to preserve.

Why dwell upon this without repentance? Once the five celestial messengers suddenly arrive and the executioner of impermanence comes abruptly, even those in the prime of youth and vigor cannot escape. At such a time, what use are magnificent halls and deep chambers?
It has nothing to do with me. How could high carriages and great horses follow me of their own accord?
My wife, children, and kinsmen are no longer my kin. These ornaments of the seven treasures appear for others. Speaking thus, the retributions of the world are all illusory transformations.

Though the heavens are pleasant, they ultimately end in decay and ruin. When life is exhausted and the soul departs, one falls into the three miserable realms. Therefore, the Buddha’s words must be heeded.
Bhadra said, "Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra possessed sharp faculties and great intelligence; he was able to subdue his afflictions and reach the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Yet, when his life ended, he was reborn as a flying cat within the realm of animals—how much more so would this be true for others?"
Therefore, know that from those who have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood and below, all must undergo transmigration; by stealing the sutras, one may fall into evil realms.

If one is not careful, suddenly one day one will personally encounter such a fate, and by then it will be too late for regret. Consider, for instance, people today who are suddenly struck by punishment.
To go to the gates of officialdom and be subjected to shackles and imprisonment is but a minor suffering;

yet it causes one to be terrified, anxious, and preoccupied, seeking salvation through hundreds of means. Compared to this, the manifold sufferings of the hells are hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater, beyond all analogy.
Since beginningless kalpas, you have all together accumulated sins as vast as Mount Sumeru; how can you hear this and remain so calm?
To neither be startled nor terrified, only to cause this spirit to again suffer such affliction—this is truly pitiable.

Therefore, we, the disciples [Name] and others, today awaken to this truth and most earnestly prostrate ourselves in repentance for all karmic obstructions from beginningless time until this very day.
Now, regarding the karma we have created, since the two assemblies of monastics and laity share both differences and similarities, at the time when retribution is received...
It is likewise so. There are aspects of the hells that are common to both monastics and laypeople, as well as those that differ between them.
Regarding the manner of suffering, there are features distinct from those experienced by laypeople; for now, we shall first repent for these common characteristics.

As for the retributions received—whether by monastics or laypeople—the most severe is, first and foremost, the Avīci Hell, as clarified in the sutras. We shall now briefly describe its characteristics.
This hell is surrounded on all sides by seven layers of iron walls. Furthermore, there are seven layers of iron nets that cover it from above and below.
There are seven layers of razor-edged tiles and immeasurable fierce fires, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. The bodies of the sinners fill its entirety;
due to the conditions of their karmic offenses, they do not obstruct one another, as the fire from above penetrates to the bottom and the fire from the bottom penetrates upward.
Above, below, east, west, south, and north, it penetrates and interweaves everywhere. Like a fish on a griddle, its fat and marrow are completely consumed;
the suffering of sin within this place is likewise so. At the four gates of that city are four great copper dogs. These dogs are four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth;
their fangs and claws are sharp as blades, and their eyes flash like lightning. Furthermore, there are immeasurable iron-beaked birds that spread their wings and strike.
Soaring up, they devour the flesh of the sinners. These ox-headed hell-wardens have forms like rākṣasas and possess nine tails;
their tails are made of iron. Furthermore, they have eight heads, each head bearing eight corners and sixty-four eyes.
From every single eye, glowing red-hot irons protrude, each one burning the flesh of the sinners. Moreover, with every flash of wrath and every outburst of rage, they let out a thunderous roar.

At that time, a sound like a thunderclap resounded. Furthermore, immeasurable wheels of natural power descended from the sky, entering through the crowns of the sinners' heads and exiting through their feet.
Thereupon, the sinners experienced pain piercing to the very marrow of their bones and agony cutting into their livers and hearts.
Thus they passed through immeasurable years, unable to seek birth and unable to seek death. Such karmic retributions as these are all to be repented.
I repent.
Next, I shall repent for the retributive offenses of the remaining hells: the falling off of head and body upon the mountains of knives and trees of swords;
I repent for the retributive offenses of being burned and boiled in the hell of iron cauldrons and glowing coals; I repent for the hell of the iron bed and the copper pillar.

I repent for the retribution of being scorched to cinders; I repent for the retribution of the agony of being split open by the wheel-blades and fiery ground of the Sūcī-mukha (Needle-mouth) and Kṣuramārga (Razor-path) hells;
I repent for the retribution of the excruciating pain of having one’s tongue plucked out and tilled with a plow in the hell of the Plowed Tongue;

I repent for the retribution of the five types of flesh being consumed and the molten copper poured into the mouth in the hell of Iron Nails and Boiling Copper; I repent for the reduction of my bones and flesh to dust and powder in the hell of the Iron Hammer and Iron Mill.
Repentance for the retribution of the Black Rope and Iron Net Hells, where the limbs and joints are severed;

Repentance for the retribution of the Ash River and Boiling Excrement Hells, where there is total distress; Repentance for the retribution of the Cold Water Hell, where the skin and flesh crack open and one is left naked;
Repentance for the retribution of the Tigris, Wolves, Hawks, and Dogs Hell, where beings prey upon and harm one another.
Repent of the retribution for the crimes of mutual grappling, seizing, hacking, and stabbing in the Hell of Weapons and Blades;

Repent of the retribution for the crimes of being roasted and broiled in the Hell of the Fire Pit; Repent of the retribution for the crimes of having one’s physical frame shattered by the clashing of two rocks in the Hell of the Crushing Stones;
Repent of the retribution for the crimes of being dismembered upon release in the Samghāta (Assembly) and Kālakaṇṇa (Black-Ear) Hells; Repent of the darkness [of ignorance].

Repentance for the retribution of being hacked and minced in the Míng-jiù Shān (Dark Meat Mountain) Hell; Repentance for the retribution of being dismembered and having the body nailed down in the Jùjiě Dìngshēn (Saw-Splitting and Nailing the Body) Hell;
Repentance for the retribution of being butchered and sliced while suspended upside down with iron clubs in the Tiěbàng Dàoxuán (Iron Club Upside-Down Suspension) Hell;

Repentance for the retribution of grievous resentment in the Jiāorè Jiàohuàn (Scorching Heat and Wailing) Hell; Repentance for the long night of darkness within the Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains.
I repent for the karmic retribution of not recognizing the three luminaries in the darkness, and for the karmic retribution of the Āpāpa Hell,
the Āvīci Hell, the Aṭaṭa Hell, and the Alala Hell. Thus, within each of all the eight cold and eight hot hells,
there are further eighty-four thousand subsidiary hells that serve as their retinue.
Belonging to this realm, there are the sufferings of being roasted, boiled, and burned; the pain of having one’s skin flayed, flesh torn away, bones scraped, and marrow beaten;

and the agony of having one’s intestines pulled out and lungs extracted—immeasurable sufferings that cannot be heard and cannot be described. *Namo Buddha*. Those who are here within this realm today...
These have been our parents throughout countless lifetimes since beginningless time, as well as all our kinsmen and associates.
After we have passed away together, we may fall into such a hell as this.

Today, with hearts purified to the utmost, we prostrate ourselves with our heads to the ground before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, entreating their compassion and repenting so that all these retributions may be extinguished.

Obstructions are now completely extinguished. Having finished repenting for the retributions of hell, we shall now, furthermore, repent for the three kinds of evil retributions: those of animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.

In the sutras, the Buddha said that because those with great desire seek many profits, their suffering and affliction are also many; whereas those who know contentment are free from [the burden of] lying down...

Such is the contemplation of the blue color; the yellow, white, and pigeon-colored [bones] are likewise so. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva performs this contemplation.

At that time, from between his eyebrows, there issued forth rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of a pigeon. Within each of these individual rays of light, the Bodhisattva saw the image of a Buddha. Having seen them, he immediately asked: "This body is composed through the combination of impure causes and conditions;

how is it able to sit, rise, walk, stand, bend, stretch, look up or down, gaze, breathe, weep, rejoice, or laugh? There is no master within this; who causes it to be so? Having asked this, the Buddhas within the rays suddenly vanished. He further thought:

"Perhaps consciousness is the self, and for that reason the Buddhas do not speak to me. He then observed that this consciousness arises and ceases in succession like a flowing stream, and thus it too is not the self. He further thought: "If consciousness is not the self... [The text continues with the emergence of the light.]

Regarding the inhalation and exhalation, one might think, "Perhaps this is the self. Then one further reflects: "These inhalations and exhalations are simply the nature of wind; this nature of wind is itself the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Among these four great elements, which is the self? The nature of earth is not the self;

the natures of water, fire, and wind are likewise not the self. Then one further reflects: "This entire body is entirely devoid of a self; it is merely a manifestation of various activities through the harmonious conjunction of mental consciousness and its conditions.

It is like that which is produced by the power of incantations or magical illusions, or like a lute that produces sound according to the will [of the player]. This body of mine is thus impure, having been formed through the temporary conjunction of various causes and conditions. In what place could craving arise for this? And if it is reviled, in what place could anger arise?"

Anger! Yet this body of mine consists of thirty-six impure and foul substances; where, then, could there be one who receives abuse? If I hear such abuse, I should immediately reflect: "By what sound am I being abused? Since no single sound can abuse me, neither can many sounds together.

For this reason, one should not give rise to anger. If another comes to strike me, I should likewise reflect: "From what does such a striker arise? Then I should further think: "It is called 'striking' because of the hands, the weapons, and my own body.

For what reason should I pointlessly direct my anger toward another? It is my own body that has invited this fault, for I have received these five aggregates. It is like how, because of a target, an arrow strikes it. I...

The body is likewise. When there is a body, there is striking. If I do not practice forbearance, my mind will become distracted. If the mind is distracted, right mindfulness is lost. If right mindfulness is lost, one cannot contemplate the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. If one cannot contemplate the meaning of what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, one practices unwholesome dharmas.

Through the causal conditions of unwholesome dharmas, one falls into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. When the Bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he attains the four foundations of mindfulness. Having attained the four foundations of mindfulness, he abides in the stage of endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he is able to endure lust and anger; furthermore, he can endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice; violent winds, harsh tactile sensations, various epidemics, abusive speech, reviling, beating, and the physical and mental afflictions of pain—all these he is able to endure.
This is called dwelling in the Stage of Endurance (Kṣānti-bhūmi).

Now, for the sake of beginners, since this doctrinal principle has not yet been fully unfolded, and because one wishes to obstruct the fault of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), it must first be clarified from where these phenomena arise.
All sentient beings possess the nature of the true mind; however, due to delusion, ignorance arises within that nature.
The harmonious union is named the *ālaya*-consciousness; This consciousness can transform objects into three layers of sensory dust.
Dust depends on deluded thought, yet dust does not exist; Deluded thought depends on the body, yet thought is empty.
The body relies upon the *ālaya*; how could the body be real? The *ālaya* relies upon the nature; in itself, it is fused and dissolved.
This is the natural course of causes and conditions: When arising, there is no trace; when ceasing, nothing remains.

Like the wealth and nobility, or the poverty and lowliness, within a dream, Or like the vermilion and crimson in a mirror’s reflection— The deluded and ignorant, crawling about, eternally reckon things as real;

Although the luminous, fundamental awakening is capable of illumination, its wondrous function covers all manifold differences;
yet, since it obstructs the omniscience of bodhi, one knows that the sin of clinging to phenomena is difficult to forgive.
Simply look at the subsequent verse which clarifies that this is not an illusion; the analogy of drawing a mirror and polishing away dust is exactly the same.
The preceding section concludes the refutation of attachments through both the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Below this, the thirteenth [section] shall clarify the principle:
"Because illusion is extinguished by extinction, that which is not illusion does not perish. It is like polishing a mirror: when the defilements are exhausted, the clarity appears."
All illusions originally arise based on true nature; when they arise, true nature is obscured and clouded.

As all illusions subsequently perish as before, true nature is thereby opened and unobstructed, causing the dust to vanish so that the mirror shines with brilliant clarity, and the clouds parting, the moon in the sky becomes luminously radiant.
That which does not arise dependent on conditions is called non-illusory; that which arises by relying on manifold conditions is the illusory form.

With a sincere heart,

Śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and others, reflect upon themselves: "By the retribution of our meager virtues, we have been born among humans;
within the Semblance Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, we have left the household life to study the Path. Yet we are unable to glorify the Sun of the Buddha, benefiting neither ourselves nor others.

Lacking cultivation in meditation and wisdom, we have wasted the offerings of the faithful in vain. Possessing neither precepts nor virtue, we are self-conceited and arrogant, [failing to attain] liberation."

They often fall short in their observance. Or, as with the *śrāmaṇera* and *śrāmaṇerī*, they violate the ten precepts. As...

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, whether acting as a scholar-monk studying and lecturing on commentaries and treatises, or...

Today, with utmost sincerity, we all repent.

They feel neither shame nor remorse, being addicted to worldly dust and devoid of conscience or integrity. Though they wear the dharma-robes, how are they different from the common laity?
Such śramaṇas commit two kinds of offenses: first, as disciples of the Buddha, they turn their backs on the Buddha’s disciplinary code.

By these causes and conditions, one shall fall into hell and encounter the suffering of iron horses, or mount the carriage of an iron ox, or ride an iron donkey, constantly being kicked and trampled.
For hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of kalpas, undergoing death and rebirth again and again—all this results from practicing hypocrisy and deception.
The vestments and insignia of those who cultivate the Path are not produced by worldly means; they are used through the faithful offerings of those with profound respect.
Therefore, a sutra says: "At that time, the flowers of the Bodhi tree suddenly fell. Bodhiruci addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, why have all the flowers of the Bodhi tree fallen?

"I am confused. I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me, so that the doubts of this great assembly of seated Bodhisattvas may all be removed.

"Regarding the Nose Hell," the Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! You may go now; you shall be permitted to see it.

One immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without relying on a teacher;

in the Sudden Teaching, delusion lasts for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, while awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa—how could it require delay? The Perfect Teaching says that birth is fundamentally Buddha:
what can the six realms, which are like flowers in the sky, do? Such are the six types of meanings regarding slowness and swiftness.

Excellent. This differs from the Buddha-body. In the holy lands of the West, the sages and worthies discuss the definition [of valid cognition] such that all three criteria are complete as a constant rule:

(1) when the principle is clearly explained, it is called *anumāna* (inference); (2) when citing the words of the Buddha, it is called *āptāgama* (authoritative testimony); (3) when seeing for oneself, it is called *pratyakṣa* (direct perception).
In establishing the teachings and citing the scriptures, only these two criteria are employed.
If direct perception were thus undermined, how could one dare to doubt the words of the Buddhas?

The *Sutra on the Names of Buddhas for Sincere Repentance* states: The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Good sons and good daughters,
those who wish to repent all karmic obstructions so that their roots are forever extinguished must first direct their minds with the desire to fulfill all [virtues]."
Pāramitās. Desiring to achieve unexcelled bodhi and desiring to fulfill all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, one should form this thought:

"I shall study the great renunciation practiced by the bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, breaking my bones and extracting my heart to give it to sentient beings, just as the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya and the Bodhisattva King of Kāśi did when they gave away their wives."
Sons, you should practice giving to the poor and destitute, just as the non-regressive Bodhisattvas, King Aśoka, the Bodhisattva Sudāna, King Śobha, and other Bodhisattvas did.
You should enter the hells to rescue suffering sentient beings, just as the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika and the Devaputra Sunetra did.
You should equally rescue sentient beings who commit evil deeds, just as the Bodhisattva Sukṛtī and Vijaya did.
Bodhisattvas such as Cāritramati gave away their jeweled celestial crowns and even flayed their scalps to bestow them [upon others].
Bodhisattvas such as Uttaramantrī and the Devaputra Ratnaśikhin gave away their eyes as alms.
Bodhisattvas such as Maitreya, Nandivardhana, and King Candraprabha gave away their ears and noses to various beggars. As did Aśoka...
Bodhisattvas such as Śreṣṭha-caryā-rāja Bodhisattva gave their teeth as alms to all sentient beings;
like Puṣpadanta-rāja Bodhisattva and the Six-Tusked Elephant King Bodhisattva, they gave their tongues as offerings;
like Avaivartika Bodhisattva and Sumukha-rāja Bodhisattva, they gave their hands and feet as alms; and like Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Aśoka-rāja, and Dṛḍhamati-rāja Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattvas such as Huashen (Destroyer-of-the-Body) who gave blood from his own body to sentient beings;
Bodhisattvas such as Ruyefa (Dharma-Action), King Shanyì (Good Intention), and the Devaputra Yuesi (Moon-Thought) who gave their flesh and marrow;

Bodhisattvas such as Anyin (Peaceful), Raoyì (Beneficial), and King Yiqieshi (All-Giver) who gave their large intestines, small intestines, liver, lungs, spleen, and kidneys; and Bodhisattvas such as Shanshi (Good Giver) who subdued... [the text continues].
The Bodhisattva Māveśvara and the Bodhisattvas such as Svayamapagatāpāyarāja offered all their bodily members, both large and small;
the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara and the Bodhisattvas such as the Devaputra Jyotiṣprabha offered their skin;
the Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha and the Bodhisattvas such as the Golden-Flank Deer King offered their level toes, just like Dṛḍhavīrya.
The Bodhisattva Jin (Progressive), the Bodhisattvas such as King Sovereign of Jambudvīpa, the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible-like who gave away his flesh-and-nail fingernails,
the Bodhisattvas such as the Devaputra Seeking the Good Dharma, and the Bodhisattva Without Regret or Weariness who gave these alms to beggars,
as well as the Bodhisattva Unobstructed King who gave his body to feed a tiger, like the Prince Mahāsattva.
Bodhisattvas break their bones to extract the marrow as an offering to the *prajñāpāramitā*, like the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita;
they weigh their own bodies to ransom a dove and act as servants for impoverished sentient beings, like the Bodhisattva King Śibi;
they sacrifice their bodies to feed five rākṣasas, like the Bodhisattva King Maitrībala; and they relinquish the four continents, the great earth, and all its adornments.

Just as when the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta and the Bodhisattvas such as the Devaputra Candravimalaśrī and others sought to receive the Dharma, they conceived the thought that it was difficult to encounter;

when someone said to them, "If you can cast yourself into a fire-pit seven fathoms deep, I shall bestow the Dharma upon you," the Bodhisattvas, having heard this, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, reflecting: "For the sake of the Dharma, I should even endure for a long time..."
They dwell even in the Avīci Hell; how much more so when they have merely entered a fire-pit among humans! How marvelous is the True Dharma—how exceedingly easy it is to obtain!

Just tell me: for the sake of entering a fire-pit, like the Bodhisattva Seeking the Good Dharma or the Bodhisattva Vajracintin when they occupied the royal throne seeking the True Dharma, even for the sake of a single phrase, a single word, or the meaning of a single sentence.
They conceive the thought that [human] birth is difficult to obtain; they are able to completely renounce everything within the seas, whether near or far:
kingdoms and cities, people and treasuries, gardens, ponds, houses and dwellings, groves, flowers, and fruits—even down to all manner of rare and wonderful objects.
They are able to renounce palaces, towers, wives, children, kinsmen, and even their royal thrones;
seeking the enduring Dharma within that which is non-enduring, they diligently seek the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
I have brought to ultimate purity the path of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-mārga*), just as the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Jayasthāmagarbha, and all other Bodhisattvas have done. Śāriputra, to speak briefly,
I have likewise fully accomplished all the *pāramitā* practices of all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, desiring to achieve [the state] such as...

Because this is the practice, one must constantly repent for all karmic obstructions from time immemorial. When wishing to repent, one should first understand the causes and conditions that gave rise to those sinful karmas;
only then, by directing the mind with sincere and profound earnestness to wash them away, can they be extinguished.
Regarding the causes and conditions of transgression: it is truly because one fails to properly guard the six sense faculties that the three outflows arise.

As these outflows and karmic actions continue in succession, one extensively commits errors and violations; all of this takes solitary ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) as the seed of affliction. We shall now first repent of this solitary ignorance.
Since beginningless time, throughout the worlds, we have received bodies and passed through immeasurable eons, one by one...
Throughout the kalpas, they have assumed various bodies; within each body, they have committed all manner of evil karmas, as numerous as the atoms of the world-system.
Each individual evil karma brings about a retribution as vast as the sands of the Ganges, and within each such retribution, they undergo immeasurable suffering. Such are their sufferings.
All these are caused by ignorance as their karma-seeds. One should now take the sun of bodhicitta to illuminate that ignorance;
when ignorance is thus enlightened, it becomes clarity. This is repentance. Since ignorance is no more, all myriad delusions are utterly exhausted.

As for the karmic offenses arising from the prior cause of ignorance, which cannot be fully remembered or known, I today sincerely disclose and repent them. May they all be extinguished. (The Upper Repentance)

Fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is that which all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) universally possess; it is innate and spontaneous, not derived from teachers or schools. What follows is the specific confession of wrong views arising from discrimination, which likewise belongs to the category of ignorance.
Furthermore, from beginningless kalpas until this very day, we have been defiled by delusions and false views, entering the doctrines of external paths.

Lost in false imaginings, we have practiced perverted teachings, following from such concepts as the obscure principle (*tattva*), the nature of the world (*loka-prakṛti*), and subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Clinging to a self that is spontaneous, pervasive, and sovereign throughout space, we have received false teachings and slandered the Buddha’s school. The six heretical masters have confounded the spirit, and the four inversions have led us into delusion.

I see that this sin is grave, as it eternally extinguishes the roots of goodness. I vow that in every future life I shall further study and practice, whether among the assembly of Śrāvakas or otherwise, and not practice the Mahāyāna.
[To hold such views as] "the fruit does not arise from the cause" or "the cause does not induce the fruit"—such views are immeasurable and boundless.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all. (The following is the repentance for the three poisons.)
Furthermore, since beginningless time, one has acted at will with the three poisons. The fires of greed, hatred, and delusion blaze day and night;

as they encounter objects and touch the mind, they incinerate the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Greed arises toward attractive forms, hatred arises toward unattractive forms, and delusion arises toward that which is neutral.
Seeking them out everywhere, there is not a moment’s respite. Or, at times...
Greed, hatred, and delusion arise from the objects of the five desires; or greed, hatred, and delusion arise through the conditions of the three types of sensation;
or greed, hatred, and delusion arise from wholesome dharmas; or greed, hatred, and delusion arise regarding unwholesome dharmas.

Due to these three states of mind, views and pride increase, becoming deeper than the great ocean and heavier than a mountain range. They cannot be fully described; they cannot be fully recounted. Now...
I daily feel shame and remorse, confessing my transgressions with a sincere heart; may they all be extinguished.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, I have indulged in the seven types of pride, which arise based on three categories of persons and the qualities of my own self.
That is to say, relying upon my own aggregates (*skandha*), I give rise to the conceit of "I am," exalting myself by relying on my own status.

(There are seven types of conceit (*māna*). The sequence differs from that in other treatises; in those treatises, the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) is placed fourth, but here it is placed first because it serves as the root of all others.
Because of the conception of a self, one gives rise to conceit toward those who are inferior. That is to say: regarding those who are inferior to oneself, one considers oneself superior;

regarding those who are equal to oneself, one considers oneself equal. Even when one is merely within their own rank, there is still a mind of conceit. Furthermore, [this applies] toward those of middling quality...
A person of superior grade gives rise to *abhimāna* (conceit). This means that toward those who are equal to oneself, one reckons oneself as superior;

and toward those who are superior to oneself, one reckons oneself as equal. Because this conceit exceeds the former, it is called *abhimāna*. Furthermore, such a person gives rise to *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit) toward those of superior grade.

This means that toward those who are superior to oneself, one reckons oneself as even more superior than them. Because this exceeds the former by a multiple, it is called *mānātimāna*. Furthermore, toward those of superior grade...

A person gives rise to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*). This refers to regarding oneself as only slightly inferior to those who are for the most part superior to oneself (the first four [types] arise from three grades of persons).
Furthermore, one gives rise to the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*) regarding qualities of excellence that have been only slightly realized;

although one has attained only a small portion, one claims to have attained much. Moreover, regarding qualities of excellence that one has not attained at all, one reckons oneself as possessing such virtues.

It arises from false pride (*mithyāmāna*)—which consists entirely of the absence of any [actual] attainment—and from overweening pride (*adhimāna*), which is the estimation of oneself as superior when one is merely equal; both of these arise from [the perception of] superior qualities.

Furthermore, through the mutual interweaving of the three types of pride previously mentioned—namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)—nine further types of pride are formed (these nine appear in the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*;
their textual basis is not found in the Mahāyāna). These are: estimating oneself as superior to those who are equal (*atimāna*); and estimating oneself as equal to those who are equal (*māna*).

To consider oneself inferior to one who is superior (*ūnamāna*); to consider oneself superior to one who is superior (*adhimāna*); to consider oneself equal to one who is equal (*māna*); to consider oneself inferior to one who is equal (*atimāna*);
to consider oneself not superior to one who is equal (*māna*); to consider oneself not equal to one who is equal (*atimāna*); and to consider oneself not inferior to one who is superior (*ūnamāna*).
Through these various types of conceit, one relies on oneself to despise others, giving rise to what are called faults and evils regarding those possessing superior qualities and dharmas.
Those who possess virtue but whose minds are not humble, who do not associate with virtuous friends, and who do not hear the sublime Dharma, obstruct the Path of the Sages.
Because of this, they transmigrate through birth and death without end, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction. Today, having attained awakening, I repent for all of these things.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, I have constantly harbored doubts; upon hearing various principles and phenomena, I was hesitant and indecisive regarding the Buddha.

Regarding the true virtues and capabilities of the Dharma and Sangha Jewels, one is unable to accept them; one cannot deeply endure or take delight in them. Because of this lack of endurance, one is obstructed from the True Dharma.

Upon hearing it taught that virtuous causes lead to pleasant fruits and evil causes lead to bitter fruits—even up to the meditative concentrations, liberations, and the various *pāramitās*—one harbors doubts and perplexity throughout.
Although one does not slander them, one is unable to resolve them through patient acceptance. Due to this hesitation, [the obstacle arises].
They ultimately do not enter [the path], remaining long submerged in birth and death with no prospect of escape.
Or, though they may turn their hearts toward the Triple Gem and believe in dependent origination, they still harbor various doubts regarding the teachings they follow and the masters they serve.

They may doubt that the teachings are not definitive and that practicing them is a wasteful expenditure of effort; or they may doubt that the master’s explanations are unclear and deviate from the true meaning; or they may doubt...
Although my teacher is clearly enlightened, he has no means to deliver me. My mind may well harbor doubts, thinking: "I am of dull faculties;
even if I practice, it will ultimately yield no benefit. Like encountering a forked road where one is uncertain whether to go left or right, in the mere blink of an eye, how can one advance?

Even if one were to take a step forward, once the two rats have shifted their grip, how could one reach the destination ahead? To fail in one's commitments and lose what was sought is the greatest loss of all.

This is the mind of doubt. To cultivate and realize while harboring doubt is likewise so. One should know that among all obstacles to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the mind of doubt is the most severe.
Once the power of concentration is lost, one willingly enters the path of subsequent karma, and many seeds of karma are produced. Good and evil become difficult to discern;

whether one is among ghosts, in hell, or among humans or devas, one knows not which path to take. Thus, with such hesitation, for immeasurable and boundless kalpas, one has been deluded and distracted.
Having now awakened to this meaning, I have formed a resolute mind. All the various doubts and afflictions mentioned above are hereby confessed.
Having already confessed the independent ignorance, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and hesitation, [I confess] because of these afflictions...
The evil karma we have produced has not yet been fully disclosed; now, with this sincere devotion, we repent in verse:
We, as lords dwelling in an age of five corruptions, Have committed various evil deeds, our sins boundless.
In killing, we were ignorant of the suffering of others; In lust, theft, and delusion, we took pleasure in what met our eyes.
False speech and frivolous talk are full of deception; Divisive words and harsh speech destroy the virtuous and noble.
The mental karma constantly cultivates greed, delusion, and anger; Failing to contemplate the wholesome conditions of good friends, Today I sincerely take refuge and repent.
May the sins of the three karmas be extinguished and the pure mind be firm.
Respectfully holding incense and flowers, I make offerings to the Buddha; repenting, we together return to the source of purity.
Having finished repentance, with a sincere heart I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
With a sincere heart, I make this vow:
May we, by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of ignorance and the three poisons, always encounter enlightened teachers throughout every life,
always hear the True Dharma, awaken in every birth, remain undeluded in every lifetime, and be free from greed, hatred, and delusion, fully possessing precepts,
concentration, and wisdom. Furthermore, may we, by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of pride and doubt, be humble in every life and every age.
Be humble and yielding; draw near to superior persons, whether they be noble or ordinary, and show them all respect. Regarding the Dharma you have heard, resolve its meaning until there is no doubt;
regarding the authentic teachings you encounter, attain decisive faith. Deeply endure and aspire to the true virtues and supreme capabilities of the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, by means of the merit produced from repenting the ten evil deeds and other transgressions, may I, in birth after birth and life after life, [attain these qualities].
The *dānapāramitā* serves as the cause for merit; the *śīlapāramitā* serves as the cause for freedom from defilement;
the *kṣāntipāramitā* serves as the cause for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); the *vīryapāramitā* serves as the cause for application (*prayoga*);
the *dhyānapāramitā* serves as the cause for realization and entry; and the *prajñāpāramitā* serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood—thus they are complete in three ways.

Having attained liberation, the fivefold Dharma-body, the accomplishment of the four wisdoms, and the perfection of the ten powers, one then employs great compassion and skillful means to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
Through the wisdom of wondrous observation, one preaches the Dharma according to their needs, so that those in the three realms of humans and devas may all realize nirvana without remainder.
Ordinary beings and sages dwell therein for a long time, together entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Having made this vow, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Addressing the assembly, listen as I recite the verses on impermanence from the sutras:
In all worlds, All who are born must return to death; Though one’s lifespan may be immeasurable, [It shall eventually come to an end.]
That which must necessarily come to an end, And that which in its fullness must inevitably decline;
Where there is meeting, there must be parting; The prime of youth does not linger long. There is no phenomenon that is permanent.
Thus, realizing impermanence, Be cautious and do not be heedless. Heedfulness is immortality.
Heedlessness is the path to death; heedfulness is supreme.
For the sake of the celestial kings, [know that] heedlessness is the root of birth and death, while vigilance is the excellent path.
Therefore, abandon heedlessness and you shall always experience happiness. (The above is from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, fascicle 30.)
Part Eleven (Upper): [Prostrating to the Fifty-three Buddhas; Self-Description of Repentance, Entreaty, Rejoicing, Dedication, and Aspiration] Praising the Buddha:

I now take refuge in all the Sugatas. I prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, oceans of virtue, who shine upon the ten directions like great mountains of gold. May you, out of compassion, graciously accept me.
Your physical form is golden light, pure and stainless; Your eyes are like clear, deep-blue lapis lazuli.
O Honored One of auspicious majesty and renown, The sun of great compassion and wisdom dispels all darkness.
The radiance of the Buddha-sun is ever-pervasive, Exceedingly pure, stainless, and free from all dust.
The Moon of the Muni shines with supreme coolness, Able to dispel the fever of afflictions in sentient beings.
Adorned throughout by the thirty-two marks, And fully perfected in the eighty secondary characteristics, His merit is inconceivable and peerless;
Like the flowing light of the sun, he illuminates the world.
As the volume of the great ocean is difficult to know, As the atoms of heaven and earth cannot be counted,
As Mount Sumeru is beyond measure, And as space has no boundaries—
So too are the merits of the Buddhas, Which all sentient beings cannot know.
Having contemplated with earnest thought for immeasurable eons, there is none who can know the shore of your ocean of virtue.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One who enters the Treasury of Great Radiance through supernormal powers, manifesting all pure lands to respond to the capacities of beings.
I take refuge in my own Original Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.

Homage to the Great Radiant Treasury within the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta Sūtra; to all Buddhas who abide in the ground of enlightenment for sentient beings, adorned with light and maintaining their vows;
and to the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas who, with bodies interpenetrating and speech unimpeded, together proclaim the Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta Sūtra.
Homage to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
who possess great compassion and have made great vows to protect the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* until the end of the future;
homage to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, who manifests his entire body through hundreds of billions of transformation bodies to respond to the capacities and conditions of beings in the Sahā world with great kindness and great compassion.
Homage to the Tathāgata Universal Radiance, the fifty-three Buddhas, and all other Buddhas.
Homage to the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa. Homage to the Buddha Samantajñāna.
Homage to the Buddha Samantaśuddha. Homage to the Buddha Tamālapatracandanagandha.
Homage to the Buddha Candanaprabha. Homage to the Buddha Maṇidhvaja.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnakūṭābhigarbharatna.
Homage to the Buddha Sarvalokābhirucitadarśana-mahāparākrama.
Homage to the Buddha Maṇidhvajapradīpa. Homage to the Buddha Prajñāpradīpāvabhāsa.
Homage to the Buddha Ocean of Virtue Radiant Light.
Homage to the Buddha Vajra Firmness Universally Scattering Golden Light.
Homage to the Buddha Great Powerful Vigor and Valor. Homage to the Buddha Great Compassionate Light.
Homage to the Buddha King of Compassionate Power. Homage to the Buddha Treasury of Compassion.
Homage to the Buddha Victorious Adorned with Sandalwood Caves. Homage to the Buddha Chief of the Virtuous and Good.
Homage to the Buddha of Noble Intent. Homage to the Buddha King of Vast Adornments.
Homage to the Buddha Golden Flower Radiance.
Homage to the Buddha Sovereign King of Jewel Canopies Illuminating Space.
Homage to the Buddha Empty Space Jewel Flower Radiance. Homage to the Buddha Vaidūrya Adorned King.
Homage to the Buddha Universal Manifestation of Form-Bodies and Light. Homage to the Buddha Immutable Wisdom Light.
Homage to the Buddha Subduer of All Mara Kings. Homage to the Buddha Talented Radiance.
Homage to the Buddha Supreme Wisdom. Homage to the Buddha Maitreya Light.
Homage to the Buddha World-Pure-Light.
Homage to the Buddha King of the Wondrous Honored Wisdom of the Well-Quiescent Moon-Sound.
Homage to the Buddha King of the Honored Wisdom of the Dragon-Lineage. Homage to the Buddha Sun-and-Moon-Light.
Homage to the Buddha Moon-Sun-Jewel-Radiance. Homage to the Buddha Wisdom-Banner-Victorious-King.
Homage to the Buddha Lion’s Roar Sovereign Power King. Homage to the Buddha Wondrous Sound Victorious King.
Homage to the Buddha Constant Light Banner. Homage to the Buddha Contemplator of the World Lamp.
Homage to the Buddha Prabhāsavikrāntagāmin. Homage to the Buddha Dharmavikrāmin.
Homage to the Buddha Meruprabhāsa. Homage to the Buddha Sumana-puṣpaprabhāsa.
Homage to the Buddha Udumbarapuṣpa-viśeṣarāja.
Homage to the Buddha King of Immeasurable Sound. Homage to the Buddha Wealth-Light.
Homage to the Buddha Golden Ocean Light.
Homage to the Buddha Sovereign King of Ocean-Mountain Wisdom and Supernatural Powers.
Homage to the Buddha Great Pervasive Radiance. Homage to the Buddha King Whose All Dharmas Are Ever Full.
Homage to the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha of the Twelve Supreme Vows in the Eastern World of the Full Moon.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of Forty-eight Vows in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Homage to the World-Honored Buddha Maitreya, who will descend to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven;

homage to all those whose number is as incalculable as the atoms within unspeakably many buddha-fields— those who, throughout the three periods of time and across the long and short kalpas within the entirety of the space-pervading realms of dust and atoms in the ten directions,
are lords of vast wisdom and vows, with their principal and retinues mutually interpenetrating.
Homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions who have entered parinirvāṇa throughout all the lands as numerous as the atoms within the entirety of space,
including all their transformation bodies, their relics from divided remains, and all their images, stūpas, and precious pagodas.
Homage to the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta-sūtra-nītārtha, also known as the Secret King Samādhi,
the Definitive Realm of the Tathāgata, the Self-Nature Differentiation of the Tathāgatagarbha, the Profound Dharma-Treasury of the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, who has attained the wisdom of realization through faith and understanding, born within the Assembly of Equality in the Pure Land manifested by the Honored One from the Great Treasury of Radiance in the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment.
Homage to the Pure Land manifested by the Honored One from the Great Treasury of Radiance in the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment.
In the assembly of the Middle Sovereign, there are Samantabhadra Bodhisattva of the Truth of Practice and Vows,
Namah to the Assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury,
as well as Universal Eye Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva, Vaśavartin-tejas Bodhisattva, Ghoṣadatta Bodhisattva, and Viśuddha Bodhisattva.
To the twelve principal bodhisattvas, including Bodhisattva Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, Bodhisattva Paripūrṇabodhi, and Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla,
and to the hundred thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly of the Pure Land of the Great Radiance Treasury— homage to you!
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion, with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, who manifests in various forms to save suffering sentient beings.
Homage to the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, who eternally dwells in the realm of Yāma, employing skillful means according to conditions to rescue and deliver those in the dark paths.
Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva,
Namo to all the assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas throughout the dust-mote lands within the entirety of the void realm of the three periods and the ten directions.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Sudhana, the vessel of perfect capacity and superior faculties within the final assembly of the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra;

who, within a single lifetime, perfected the bodhisattva practices by seeking the Dharma through a hundred cities, serving as the model for cultivation and realization for the sudden teaching of the final age;
and homage to all those in training and those beyond training throughout the three times, the ten directions, and all lands as vast as space.

I turn toward the Sangha of all worthy sages—the three fruits of the path, the Arhats, and the Pratyekabuddhas—and for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the beings of the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, I universally pray that they may sever the three hindrances. I take refuge and repent.

(These five gates—repentance, exhortation, sympathetic joy, dedication, and the making of vows—are all by Zongmi. In the first year of the Dahe era, from the end of the ninth month through the winter, he entered Guifeng alone; there he constructed a thatched hut as a private chamber and personally composed this.)

Regarding the traces of the mind: from the beginning until now, these have been deluded thoughts. Once the texts for repentance and vows were completed, I later realized that these writings also apply universally to the minds of all practitioners. Therefore, I have deleted portions that were biased toward my own personal affairs and polished the text so that it may be used by everyone.

With a sincere heart, I repent and contemplate that my aggregates are fundamentally empty and still; they are merely the perfectly luminous and wondrous enlightened mind, which from time immemorial has remained unaware.
In a single thought-moment, the karmic consciousness suddenly arises.
Through mindfulness, it transforms into the aspect of the perceiver; because there is a perceiver, objects appear before one.
Failing to realize that these are produced by one's own mind, one resolutely clings to them as external objects.
From this point on, they continue in constant succession from moment to moment, and through deep-seated attachment, one conceives of a self and persons.
Grasping at signs and following after names leads to views that are contradictory; greed, hatred, delusion, and pride only cause the weeds to flourish.
As one encounters objects and gives rise to emotions, various karmas are created; both good and evil depend entirely upon the tainted mind.
Marked by birth and death, one sinks into the six realms of existence; life after life, from birth to birth, one is bound by karma and suffers.
Relying on this body of suffering, one clings back to it; from clinging, attachment to pleasant and unpleasant bodies arises again.

Take to heart the shifting dynamics described above; Examine closely where the benefit truly lies.

from the beginningless past, one has been biased toward and attached to them. They are nothing other than the lustful mind—do not go beyond this.
Do not say, "I myself have committed no such act," for although the specific deeds differ, the offense is categorized as equal.

Even the royal law does not escape the net; how could the True Administrator ever allow such negligence?
All people must grasp the meaning of the preceding text: as soon as an emotion arises, one must immediately reproach oneself.
One must ensure that the root of the mind severs this thought; for a time, do not even bring Amitābha to mind.
One's own wife must not be violated through improper means; furthermore, as for other rulers who indulge in concubines and mistresses, this is merely a corruption of the Way.

A husband and wife are matched as a pair, following the patterns of Heaven and Earth and attuning with the harmony of the Yang.

Five thousand great demons constantly obstruct and intercept; they openly defy the Buddha and bring ruin to Śākyamuni’s teachings.
One should know that desire for form brings many calamities; it harms both the laity and those who have left the home life.

In ancient times, Jieyi was truly lamentable; in recent times, Lady Yang is likewise pitiable.
