Monks and nuns disregard both calamity and misfortune; they violate both the *Prātimokṣa* rules and the nature-restraining prohibitions.
In conduct, he was biased and private, lacking true virtue; his outward demeanor was a display of empty vanity.
Amidst the dust of the world, he continued the root of saṃsāra; though the secular net had collapsed, he turned toward the Buddha-dharma.
Yet, who would have thought that one in black robes would belong to the demonic and heterodox?
Those who have never revealed the Tathāgatagarbha, but merely nourish and perfume the Ālayavijñāna—such deluded interpreters shall immediately undergo excruciating severance.
They need not wait until the Aṭaṭa hell for their passions to be fully vented;
in a mere instant, they must endure suffering for billions of kalpas.
The latter portion of the verses explains this in full; one should know that these are the transgressions of craving and desire.
*Vandanā* to the Great Compassionate One (and so forth). (The following twelve prostrations are according to the previous pattern.)
Repent with a sincere heart.
Now, the method of repentance is not a minor matter. Among the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, there was none who attained the Way without relying on repentance.
This principle is taught in various Mahāyāna sūtras; for instance, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇabherī-sūtra*.
Repentance. From the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, the "Heavenly Drum Repentance.

Now, I shall briefly explain the Dharma-gate of the Golden Drum, employing the exquisite words of the Bodhisattva Subhaketu to express the earnest intentions of our assembly. First, I shall recount the origin of the Golden Drum;
subsequently, following the account of the Golden Drum’s origin as presented by that Bodhisattva, there is the dream-vision repentance found in that sutra.
The chapter states: At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, having personally heard the sublime Dharma before the Buddha, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
With single-minded concentration, he contemplated it and returned to his own abode. During the night, in a dream, he saw a great golden drum, its radiance dazzlingly brilliant.

It was like the orb of the sun. Within this light, one could see the Buddhas of the ten directions sitting upon lapis lazuli thrones beneath jeweled trees, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of assemblies as they preached the Dharma.
One also saw a brahmin striking a golden drum with a mallet, producing a great sound; from within that sound, he recited subtle and wondrous verses explaining the method of repentance.
Having heard this, Sudarśana retained it all in memory and remained there with focused mindfulness.

When dawn broke, he set out from the city of Rājagṛha surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, carrying various offerings. He proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain to the place where the World-Honored One was;
having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he arranged incense and flowers, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit to one side with palms joined in reverence.
With reverence, gazing up at the Honored Countenance, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, in a dream I saw a brāhmaṇa who took a mallet in his hand and struck a wondrous golden drum, producing a great sound. Within that sound, he recited subtle and wondrous verses explaining the Dharma of repentance;
I have memorized them all. I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow great compassion and grant me leave to speak what I have said. Thus he spoke.
Before the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
"Last night, in my dream, I saw a great golden drum;
Its form was exceedingly sublime, And it was entirely suffused with golden light, Like the orb of the blazing sun, Its radiance shining everywhere."

Light fills the worlds of the ten directions, And all behold the various Buddhas, Seated beneath jeweled trees upon individual lapis lazuli thrones, Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of countless beings in reverent attendance.
There was a brahmin who struck a celestial drum with a mallet; Within the sound of that drum, [he heard:]
When these sublime verses are spoken,
the sound emerging from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* drum reaches throughout the trichiliocosm,
able to extinguish the most grievous sins of the three miserable realms as well as all the sufferings and calamities among human beings.
By the power of the sound of this golden drum, may all afflictive obscurations be forever extinguished;
may fears be severed and beings be brought to security.
Just as when the Sovereign Muni is present, if there are sentient beings dwelling in the evil realms with their bodies entirely enveloped by the fierce flames of a great fire, [may they find relief].
If one hears this wondrous sound of the drum, one immediately leaves suffering behind and takes refuge in the Buddha.

All shall attain the wisdom of recollecting past lives and be able to remember hundreds of thousands of previous existences with perfect mindfulness before the Honored One of the Munis, having heard the Tathāgata’s most profound teaching.
By hearing the sublime and wondrous sound of the golden drum, one shall always be able to draw near to all Buddhas;
having completely abandoned all evil karma, one shall purely cultivate all categories of pure virtues.
For all sentient beings among gods and humans who pray with profound gravity and utmost sincerity—
Having heard the wondrous sound of the golden drum, it is able to cause all prayers and requests to be fulfilled.
Thus far, based on the scriptural text, the account of the causes and conditions of the Golden Drum has been completed.
Now, we shall proceed according to the Bodhisattva’s lamenting petition to the Buddha and his confession as if in a dream.
To the Two-legged Honored Ones who eternally abide throughout the worlds of the ten directions:
May you, with a heart of great compassion, take pity upon me and keep me in mind.
For those such as myself—beings without refuge and without protection— May you be able to act as a great refuge. Whatever transgressions I have now committed...
All these most grievous evil karmas, I now confess with a sincere heart Before the One of Ten Powers.
In the past, I did not believe in the Buddha, Nor did I revere my elders or kin; I failed to cultivate various virtues And constantly committed all manner of evil deeds.
Whether out of self-reliance on my own nobility, My lineage, or my wealth and status, I acted thus.
In the prime of one’s life, one acts with heedlessness, constantly creating various evil karmas;

the mind perpetually gives rise to wrong thoughts and the mouth utters evil words. Seeing no fault or transgression, one constantly creates various evil karmas and always performs the deeds of a fool.
With the heart shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, one follows along with unwholesome friends.

I have constantly committed various evil deeds, whether out of various forms of play and pleasure, or again, out of harboring grief and distress, being entangled by greed and hatred; thus I have created these evil karmas.
Although I did not delight in these manifold faults, because of the presence of fear, and because I lacked self-mastery, I have created these evil karmas.
Whether out of a restless mind, or due to anger and resentment, or because of the affliction of hunger and thirst,
I have committed evil deeds; Driven by the fires of affliction— namely food and clothing, as well as craving for women—
I have committed evil deeds against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Lacking a heart of reverence, I have committed such manifold sins; I now confess them all before the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Likewise, lacking a heart of reverence, I have committed such manifold sins;
I now confess them all. Driven by the power of ignorance, pride, greed, and hatred, I have committed these transgressions.
Having committed such manifold transgressions, I now repent them all.
Having repented, I take refuge and pay homage with a sincere heart.
Disciples, having finished the full confession of all karmic obstacles from beginningless time according to the scriptural text, we shall now...
Furthermore, based on the subsequent text of this scripture, we shall set forth our own hearts and make great vows (following the two levels of repentance and the hymn of praise to the Buddha).
By all my accumulated roots of goodness, may I swiftly attain the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One;
may I extensively proclaim the True Dharma to benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to be liberated from manifold sufferings;
may I subdue the hosts of powerful Māra armies and constantly turn the unsurpassed, wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
Abiding for inconceivable numbers of kalpas, you satisfy sentient beings with the flavor of ambrosia;
just like all the Victors of the past, you have perfected the six pāramitās,
extinguished all greed, hatred, and delusion, subdued the afflictions, and eliminated all suffering.
May I always attain the knowledge of past lives, And be able to remember hundreds of thousands of past existences;
May I also constantly call to mind the Honored Sage, And hear the profound Dharma of all Buddhas.
By means of these various roots of goodness, May I serve the boundless and most supreme Honored One.
May they remain far removed from all unwholesome causes and constantly practice the truly wondrous Dharma;
may all sentient beings in every world be entirely freed from suffering and attain peace and happiness;
and may those whose sense faculties are incomplete have their physical forms made perfectly complete.
If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of illness, Their bodies emaciated and with no one to rely upon,
May all their sickness and pain be eliminated, And their faculties, complexion, and strength be fully restored.
If they have violated the king’s law and face execution, Oppressed by manifold sufferings and filled with grief—
When they undergo such extreme suffering, there is no refuge or protector to save them;
when they are subjected to whips, staves, shackles, and fetters, and their bodies are tormented by various instruments of pain,
amidst immeasurable hundreds of thousands of anxieties and afflictions, their bodies and minds are oppressed without a moment’s respite of joy.
May all be made free from bondage, And from the scourge of whips and staves;
may those facing execution Obtain the preservation of their lives. May all sufferings be forever and completely eliminated.
If there are sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, May they obtain various kinds of exquisite flavors.
The blind shall gain sight and the deaf hear; the lame shall walk and the mute speak.
Destitute beings shall obtain the treasury of the Dharma; their storehouses overflowing, they shall lack for nothing.
All shall be able to receive the most sublime medicine, so that not a single being suffers affliction.
All humans and devas delight in beholding him; his countenance is gentle, refined, and most majestic.
All experience immeasurable bliss, enjoying abundant prosperity and endowed with merit.
According to the inclinations of those sentient beings, musical instruments and myriad wondrous sounds all appear before them.
Upon merely thinking of water, a cool, refreshing pool appears, with golden lotuses sinking upon its surface.
According to the mental inclinations of sentient beings, food, drink, clothing, bedding,
and various forms of gold, silver, precious gems, and exquisite lapis lazuli— along with necklaces and all manner of ornaments— are fully provided.
May sentient beings never hear evil sounds, nor shall they ever encounter anything discordant;
may their physical appearances be entirely dignified and majestic, and may they each cherish one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
May all the worldly necessities for life and every form of pleasure be fully satisfied whenever they are thought of according to their wishes.
Without any stinginess regarding all their wealth and resources, they distribute them as gifts to all sentient beings.
Incense for burning, powdered incense, and unguents, along with various exquisite flowers of many colors, fall from the trees three times every day;
according to their hearts' desire, they enjoy these and give rise to joy.
Having made this vow, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Addressing the assembly, please listen to these verses on impermanence for this moment:
A lifetime is passing away; one must be aware of this. Exert yourself in cultivating goodness to create the causes for the future.
Life is like a flowing stream, difficult to turn back; impermanence arrives with urgent haste upon your person.
Though husband and wife share deep affection, they must ultimately part; kinsmen are but temporary companions.
One sees only desolate fields and tombs of a thousand years; who among all households can possess a person for a hundred?
Having realized the characteristic of impermanence, one should discipline the heedless mind; for heedlessness is the root of all evils, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"If a person were to throw himself from a mountain cliff, there might be some who do not lose their life; but those who fall into the state of heedlessness [are lost]."
One who practices heedlessness will not avoid suffering;
even if one has companions in one's undertakings throughout the day and night, there will ultimately be no reward of happiness.
All worldly and world-transcending dharmas of happiness can be destroyed by heedlessness; therefore, one should abandon it.

Upon his crown is the mark of a Great Man adorned with thirty-two jewels. Among these marks of a Great Man, it is named...
The light illuminates all ten directions, universally emitting immeasurable nets of great radiance, adorned with every kind of exquisite jewel.

The mark of a person is named "Cloud of Adornments Universally Illuminating the Entire Dharma Realm.
It is situated at the very center, gradually rising upward, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold Indra-nets that emit clouds of pure light filling the dharma realm.
In every thought-moment, it constantly manifests the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds. This is the thirty-second.

First: [Section] 18: Discourse on the Faults of Stealing;
within the gateway of favorable conditions, this is one section concerning the manifold faults of desire and form.
Miserliness, theft, and all manner of greed—these follow one after another in clear succession.
When they oppose one's desires, anger arises; when they accord with the mind, craving is born from dawn until dusk.
By reflecting thus upon the origins of karma, one sees that it is mostly due to the tracks of thieves that [suffering] increases day by day.
Zhang Mo and Li Jia abound in wealth and treasure; Zhao Shi and Wang Sheng are replete with riches and pride.

As thoughts arise from knowing their gold and silver, and as the fire of passion burns upon seeing his silk and brocade, the intent for theft rises unchecked, leading his companions to instruct one another in turn.
Since our mutual agreement has already been reached at this time, how could the distance to that place be a cause for refusal?
Even if there are three layers of locks on the outside, one must first devise a bridge a zhang wide within.
Let wealth and goods be taken by whoever desires them; why must the host strike so hard?
Treasures at the head of the bed are received one after another; From the shelf, bodies are bent low as they are tossed away one by one.
Five or six bundles are crushed before and behind; Two or three bundles remain on shoulders and backs.
This time, though not yet ruined, they are still given away repeatedly; There are also poor households whose homes have been plundered and burned.
Originally, when he was in extreme poverty and distress, he led this ox intending to sell it for three thousand coins and five bolts of silk;
yet, realizing the truth that very night, he immediately released it.
How could he have been willing to think of its heavy debt? Why would he ever have felt pity for its unpaid taxes and corvée labor?
Two men step through the gate, brandishing staffs and ropes; In a panic, they strike him, while he lets them bind his waist.
Afterward, husband and wife weep in bitter lamentation; Reflecting on the thief’s tax, their five hearts burn with anxiety.
Because his cruelty exceeds all bounds, Neither Heaven nor Earth, nor any deity, will show him mercy.
This thief has indeed brought his own ruin; Through successive interrogations, his entire nest is laid bare.
He still seeks to extend the grace period to hide his stolen goods; Only after repeated, agonizing torture does he finally admit to one plank [of evidence].
Furthermore, he implicates innocent people as "deposits"; The prisons are filled with his frantic clamor.
Subjected to repeated heavy floggings until the end of their lives, their two ribs shake like bellows;
though the master of wealth collects a meager half of what was gathered, the remainder is entirely wasted and dissipated.
Although this single episode has come to an end, the calamities of kalpas past cannot yet be escaped.
Such faults from beginning to end all sprout from craving and attachment;
One must know that there are many varieties of robbery and theft— Whenever there is encroachment or deception, these are the ranks of thieves.
The executioner’s blade is the pen used by the master thief; The cruelty and tyranny of officials are answered as being his blades.
They tunnel through walls to steal secrets with clever artifice; At their desks, they feign public integrity while privately wielding power.
High and low officials line up, many full of guile; Under the great officials, the powerful and arrogant run wild.
In urging the grain tax, they do not wait for the stalks to be cut; For the silk tribute, the cocoons have not yet been spun.
Weaving fine silks with our hands while wearing coarse cloth ourselves; Reaping rice and wheat with our blades while eating mugwort with our mouths.
The celestial palaces are not devoid of divine vision, Yet in hell one inevitably suffers beneath the earth.
How could such matters be tolerated within the Middle Way? Heaven collapses and earth cracks as ghosts and gods wail.
Part Two, Chapter Sixteen: An Exposition on the Karmic Offense of Killing.
When the objective conditions are favorable, they mostly invite the offenses of sexual misconduct and theft;

when the objective conditions are adverse, they lead to reviling, abuse, contention, and killing—all of which arise from two sources. Therefore, they are now all treated as a single section for clarification.
The Buddhas take compassion as their essential nature, while sentient beings constantly harbor poisonous malice;
whether out of greed for fine flavors or driven by anger, they may kill humans or even animals.
Those who actually violate the penal codes willingly accept death, yet those who are slain without cause shall have their spirits investigated.
Peng Sheng, Du Bo, Gongsun Sheng, Lady Hou of Song, Su E, and Dou Ying—these six individuals were all recorded in the historical annals as having been falsely executed.
Subsequently, their vengeful spirits petitioned the Supreme Deity on their behalf.
And as for taking revenge: Pengsheng was a prince of Qi. Lady Wenjiang, the wife of Duke Huan of Lu, was the younger sister of Duke Xiang of Qi.
When Duke Huan and Wenjiang were attending court at Qi, Duke Xiang had an illicit affair with her. Duke Huan reprimanded Wenjiang, and she informed Duke Xiang.
Duke Xiang became enraged and drank wine with Duke Huan. As Duke Huan was leaving, Duke Xiang ordered his son, Prince Pengsheng, to pull Duke Huan up onto the carriage.
Peng Sheng possessed great strength; he subsequently caused Huan to be crushed to death inside the chariot. The people of Lu rebuked Qi, but Qi had no words with which to respond.
They cast the blame upon Peng Sheng and killed him. Later, when Duke Xiang was hunting and saw a large boar, his attendants realized it was Peng Sheng.

Xiang was practicing archery when a boar stood upright on its hind legs and cried out. Xiang was terrified and fell from his chariot, injuring his foot. His ministers then incited a rebellion and murdered Duke Xiang.
As for Du Bo: he was the lord of the state of Du, named Heng. He entered the service as a Great Officer of Zhou.

A concubine of King Xuan named Nüjiu desired to have an affair with him, but Bo refused her. Nüjiu became enraged and slandered him in turn. King Xuan believed her and dispatched Xue Fu together with the Minister of Justice...
Gong Qi killed Duke Bo. When Duke Bo died, he transformed into a human being and reported this to the King. The King informed the Ritual Master (Zhū). The Ritual Master then killed Qi.
Qi thanked him, but Qi again brought a complaint against him on behalf of the people. He was killed once more. The Ritual Master again brought a complaint on behalf of the people.

Later, when the King was traveling through Tuanyou, Duke Bo rode a white horse with a plain carriage, while Qi was on the left and the Ritual Master on the right, rising up upon the road. With a vermilion bow and arrows, he shot King Xuan, hitting him.
His heart split and he died. Gongsun Sheng was a minister of Fu Chai. The King did not execute him for his crimes but cast him beneath Mount Xu.
Later, when Yue attacked Wu, King Fu Chai fled in defeat; as he passed this mountain, he could not take another step forward.
He ordered the Grand Chancellor Pi to call out to Sheng three times. Sheng responded. Terrified, the King looked up to heaven, sighed, and then died.
He did not return to Wu. As for the Marquis of Song, she was the Empress Dowager of Emperor Ling of the Han.
Having no favor, yet occupying the position of sovereign, she was slandered by the favored concubines of the inner palace.

Initially, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Wang Fu, having falsely incited [the charges against] Prince Kai of Hai and his consort the Lady Song—the latter being the *ji* clan of the Empress—Wang Fu, fearing the Empress’s resentment, then fabricated a story claiming that the Empress practiced heterodox arts and incantations.
Zu. Xin subsequently surrendered his seal and ribbon of office. Later, he died of grief; his father and brothers were all executed.

Afterwards, the Emperor saw a dream in which Emperor Huan appeared in a rage, saying: "What crime has Empress Song committed? You allowed wicked flatterers to take her life. Empress Song and Kui have appealed to Heaven themselves;
the Supreme Deity is struck with indignation, and their guilt is beyond redemption. The dream was extremely vivid. Upon waking, the Emperor questioned [his advisors].
Xu Shui, the Left Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (Yulin Zojian), asked: "What omen is this? Can it be averted? Xu Shui replied:

"The Empress Dowager Song and King Jihai should both be reinterred to pacify their vengeful spirits. He further suggested that the Song family's estate be returned and the former fief of King Jihai restored.
The Emperor would not accept his advice and soon passed away. As for Su E, when He Chang was serving as a magistrate during the Han dynasty, he... [removed]... removed [her].
When Governor Jiaozhi was on tour and arrived at Gaoyao County in Cangwu Commandery, he stayed overnight at Queben Pavilion as dusk fell.
At midnight, a woman suddenly appeared from beneath the pavilion and said, "I am surnamed Su, named E, with the style name Shizhen. I am originally a native of Guangxin County.
My parents and husband have all passed away; I have no brothers. I possess one hundred and twenty pieces of miscellaneous silk."
I have a maidservant named Zhifu. Being orphaned and destitute, she was unable to support herself.

She wished to go to a neighboring county to sell silk and hired a carriage and ox from Wang Bo, a resident of the same county, for a fee of twelve thousand coins. I myself carried the silk in a basket and ordered the maid to hold the reins.
On the tenth day of the fourth month of the previous year, we arrived outside this pavilion. As evening fell, all travelers had ceased their journey; not daring [to proceed further],...
They set out and stayed overnight there. Zhi Fu suddenly developed a stomachache. His wife went to the house of the village head, Gong Shou, to beg for fire.
Gong Shou drew his knife and reached toward her carriage, seizing his wife by the arm. Terrified, she refused to comply; he then killed both her and the maidservant.

They buried him beneath the building and took his property. They slaughtered an ox and burned the carriage; the nails from the carriage were placed within the bones of the ox and discarded among the mustard plants to the east of the pavilion.
The concubine, both above and below, wore white garments and green silk sandals; she then dug it up exactly as instructed. They arrested Shou and interrogated him, and he fully confessed.
He was sent down to Guangxin County, where the account matched that given by E. His parents and brothers were also arrested, and the report was submitted to the authorities. If...
According to the eternal laws, they do not deserve execution by their clansmen; however, they have lived out their lives committing evil in secret for years.

Ghosts and spirits have come to petition that not one in a thousand years has done so, and they request that all such people be executed to assist in the accumulation of hidden virtue (*yin-de*) as a means of repaying the sovereign. The Emperor granted this request. As for Dou Ying:
he was the nephew of the paternal uncle of the Empress Dowager of Emperor Xiaowen of the Han dynasty. He served as Chancellor, and later resigned from his post. When Empress Dou passed away, Ying...

Their relationship became increasingly distant and thin. At that time, Tian Fen, the younger brother of Empress Dowager of Emperor Xiaojing, was a high-ranking minister and enjoyed the sovereign's favor.
He sent someone to Ying to request several *qǐng* of land south of the city; Ying did not grant it.

Later, when Dou Gan took a wife, the various marquises went to offer their congratulations. Both Gan’s husband and Yin went out together and spoke insolent words. Gan reported their wicked speech to the authorities, and both the husband and Yin were executed by being cast to the market to die.
More than a month later, Gan fell ill; his entire body was in pain as if it were being struck with blows, and he cried out in agony.
He prostrated himself in apology. The Emperor sent a spirit-seer to examine the matter; he saw Ying and her husband together guarding the flogging.
Cao Fen subsequently died, and the Emperor also saw Ying in a dream and apologized to her.
The Case of Mr. and Mrs. Su and Lady Zhang: Brightly manifest before both men and ghosts, they all swallow their cries;
Such cases exist throughout the tens of millions of ages past and present, Yet among ten thousand, not one finds impartiality.
Beasts and humans alike fear pain and suffering without distinction; In killing another, they do not consider their own form.
Born, skinned, and flayed; their throats slit and blood drained—how can one bear to hear the lingering cries of those left for dead?
Hundreds of wild beasts roam the mountain forests; thousands of fish dwell in the rivers and seas.
Yet none have ever interfered in the affairs of others, nor have they ever committed even the slightest transgression punishable by law.
How can they be surrounded so completely that there is no way to flee, trapped and terrified?
How can you bear to cut off their passage with a horizontal net, entangling them before they have even leaped from the field?
Of these small fish, shrimp, and clams—over a thousand lives—their greedy tongues serve as but a single meal of broth.
The pigeon and the sparrow wait upon all small creatures; To kill many to provide for one is an injustice beyond naming.
Do not rely on those who do not use their own hands and bodies to kill, Yet whose offenses are overflowing as they conscript labor and seize property.
If officials unjustly beat and kill innocent people, How can one hope to succeed when investigating miscellaneous duties?
Among the Three Jewels of the Daoist gate, Compassion is foremost; in the Five Constant Virtues of Confucianism, Benevolence is most refined.
Yet the Bodhisattva’s Great Compassion taught by the Buddha and the bequeathed words of the Supreme Sage are not practiced at all.
Since one cannot practice the conduct of a gentleman, how can one occupy the rank of a high official?
When fishing, one does not use nets; one does not shoot at birds that have roosted overnight. To gaze at a flock and divine their fate is contrary to the righteousness within one's heart;
since the Rites (Li Jing) forbid killing without cause, how could one permit slaughter? A female pheasant was caught in its season—how could it be made into a stew?
To contend for union with such abandon is the nature of wolves and tigers; forty thousand of the multitudes were thus casually cast into pits.
All other sinful karmas may be universally repented; however, the matter of killing those who harbor resentment is not light.
When enmity turns back upon one and continues through successive lifetimes, when will this be resolved?
To lament at the time of death is to settle the karmic offense only now; the retribution for calamity in the three evil paths will be clear in the future.
If one wishes to know thoroughly the sufferings of many kalpas, the scriptural texts and verses are most earnest:
the precept against killing is the foremost of the Mahāyāna; one who violates it has no means of entering the City of Enlightenment. (The scriptural text below says:)

For this reason, there is much delusion and distress; one cannot enter the City of Enlightenment. To oppose and harm Great Compassion is to invite a hundred thousand hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"To give rise to a single thought of anger is to open a hundred thousand doors of hindrance. When sentient beings see such a person, it is like seeing a comet;
how can one transform those separated by such resentment? If they are not transformed, how can one accord with the teachings of the various sūtras?
The Buddha extensively praised the roots of goodness of the power of loving-kindness (as stated in the sixteenth fascicle of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, etc.). However,
because one must cultivate [merit] that accords with the dark realms,
one consequently returns to birth in the hells and as hungry ghosts.

Chapter Three: Thirty-five Verses Part One: General Presentation of the Three Evil Realms The preceding treatise extensively explained the causes and conditions of evil karma; here it is stated that the suffering experienced in future lives is manifold.
"Evil" refers to the seven branches and the three poisons; suffering pertains exclusively to the three categories of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.
Regarding the omissions concerning animals in the sutras: due to errors in the transmission and transcription of the translated texts, various teachings all speak of "three realms of suffering.
In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, this is most definitively established and cannot be a corruption (as explained below).
The ten unwholesome causes are assigned to three grades; those of light offenses belong to the lower grade: ghosts, spirits, and māras.
Among karmic actions, those of medium weight result in birth as various birds or livestock; those of superior weight lead to rebirth in the hells (*naraka*)—the three miserable realms.
Once these retributions are exhausted, one is born into the human path. Yet, even after receiving the remaining superior retributions, how could one avoid them?
Among the sufferings of the three evil states, the hells are the most grave. First, let us discuss how the suffering of the hells is.
Hereafter, we shall discuss only the offenses of the hells (*naraka*). *Naraka* is a term from the Sanskrit language;
because the hells are located beneath the earth, it corresponds to the Chinese expression "earth-hell" (which follows the nomenclature of the penal systems of this region).

Translating it according to its essential nature, it is rendered as "instrument of suffering. It is an instrument for containing those who suffer. As for "nest" (*ko*), it refers to a hollow or dwelling.

It is "reception" (vedanā). Therefore, it is likened to a nest or den. Furthermore, the metaphor of the "nest" also refers to the punishment of offenders—the general term for the instruments through which suffering is endured.

These include such things as swords, arrows, bowstrings, and glowing coals; they are the implements used for hacking, cutting, burning, and boiling. All of these are explained in terms of the *niraya* (the external environment or *upabhoga*). If one speaks in terms of the *sambhoga* (the primary physical existence itself), it is called *naraka*, which translates as "the evil place."
That is to say, those who commit evil deeds undergo this suffering. These vessels of suffering consist of three fundamental categories:

the *upapīḍa* (nearby), the *pratyeka* (solitary), and the *pṛthag-jāta* (separately born)—the latter being so called because they are places of solitary confinement and hellish descent, as will be explained in detail below.

The fundamental [category] consists of the eight cold hells combined with the eight hot hells. (The following descriptions of their dimensions, vertical and horizontal distances, and so forth, are all based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; therefore, they differ from those in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.)
Each hell has a dimension of ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth (the size of the body of each individual hell).

From this [continent] downward, there are thirty-two thousand [yojanas] (according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says twenty-two thousand) until reaching the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell. There, many sufferings accumulate;

karmic causes produce instruments of torture that inflict harm and cause one to faint and fall to the ground. A voice from the sky cries out, "You may revive! and suddenly they rise again, only to be subjected once more to the aforementioned instruments of torture and to slaughter one another.

Below, the seven hells are arranged side by side. (Starting from Saṃjīva at a depth of four thousand yojanas, extending horizontally to the Kālasūtra hell, and so on down to the Avīci hell, they are aligned in a lateral row.

First is Kālasūtra: beings are bound with cords and then cut or pierced. Second is Saṃghāta: many people gather together, and then hell-wardens drive them between two great mountains shaped like rams’ heads;

they are pressed until blood flows, and this continues through mountains shaped like horses, elephants, lions, tigers, and so forth. Afterwards, they are made to enter a great iron trough and are likewise crushed. Third is Raurava: seeking shelter, they enter an iron chamber where fire breaks out and burns them, causing them to cry out in lamentation. Fourth...

The Great Screaming Hell is like a dwelling place; its suffering exceeds that of the previous hells. Fifth, they are roasted on large, glowing iron pans, turned over and over to be scorched thin. Furthermore, they are impaled on iron skewers and grilled repeatedly, until flames erupt from their entire bodies.

Furthermore, upon a ground of glowing iron, they are struck with iron clubs until their flesh becomes a mass, burning intensely. This refers to three iron skewers piercing them from below, emerging from the shoulders and the crown of the head. Moreover, they are boiled in an iron cauldron filled with ash-water until only the bones remain;
these are then strained out onto the iron ground. Then they are reborn as before.
Regarding the seventh, Avīci, it is explained in the following verse.
The lateral distance is two thousand [yojanas], which constitutes the measurement (the distance between each hell).

Four thousand [yojanas] extend directly downward without deviation (the Saṃjīva hell extends four thousand yojanas directly downward; the cold hells are likewise ten thousand yojanas wide, and they also extend from three thousand two hundred yojanas below [the surface] down to the Arbuda hell, which is level with the Saṃjīva.

Furthermore, two thousand yojanas further down, seven hells are distributed laterally. Based on this, they should properly be situated beneath the Saṃjīva and above the Kālasūtra, exactly in the center. The Kālasūtra is four thousand [yojanas] from the Saṃjīva).

Therefore, according to the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośa*, starting from this surface of the earth and descending twenty thousand *yojana*s, one reaches Avīci; Avīci is both deep and wide by twenty thousand [yojanas] each, so its bottom is forty thousand [yojanas] from here. Thus, the verse says:

Twenty thousand [yojanas] below this is the Avīci Hell; its depth and breadth are equal. Above it are the seven *naraka*s, and all eight [hot hells] have sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*). According to this verse, the Kālasūtra and other hells are situated above Avīci, stacked one upon another.

Furthermore, there is another explanation: that Avīci extends throughout the entire perimeter, and the eight cold hells are likewise so. That treatise further asks: "What is the measurement of this Jambudvīpa? How can it accommodate Avīci and the others below? The answer is:
"The continent is like a heap of grain—broad at the base and tapering at the top; therefore, the great ocean gradually deepens and narrows."
Of the eight cold hells, I have first enumerated the number; to further describe their painful manifestations—how could one remain indifferent?

Each manifestation of suffering transforms according to the karma of the individual; ultimately, there are no waves of calamity outside the waters of the mind. (The waves do not exist apart from the water.)

Calamity does not leave the mind. In the previous chapter, regarding the ailments of killing, stealing, lust, and deception, the deceased soul is separated from the kṣaṇa (the preceding thought-moment is still the sick body; the succeeding thought-moment is the deceased soul).
The mind follows the conditions of karma without fixed form—appearing as ropes, clubs, or weapons (all manifested by the power of karma).
[There are] thousands of differences. Although there is no gate, there is a place;

the path is dark and obscure as one crosses the Naihe River (the River of Blood). [This country has been so transmitted from antiquity, though it has never been seen in the commentaries of various masters who cite the sutras and śāstras. Forgetting the true point:

moreover, after a person dies, the various manifestations that appear according to their mind and karma are all their own natural lot—why doubt this river? All strip away the clothes and garments from their bodies.
It must all be hung upon the branches and twigs of trees; driven by the staff, blown by the wind, it moves with rapidity.

In its frantic confusion, rising and falling, it is dragged and seized—sometimes passing through the Five Paths of the Underworld, sometimes saying that Yama is in the palace, or else immediately plunging into hell.
The mind and spirit transform of their own accord, not through another's hand. (From here, the eight hot hells are described: first, Saṃjīva; second, Kālasūtra; third, Raurava; fourth, Mahāraurava;
fifth, Tapana; sixth, Pratāpana; seventh, Avīci; eighth, Abīci. Undergoing all manner of suffering, they pray for death, yet they all return to life;

what can anyone do? (A multitude of sufferings accumulate due to the ripening of karma; the instruments of torture inflict harm, causing them to faint and fall to the ground. A voice from the sky says: "You may return.")

In the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell, beings suddenly rise up again and once more inflict mutual harm upon one another with the instruments of torture as before. In the Kālasūtra (Black Rope) hell, they are marked with lines;
these lines are drawn to form various patterns and shapes such as squares and circles. According to these marks, they are cut, gouged, sliced, and planed—or perhaps pounded or severed.
When many people gather together, they are crushed between two iron rams.

There are hell-wardens who drive them into this place and force them until they bleed; this occurs even with mountains of horses and elephants, and likewise when they are crushed by great iron troughs.
Then they are made to reunite and ground once more (crushed until they bleed; once shattered, they are made to join together again; then they are driven back in and crushed—this is the third).

Iron chambers burst into flames, and they wail in agony (they immediately enter iron chambers from their dwellings; as fire breaks out and burns them, their afflictions cause them to cry out—this is the fourth). Great [Hell] (the full name is Mahāraurava; immediately...).

5) Their dwellings are like a womb; because their suffering exceeds that of the former [hells], the sound is great. 6) They are roasted on iron griddles with their fat, blood, and marrow (the term "burning" refers to this).

Using flaming iron griddles and skewers, they are impaled and roasted repeatedly. Flames erupt from all seven orifices of their bodies. Furthermore, upon a floor of red-hot iron, they are beaten with clubs until their flesh, bones, fat, and blood mingle together like a lump of mud.

7) Three iron skewers pierce through their shoulders and crowns (passing from the soles of both feet, through the anus, and piercing out through both shoulders and the crown of the head). From these seven orifices, fierce flames stream forth.

Copper leaves wrap the body (furthermore, one’s entire body is enveloped in three types of large, heated copper sheets). Iron clubs strike [the body] (these two characters refer to events from the previous hell; they are placed here for the sake of the rhyme.

In this hell, the body is bound with iron and then cast upside down into a great cauldron. One is boiled in ash-water; as the broth surges and boils, one sinks and emerges. Once completely decomposed, one is reborn; having been reborn, one is boiled once more).
Seventh: Next, the Avīci Great Hell is explained.
(In various sūtras) it is also called Mahānaraka (*Dà Luòjiā*). (The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Twenty thousand [yojanas] below the northern continent, there is Avīci," referring to the Great Naraka.

It is surrounded by seven layers of iron walls. (Below this, based on the *Newly Compiled Sūtra of Buddha Names* and other sūtras, its characteristics are described; these differ slightly from those in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.)
[They are] in different locations. Furthermore, above [the hells] are seven layers of iron nets and seven rows of sword-forests, combined with fierce fires.
Eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep, the bodies of the sinners fill [the space] without obstruction.
Due to the causes and conditions of their sinful karma, one person may be many people, and many people may be one person.
All return [to the fire]; the upper fire penetrates downward and the lower fire penetrates upward;
east, west, south, and north interconnect and pass through one another. At its four gates are four copper dogs forty *yojanas* long, with sharp claws and fangs;
furthermore, there are iron-beaked birds that fly and soar about.
They devour human flesh in numbers as vast as hemp seeds; the ox-headed hell-wardens, with nine tails and eight heads, brandish iron pitchforks.
Their eight corners possess sixty-four eyes, from each of which iron pellets erupt, searing with a fierce, blazing heat.
(The character *xiàn* [煅] denotes a violent fire-gas; it is pronounced *hǔ jiā fǎn*.)
A single slave’s anger is like a thunderbolt; To casually count such outbursts would fill immeasurable *taṭaṭa* hells.
Countless wheels of swords descend from the sky; Entering the head and exiting through the feet—how could they be warded off?
(The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states there are six kinds of suffering: Fire from the four directions pierces the sinews and bones. (First, the East.)

Extending for many hundreds of yojanas, upon the great iron ground of the Three Heats, there are fierce fire-spikes. Blazing flames pierce the flesh and penetrate deep within it, severing tendons, breaking bones, and reaching the marrow. They burn like finger-candles, forming intense conflagrations; the same occurs in all other directions as well.

Because the people and the fire are intermingled without any interval, and their suffering is without interval, and one hears only the sounds of wailing in agony, it is therefore called "Avīci" (Without Interval).
Second: iron winnowing baskets and iron coals are sifted like sand; that is, they fill iron winnowing baskets with fiercely blazing iron coals and sift them together.
Third: ascending a hot iron mountain and then descending; that is, they place them upon a hot iron ground and make them ascend and descend, and descend and ascend, across the great hot iron ground.

4. "A hundred needles pierce the tongue, which is then stretched out and [kǎo] (the character is *zhāng*, meaning to spread). As for *tà*, it refers to the sound; it means that the tongue is pulled from the mouth and pierced with a hundred needles, stretching it out like the skin of an ox.
5. "Copper liquid burns the throat and pierces the internal organs. (The fifth stage:

Molten copper is poured into the mouth, burning the throat and tongue, penetrating through the internal organs until it exits from below. 6. "An iron ball enters the belly as the mouth first gapes open. (The sixth stage: Furthermore, [the victim] looks upward..."

They are laid upon a floor of glowing red-hot iron and forced to open their mouths with pincers. A great iron ball is placed within their mouths, burning their mouths, throats, and internal organs until it passes out from below.
The remaining sufferings are like those of extreme conflagration; only when their karma is exhausted do they emerge. Only here is there suffering that is constant and without interval (*ānantarya*).

As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is not like the sufferings of the seven hells, which are not constant; therefore, it is called 'without interval. For instance, in the Saṃjīva hell, one may temporarily encounter a cool breeze and be revived by its blowing, but in the Avīci hell this is not so; hence it is called 'without interval. Furthermore, there is no interval of pleasure between the sufferings, unlike [the other hells]."

In other hells, pleasure arises intermittently. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because their physical forms are vast and occupy many locations without any intervening gaps, it is called 'Avīci' (Without Interval). Although one person fills [the space], due to the power of karma, many people find no room.

The text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Precisely because they have repaid kindness with ingratitude and committed the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*), the pain pierces the liver and heart, and the suffering cuts through the marrow.
Their lifespan lasts for an intermediate kalpa; this is their home. (From the *Five Kinds of Suffering*).
The Sūtra says: "The three evil realms are the home of sentient beings. To temporarily obtain human form is like being a traveler who spends few days away and many days at home.
Let the student reflect on this; only by striving with diligent cultivation can one escape suffering. A human body is difficult to obtain, and the six sense faculties are difficult to possess.

[The section on] Extreme Cold (the following describes the eight cold hells: 1. Arbuda; 2. Nirarbuda; 3. Aṭaṭa; 4. Hahava; 5. Huhuva; 6. Padma; 7. Mahāpadma; 8. Mahāmahāpadma). Arbuda (the first): Vast cold touches the body, causing blisters [and sores].
And when the fetus bursts (the second stage; the suffering from the cold is greater than before, like a blister bursting with pus and blood flowing out, and the wound contracting).

*He* (third stage; *he* pronounced as *xie* [許葛反] and *chi* [叱涉反]; the *Abhidharmakośa* calls it *Arbuda*; *ar* [烏葛反] and *bu* [吒涉吽反]; this is the sound of enduring the cold. When the cold reaches its extreme, one cannot even open the mouth).
One can merely move the tongue to produce this sound. (4) *Jianhao* (*jiānhào*): The *Abhidharmakośa* calls it *huòhuòpó*. One cannot move the tongue; one merely makes this sound. (5) *Hǔ* (*hǔ*):

A sound like "han" and "kǔ," as death approaches its end. (6, 7, 8) *Sìliánhuá* (*sìliánhuá*): (6) Blue Lotus—cold touches the body, and the blue skin cracks and peels. (7) Red Lotus—the color turns crimson and the skin splits, perhaps ten times or more.
(8) Great Lotus—meaning the body parts become extremely large and the red skin splits, perhaps a hundred times or more.

The Flower Color (*Utpala*) and Cold Sound (*Araṭa*) each have three types; together with the two preceding blistering hells, these constitute the eight cold hells (the two [types of] sound and the three colors thus make eight).

The above concludes the fundamental hells. Next are the neighboring hells (*utsada*), which are adjacent to the eight fundamental hot hells, like the suburbs and parks surrounding a city wall; they are the places where the sinners wander.
Outside the four gates of the neighboring areas of the eight hot hells (these are the prisons), there are many more individual hells at each gate (four times four makes sixteen).

The eight hot hells comprise one hundred twenty-eight sub-hells. In the *Abhidharmakośa*, these are termed "Augmentations" (*utsada*). The verse therein states: "The eight augmentations each have sixteen; namely, the Augmentation of Hot Ashes (*kukūla*), the Augmentation of Corpses and Excrement (*kuṇapa*), the Augmentation of Razor Blades (*kṣuramārga*), and the Augmentation of the River of Cracking [Blood] (*nadī*).

The prose commentary explains this as follows: "These are places where beings suffer further torture. In the Augmentation of Hot Ashes, the ashes reach up to the knees; the sinews and skin rot away when one steps down, and are restored to their original state when one lifts the foot. In the eight cold hells, sentient beings seek shelter from the cold;
as they wander here, their feet dissolve and rot upon stepping down, and are restored to their original state when they lift them.

Mud made of corpses and excrement gives rise to *kūṭa* insects (because they seek shelter, having emerged from the previous [hell], they gradually wander and enter this [mud]; their heads and feet sink entirely. Furthermore, within the mud there are *narakūṭa* insects;
they are one zhang in length, with white beaks and black heads; they pierce the skin, enter the flesh, break the bones, and eat the marrow).

The Razor-Blade Road (sharp knives and swords have their blades pointing upward to form a path; from the previous [hell] one arrives here, and as one places a foot down, the skin and bone are consumed and rotted away; lifting the foot, they are restored to their former state). The Forest of Swords (one emerges and proceeds toward...).

In that forest, as soon as one sits beneath its shade, the wind blows the leaves down; they sever the limbs and joints of the body, which fall to the ground. There are black brindled dogs that seize and devour them. [This is] the Forest of Iron Mālatī (Iron Soapberry Trees).

[The trees] resemble black-wooden pincers; they thrust out from the front. Because dogs and other beasts pursue [the beings], the thorns point their tips downward and pierce them. When they try to pull back down, the thorns turn upward and pierce them again.
Their entire bodies and limbs are mangled as iron-beaked birds peck and devour them at will. The boiling cauldron of ash-water forms the Ash River (Kāpota-nadī).

This great river of boiling ash-water is where they fall as soon as they approach it, like beans in a boiling cauldron. The fierce fire heats the water until it surges and boils, causing them to swirl and sink. On the banks of the river stand the hell-wardens with staves, ropes, and large nets, standing in rows to block them and prevent them from escaping. Or...

Fishing them out with a net, they are placed upon the ground of the six hot cauldrons and laid face-up. When asked, "What do you require? they reply, "I suffer from hunger. The wardens immediately force their mouths open and place glowing iron balls inside.

When they reply, "I suffer from thirst," molten copper is poured into their mouths. Only when their karma is exhausted do they emerge. The sentient beings of the eight hot hells seek refuge, yet they fall into these four prisons where suffering is difficult to transcend.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Like the Ash River, like a moat; the other three resemble gardens. Furthermore, citing a sutra, it says: "These eight *naraka*s..."

It is said to be extremely difficult to cross. Its ground is made of glowing iron, surrounded by iron walls. On its four sides are four gates, closed with iron doors. Its dimensions and layout are skillfully arranged, each having sixteen *utsada* (supplementary hells) extending for many hundreds of *yojanas*.
Within it dwell those who have committed evil deeds; everywhere the flames interpenetrate, and fierce fires blaze perpetually.

Furthermore, there are various types of hells according to the time, such as empty spaces, wildernesses, mountains, and rivers—whether in mountain valleys, wildernesses, under trees, or in the air. These places of retribution may be singular or multiple; though the locations themselves are small, the instruments of suffering are vast.

Because they are not like those who have companions as their retinue—whereas the eight hot hells have [other hells] as their retinue, and although the eight cold hells lack such retinues in terms of location, these [isolated hells] alone are not like that—they are called the *ekākin* (solitary) *naraka* (hells).

The *Abhidharmakośa* further states: "The solitary hells are produced by the individual karma of each being; they are of many varieties, their locations are indefinite, and they may be on the earth..."
In the lower void and other locations, eighteen layers of hells are further described;
their similarities and differences with the previous accounts appear intermingled (as explained below, the translations vary according to the occasion).

Regarding the eight cold and hot hells discussed in various teachings, there are also discrepancies in their names across earlier and later translations of the sutras. One of shallow learning might ask: [Why is this?]

Question: During the early Tang dynasty, Ma Zhou was the first to invent the *cuò* (a small mortar) and the *duì* (a water-powered pestle). How is it that the Buddha already spoke of this hell during his lifetime? Answer: The Buddha was in India, and what he taught followed the local customs, sounds, and terminology of that land.

When these teachings were transmitted to this region, they were adapted to the phonetics and nomenclature of this country. In that [Indian] land, there were also tools for crushing grass, though they were not the same as these; the translators used the local term here. Furthermore, it is asked: If this is so, what does the perpetrator of a crime see when their life ends that is then hacked and chopped?
The following verse answers: "The instruments of suffering each correspond to what was previously seen."
When karma is completed, one receives its fruit without partiality:
having seen a mortar and pestle in a previous life, one is then pounded by the mortar and ground by the pestle;
or, having seen the world’s shackles and clubs, one encounters iron bars and an iron cage; all other instruments of suffering are likewise so.

How could one limit [the punishments] to the Mountain of Knives or the Burning Chariots? (In this country, prior to the Sui dynasty, when evil-doers died, they would immediately see themselves being hacked and stabbed;

they did not see themselves being ground in mills. Since the Tang dynasty, those who die after committing evil may or may not see such things. This is the case in each and every world. Hells follow karma and the mind; how could there be fixed numbers or fixed characteristics? For this reason, the terminology used in the translations of the scriptures differs slightly between earlier and later periods.
To have one’s tongue pulled out and to be ploughed with it is truly agonizing pain.
In the cauldrons of boiling water and the glowing coals, who can offer any help? The copper pillars and iron beds arise from one's own karma.
Being roasted in the fiery pit, do not blame others;
those with mouths like blood-basins are called rākṣasas, and those with fierce and perilous forms are yakṣas. They tear out the flesh, flay the skin, and hammer the joints of the bones.
Intestines pulled out and lungs torn from their places, as numerous as hemp seeds; the agony is so difficult it cannot be described.
Boils and sores split open with a *ap-p'o*; the skin is bruised and dark blue, the body trembling and shivering.
Red lotuses amidst mangled flesh, *a-po-po*; like ice on a bank or ice in a pond, it pierces to the very marrow of the bones.
The wind-mill, the wind-arrow, and the *aṭṭaṭṭa*—one cannot speak, for the tongue does not move;

enduring the cold without penetration, the *arara*. Within the great and small Iron Ring Mountains, there is long-lasting darkness where the three luminaries do not reach for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This above is merely a brief indication by way of analogy.
I have fully discussed the instruments of suffering, their number being boundless; they are all the karma created in previous chapters.
At that time, one was bold and fierce, boasting of one's prowess; now, having arrived at this place of terror and dread, it is too late for regret—vain is the lamentation.
Chapter Four: Sixteen Verses on the Intermediate State of Animals and the Unwholesome Karma of the Middle Grade, Which Results in Rebirth Among Animals in the Future.
They are called "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*) because they are raised by humans; furthermore, they are called "lateral" (*tiryak*) because their bodies are oriented horizontally.
Secondly, let us consider what is commonly observed among the majority. To explain in detail: how could one ever be restricted by this name?
It encompasses all those dwelling in water, on land, and in the air—beings with no feet, many feet, and myriad forms.
Originally, they all flowed forth from the great ocean (at the beginning of the kalpa of formation, aquatic life first arose).
The three thousand rivers gradually fill; birds, beasts, fish, dragons, insects, ants, and all that wriggles, flies, or stirs—all contain spirit.
Those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
even within fire and within material objects, they take birth—beings of the greatest magnitude and the most minute, numbering in the trillions.

From the *kūṇa* and *páng* with golden wings (the largest) down to the *yòu* and *míng* insects (the smallest), though there may be occasional pleasures according to the time (these being distinct retributions,
such as the dogs and horses of the wealthy), all are characterized by a degree of ignorance and are termed "lowly" (collectively called animals because they lack self-mastery).
Their individual karma drives them into this realm of suffering.
Controlled by others, how can there be honor? Dragging loads and bearing heavy burdens, one must repay debts;
With rotting backs and pierced hooves, how can one express one’s plight? (Until life ends, how can one escape?
On steep roads and deep mud, the carriage does not move; Strength exhausted and breath spent, the blows of the cudgel are no less severe.
The journey continues for three stages; though the ball is full, the tally has not yet ceased.
Because the millstone is dragged by the weak, the eyes are covered and pitch-black.
Having dwelt through the winter nights amidst frost and dew, one has lain for many years throughout the night in a pit of filth.
People hasten along the road, their bodies weary from the whip; The wind blows upon their aged, emaciated, and chilled forms.
For clothing they use only skin and fur; Yet even for food and drink, grass and water are scarce.
Hunger, satiety, life, and death are not within their own control; Safety, peril, rest, and exhaustion depend on the whims of others.
Driven by clubs and bound with ropes, their faces are filled with terror; pierced by blades and scalded in boiling water, they cry out in bitter resentment and pain.
With four limbs hanging upside down, they remain barely alive;
as their bodies are spun and flayed until the skin falls away, they are surrounded by bows and knives that crush their very souls. Hawks and dogs roam about at will, striking fear into their hearts.
The mounted cavalry feared only pursuit from behind; they never imagined an archer would meet them head-on.
Pressed from both front and rear, with chariots blocked from the west, where could they go?
Arrows pierced their backs and emerged through their chests; in such frantic agony, how could they possibly survive?
They also turn back fires that scorch mountains and fields; they divide beasts and thousands of snakes, how many in their frantic haste (ping, with the tone of pu-geng).
Nesting sparrows and creatures in burrows, numbering in the billions, all crave life and dread death, being equal to humans in this regard. Long-lived scaly insects and various worms swarm about.
Crushed in hot sands, their pain awakens them again; the powerful harm the weak, who devour one another without ever ceasing.
What has been described above is but a brief indication of these types;
as the categories are numerous, how could they all be fully explained? There are, in total, thirty-six billion kinds (as recorded in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*).
From the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Sutra on Abiding):

If one encounters extraordinary suffering, or if having already lost this human form it is difficult to regain, and as one wanders through successive lives, evil and delusion easily take root—then observing how that carriage has overturned, one must change its course;
for while the six faculties are fully intact, one must surely cultivate and strive.
Chapter Five, Section Sixteen:
Describing the Ten Kinds of Inferior Unwholesome Karma of the Preta Realm. This constitutes the primary cause and condition for pretas:
long lifespans, hunger and thirst, and much fear; they seek relief from others to satisfy their parched throats.

The root source lies solely in the realm of Yama (alternatively called *Yamā*, which means "cessation of dispute," or "equality"; the *Abhidharmakośa* states that sentient beings have not yet reached it).

All say they are without fault; yet as soon as they reach the impartial Mirror of Karma (*karmādarśa*), their transgressions manifest of themselves. They dare no longer claim [to be innocent], and thus it is named "Quiescent Rest" (*jìngxī*).

From there, they pass through successive branches of existence into the great trichiliocosm. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Five hundred yojanas below this is the kingdom of King Yama. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:

"The various abodes of the pretas are scattered from here to other places. Some are dignified, majestic, wealthy, and happy like devas; others are emaciated by hunger and hideous. In the east and west, there are likewise two types; in the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), there are only those who possess majesty and virtue."
Half [of them] constantly dwell beneath the earth (the Yellow Springs;
there is also the Kingdom of King Yama), while half participate in the human world, remaining by the side of humans. Because their karmic retributions differ, they do not see one another.

When their shared capacities manifest before them—such as when a person’s primary retribution is in the human realm yet they possess the shared capacity of the ghost realm, they can see ghosts; or when a ghost possesses the shared capacity of the human realm, they can [see humans].
When seeing people, their dwellings are distant; (due to conditions of seeing) they are constantly separated.

(The dwellings where humans and ghosts reside are each the result of their dependent retribution. Since these are distant, they do not see one another. They suspect each other’s supernatural powers, comparing them to the ability to tunnel through walls. (Those who see ghosts do not realize that ghosts cannot see their own houses.

When they encounter someone passing by after tunneling through a wall or partition, they immediately say, "The ghost possesses spiritual powers. People do not realize that ghosts can see; it is merely that the person passes through the open space of the ground. Yet when a ghost sees a person tunneling [through a wall],...)
One passes through their own walls; ghosts do not know humans and do not see their own houses, yet they say that a person possesses supernatural powers and has pierced their walls.
The kingdom of Yama lies five hundred *yojanas* beneath Jambudvīpa, both in length and breadth;

it is here that the good and evil of all beings are determined. Some say that those in the heavens and those in Avīci do not pass through this place, just as officials of the fifth rank or below do not pass through the main hall of the Ministry of Personnel.
Cáo. The rebel traitor Jù has not yet arrived at the Imperial Secretariat, the Court of Judicial Review, or other such offices.
Since ancient times, the world has called this place the Yellow Springs; though life has ended, one has not yet spoken of the place of rebirth.
For a time, one finds reunion here with loved ones, enemies, and kinsmen alike.
Whether meeting face-to-face or drawn together by fate, from this parting many eons have passed;
some are born in the hells or as animals, some are born in the heavens, some enter the *āśvalaka* [ocean] within the sea,
some ascend as five-fold supernatural sages upon the ocean, and if born in the realm of ghosts, it is as previously described.

Some dwell in their own realm (the kingdom of King Yama), some in the human world (all beings), and some are employed as servants by the Iron Wheel-turning Kings. They take turns serving one another for years on end;

as the *Abhidharmakośa* states, the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have powerful spirits who guard and patrol [them]. Carrying stones and bearing sand, they endure many hardships.
Filling rivers and damming seas, they stretch out in continuous succession; these three types are further divided into nine distinct varieties.
It is said that among the hungry ghosts, those who suffer from loathsome odors come first.
The first of the nine is the *ulkāmukha* (torch-mouth) ghost, whose mouth constantly blazes with flaming torches, burning down villages, towns, and wildernesses.
Having first passed through hell, one now endures this: with a belly as vast as a mountain and a throat-pore as narrow as a needle, one suffers for stealing the food of the Sangha;
from one’s own evil mouth there is constant putrid stench, for one praised wicked factions and slandered the virtuous and wise; with hair as sharp as nails, one pierces oneself as one walks.
Applying acupuncture and moxibustion perversely leaves illness unhealed;
The stench of pricking the hairy body makes one loathe it, yet one plucks at oneself like a pig or sheep being flayed by knife and spear (the small spear is pronounced *shìlián*).
One drains pus from a goiter and eats it; Envy toward others and resentment become heavy latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
These six types of beings above are all extremely hungry; their lifespan lasts for fifteen thousand years.
(One month in the human realm constitutes one day for them; their lifespan is five hundred years, which corresponds to fifteen thousand years in the human realm.

Their two ears do not hear the word "gruel," and their single body consists only of skin and bone joined together. When they see food, it transforms into fierce fire as soon as they attempt to eat it.
When approaching a river wishing to drink, it immediately dries up;
having obtained food left over from sacrifices to the gods, they are stingy and give little, yet when asked for alms, they point toward it. There is food discarded on steps and in alleys;
because they harbor doubts that it was lost, it remains as such. The ninth is named the Ghost of the Sword of Power.
Their transformations, prosperity, and pleasures resemble those of the heavens;

they include rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and others dwelling in mountain forests, spirit temples, and along the shores of mountains and rivers (*ruān*—meaning the edges of rivers and seas). As stated in the *Dharmapada-vaṃśa-sūtra*:

"The bhikṣu Saṃghayaśas traveled to the shore of the great ocean and saw a wondrous palace, within which two ghosts were bound with chains," and so forth. Their transgressions and blessings are not fixed, and their mental speech is a mixture of the pure and the defiled.
Although individual retributions may be severe, collective retributions are all-pervasive; the six types of hunger and two types of deprivation can only be satisfied through sufficiency.
To emphasize the point, "hunger" is specifically mentioned, for it must be proclaimed (the term *xuyan* refers to the circulation of the Buddha’s words).
O assembly, what has been presented above from the *Suvarṇabhāsa-sūtra* on Repentance is so vast and extensive that it cannot be set forth all at once. Now, furthermore...

Based on the remaining scriptural passages from the preceding chapter, we repent to remove all other hindrances. Disciple [Name] and others, together with all sentient beings, repent with a sincere heart.
If a person, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, Commits various most grievous sins, By revealing them for a brief moment, all evils are completely eliminated.
Relying upon this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, And performing such repentance, one is thereby able to swiftly exhaust All karmas of suffering.
I only pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions [will bear witness].
Observe and protect me; Compassionately accept my confession.
With a heart of great compassion, May you, out of pity, eliminate all the evil karma I have created throughout many kalpas, Which causes me constant suffering and distress.
For having committed these various evil deeds, I am perpetually born into a state of sorrow and fear.
Within these modes of conduct, you have always harbored thoughts of joy;
You who possess great compassion and can remove the fears of all sentient beings, I pray that you accept my confession and cause me to be free from sorrow and suffering.
Whatever afflictions I possess, as well as all karmic retributions, I pray that you will wash them away with the water of your great compassion.
I wash myself clean; all the various sins I have committed in the past, as well as the evil karma I am currently creating, I confess with a sincere heart—may they all be completely eliminated.
Regarding all future evil karma, I shall guard against it so that it does not arise; even if I should happen to transgress, I shall never dare to conceal it.
The three types of bodily action, the four kinds of vocal action, and the three types of mental action—these tightly bind all sentient beings, continuing in succession from beginningless time.
Through these three modes of conduct, I have committed the ten non-virtuous karmas and such a multitude of sins;
I now confess them all. Whatever evil deeds I have committed, [I now repent].
One must personally undergo the retribution of suffering; now, before all the Buddhas, I sincerely repent.
Having repented, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

The confession and removal of the four categories [of obstacles] have already been completed above. Now, following the sequence of the sutra text, we shall further confess and remove twelve kinds of difficulties.
These were all presented by the Bodhisattva King of the Golden Drum Dream to the Buddha; therefore, one should perform this repentance with a sincere heart.
Now, in the presence of the One of Ten Powers, I confess the many hardships and miseries:
The hardship of delusion for ordinary fools within the three realms of existence; The hardship of constantly creating extremely grave evil karma;
The hardship of the accumulation of perverse desires by myself; And the hardship of the afflictions of all foolish beings.
The difficulty of a deranged mind, distraction, and perversion; The difficulty of associating with evil friends;
The difficulty of being stained by craving within saṃsāra; The difficulty of committing sins through the darkness and dullness of hatred and delusion;
The difficulty of being born in the eight states of non-leisure or evil realms; And the difficulty of never having accumulated merit.
I now, before all the Most Victorious Ones, repent of my boundless evil karmic offenses (these twelve difficulties occur before the preceding section on repentance, prior to the making of vows).
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
With a sincere heart,
I entreat you to always behold the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, dwelling peacefully beneath the precious king-tree.
Seated upon a sublime lion throne of lapis lazuli, may you eternally remain in the world to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having made this request, with a sincere heart, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem;
with a sincere heart, I rejoice.
Whatever various causes for supreme merit beings have performed here within this Jambudvīpa, or in other world-systems,
I now rejoice in them all with a heart of sympathetic joy; having rejoiced,
I take refuge and pay homage with a sincere mind to the Triple Gem.
Through these merits of rejoicing, And the various virtues created by body, speech, and mind, May this supreme karma always increase; I dedicate it toward unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
All the merit of praising the Buddhas, With a profound mind pure and free from stain—
Through this dedication and aspiration, merit shall be boundless; one shall transcend the evil realms for sixty kalpas.
(These three gates belong to the preceding section; this section falls within the midst of the aspiration.)
May I eliminate the ten unwholesome deeds And practice the path of the ten wholesome deeds.
Abiding securely within the ten stages, may I constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions. With my body, speech, and mind, I dedicate the merit and wisdom thus cultivated;
May these roots of goodness cause me to swiftly attain the Unsurpassed Way. (The following verses are, in fact, the preceding text on repentance.)
Having performed the dedication, with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
With a sincere heart, make this vow:
may all sentient beings universally make offerings to all the Most Victorious Honored Ones of the ten directions.
The sublime Dharma-gate of the three vehicles— may the assembly of bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas,
and śrāvakas always vow not to dwell in lowly states; may they not be born amidst the eight difficulties of the lack of leisure,
but be born as honored ones among those with leisure, and may they forever be able to personally attend upon the Buddhas of the ten directions.
May I always be born into wealthy and noble families, With treasuries and storehouses all filled to overflowing;
May my appearance and reputation be peerless, And may my lifespan extend through kalpas.
May all women be transformed into men, Brave, vigorous, intelligent, and possessed of great wisdom.
May all constantly practice the bodhisattva path, Thoroughly cultivating the six perfections to reach the other shore.
Whatever karma they have created throughout the three realms of existence In the past and the present,
May they transcend these loathsome and unwholesome destinies, And may it be utterly extinguished without remainder.
May all sentient beings within the ocean of existence, Firmly bound by the net of birth and death,
Have their bonds severed by the sword of wisdom, And, free from suffering, swiftly realize the state of Bodhi.
Whether they be men or women, Or those of the noble castes such as the Brahmins—
With palms joined and single-minded devotion, I praise the Buddha; May I constantly remember my past lives in every birth.
May my faculties be pure and ever-perfected, And may all supreme merits be fully accomplished.
In all future places of rebirth, May I always be gazed upon by gods and humans alike. (This passage continues from the preceding text.)
[This refers to the period] after Duan had made his vow.
Having made the vow, he paid homage with a sincere heart, taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, having heard this, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
Just as in your dream, the golden drum produced a sound that praised the true merits of the Tathāgata and included the method for repentance.
Anyone who hears it will obtain immense merit, bring great benefit to sentient beings, and eliminate their karmic obstructions. You should now know this.
This supreme karma is entirely due to the causes and conditions of past praise, aspiration, and habitual practice, as well as the majestic empowerment and protection of all Buddhas.
I shall now explain these causes and conditions for you. When the great assembly heard this Dharma, they were moved.
All were filled with joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced [the teaching].
[The Preacher] addressed the assembly, saying: "Listen to the verses on impermanence from within the Sūtra:
Whether in pleasure or in suffering, Whether old or young, Whether of great lineage or humble birth."
The King of Death can kill all— whether handsome or ugly, whether of great strength or little strength,
whether alone or accompanied; the King of Death can kill all— whether king or servant,
whether layperson or renunciant, whether firm or soft.
Whether rich or poor, whether possessing merit or lacking it, whether male or female—the King of Death can slay them all.
Whether walking or staying at home, whether in water, on land, in the mountains, or within a city—the King of Death can slay them all. Whether asleep or awake.
Whether eating or not eating, one is able to traverse the chaotic world; yet the King of Death can slay all.
