Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
Part 14: Praising the Buddha’s Merits.
O Great Physician King who has compassion for the world, whose body is entirely wisdom and tranquility;

in the dharma of selflessness, there is a true self—therefore I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Savior of the World, whom those seeking refuge find only after long aspiration; I take my refuge in the Unsurpassed Tathāgata.
Following the Buddha through the world like a calf, he is therefore named the Great Compassionate Cow;
his merit fills the ten directions, yet ordinary, inferior, and ignorant beings lack the power to praise him.
Now I shall praise his heart of loving-kindness and compassion, as an offering for my two types of karma—body and speech.
The world constantly seeks its own benefit; the Tathāgata never acts for such purposes.
He is able to sever the worldly karmic retributions of sentient beings; therefore, I pay homage to him who benefits both self and others.
The world pursues its kin and bestows thick favors upon them; the Tathāgata’s benefit extends to all, without distinction between enemy and kin.
The Buddha does not possess such characteristics as worldly people do; therefore, his mind is equal and without duality.
The world speaks of diverse karmic actions and diverse results, yet for the Tathāgata, there is no discrepancy between what he teaches and the karma [he embodies].
Whatever practices he cultivates sever all conditioned formations; for this reason, he is named the Tathāgata.
Having already understood the faults of afflictions, he manifests in order to benefit sentient beings;
though he has long attained liberation within the world, he remains out of his compassion for those dwelling in birth and death.
Although he appears in celestial and human forms, his compassion follows him like a calf follows its mother.
The Tathāgata is the mother of all sentient beings, And his compassionate heart is like a young calf.
He personally undergoes manifold sufferings while mindful of sentient beings; In moments of compassionate thought, he never regrets or sinks in spirit.
His heart of pity is so intense that he is unaware of his own suffering; Therefore, I prostrate to the one who uproots suffering.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one should weary of craving and the path of karma, abandoning evil and delighting in the good.
(First) Singing eleven verses:
Describing virtuous karma—having taken refuge in the Triple Gem in previous lives, One now encounters past conditions and right faith arises.
Seeing talk of humans and devas, one smiles with delight (the *Lunyu* says: "The Master smiled with a *wan-er* smile");
hearing discourse on ghosts and hells, one is struck with a sigh of awe (*quai* is a sound of sighing; the *Lunyu* says: "Yan Yuan sighed deeply and said").
One must deeply realize that worldly desires must be rebuked and loathed, and one must deeply believe that the Gate of Truth may be served with utmost sincerity.
Abandoning evil and turning the mind toward goodness alone, one desires to fulfill the most honored and glorious state of Buddhahood.

(Having seen various Mahāyāna sūtras, one is exhorted to arouse the great bodhicitta and thus seeks to attain Buddhahood; yet, because the fundamental nature has not been realized, one cannot avoid falling back into tainted actions.
One should receive the Three Refuges and the precepts with single-minded diligence, and cease the causes and conditions of the ten non-virtuous actions with a sincere heart.
The wayward son, Yaolang, has long remained far away; he has repeatedly consulted with his teachers as mentioned above, yet for years he has frequented singing halls and wine shops.
He visits temples and monasteries every month, and whether busy in the morning or evening, he constantly recites the Buddha’s name.
Whenever there is a slight moment of leisure, whether for public or private affairs, he immediately upholds the sutras.
He often declined invitations to weddings and gatherings; when dhyāna or lecture sessions were held, he would go at once to listen.
Encountering the eight precepts, he never grew lax; on the six fast days, he was invariably diligent.
When monks arrived with alms bowls, he never let them pass empty-handed; when people prepared offerings together, he would ensure they were properly recorded.
He frequently relieves the poor and the sick through wisdom, And repeatedly repairs meditation halls and Buddha shrines.
(The following two lines describe the farming family.

He is dedicated to preventing damage from insects and snakes during cultivation, And when opening scales and measures, he ensures they are always level and fair. (The following two lines apply generally to all people.)
Relieving the destitute and aiding the needy according to one's power; rescuing the weak in peril and supporting those on the verge of collapse (these two lines describe officials).
Vowing to act with integrity alone while serving as an official;
maintaining one’s post, living in poverty, and preserving purity (the following two lines apply generally to all).
Regarding my kin, I have no deceit or falsehood; among my friends, I never engage in clamorous strife until death.
(The following verse describes being urged by relatives toward wine and meat, yet maintaining my resolve without compliance: Though wind and frost may blow, fine wine is poured deep into the cup;
though hunger and exhaustion prevail, rich broth fills the bowl. I was once urged by my relatives to join in their gathering.
Subduing the mind and restraining the mouth so that no passions arise—how much less would one commit even a fraction of the grave or light offenses such as killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct?
For such a person, though they practice the precepts, there may be variations in the fullness or deficiency of their upper, middle, or lower grades;
yet, although they originally sought Buddhahood through such cultivation, [the result remains].

Furthermore, because the principles of the Three Vehicles have not yet been clarified, beings follow the gradations of the stages and undergo empty retributions, being born into the human realm and the celestial courts; thus they manifest again as devas and humans.
[End of] Section Two: Chanting the Twenty-four Verses, Describing the Human Realm.
If one wishes to discern the distinctions between the karmic rewards of humans and devas, one must first know upon what they depend.
(The following is described point by point according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, using either verse or prose as appropriate. The receptacle world has the wind-circle at its very bottom.

(This means that through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, first, supported by space at the lowest level, a wind-circle arises. It is sixteen hundred million [yojanas] thick. (This wind-circle is sixteen hundred million yojanas in thickness.)

In the following text, every instance where a number is cited refers to *yojanas*. "Difficult to perceive" means that the number is immeasurable; thus the verse says: "The receptacle world is established with the wind-circle at its very bottom;
its breadth is incalculable, and its thickness is sixteen *lakṣas*. *Lakṣa* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "hundred million. This wheel’s essential nature is exceptionally firm and dense;
even if struck by a vajra-pestle, it is difficult to destroy (*huī*, meaning to ruin). (From the *Śāstra*)

It is said: "The substance of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) is firm and dense. Even if a great Nārāyaṇa were to brandish a vajra-wheel and strike it with fierce power, the vajra might shatter, but the wind-circle would suffer no damage.

Great clouds pour down rain upon the wind-circle; Drops as large as axle-trees form a lake. The *Śāstra* says: "Furthermore, through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds and rain arise and pour down upon the wind-circle.

While the water has not yet solidified, its depth is one billion one hundred and twenty-two thousand *yojanas*. Question: How is it that the water-circle does not flow out sideways? Answer: [As follows:]

The karma of sentient beings, sustained by the power of the wind, prevents it from flowing or dispersing, just as a granary holds grain. Furthermore, through the power of karma, a strike arises upon this water, forming a golden wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*).

It is like a film that forms on top of boiled honey as it cools. Therefore, the water-wheel is only eight hundred million [yojanas] thick; the remainder solidifies into the golden wheel, which is three hundred and twenty-two million [yojanas] thick. Thus the verse says: "Above that, the water-wheel is eleven hundred and twenty million deep; the lower eight lakhs of water [solidify], and the remainder congeals to form the gold.
Its diameter (length) is twelve hundred and thirty-four million [yojanas], and its depth is ten [million].
[The water wheel] is one [billion] yojanas in depth and is supported on its four sides by wind;

above, it is bound together with gold, forming a membrane like that of milk. Its thickness is three hundred and twenty-two thousand [yojanas], and its diameter is no less [than its depth, being equal to that of the water].

As the *Śāstra* says: "The dimensions of these two wheels are identical. Their diameter is twelve billion, thirty-four million, and fifty thousand yojanas. Therefore, the verse states: "The extent of this water and gold wheel is twelve lakṣas in diameter."
[The circumference] is three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas]. The perimeter is three times this amount; it totals thirty-six *koṭis*, with a remainder.
(The character *qí* [pronounced *jī*] means "odd"; because it is not even or complete, it refers to these two wheels. Their straight length is twelve *koṭis*, three thousand four hundred *yojanas*.

If one calculates the measure of the fourfold perimeter, it is three [times that], which equals thirty-six *koṭis*, ten thousand three hundred and fifty *yojanas*. Therefore, the verse says: "The perimeter is three times this. This...)

"Zhe" (者) refers to the number of straight lengths. Now, in this verse, because of the desire to complete the phrasing and the meter, it simply says "three hundred and sixty *billion*. It mentions the remainder of the count, hence saying "there still remain the odd ones. "The remainder" refers to ten thousand, three hundred, and fifty. The calculation is thus.
The great clouds of collective karma again arise, raining drops upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*).

Regarding the "nine [尸@垂][厂@義]": the "nine" refers to Mount Sumeru and the seven mountain ranges of gold and iron. As for the "seven gold [mountains]," following Sumeru, they are: first, Yugandhara; second, Īṣādhāra; third, Khadiraka... [text fragment ends].

1. Yugandhara, 2. Īṣādhara, 3. Khadiraka, 4. Sudarśana, 5. Aśvakarṇa, 6. Vinataka, 7. Nimindhara. These distinct winds separate the accumulations of gold and silver into mountain shapes and the foundations of the continents;
they divide the waters into sweet and salt to form the inner and outer oceans, all of which are established simultaneously.
(The *Śāstra* says: Upon the Golden Wheel there are nine great mountains. Sumeru, the King of Mountains, dwells in the center, while the other eight surround it.)

Among these eight, the first seven are called "inner. Outside the seventh mountain are the great continents and so forth. Beyond these is the Iron Rim Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*), which encircles the entire world-system like a wheel. The [first] seven are composed solely of gold, while Sumeru is made of four jewels.

Question: From what do these arise? Answer: Through the power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds and rain are produced and pour down upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), with drops as large as chariot axles.

The surging waves of accumulated water become a treasury of various jewels. Due to the impact of various powerful winds possessing diverse majesties, the various classes of jewels are produced. Furthermore, through the power of karma, distinct winds are aroused which separate the jewels and other substances, gathering them together to form the continents (*dvīpa*) and dividing the waters to establish the inner and outer oceans separately.

Thus, the nine mountains rest upon the Golden Wheel; the depth of their immersion in the water is equal to eighty thousand *yojana*s. Only Mount Sumeru rises above the water by that same amount; for the remaining eight mountains, the height above the water decreases by half for each successive one.

The Yugandhara Mountains emerge from the water forty thousand [yojanas], up to the Cakravāḍa Mountains, which emerge three hundred twelve and a half [yojanas]. Thus, for each of these nine mountains, the breadth is equal to its respective height above the water.

Sumeru has the four precious substances as its body: its southern face is of vaidūrya, its northern side is of gold, its eastern body is of silver, and the precious substance on its western side is called sphatika (crystal). [The Śāstra says: "According to the precious substance..."]

Its majestic power causes its color to manifest externally; thus, the sky over Jambudvīpa appears like the color of lapis lazuli. The four sides of the Golden Mountain are encircled by seven tiers, with a sea intervening between each mountain.
The inner mountains are high and broad, while those on the outside are low and narrow. [Mount] Sumeru is eighty thousand [yojanas].

From Yugaṃdhara, the dimensions of the portions of the oceans decrease respectively by forty thousand, twenty thousand, ten thousand, five thousand, two thousand five hundred, one thousand two hundred fifty, and six hundred twenty-five, down to the Cakravāḍa, which is three hundred twelve and a half [yojanas].

The proportions of the seven inner seas also follow this sequence from the innermost to the outermost: eighty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, ten thousand, five thousand, two thousand five hundred, and finally one thousand two hundred fifty for the seventh sea.

Thus the verse says: "In between there are eight seas; the first seven are called 'inner. The first is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide, and each of its four sides is three times that. The remainder follows accordingly.

The six [seas] decrease by half and half [successively]. "O Son of Good Family, you should know that when a Bodhisattva manifests transformations in the world, it is not rooted in craving; rather, it is solely out of compassion."
He abandons craving; yet, by means of various desires, he enters into birth and death.
Ninth: Sixteen Verses on the Middle Way. A General Explanation of the Previous Doubts and Difficulties.
First: A General Resolution of All Doubts.
All you great beings of the Mahāyāna, contemplate in your minds that the two types of grasping are fundamentally empty and void.
Once you know that the mark of self (*ātman*) possesses nothing at all, how could you not first eliminate the root of craving? (For craving arises from the grasping at a self.
One must simply rely on compassion and wisdom, which must be practiced in tandem.
"Retaining delusions to undergo rebirth and dwelling together with the world" (this is praised in all Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras as the means of moistening birth through retained delusions).
If one were to show this [practice] as being identical to worldly affairs:

"To save those deluded followers who have not attained liberation, one would rather cast oneself into the water to rescue a drowning man; to support the intoxicated, one must lift them up from within the mud."
To save others, how could one decline to provide abundant clothing? To support another, how can one avoid the mire?
(Falling drunk into places such as filth and excrement—this is why one must support them. When sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is ill (as extensively explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
Desiring to deliver those of coarse character, his traces appear coarse; From the sacred he enters the mundane—truly unfathomable. (Truly, it is as it ought to be.)
[It is] immeasurable. The transition from the mundane to the sacred is likewise not distinct. There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:

first, those above the [first] stage who possess supernormal powers and manifest as mundane beings from their state of sanctity to deliver sentient beings; second, ordinary beings bound by fetters who are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata and, with superior great compassion, extensively transform sentient beings.

Although these two types deliver sentient beings, their skillful means (*upāya*) are no different; thus it is said they are "not distinct. "Mutually hearing [the truth], greed and love are fundamentally non-existent;
Beaten and toyed with as slaves, how could one truly be a slave? (This metaphor refers to those at the upper level of ordinary beings.
"Like that which restrains a venomous snake while its life remains, Having controlled its poisonous breath, it is rendered powerless. (This praises the non-formation of karma.)

Next, regarding the specific application of food, clothing, medicine, and the prohibitions against poison, it is like first severing craving (the definitive cutting of the resolve; though one does not dwell upon objects of attachment, the performance of a bodhisattva’s deeds cannot help but appear as if they still exist—this is not something that ordinary deluded beings can understand).
Life remaining is just like maintaining a physical body (as long as the snake’s life remains...).

Just as a bodhisattva cherishes and protects his physical body, nourishing it with food and clothing and treating it with medicine when ill, so too does he maintain himself solely for the purpose of propagating the Buddha-dharma, entering and exiting birth and death to transform ordinary beings.
(The following details the reasons for maintaining the physical form: The faculty of sight is essential for examining the scriptures and teachings.
The karmic activity of speech must be employed to expound the extraordinary meaning; How could one without feet travel through the world?
How could one without a body gather disciples? This body, which serves as a support, requires food and clothing;
Unlike grasses and trees which have roots and trunks (unlike a gourd that is tied up but not eaten).
Next, regarding the general application of speech that accords with people's intentions:
when one encounters doubt as to whether something is right or wrong, the beginner responding to circumstances must employ skillful means.
Unlike birds and beasts, which are merely ignorant and do not provide food or clothing for their own greedy desires, [humans] do not engage in social interactions with the aim of personal gain.
If one opposes the sentiments of others, they will distance themselves; how then can one be led into the profound pivot?
Furthermore, regarding doubts about receiving birth in future lives, one might study the Two Vehicles in their entirety to cultivate quiescence, or be born in a Pure Land to enjoy oneself.
Who would be willing to cast their body into the five turbidities?
Who can rescue others and deliver them from the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties where the Buddha-dharma cannot be transmitted?

It is through the power of the Three Vehicles that Bodhisattvas take birth by entrusting themselves to a womb here in Jambudvīpa; it is solely because of their compassionate salvation that they undergo such hardships.

To summarize the preceding meaning and give rise to the subsequent thought, one should know that this present life, together with the future life, exists solely for the sake of him [the Buddha]. To protect one's life and preserve the body is done only for his sake.
If doubt regarding the final age has not yet been resolved, listen further to an analogy; how could its principle be otherwise?
Like a person falling into the sea on the verge of death, who suddenly encounters a human corpse floating upon the great ocean—the vast sea will not allow the corpse to remain long;
it will surely be driven by the wind to rest upon a shore.
That person must embrace it firmly, holding fast without letting go for even a moment.
Though one may loathe a corpse infested with maggots, one still seeks to reach the shore by means of a raft;
Birth and death are boundless like the great ocean— viewing the body as impure as a corpse with maggots,
One takes Great Parinirvāṇa as the shore, delivering others and oneself like those who board a raft.
Caring for one's body with food and clothing is like holding onto a prison; how can this differ from having no attachment in the mind?
If the great assembly suspects that others have not severed their attachments, simply examine this analogy and they will naturally be dispelled.
If all sentient beings in the final age are able to renounce all desires and eliminate both hatred and love, they will forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra.
Diligently seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, one attains awakening within the pure mind.
Chapter Ten: Four Verses on the Middle.
First, it is inferred that craving is the root of saṃsāra; the causes and conditions of its faults are manifold.
Since this has already been personally witnessed and severed by the Tathāgata, what further merit is there now in explaining the means of severance?
If sentient beings of the final age encounter the True Vehicle of the Perfect and Sudden School,
they will externally remain unbound by the dusts of desire, and internally eliminate the feverish afflictions of hatred and attachment from their hearts.
Moment by moment, one forever severs the views of saṃsāra; In every thought, one contemplates only the emptiness of the fundamental nature.

Thereafter, one diligently seeks unsurpassed enlightenment; Furthermore, meeting virtuous friends who open the mind’s ignorance, The dust of the emotions is already departed and the mind is pure; All phenomena are suddenly and simultaneously realized.
The rising sun reveals a dense array of a single form; The bright mirror clearly manifests a thousand appearances.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One (as before, perform twelve prostrations).

With a sincere heart, I have completed the repentance for the karmic obstructions regarding the previously detailed, sublime causes and conditions of the golden drum seen by the Bodhisattva Subhaketu. Having finished this repentance for karmic obstructions,

I shall now, furthermore, according to that same scripture, the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions" (the chapter immediately preceding the one above), perform the repentance taught by the Buddha to Śakra, Lord of Devas.
...the Dharma, and performed repentance (this is the opening text of the chapter).
At that time, the World-Honored One dwelt in correct discernment and entered a profound, subtle, and tranquil meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
From the pores of his body, he emitted a great radiance; within that light, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various colors and all Buddha-fields appeared. Ten...
Even ten thousand Ganges-sands of such beings cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.

In this world of five turbidities, those who were illuminated by the light—including those who committed the ten evil deeds, the five crimes of immediate retribution, slandered the Triple Gem, were unfilial toward their parents and elders, or treated their teachers and the assembly of Brahmins with contempt, and who were destined to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals—each received the illumination of the light. Upon reaching...
In whatever places these sentient beings dwell, once they have seen this light, by the power of that light, they all attain peace and happiness;
they become upright and exquisite, their physical forms and characteristics become stable, and adorned with merit and wisdom, they are able to see the Buddhas.
At that time, Śakra, the assembly of all the devas, the Goddess of the Ganges, and the great multitude, having been graced by this rare light, all went to the Buddha.
Having circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, he withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One, how do sons and daughters of good family who aspire to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practice the Mahāyāna proceed?"
Regarding those who have gathered all the karmic obstructions and transgressions committed by sentient beings who are deluded and inverted:
how should they repent so that these may be eliminated? The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you are now practicing."
I desire that immeasurable and boundless sentient beings may attain pure liberation and peace and happiness. Out of compassion for the world, I seek the welfare and benefit of all.
If there are sentient beings who, due to karmic obstructions, have committed various transgressions, they should exert themselves with diligence.

During the six periods of day and night, with the right shoulder bared, the right knee touching the ground, and palms joined in reverence, one should single-mindedly focus the mind and speak these words:
"I take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
who turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, uphold and illuminate the wheel of Dharma, and rain down the great rain of the Dharma."
Beating the great Dharma drum, blowing the great Dharma conch, erecting the great Dharma banner, and holding aloft the great Dharma torch—
for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings— they constantly practice the gift of Dharma to guide and advance the deluded masses,
enabling them to attain the great fruit and realize eternal bliss. To all such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, I prostrate my body, speech, and mind, bowing with sincerity and a devoted heart.

I pay homage to those World-Honored Ones with true wisdom, with the true eye, through true realization, and with true equanimity, fully knowing and fully seeing the wholesome and unwholesome karma of all sentient beings.
(The above is the complete transcription of the scripture text; the following line consists of the compiler’s words.)
Therefore, we, together with all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu*, perform this confession according to the words of repentance taught by the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*).

[The following text is the full scripture; that is, the text of the Lotus Sūtra. These words are repeated and detailed three times; this is a confession made during the final age of the Buddha’s teaching.

From beginningless birth and death, I have followed along with the evil currents. Together with all sentient beings, I have created karmic obstructions and transgressions through greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha*, *dveṣa*, *moha*).
Bound by these fetters, while they did not yet recognize the Buddha, did not yet recognize the Dharma, did not yet recognize the Saṅgha, and did not yet recognize good and evil,

they committed crimes of immediate retribution through the actions of body, speech, and mind: shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil intent, slandering the True Dharma, causing schism in the harmonious Saṅgha,
killing an Arhat, and killing one’s father or mother— performing the three types of bodily, four types of verbal, and three types of mental actions.
The ten non-virtuous actions: committing them oneself, inciting others to do so, or rejoicing upon seeing them committed; groundlessly slandering virtuous persons;

deceiving through false weights and measures or passing off the counterfeit as genuine; giving impure food and drink to anyone; and mutually afflicting or harming one's parents within the six realms of existence;
stealing property from a stūpa, property belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters, or property belonging to the present Sangha.
They act with self-will; they take no pleasure in following the Dharma and Vinaya of the World-Honored One, nor do they comply with the instructions of their teachers.
Upon seeing practitioners of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna vehicles, they delight in reviling them, causing those practitioners to feel regret and distress.

When they see someone superior to themselves, they harbor jealousy. Regarding the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth, they are constantly stingy and parsimonious. They are shrouded in ignorance.
Their minds are shrouded by the delusions of false views; they do not cultivate wholesome causes, allowing evil to increase.
Toward the Buddhas, they give rise to slander, declaring the Dharma to be non-Dharma and non-Dharma to be Dharma.
All such transgressions, the Buddha knows and sees entirely through his true wisdom, true eye, true realization, and true equanimity. I now take refuge before all [the Buddhas].
Before the Buddha, they all confessed and revealed their faults, not daring to conceal them. Regarding sins not yet committed, they vowed never to commit them again;

regarding sins already committed, they now repent them all. May all karmic obstructions created by these deeds—those that would cause one to fall into the evil realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the realm of hungry ghosts, the asura hosts, or the eight difficult conditions—be entirely purified within this very life.
May all evil retributions be extinguished and never experienced again in the future.

Just as all the great Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have cultivated the Bodhisattva path and fully repented all their karmic obstructions, so do I now repent my own karmic obstructions.
I disclose them all completely and dare not conceal them. May the sins already committed be eliminated; as for those yet to come—
I dare not commit evil again.
Having finished my repentance, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
After the Buddha had instructed him to repent as above, he further addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, saying: "Good son, by these causes and conditions..."
If one has committed a transgression, it must not be concealed for even a single moment, let alone for a day and night or for many days.

If one has committed an offense and seeks purification, one should harbor a sense of shame and remorse, believing that there will inevitably be a retribution in the future and giving rise to great dread;
one should perform repentance in this manner, just as when a person's head is being burned by fire, they strive to extinguish it with all speed.
If the fire is not extinguished, the mind finds no peace. It is the same for one who has committed an offense: one should immediately repent so that it may be swiftly extinguished and eliminated.

If there is a wish to be born into a wealthy and prosperous family with abundant riches and treasures, and if one further desires to resolve to practice the Mahāyāna, one should likewise repent to eliminate karmic obstructions. If one wishes to be born into a noble and eminent Brahmin family...
...caste. Even those born into a Kṣatriya family or as a Wheel-Turning King endowed with the seven treasures should likewise repent and eliminate their karmic obstructions.
Good son, if one wishes to be reborn among the various devas, even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one must also repent and eliminate karmic obstructions.
If one seeks the fruit of a Stream-enterer, or even the stage of a sovereign Bodhisattva, up to the ultimate...

Throughout the entire earth, those who seek all-knowledge and are perfectly awakened ones (*samyaksambuddha*)—the possessors of universal knowledge—should likewise repent and eliminate their karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Why is this? Good son, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
As the Tathāgata has taught, distinct characteristics give rise to distinct perceptions, and causes and conditions cease. Therefore, all such past phenomena have already ceased.
All karmic obstructions are exhausted, leaving nothing remaining. These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*), which had not yet manifested in the present life, now arise;
future karmic obstructions shall never again arise. Why is this? Good son, all dharmas are empty, as the Tathāgata has taught.

Therein is no self (*ātman*), no person (*pudgala*), no sentient being (*sattva*), and no life-span (*jīva*). Furthermore, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor even the dharma of emptiness itself. Good son...
"Son of good family, all phenomena rely upon the fundamental source, yet they cannot be described. Why is this? Because they transcend all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

If there are sons or daughters of good family who thus enter into the subtle and wondrous True Principle and give rise to a heart of faith and reverence, this is called 'sentient beings possessing the fundamental source.
For this reason, it is said that through repentance, [faults] are extinguished and eliminated."
Regarding the karmic obstructions: the assembly of disciples has already completed the recitation of the sūtra text for the repentance of karmic obstructions.
Now, returning to the sequence of the following sūtra text, I shall personally express our intention of sympathetic joy, exhortation, and dedication. The sūtra says: "Good son..."
There are four types of karmic obstructions that are difficult to repent and eliminate. What are the four? First, committing grave offenses against the bodhisattva vows;
second, giving rise to slanderous thoughts toward the Mahāyāna sūtras; third, being unable to develop one's own faculties;
and fourth, being greedily attached to the three realms of existence and lacking the mind of renunciation. Furthermore, there are four kinds of remedial measures for these karmic obstructions.

What are the four? (Confession, Entreaty, Rejoicing, and Dedication. First, with a sincere heart, one approaches all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and confesses all transgressions.
Second, for the sake of all sentient beings, one entreats all Buddhas to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma.
Third, one rejoices in all the merits and virtues possessed by all sentient beings. Fourth, [all that...]
All merits and roots of goodness are entirely dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

(Various commentators have followed the texts of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and others by first performing the request for teaching and subsequently rejoicing; however, following this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the "Chapter on Vows" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, one first rejoices and subsequently makes the requests.
Therefore, we, fully relying upon the method of rejoicing taught by the Tathāgata to Śakra Devendra, perform this act of rejoicing.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, among all the sons and daughters of good family in the world who practice the Mahāyāna, there are those who are able to practice it and those who are not.
How can they obtain the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) for the roots of goodness and merit of all sentient beings?
The Buddha said: "Sons and daughters of good family, if the assembly, though not yet [established] in the Mahāyāna..."

One is able to practice this. Thus, throughout the six periods of day and night, one should bare the right shoulder, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms in reverence, and with single-minded concentration, cultivate sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
At that time, one will obtain immeasurable merit. One should speak as follows:
"I have now deeply given rise to sympathetic joy for all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are currently practicing giving, morality, mental cultivation, and wisdom."
By virtue of performing such rejoicing in merit, one will certainly obtain a result that is honored, distinguished, unsurpassed, peerless, and most excellent.
In this way, I rejoice in all the roots of goodness belonging to all sentient beings of the past and the future.
Furthermore, regarding those bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who have first set out on the path and generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*)...
I wholeheartedly rejoice in and praise all the merits of those who dwell in the stage of being born only once more before attaining Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Furthermore, regarding all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions— who have realized wondrous Bodhi and, for the sake of delivering boundless sentient beings,
turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and practice unimpeded Dharma-giving— I, out of compassion, exhort and transform them...
I rejoice in all the merits that cause all sentient beings to believe and accept [the Dharma], so that they may all receive the gift of the Dharma, be fully satisfied,
and attain inexhaustible peace and happiness. I likewise rejoice with a sincere heart in all the merits of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
praising them all.
Having expressed sympathetic joy, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

We have thus far followed the teachings in our expression of sympathetic joy; if our minds and their objects are in accord and correspond to the principle, we shall know that the merits spoken of by the Buddha are immeasurable.
Therefore, the subsequent passage of the sutra states: "Good son, having expressed sympathetic joy in this manner, you should..."

One attains a holy assembly of immeasurable merit. Suppose all sentient beings within as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were to sever their afflictions and become arhats.
If a son or daughter of good family were to provide them with offerings of the finest clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for as long as they live, it would be thus.
This merit does not equal even one-thousandth of the merit of rejoicing as previously described. Why is this?

The merit of making offerings is finite and measurable, for it does not encompass all merits; whereas the merit of rejoicing is immeasurable and infinite, capable of encompassing all merits of the three periods of time.
Therefore, if a person desires to increase their superior roots of goodness, [they should practice rejoicing].
One should cultivate such merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
With a sincere heart, one should exhort all [beings].

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you have already fully explained the merit of sympathetic joy. [Now please explain] the merit of exhortation..."
“O Virtuous One, I pray that you will explain this, so that all bodhisattvas of the future may turn the wheel of Dharma, and those bodhisattvas of the present may correctly practice it.

The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of the Devas: “If there are sons or daughters of good family who aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should practice the path of the three vehicles. Such a person...”
During the six periods of day and night, maintaining the same dignified posture as before, one should single-mindedly focus the mind and speak these words:

"I now take refuge in all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions—those who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma, and those who wish to relinquish their reward bodies (*vipākakāya*) and enter *nirvāṇa*. To all of them, I pay homage with utmost sincerity."

I respectfully entreat you to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, to rain down the great rain of Dharma, to kindle the great torch of Dharma, to illuminate the principles of reality, and to bestow the unimpeded Dharma.

May you enter true *parinirvāṇa* while remaining long in this world to deliver, liberate, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, as previously described, until their ultimate and inexhaustible peace and happiness.
Having made these entreaties, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Triple Gem and the assembly.
...and so forth. Thus far, we have relied upon the sūtra to offer this exhortation. If one can bring the mind and its objects into correspondence, the merit will be immeasurable.
Therefore, the sūtra below states: "Good son, suppose there were a person who offered the seven treasures, filling the entirety of the trichiliocosm, as an offering to the Tathāgata;
yet, if there were another person who exhorted the Tathāgata to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, the merit obtained by the latter would [far exceed that of the former]."

...its merit is superior to that. Why is this? That is the gift of material wealth; this is the gift of the Dharma. Son of good family, let alone the gift of the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm;

if a person were to take the seven treasures filling as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and offer them to all Buddhas, even the merit of such an exhortation would be superior to [the former].
That Dharma-giving possesses five benefits. What are the five? First, Dharma-giving benefits both oneself and others, whereas material giving does not.
Second, Dharma-giving enables sentient beings to transcend the triple world, while the merit of material giving does not extend beyond the desire realm.
Third, Dharma-giving can purify the Dharma-body, whereas material giving only increases [the physical body].

First, form [is perishable]. Second, the Dharma-gift is inexhaustible, whereas the material gift is finite. Third, the Dharma-gift can sever ignorance, while the material gift merely suppresses craving and attachment.
Therefore, son of good family, the merit of exhortation and entreaty is boundless and difficult to illustrate by analogy.
When I was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, I exhorted the Buddhas and the Brahma Kings and others to turn the great wheel of Dharma for me.
Good son, I requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma because I desired to deliver, liberate, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
In the past, for the sake of practicing for enlightenment, I exhorted the Tathāgata to remain long in the world and not enter parinirvāṇa.
By virtue of this root of goodness, I have attained the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, and even the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
After my nirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall abide for a long time; my Dharma-body and sublime marks are pure beyond compare, emerging from—
The realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the practice of the great bodhisattvas, and all such things as these are, in their essence, no different from non-existence.
All of this is due to the power of the roots of goodness resulting from the merit of exhortation. Such a dharmakāya as this I have now attained.
Therefore, if there are those who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, regarding all [phenomena]...
If the roots of merit and goodness from explaining even a single sentence or a single verse of a sutra to others are already boundless,
how much more so when one exhorts the Tathāgata to turn the great wheel of Dharma, to remain long in the world, and not to enter parinirvāṇa?
With a sincere heart, he dedicated [the merit].

At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if good sons and good daughters, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, cultivate the path of the three vehicles, how should they dedicate all their roots of goodness?"
[They] are directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). The Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"Good son, if there are sentient beings who, desiring to seek awakening (*bodhi*), cultivate the path of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and wish to dedicate all their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), they should, during the six periods of day and night, with profound respect and a most sincere mind, speak as follows:
'From beginningless saṃsāra until now, regarding the Three Jewels (*triratna*), I have practiced...'"
All roots of goodness thus accomplished— even giving a single morsel of food to an animal, or reconciling others with kind words through the pure Dharma,
or taking the three refuges and the various precepts, or likewise performing confession, entreaty, and sympathetic joy— [are dedicated].
I now bring all roots of goodness to mind and fully embrace them. With a heart free from regret or stinginess, I dedicate them for the benefit of all sentient beings.
These roots of goodness conducive to liberation are as they are known and seen by the Buddha, the World-Honored One—inconceivable, unimpeded, and pure.
All such meritorious roots of goodness I entirely dedicate to all [sentient beings].
Sentient beings do not abide in a mind of signs, nor do they abandon a mind of signs. I likewise dedicate all these roots of merit and virtue to all sentient beings.

May they all obtain wish-fulfilling jewels that emerge from space, fulfilling the aspirations of all beings with inexhaustible wealth and joy, and infinite wisdom, such that their eloquence in the sublime Dharma is entirely unimpeded. Together with all...
May all sentient beings together realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Furthermore,
just as the merits and roots of goodness of all the great bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present were entirely dedicated toward all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*),
so too shall I now dedicate all my merits and roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (from this point onward, one should form the following vow): "May I, together with all sentient beings, collectively attain perfect enlightenment.
Just as the other Buddhas sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and defeated the immeasurable hosts of the Māra Pāpīyān;
may I likewise perceive, awaken to, and thoroughly penetrate all such things, illuminating them all within a single kṣaṇa."
At the end of the night, I attained the Dharma of Ambrosia and realized its meaning. May I and all sentient beings together realize the wondrous enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
Having completed the dedication and the making of vows, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
The four sections of the Dharma gate, beginning from the confession and ending with the dedication, are collectively titled "The Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions."
This very wisdom removes the remaining obstacles. One must possess the four gates. At the conclusion of these four gates, the merits are praised in general, saying:
