Although (although is a concessive particle used to introduce the following phrase; although he has surpassed the preceding stages, he has not yet reached the tenth bhūmi), he is steadfast.

"Solid" (*dṛḍha*) has the meaning of "vajra. Because of the three types of dedication, one's practice and understanding become solid, making it possible to enter the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). For this reason, within the *Śīla* [section], they are called the "Ten Vajras," while in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (*Benevolent Kings Sūtra*), they are called the "Ten Solids" (*daśadṛḍha*).

"Before ascending to the noble realm of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), Since these are worthy persons (*bhadra*) who accord with awakening, The name 'worthy position' (*bhadrapada*) first becomes appropriate.

This sūtra merely says "those who have not yet entered the stages" (*apraviṣṭabhūmika*) because they accord with the nature of awakening; it does not explicitly mention the "worthy positions. Other sūtras, however, speak of the "three worthies" (*traya-bhadra*).
Therefore, these two phrases harmonize and integrate these two meanings.
Good son, that which has illumination and that which has awareness are both termed obstructions. For this reason, the Bodhisattva dwells in constant awareness without abiding;
illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescent extinction. It is like a person who severs their own head: because the head has already been severed, there is [no longer any subject].

As for "one who can sever": it is by means of an obstructing mind that one causes all obstructions to cease of themselves. Once the obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no longer anyone who extinguishes the obstructions.
The teachings of the *Sūtras* are like a finger pointing at the moon; once one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon.
All the various verbal expressions of the Tathāgatas used to instruct Bodhisattvas are likewise so. This is called the Bodhisattva’s [realization].
Regarding "entering the stages" (*bhūmi*): it is to accord with the nature of awakening.
The first two [stages] describe the stage of application (*prayoga*) as the cause and condition for entering the Path;

through the power of dedication, the mind becomes vast and empty. Through diligent application, one enters the stream of the sages (the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*).

The first set of four dharmas constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the proximate means for entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*). These dharmas rely upon the four types of discursive investigation (*vitarka*) and the four types of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Regarding the establishment of the four types of discursive investigation in the initial and final stages:

one investigates name (*nāman*), object (*artha*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and particularity (*viśeṣa*) as being conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent. Because one thoroughly knows these four to be devoid of consciousness and that consciousness itself does not exist, this is called "knowledge of reality. Since name and object differ in character, they are sought separately; since the two pairs share similar characteristics, they are considered together.

Based on the concentration of "attainment of clarity" (*vidarśana-labdha-samādhi*), one initiates inferior discursive investigation and contemplates the absence of an apprehended object (*grāhya*); this is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). This means that within this stage, one first contemplates that the four dharmas—name and so forth—which constitute the apprehended object, are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as conventional designations and being ultimately unfindable.

It is called "Illumination" (*āloka*) because it is the precursor to the attainment of the sun of wisdom. Since it is also the precursor to the fire of the path thus attained, it is further named "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Next, relying on the concentration of Increasing Illumination (*ālokavṛddhi-samādhi*), one gives rise to superior reflection and contemplates the absence of an object of apprehension; this is established as the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).

That is to say, within this stage, one repeatedly contemplates that the four factors—name and so forth—which constitute the object of apprehension, are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations and being ultimately unfindable. Because the signs of illumination become increasingly intense, it is called "Increasing Illumination. This marks the culmination of the stage of reflection.

Therefore, it is further called "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). Relying on the concentration of "conformity" (*ānulomika-samādhi*), one gives rise to the lower "knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and definitively confirms the absence of the grasped object (*grāhya*). Within the absence of the grasper (*grāhaka*), one likewise conforms to and endures this state. Since there is no real object, how could there be a real consciousness apart from the grasper-consciousness? For the grasped and the grasper are established only in mutual dependence.

At the time of this confirmation, conformity, and endurance, these are collectively termed "Endurance" (*kṣānti*). Because it confirms the preceding stage and conforms to the subsequent one, it is given the name "Conformity-Endurance. Furthermore, because it endures the emptiness of both object and consciousness, it is also called "Endurance.

Relying on the "uninterrupted" concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the higher "knowledge of reality as it is," which confirms the emptiness of both types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). This establishes the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). That is to say, while the preceding "Higher Endurance" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) only confirms the emptiness of the grasper, the present Supreme Mundane Dharma doubly confirms the emptiness of both. From...

This is the "uninterrupted" [stage], for one must necessarily enter the Path of Seeing; thus it is given the name "uninterrupted. Because it is the most excellent among the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

In this way, during the stages of Heat (*ūṣmagata*) and Peak (*mūrdhan*), based on the grasping consciousness, one contemplates the emptiness of the grasped object. When the lower stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) arises, one confirms the empty characteristic of the object. At the stage of the middle stage of Patience, regarding the grasping consciousness, one confirms that the object is empty and accords with the joyful acceptance [of that truth].

When the upper stage of Patience arises, one confirms the emptiness of the grasping [consciousness]. The Supreme Mundane Dharma confirms the empty characteristic of both. Since all of these still involve mental images (*nimitta*), they have not yet realized the ultimate reality. Therefore, it is said that within these four stages, the Bodhisattva still establishes a slight entity before them, namely, that which is the true ultimate nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). This is because those two—emptiness and existence—[are still being held as dualities].

The characteristics have not yet been eliminated; because one observes the mind while still retaining these characteristics, there is something apprehended. Therefore, one does not truly abide in the principle of true *vijñapti-mātratā*. Thus, that verse says: "To posit a slight object before oneself, claiming it to be the nature of *vijñapti-mātratā*, is due to the fact that there is something apprehended."

It is not yet truly abiding in consciousness-only; only after that consciousness has ceased does one truly abide [in suchness]. Therefore, it is now said that one has "entered the stream of the noble ones" (*ārya-srotas*).

Names, meanings, and natures differ, yet there is nothing to be grasped. Having reached the pinnacle through investigation, the seal [of realization] accords with former practice and is empty of both past and future.
There is no question regarding what remains; even the slightest thing appearing before one still lingers.

Although it belongs to the world, it is the most supreme; in the moment immediately following, it is the peer of the Dharma (where "peer" [chou] means companion or classmate, referring to its outflow and kind).
The next four lines describe the realization of the Path (the first half clarifies what was previously non-existent, while the remainder explicitly explains the characteristics of realization).

Only now do we know that both illumination and awareness are termed "obstructions. When you look with your eyes—the pupils within the eyes—there is truly something to be grasped (for awareness to illuminate awareness and for the eyes to look at the eyes is to be ashamed of one's own folly).
Just as the eye cannot see itself yet is not hindered from seeing what is present, so too, while nature does not self-awaken, it is not hindered from being eternally aware; thus it is said below:
"Eternal awareness does not abide. Eternal awareness does not preclude eternal non-abiding.
The illumination and the illuminator cease simultaneously; wisdom finds nothing to be apprehended within its objects. (As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states in the verse on the Path of Vision:
"When, with respect to the object, wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended... Free from both the grasped and the grasper, it is profoundly secluded and deep. (The following verse says:

"Because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings, at that time one abides in consciousness-only. Below this, the prose commentary on Consciousness-Only harmonizes this sutra passage as follows:)
"Constantly awakening to this sutra" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (this is from that treatise).

"Not abiding in this sutra" has no connection with being subsumed under frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) (this is the treatise’s own commentary on the verse: "because there is nothing among the various phenomena of frivolous proliferation to be abandoned";

it is precisely this phrase "not abiding" in the sutra). "Non-apprehension" is also the meaning of "not abiding. At that time, one attains the dwelling in perfectly luminous awakening (the treatise says: "At that time...").

At that time, one abides in the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). This nature of consciousness is precisely this *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment). Now, following the tenet of the Sūtra, it is called "Awakening.
Wisdom is equal to and pervasive throughout True Suchness (*tathatā*), as it is said: "Wisdom and True Suchness are equal and equal.
It is like the sun shining upon the sky, or a luminous pearl illuminating its own substance; it is also like a person attempting to sever their own head.
The sun of wisdom and true emptiness are without dual characteristics; the pearl of the mind fundamentally illuminates, free from causes and conditions.
When the obstructing mind is extinguished within the mind itself, once extinguished, there is no longer an enemy to be extinguished (such as someone who would destroy me).
That [previous case] was like an enemy; now it is not so.

The following three verses take the aforementioned path of realization (pramāṇa-mārga) and contrast it with the subsequent path of teaching (deśanā-mārga), thereby synthesizing and harmonizing them according to the scriptural passages of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, specifically the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
As the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "One attains the wisdom of the sūtras and śāstras."

Within the stages (*bhūmi*) of the two paths—teaching (*deśanā-mārga*) and realization (*adhigama-mārga*)—"superior" (*viśiṣṭa*) means preeminent. Vasubandhu’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* explains this by opening it into nine pairs. Regarding each instance of "realization," it says: "The path of teaching and the path of realization are called the two paths;

since the stage of entry (*praveśa-bhūmi*) is particularly superior, it is here termed 'superior'. The path of realization is profoundly deep, thereby perfecting the path of teaching. Vasubandhu composed this treatise in nine times nine [sections].
When the illumination occurs, it is solely for the purpose of eliminating subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

Universally illuminating billions of boundless [lands]—[as that sutra says: "This vision [sees] many hundreds of Buddha-lands and rules over many hundreds of worlds"]—one awakens to the scriptural texts of the Buddha’s teaching, which are free from words and phrases.
Having attained the wisdom of the sutras and śāstras, one continues to seek diligently;
though this present sutra is brief, it is nonetheless identical to the two [other versions]. One should know that it is the stream praised by the noble principles.
The former is the gate of realization (shōmon) and the latter is the gate of teaching (kyōmon); both are non-abiding, which is precisely their mutual inclusion.
(Non-abiding in these two means that the two paths are perfected. Since teaching is realization and realization is teaching, they are mutually identical, and thus mutually inclusive.
Next, the teaching path is explained individually.
Just as when a person points with their finger at the new moon, the wise look toward the crescent moon in the sky;
yet if they become fixated on the tip of the finger, they do not see the moon. To lose both paths is to turn them into a burden.
The principle resides in the ground of the mind, not in words; how could one search for truth within words?
The moon is in the sky and not upon the finger; seeking the moon at the fingertip is truly in vain.
When one’s words and realization accord with this non-abiding, only then can it be called the healing of the disease of the Dharma (*dharma-glāna*).
This is the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) by one who accords with awakening.
“O son of good family, the sun of true wisdom has already shone;
all hindrances are themselves ultimate awakening. Whether mindfulness is maintained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation.
Whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvana. Wisdom and folly are both universally the *prajñā*. As for Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists...”

The Dharma of Accomplishment: Awakening is one and the same; ignorance and suchness are not distinct realms. All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and delusion, are collectively the Brahma-conduct.
Sentient beings and their lands share the same dharma-nature; the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands.
Those with nature and those without nature alike achieve the Buddha-way. All afflictions are ultimately liberated. The Dharma...
Dhātusāgaraprajñā, you clearly illuminate all marks as being like empty space; this is called the Tathāgata’s awakening in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Having previously departed from the realms of toil and affliction throughout vast eons, you have now for the first time entered the Tathāgata’s *dharmatā*.
Moving solely toward the path of the sages and forever departing from the state of ordinary beings, you single-mindedly accord with principle and are liberated from the cage of bondage.
Next, regarding the differences between cause and effect within the "Pervading the Holy" (tōjō):

now that the fruit of Buddhahood is realized, ordinary beings and sages are fused; therefore, there are both similarities and differences compared to the causal gate. (The similarity lies in the identical principle of the purity of the sages;
the difference lies in its encompassing of the defilements of ordinary beings. It is entirely in accord with the spontaneous (*jinen*), eternally ultimate. (Spontaneity is the fundamental...)
Awakening. That which is "completely merged" is called ultimate awakening because it does not abide in initial awakening. Because consciousness and wisdom do not coexist, it is perfectly penetrating.
Next, the characteristics of the Buddha-fruit are correctly described:
all obstacles are themselves numinous awareness; all *tathatā* (suchness) is entirely interfused. (This explains the initial general heading.)
The following explains that the ten pairs of dual characteristics are not different: 1. The power of mindfulness brings liberation whether in existence or non-existence;
2. The formation and destruction of the dharma-realm are both entirely true emptiness; 3–4. Folly and wisdom, the heterodox and the orthodox, all constitute prajñā;
5. Ignorance and true nature are both equally honored; 6–7. Precepts and concentration, as well as greed and anger, are all pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
The dark paths of hell and the celestial palaces, sentient and non-sentient (realms)—all are one *dharmatā* (the seventh point restated).
Whether possessing nature or lacking nature, they realize the Perfect Teaching (the ninth).
All together achieve the Unsurpassed Way; what further afflictions could there be to obscure them? (the tenth).
Later, through comprehensive discernment, the dharmadhātu is established;
the light of wisdom constantly shines, clearly illuminating it. Thus, all phenomena are made equal to space;
this is the Tathāgata’s awakening in accordance with reality—the Great Majestic Hero in the state of Vairocana’s fruition.
Good son, it is simply that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts;
yet they do not suppress or extinguish these deluded minds. They abide within the realm of delusive thought, which cannot be fully known, and thus remain in a state of non-knowing.
They do not discern the reality. Yet those sentient beings, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear;

this is precisely what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening. Good sons, you should know that such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as to great Bodhisattvas, and have planted the roots of all virtues.
The Buddha said that such a person is called one who has accomplished all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Although their stages and positions vary according to conditions, during cultivation one cannot calculate the distance traveled;
for when in accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), there are originally no discriminatory thoughts, yet this does not hinder the various levels from naturally increasing in clarity.
The Buddha said: "You bodhisattvas and the multitude of ordinary beings in future times—throughout all time, do not give rise to thoughts.
Even if the deluded mind does not cease, teach it to abide in stillness;
yet within this state of non-discrimination, there remains a deluded sentiment."
The World-Honored One himself has taught the Dharma for settling the mind: The Southern School and the Northern Patriarchs should not contend.

When sentient beings hear this Dharma, If they believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without alarm, This is truly called "conforming to awakening. How could the stages of the sages and worthies be difficult to achieve?
This person has already made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having planted all roots of virtue, their merit is full.
The Buddha himself grants them a clear prediction of enlightenment; "All-Knowledge" (Sarvākārajñatā) is their name.
With a sincere heart, they repent.
The assembly has come forward to rely upon the instructions of the Heavenly Drum to universally purify the three karmas of all sentient beings throughout the peripheral reaches of the Dharma-realm.

Having completed this general confession, we shall now proceed with the following scriptural text to once again rely upon the Heavenly Drum for a specific exposition of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
By observing the root source of sinful karma, we shall sweep away subtle delusions and extinguish all views, thereby performing our confession.
At that time, having heard these words, the sons of the gods attained a realization of the Dharma and their hearts were filled with great joy.
They asked, "How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva repent and eliminate all faults and evils?

Then, by the power of the roots of goodness from the bodhisattva’s samādhi, the celestial drum emitted a voice and declared, "Sons of the gods, the bodhisattva knows that all karmas do not [arise] from..."
They do not come from the east, nor from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below; yet they gather together and abide upon the mind.
They arise solely from inversion and have no place of abiding. The Bodhisattva thus perceives with certainty and clarity, free from doubt or confusion.
O sons of the gods, it is like my celestial drum, which speaks of karma, speaks of retribution, speaks of conduct, speaks of precepts, and speaks of joy.
They speak of peace; they speak of various samādhis. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are likewise:

they speak of a self, they speak of what belongs to a self, they speak of sentient beings, and they speak of the various karmas of greed, hatred, and delusion. Yet in reality, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
All the karmas performed and the retributions of the six realms of existence cannot be found when sought throughout the ten directions. O sons of the gods, it is like the sound of the word "self."
Neither arising nor ceasing, the various devas who have committed evil hear no other sound; they hear only the sounds that awaken them regarding the hells.
All karmic actions are likewise neither arising nor ceasing; according to what has been cultivated and accumulated, one receives its retribution.
O sons of the gods, just as the sounds produced by my celestial drum cannot be exhausted throughout immeasurable kalpas.
There is no interruption; whether coming or going, they are all ungraspable. Yet, throughout immeasurable worlds, according to the minds of sentient beings, they enable all to hear them.
It is the same for all Buddhas: according to the minds of sentient beings, they cause all to see them.
O sons of the gods, it is as if there were a crystal mirror; how could it not reflect? Pure, clear, and transparent, it is like [the ten...]
The dimensions of its boundaries are perfectly equal, immeasurable, and boundless.
Within it, all mountains and rivers, all sentient beings, and even those in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts—all their reflected images—appear therein.
O sons of the gods, what do you think? Can it be said that those various images come and enter into the mirror, or [depart from] the mirror?
"Does it go? He replied, "No. "O sons of the gods, all karmic actions are likewise:
although they can produce various virtuous fruits and retributions, they have no place from which they come or to which they go. To know this is true repentance;
thereby all evils and transgressions become entirely purified. Now, relying on the principle and wisdom of this chapter, one further employs the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
The verses for repentance within this chapter are as follows:

I now repent of all the evil karma I have created in the past, which arose from my body, speech, and mind, and was caused by beginningless greed, anger, and delusion. All of it, I now confess and repent.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

When the Celestial Drum expounded this method of repentance on the nature-emptiness of karmic retribution, within worlds as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields,
the various devaputras of Tuṣita attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), which is immeasurable and inconceivable.
During the discussion on the *asaṃkhyeya* [aeons], the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāma-deva*) resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Within the six heavens of desire, all the celestial maidens (*devī*) likewise relinquished their female bodies and gave rise to the aspiration for supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi-citta*).

At that time, because the sons of the gods heard the exposition of Samantabhadra’s vast and great dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), they attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and acquired the adornments of the various powers (*bala*).
The Samādhi of Adornment: By means of the three pure karmas equal in number to all sentient beings, one repents and eliminates all heavy obstructions.
Consequently, one immediately sees lotus flowers made of the seven treasures, as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields.
Upon each flower sits a bodhisattva in the full lotus posture, emitting great radiance. Each of those bodhisattvas, in turn, follows...

Excellent. He emits rays of light equal in number to all sentient beings. Within those rays of light, there are Buddhas equal in number to all sentient beings, sitting in the full lotus posture, preaching the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings' minds.

Make this vow with a sincere heart (from the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the fourth of the ten vows: the vow not to be separated from the conditions of virtuous friends; and the third: the vow to diligently cultivate the two benefits).
May those who share my same path be gathered together in all places (the original text says: "always assembled");
may their actions of body, speech, and mind be entirely identical, and may they practice and study together all their deeds and vows—those very spiritual friends who benefit me.
Reveal to me the gateway of Samantabhadra (the text reads "conduct"), and may you also join me in assembly;
may I always give rise to a mind of joy (the text reads "heart").
May I cultivate the pure pāramitās and never forget the bodhicitta, eradicating all defilements and obscurations without remainder.
All sublime practices are fully accomplished;
the mind is liberated from all afflictions, karma, demonic realms, and the worldly path—
like the sun and moon that do not abide in the sky, and like the lotus flower that is not stained by water.
Having made this vow above, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
I address the assembly: please listen as I recite these verses on impermanence at this moment.
Ordinary people frequently encounter the hardships of illness; In recent times, I have seen many pass away.
The sound of wailing in the streets and alleys is ever in my ears; Graveyards in the desolate outskirts gradually form long rows.
Knowing for certain that neither young nor old can ultimately escape this, How could one not feel sorrow upon reflection?
All those gathered in this hall are guests from the Yellow Springs; Who can guarantee that their own bodies shall endure for long?
Awakening to this matter of impermanence, One should early seek to realize the True Constant. Eternal bliss lies within impermanence; suffering and joy reside in the human heart.
(Below this, it quotes the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, saying: All things depend largely upon the mind.
Just as wind, water, and fire, Following whatever causes and conditions they encounter, The mind likewise moves and turns;
It can depart with great speed, And it can also return with great speed.
It quickly leads one to the heavens, And quickly causes one to enter the evil realms. If one can guard and protect the mind, There is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

Seventeenth: He praised the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, saying that the mind, consciousness, and mentation are all unapprehendable; yet, by virtue of knowing the immeasurable, he knows the mind of the Tathāgata.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is the basis for all mundane and supramundane wisdoms. And...

The Tathāgata’s wisdom has no basis (1). Furthermore, it constantly gives rise to both mundane and supramundane wisdom, yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom neither increases nor decreases (2), like the great ocean.
Its waters flow secretly through the lands of the four continents and the eighty billion sub-continents;
wherever one digs, there is none who does not find water. Yet that great ocean does not form the discrimination: "I am producing [this water]."
Water. The ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it flows into the hearts of all sentient beings.
If sentient beings observe their objects and cultivate the Dharma-gates, they immediately attain wisdom that is pure and lucid.
Yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom is equal and non-dual, devoid of discrimination; it is only because the mental activities of sentient beings differ that the wisdom they obtain varies accordingly.
Wisdom is distinct in each case (the third). With a sincere heart,

I take refuge and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha-viśvārāja, who asks about the expedient means for cultivation and realization within the Great Treasury of Radiance in the Mahāvaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates outside;
those who come from the various directions do not follow only a single path. Likewise, all bodhisattvas adorn buddha-lands and realize enlightenment through manifold skillful means.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim for us all these gradual skillful means."

Furthermore, how many types of practitioners are there in total, so that the bodhisattvas in this assembly and those sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who seek the Mahāyāna may swiftly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s ocean of great nirvāṇa?
The preceding exposition on the universal clarity of contemplative practice is concluded.

Because it encompasses both those of sharp and dull faculties, it is termed "universal," referring to the stages of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, as well as what is abandoned and realized. From cause to fruit, throughout this single period of life, those of superior capacity are able to cultivate and abandon based upon this;
while those of middling capacity, though they do practice, have dense residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
With majestic virtue, he took pity on them and reverently entreated the Buddha; He separately opened up expedient means to assist their prior efforts.

Although the words of the Buddhas and sages are complete for those who follow awakening, Because the faculties of the sharp and dull differ and the power of their minds varies, He accordingly divided the paths as was appropriate, So that each may enter according to their capacity and all return to the ultimate source.
Just as there is a great city that, though being one, Must have gates on all four sides;
one cannot enter from the south if one has approached from the east, nor from the north. Each follows its respective direction—how could it deviate from the center?
I pray that the World-Honored One will explain extensively The skillful means and gradual stages that accord with true emptiness.
"And how many kinds of practitioners are there who are all led to awaken and enter the palace of Nirvāṇa?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. Son of good family, the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades the ten directions and gives birth [to all things]."
The Tathāgata is of one essence and equal to all phenomena; regarding all practices, there is truly no duality.
While the skillful means that accord with them are immeasurable in number, when fully encompassing their ultimate destination, there are three types of distinctions between cultivation and nature.
His majestic virtue and speech accorded with the Sage’s intent; The World-Honored One immediately granted permission to proclaim it.
Although various practices were opened according to the ailments, Do not allow yourself to be deluded by desire; awaken the King of Minds.
The awakened mind is subtle, wondrous, and originally supreme; It fills the void and pervades the ten directions.
This alone is that which transcends all Buddhas; it is equal in number to all dharmas, true and eternal.
Sentient beings are deluded by this and give rise to false views;

Since this is but a floating thought, how could it reach True quiescence?
Only when one can know the absolute, numinous mind And the Middle Way contemplation—its function perfected and its manifestation thus— Is the goal truly attained."
Eight: Five. The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are called by this skillful means *dhyāna*.
This is translated as "meditative concentration" (*zhènglù*); its meaning corresponds to the equilibrium of meditative stabilization (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), without partiality.
The Master [Zhiyi] spoke of the "Numinous Mind of the Middle Way" to manifest its true creation from the single source of ultimate reality;
within the text on the arising of practice, it is absolute and without dependence precisely because both extremes are extinguished and both are fully preserved.
Thus, the three layers of negation serve the two meanings, and the principle of absolute non-dependence is clearly evident.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is titled "The Characteristic of Renunciation" (*śe-ming*).

It is also titled "The Abandonment of Both Motion and Stillness" (*yung-ching-erh-ju-tuan*). *Upekṣā* (translated here as *yōu-pi-ch'a*) means "equanimity" (*samaprasthāna*). [This is the original text's "equanimity," which refers to the simultaneous preservation of both; this is the meaning of *dhyāna*.

Furthermore, it is said that *upekṣā* means "non-contention," "non-contemplation," and "non-practice"; this is the meaning of absolute transcendence. It further teaches the equalizing of concentration and wisdom, with the mind focused single-mindedly.

The "double negation that transcends dependence" above (referring to the commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) intends to facilitate the cultivation of the practice by eliminating forgetfulness regarding conditions.

The "double affirmation of simultaneous integration" (referring to *dhyāna-samādhi*) signifies that the meaning is only perfected when both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are embraced together.
Both double negation and double affirmation are the Middle Way.
Transcending dependence, all things are unified and harmonized, entirely free from extremes; simply examine the meaning of the three sections of the scriptural text:

(1) "Transcending dependence" refers back to the aforementioned three layers—this is the double negation (*ubhayānta-varjana*). (2) "The numinous mind" refers back to the character for "gate" (*mukha*)—this is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). (3) "Samādhi and Prajñā, etc. concludes with the name *dhyāna*—this is the simultaneous unification (*samatā-saṃyoga*).
One will find that my own interpretation is highly refined and precise.

Chapter Nine: Eight. Having concluded the three gates by explaining the preceding text and various teachings according to their respective sections, from here on we shall evaluate the three types of names;
these are all designated as "Awakening. One has already heard the six chapters of the sutra from the preceding section.

The first chapter awakens to the realization of non-arising and non-ceasing (answering Mañjuśrī, it says: "Within non-arising, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing"; and further: "There is also no body or mind that undergoes birth and death").
"Because there is ultimately no arising or ceasing, and no knowing or seeing. Therefore, this clarity and auspiciousness quells deluded sentiments;

secondly, one realizes that all phenomena are illusory. (The answer to Samantabhadra says: "The illusion of sentient beings is extinguished by relying on illusion itself. ... continuing until the answer to Samantabhadra says:

"Because the illusory body is extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; the illusory objects are also extinguished; even the extinction of illusion is extinguished," concluding with "because of manifesting clarity. Consequently, illusory wisdom arises to transform all living beings. (At the end of this chapter it says:)

The illusory appearances are forever departed; this refers to the previous statement that when illusion ceases, it too ceases. Furthermore, it says: "This is the perfect and wondrous practice of all Bodhisattvas," which corresponds to the previous statement that what is not illusory does not cease, and that when defilements are exhausted, clarity manifests.

"Shadows vanish and emptiness dissolves, and awakening is revealed. (In response to Puyan, it further states: When defilements are exhausted, their opposites are eliminated; thus there is no opposing defilement. Because Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas who teach through names and doctrines, as well as the cessation of images, have been removed, there is purity without direction and pervasiveness throughout empty space.

That which is revealed by awakening is because awakening is perfectly luminous; thus the mind's purity is revealed. This applies to the sense organs, objects, consciousnesses, locations, and elements, and so forth.)
All serve to eliminate doubt (Vajragarbha Chapter); desire to sever craving (Maitreya Chapter);
from beginning to end, they accord with awakening to realize perfect clarity (Viśuddhamati Chapter—meaning that the final three chapters also merely fulfill the preceding three).

This corresponds to the three characteristics of *Nirvāṇa* (where it says: "Because it is devoid of the ten characteristics, it is called Great *Nirvāṇa*"). [The practitioner] constantly cultivates the characteristics of meditative concentration, wisdom, and equanimity among the ranks of monks. Then...

The severance of the ten marks is called concentration (*samādhi*). If one grasps at the mark of form but does not contemplate the marks of form’s permanence or impermanence, this is called the mark of concentration. If one can contemplate the marks of form’s permanence or impermanence, this is called the mark of wisdom (*prajñā*). When concentration and wisdom are in equilibrium, it is [true samādhi].
To contemplate all phenomena is called the mark of relinquishment (*tyāga-lakṣaṇa*). Next, the detailed explanation is as cited above. As previously assigned, there is neither deficiency nor excess;

this is merely the gradual gate (*anupūrva-mukha*), which is the ultimate meaning within the gradual teachings of *Nirvāṇa*. One contemplates the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha-dharma*)—that is, contemplating the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
This is practiced based on pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*). Furthermore, it corresponds to the Three Contemplations (*tri-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of Tiantai.
The principles of the Dharma are harmonized from beginning to end;

however, one first contemplates the relative nature of all phenomena and thereby cultivates the realization of the Three Truths. This awakening to one's own mind does not establish an object (the observed realm).

This refers to the three truths. One should investigate and refine [the mind] based solely on the point of awakening (at the time of initial sudden awakening, one has already been exhorted to resolve all doubts).
Furthermore, these do not specifically designate the "three cessations," for the specific characteristics of cessation and contemplation are inherent in every gate.
Moreover, examine the three contemplations in detail according to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng).
The names of the Three Truths in the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma):
Each of these three sets is sequentially assigned such that they all correspond perfectly and do not conflict with one another. Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all cultivate this;
apart from this, there is no way to enter the City of Enlightenment. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have realized it through this.
Thus, as the Buddha has spoken, this concludes the tenth chapter, "The Three Quotations Illustrating Perfect Goodness.
Good son, these three dharma-gates are all Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). By drawing near to and following them, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions [attained it].

This is the attainment of Buddhahood. The various skillful means of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, in all their similarities and differences, are entirely based upon these three kinds of practice.
If one attains perfect realization through them, one immediately achieves Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
First, the main text explains that by relying on awakening to cultivate practice, one returns to realize awakening;
because from beginning to end one eternally relies upon and follows awakening, it is called "conforming" and "intimate approach. Apart from this cultivation, there is nothing to rely upon.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, the factors of enlightenment, the perfections, wisdom, and compassion—
the eighty-four thousand diverse practices— all take the three contemplations as their foundation;
this is the practitioner’s undertaking, cultivated either sequentially or simultaneously.
The practice of alternating between the single and the multiple is called "conformity" (as in the twenty-five wheels below).
Upon the perfect realization and tranquil accomplishment of *Acalā* (the Unshakable), one becomes a supreme teacher;
this subsequently explains the teaching on the three numbers.
This scripture—the *Mūlakarma* and the teachings on *Nirvāṇa*, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, the *Tiantai* [teachings], and so forth—regarding their methods of transformation and guidance:
how could they fail to take the "three numbers" as their standard for the expedient methods of the gate of contemplation?

For the Dharma-nature of these excellent conditions is fundamentally the Three Greats (the three characters of the *Avataṃsaka*—*Mahāvaipulya*—are the Greatness of Essence, the Greatness of Characteristics, and the Greatness of Function; the *Awakening of Faith* also enumerates the Three Greats).

Delusion forms the three paths, which are eternally opposed [to the three greatnesses] (the twelve links of dependent origination comprise the path of afflictions, the path of karma, and the path of suffering; these three are perpetually remote from the three greatnesses).

Therefore, it is said that the three causes are all Buddha-nature (although the three paths are long separated from the three greatnesses, they do not lose their own nature therein; thus they are called the three causes of Buddha-nature: first, the causal Buddha-nature, which is the original nature—this refers to the numinous mind;

second, the revealing cause, which realizes that delusive phenomena are all empty—this refers to this very tranquil contemplation; third, the conditional cause, which consists of the six perfections and myriad practices—delusion is this very illusory contemplation).
One should uphold the three clusters of precepts (the restraint of conduct, the gathering of wholesome dharmas, and the gathering of sentient beings),
cause them to rely on the three supreme [refuges] to cultivate the three contemplations, dedicate [merit] to the three destinations (enlightenment, sentient beings, and the limit of reality),
expand the three refuges (the Triple Gem), extinguish the three paths, and realize the three wisdoms (the wisdom of all modes).
The Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Possessing the three virtues, one inconceivably attains the three sublime awakenings (the awakening of true reality, the awakening of skillful means, and the awakening of true wisdom), the three types of parinirvāṇa (naturally pure nirvāṇa, nirvāṇa purified by skillful means, and perfectly pure nirvāṇa), and abides in the three secrets (mahāprajñā, liberation, and the dharma-body). This is it.

Eight: Examining the Merits of the Three Contemplations.

"Good son, suppose there were someone who cultivated the noble path (the noble path of the two vehicles) and taught and brought to fruition hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of arhats (translated as 'thiefless' or 'slayer of thieves') and pratyekabuddhas (translated as 'enlightened by conditions' or 'awakened ones,' meaning those who awaken to conditions).

The first three verses briefly explain the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha.
"A" means "no"; an "Arhat" (a-han) is one who has killed the enemy. Killing the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is his achievement;

the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) have already been eliminated—namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, false views, the grasping of views, and the grasping of precepts and observances—and he possesses the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Having fully prepared the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, those called *pratyekabuddhas* (solitary realizers) awaken to the fact that the self-nature of causes and conditions is empty.

By practicing these two vehicles, they achieve the ultimate fruit, completely transcending the three fruits and escaping the cage of afflictions; they are worthy of receiving vast offerings from humans and devas.
Worthy to be the ancestral refuge for dragons and ghosts, those who pay homage shall have their calamities and decline utterly extinguished;
by making offerings, the retribution of merit will naturally flourish.
The following two verses describe the merit of delivering others so that they may attain the two kinds of noble fruits.

If a person teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to enter such a noble stage—from one, two, three, up to a hundred million, and finally reaching hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and millions of billions—only then does it conclude. (Counting from one up to ten million;

then counting from one hundred million and two hundred million, until hundreds of thousands of billions, only then does one succeed in delivering that many people, all of whom become Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.)

The worldly merits can only be fully understood by a Buddha; if ordinary people wish to fathom their true conditions, it is like comparing a molehill to a high peak when set against the causes of giving and precepts.
(Note: The above clarifies the nature of the merit; the following clarifies its transcendence over the realms of humans and devas.)

The three existences (triloka) comprise eight phrases clarifying the merit of practicing the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, this merit surpasses that of saving sentient beings.
Moreover, there was another person who initiated a distinct practice, seeking solely the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) doctrine of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*).

Upon hearing the exposition of the aforementioned three types of contemplation, his mind realized them moment by moment, rejoicing at the rare encounter with such a teaching. (The Root of the Three Contemplations)

This refers to what was explained in the preceding six chapters; as one arrives here, accomplishment is attained, and thus the merit is exceedingly great. First, the will does not follow the attachments to the myriad objects.

(The Sūtra says that "conformity" refers to what was explained in the preceding six chapters; it is conformity with reality, not the non-conforming, pervasive conceptual attachments. As for the Dharma-gate of non-obstruction, it means the myriad objects are merged into the One Mind. By relying on this, the three contemplations are unimpeded.)

The phrase "cultivating this mind for even a single thought-moment" (the Sūtra says "in a single kṣaṇa") surpasses the aforementioned merit (the merit of saving people and realizing the fruit of sainthood) by an infinite number.
The two lines beginning with "Five" express a state of doubt.
How can the merit of a single moment be like this? Although the mind wishes to believe, the will finds it difficult to follow.
(The latter two lines address pervasive doubt.

All things are properly within the sphere of compliance: first, in compliance with the external objects of body and mind, which are entirely empty and illusory; they are simply the realm of the pure mind of Perfect Enlightenment.

With a sincere heart, perform repentance.
We, the disciples, from time immemorial until this very day, have been conditioned by ignorance, which obscures the eyes and mind;

we have followed after the afflictions and committed transgressions throughout the three periods of time. Whether through indulging in and becoming attached to defiled cravings, giving rise to the affliction of greed and desire;

or through hatred, anger, and harboring malice, giving rise to the affliction of resentment; or through being dazed, bewildered, and lacking understanding of the meaning of the afflictions; or through the affliction of pride—[we have thus fallen into error].
The affliction of self-exaltation and arrogance; the affliction of doubting the right path and being indecisive; the affliction of the false view that denies cause and effect;

the affliction of failing to recognize dependent origination and clinging to a self; the affliction of being deluded regarding the three periods of time and adhering to the views of nihilism or eternalism;

the affliction of intimacy with evil dharmas and giving rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and the affliction of following a perverse teacher and creating the grasping of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Even unto one...
These four attachments are afflictions born of arbitrary conceptualization. Such afflictions are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I repent for them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, I have guarded and cherished [possessions] with firm attachment, giving rise to the affliction of stinginess. I do not...

The affliction of indulging the six sense-faculties in extravagance; the affliction of mental conduct that is base and evil, lacking forbearance; the affliction of indolence and laxity due to lack of self-restraint;
the affliction of discursive thought and examination arising from the agitation of the mind; and the affliction of confusion and ignorance when encountering sensory objects.
Following the eight winds of the world, they give rise to the afflictions of self and other. They are devious and crooked, praising others without a straightforward mind;

these are the afflictions of dishonesty. They are rigid and difficult to approach, being unrefined; these are the afflictions of lack of discipline. They are quick to anger and difficult to please, possessing much greed and resentment; these are the afflictions of covetousness and hatred. They are swift in jealousy and maliciously piercing; these are the afflictions of ferocity and cruelty.

They are fierce, perilous, violent, and harmful, being deceitful and poisonous; these are the afflictions of treachery and toxicity. They are contrary to the two truths and cling to signs; these are the afflictions of attachment to characteristics. Following...

From the afflictions that flow through the twelve links of dependent origination within birth and death, up to the *asaṃkhyeya-saṃsāra* (Ganges-sand-like) afflictions of the *anādikāla-avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (beginningless ignorance-abiding ground), the four *vāsabhūmis* (abiding grounds) arise, constructing the afflictions of the bitter fruits of the triple world. Such are these various afflictions.
Immeasurable and boundless, they have afflicted and disturbed the worthy and holy ones throughout the six paths and four modes of birth. Today we reveal these transgressions;
before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, we repent them all. May they all be extinguished.
Furthermore, disciples and others, from time immemorial until this very day, have nurtured afflictions that grow deeper by the day and thicker by the month.

Not only have they transmigrated through birth and death, enduring endless suffering, but these afflictions have also shrouded the eye of wisdom, rendering it sightless, severing all roots of goodness, and forming various hindrances.
Today, having attained awakening, we repent each and every one of them—namely, those which are...

The affliction of having seen the Buddha, yet not hearing the True Dharma, and not encountering the Noble Sangha (while at first glance it appears that the character "zhàng" [obstruction] stands at the end of the sentence, upon careful examination of the meaning of "zhàng," [it is understood as "affliction"]).

the afflictive hindrances to studying the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience within the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*); and the afflictive hindrances to studying hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
Cultivating the first dharma obstructs the afflictions; learning the equality of emptiness and the Middle Way resolves the obstruction of afflictions;
learning the Eightfold Noble Path obstructs the afflictions of manifesting signs; learning the Seven Factors of Enlightenment obstructs the afflictions of non-manifestation of signs;

the afflictive hindrances of training in the various knowledges and views of the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages;

Regarding the afflictions that obstruct the practice of the myriad practices of a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas toward the fruit of Buddhahood— such obstacles to practice being immeasurable and boundless—
I today prostrate myself with utmost reverence. Facing the Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Sangha of the ten directions, I feel shame and remorse,
repenting so that all [obstacles] may be completely extinguished.
With a sincere heart, we make this vow: may our disciples, by virtue of this repentance for all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, in birth after birth and life after life,
break down the banner of pride, dry up the waters of craving and desire, extinguish the fire of anger, shatter the darkness of ignorance, and uproot the very source of doubt.

He tears asunder the net of all views and deeply realizes that the three realms are like a prison, the four great elements are like venomous snakes, the five aggregates are like hostile thieves, the six sense bases are like an empty village, and craving feigns the intimacy of a friend.
He cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, severs the source of ignorance, and proceeds directly toward Nirvana.

Without ceasing or resting, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ) and the ten perfections (daśa-pāramitāḥ) shall constantly manifest before the mind at every moment.
Furthermore, I pray that my disciples, by means of this repentance, may have all afflictions (kleśa) obstructed within their various activities;

and that wherever they may be reborn, they may attain mastery over their births and not be turned about by the bonds of karma. By means of the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna)...
In the space of a single thought-moment, they travel everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions to gather and transform sentient beings.
Regarding the profound realms of all meditative concentrations, up to all-encompassing knowledge and vision, their minds attain unimpeded penetration.

They are able to universally pervade all phenomena with inexhaustible delight in teaching, yet remain unstained by attachment. Thus they attain mastery over the mind and mastery over the Dharma, and their wisdom is autonomous.

Through mastery in skillful means, these afflictions and the habitual tendencies of the fetters of ignorance are brought to ultimate and permanent cessation, so that they no longer continue in succession;
the untainted noble path shines forth clearly like the sun.
Having made this vow, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
I address the assembly: listen now to these verses on impermanence.
Do not say that you shall preserve one another year after year; rather, each of you must personally cultivate and practice meritorious deeds.
Once this assembly of followers has dispersed, who knows who will die and who will live?
One day, entering the Jade City as a mound of dust, the home will be silent and no sound shall be heard;
even if a spirit-bed is prepared at the place of weeping, by what means can one behold the true form?
Ordinary fools do not awaken to this; they constantly indulge in the pleasures of the five desires.
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* (Chapter Thirty-Seven), a verse is spoken in reprimand:
"If a person does not contemplate the mind but constantly pursues the enjoyment of desire, They sleep for a long night through vast time, and their suffering and affliction are never extinguished."
Out of delusion, one delights in pleasant sensations and fails to perceive suffering and affliction;
only later, when faced with decline and distress, does one realize what fruit has been obtained. Desire appears virtuous at first, yet it is unreal and exceedingly evil;
it is the messenger of hell, solely intent on doing harm. The blind man places his trust in this desire.
One whose eye of wisdom is thus detached is like a precarious cliff; such a person falls into hell.
Heedfulness is the foremost friend, for it can always bring benefit, while negligence is the foremost enemy.
Therefore, one should draw near to virtuous friends. For those who desire to pervade their entire bodies [with virtue], heedlessness is like the most virulent poison.
The foremost path to the evil realms is what is called heedlessness.
If one practices heedlessness and becomes deeply attached to sense objects, then because of that delusion, one constantly undergoes all manner of suffering;
all life is lost, all happiness is exhausted, and one is separated from all that is dear.
When you die, you desire to be reborn; death is the ultimate evil. Upon reaching the vast wilderness of the great road, there is no refuge other than the Dharma.
Therefore, you should accord with the Dharma and cultivate and realize the path of the Perfect Enlightenment Maṇḍala. [End of] Fascicle Twelve of the Extensive Text.

Part Nineteen: An Upward Praise of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha acts as the unsurpassed King of Physicians.

Having refined the medicinal elixir of the Dharma across immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of eons, he has attained mastery in all skillful means and the power of the Great Vidyā-mantra;
having reached the further shore, he is well able to eliminate the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings, and thus abides.
His lifespan lasts for countless eons; his body is pure, free from conceptual thought, and devoid of active exertion.
Yet, he never ceases to perform any of the Buddha-works. Sentient beings who behold him find all their afflictions and diseases completely extinguished.
This is the eighth mark of the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

With sincere repentance, may the assembly together now attain tranquility of body and mind; being free from deception and hindrance, this is precisely the time for generating goodness and extinguishing evil.

Furthermore, each person should give rise to four kinds of contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) as a means to extinguish transgressions and serve as the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*). What are they?
There are four: first, contemplating causes and conditions; second, contemplating karmic retribution; third, contemplating one's own body;
and fourth, contemplating the body of the Tathāgata.

First, regarding the contemplation of causes and conditions: I recognize that these transgressions of mine arose by relying on ignorance, improper reflection, and a lack of the power of right observation;

I practiced what is deviant and perilous, like a fish biting the hook without knowing its danger, or like a silkworm making its cocoon, entangling and binding itself, or like a moth leaping into the flame.
Fire. One burns and rots oneself; by these causes and conditions, one cannot escape on one's own.

Second, regarding the contemplation of karmic retribution: all evil and unwholesome karma flows through the three periods of time, resulting in endless suffering and boundless immersion in the great ocean of the vast night, where one is devoured by the rākṣasas of the various afflictions. Not yet...

Coming and going through birth and death, it is thus without end. Upon passing away, one receives the retribution of becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), ruling over the four continents with sovereign power to fly, fully endowed with the seven treasures. Yet, after the end of his life, he cannot avoid the evil realms;

even with the fruits of the four formless attainments, once the merit of his supreme status is exhausted within the three realms, he returns to become a worm on the hump of an ox—how much more so for others who possess no merit or virtue?
Furthermore, they are indolent and do not diligently practice repentance. This is also like carrying a stone and sinking into a deep abyss; it is extremely difficult to seek escape.

Third, regarding the contemplation of one's own body: one reflects that although within this body there exists the nature of the numinous awakening which is the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*), it is shrouded by the dark forest of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Lacking the power of the liberating cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), one is unable to attain [awakening].
Manifesting this, I should now give rise to the supreme mind: to shatter the heavy obstructions of ignorance and perversion;
to sever and extinguish the false causes of birth, death, and suffering; to manifest the great, luminous wisdom of the Tathāgata; and to establish the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the Tathāgata’s body: The body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned, quiescent, and luminous; it transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.

It is replete with all virtues and remains eternally in a state of profound stillness. Although he manifests entry into parinirvāṇa through skillful means, his compassionate salvation and protection have never for a moment ceased.
To give rise to such a mind may be called an excellent ford for extinguishing transgressions and an essential method for removing hindrances.
Thus it is. Therefore, disciples, today we take refuge in the Triple Gem with utmost sincerity and seek compassionate repentance.
Disciples, having already repented for various kinds of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), we shall now proceed in order to repent for the hindrance of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
Indeed, karma adorns the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence; wherever one may be bound, one receives a body and fails to attain liberation.
It is like a skilled painter who can depict all the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the world; there is no phenomenon arising from birth that he does not create.

Thus, one knows that the various forms and types within the three realms (*tridhātu*) are all produced by the power of karma (*karma-vaśa*). Therefore, although the power of the Buddha is supreme, it does not surpass the power of karma.
Furthermore, the karmic actions created—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are different in their lightness or gravity; all must first be [addressed with]...
First, through one's own power, one must give rise to a mind of intense remorse; thereafter, relying upon the power of the Buddha, one must subdue oneself and repent for one's failings.

One should transform conditions, punish transgressions, and rectify past errors by preemptively restraining the former mind. Regarding those offenses that are not yet covered by the *vinaya* or the rules for non-regret, there are texts concerning the repentance of even grave crimes such as the five rebellious acts (*ānantarya*).
Since these methods encompass great and small offenses without exception, one must approach the Three Jewels with utmost sincerity and profound reverence.

First, one should repent and reproach one's former mind, confessing the offenses committed. Regarding grave (upper-grade) offenses: the preparatory intention is heavy; at the time of the act and after the act, all three periods are heavy.

When the mind and its object correspond, and furthermore, when the actions involve the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the slandering of the Vaipulya sutras, or the acts of an icchantika—actions that are numerous and beneficial [to oneself] while being deluded about causes and mistaken about effects, failing to recognize the offense and failing to recognize the Dharma—this is termed [grave].

Regarding those of superior and middling grades: for a crime of the middling grade, the preparatory effort and the actual performance are both grave at two stages; after the act is completed, the mind is light; the object is grave while the mental state is slight;
furthermore, it does not involve the three extremes of sharpness, nor is it frequent, nor is there delusion regarding cause and effect—this is termed "middling.

As for what is called "inferior": the mind is grave before and after, while the actual performance is light; the object and the mind are in opposition; furthermore, it is not an offense involving the community.
To enumerate them, they are not beneficial. To recognize the dharmas and recognize one's offenses, clearly understanding cause and effect, constitutes the lowest grade.

Now, for those who wish to repent of the three preceding grades, there are three types of gates of repentance: first, the repentance that suppresses karma; second, the repentance that transforms karma;

and third, the repentance that extinguishes karma. Regarding what is called "suppressing": this refers to repenting according to the limited teachings of the Two Vehicles; regarding the first four categories [of offenses], one merely suppresses them and does not...
To "arise" [from transgression] is called *chan* (repentance). Having already undergone disclosure (*pratikarma*), the original offense does not increase, as there is no concealment of faults;
because of such concealment, the offense that ought to arise fails to do so—this is called "subduing. Regarding the "twofold transformation of karma":

by substituting a short period for a long one, and using light suffering to suppress heavy suffering, whatever retribution should have been experienced within the three evil realms, one vows to repay it in this present body. It does not... [continue].
"Entering the evil realms to receive [retribution]" clarifies the repentance for the transformation of karma. Third, regarding the extinction of karma:
the mind must clearly understand through contemplation and resolve, deeply generating the great bodhicitta. All sins committed since beginningless time are like darkness in the sky;
the wisdom of repentance is likened to a bright lamp. Once the bright lamp shines, all gloom is dispelled; one cannot resist it simply because the darkness is thick.
It is like a lamp. Because of delusion, one produces erroneous results and commits all manner of transgressions; thus, the Buddha-nature remains hidden in its radiance.

Therefore, know that it is like the matter of lighting a true wisdom-fire in a dark room: as the lamp is lit and the light arises, darkness is dispelled; as understanding is born, delusion perishes, and there is no karma that is not extinguished.
We disciples reflect upon ourselves: from time immemorial until this very day, we have accumulated evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and committed sins that fill the heavens and the earth.

Karma that destroys and annihilates the Triple Gem and subverts the True Dharma; karma of disbelief in sin and merit that gives rise to the ten non-virtuous actions;

The activity of failing to provide protection; the activity of a corrupted mind characterized by envy, forgetfulness, and lack of restraint toward others;

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhakarmāvaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if the intrinsic nature of this awakened mind is fundamentally pure, by what cause is it defiled such that all sentient beings are bewildered and fail to enter [it]?

Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have through deluded imagination clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
