At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately commanded his great ministers to prepare the ritual offerings; together with his consort, he solemnly prepared his carriage and mount.
The people followed him. From afar, the great assembly at Kuśinagara saw the King approaching. The Buddha addressed the assembly:

"Regarding the proximate causes and conditions for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, none is more primary than a virtuous friend. Had King Ajātaśatru not followed the words of Jīvaka, on the seventh day of the coming month—"
He will certainly meet his end and fall into the Avīci Hell. At that time, the Great King went to the Buddha’s dwelling and gazed up at his marks and signs, which were like a mountain of pure gold.
The World-Honored One addressed him, saying, "Great King Ajātaśatru. Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and spoke these words: "The Tathāgata has looked upon me and charged me;
I truly know that his compassion and pity are equal and without distinction. He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if by chance..."
Even if I were now permitted to sit, rise, eat, and drink together with Brahmā and Śakra, I would still not feel such joy;
yet, having encountered a single word of the Tathāgata’s personal summons, I am profoundly delighted and filled with celebration.

The Buddha said to the Great King: "I shall now explain for you the essentials of the True Dharma. An ordinary person should constantly maintain mindfulness that there are twenty matters regarding the body.

Namely: [one phrase per item] it is empty and non-existent; it is without outflows; it lacks the roots of all goodness; birth and death have not been subdued; one has not emerged from the deep pit. How can one see one's nature?
How can one cultivate meditative concentration? It is impermanent and without self; the eight difficulties are hard to escape; and there is enmity."
Daily life is pursued in vain; there is no dharma to block existence. One has not yet escaped the three evil realms and possesses wicked, heterodox views.

One has not yet crossed over the five heinous crimes, and birth and death have no end (the following two phrases refer to a single matter). If one does not perform wholesome karma, one will not obtain its fruit and retribution. It is not the case that I perform the action while another receives the fruit.
If one does not create the cause for happiness, there will ultimately be no retribution of joy. If one creates karma, the fruit is never lost; it is because there is no [other] cause.

One who has attained clarity also dies because of it. Having observed that those of the past, future, and present constantly practice heedlessness, one no longer delights in birth and death and immediately attains right contemplation.
At that time, one sequentially contemplates the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind, as well as the characteristics of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom.
If one does not commit evil, there will be no fear of death nor fear of the three evil realms.
If one does not fix the mind to observe these twenty matters, the mind will become negligent, and there is no evil that will not be committed. Ajātaśatru said:
"From the past until now, I have never observed these twenty matters; therefore, I have committed many evils. Now I have the fear of death and the fear of the three evil realms. From myself...
This invites calamity. To commit grave evils while practicing compassion—regardless of whether these twenty matters are contemplated or not—one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha told the Great King: "The nature and characteristics of all phenomena are impermanent; there is no fixed certainty. The Great King asked:
"How then can you say that there is a fixed certainty of falling? The King addressed the Buddha, saying: "If that is so, then my own sin of killing should also [be considered non-existent]."

[The interlocutor says: It is indeterminate. The Buddha said, "Excellent! Killing has no fixed characteristic. What is it that constitutes a father? One merely gives rise to the false notion of 'father' with respect to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If form (*rūpa*) were the father, then the other four aggregates would not be; the same applies to the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). Thus, form cannot be harmed."

The aggregates (*skandhas*) are likewise incapable of being harmed; their nature does not abide. The past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present perishes moment by moment.
Since form (*rūpa*) is thus unstable, killing is also indeterminate, and its retribution is likewise indeterminate.

Your father formerly cultivated wholesome roots in the presence of the Buddha, and it is because of this that he has now become king. If the Buddhas had not accepted his offerings, he would not have become king. If...
If you were the king, you would not have become king; if you had not become king, you would not have committed this harm. If you are guilty, then the Buddhas are also guilty.
Your father previously harbored an evil mind and killed a seer possessing the five supernatural powers, causing him to lose his spiritual faculties;
he reaps what he himself has sown. How can you say that your royal father was innocent? If there were no evil karma, there would be no evil retribution.

There are four kinds of madness among sentient beings: first, madness from desire; second, madness from drugs; third, madness from incantations; and fourth, madness from karma. When a madman commits evil, he ultimately does not violate the precepts.
If he regains his senses, he is likewise not said to have violated them. Your Majesty originally coveted the kingdom and treacherously harmed your father king;
this was done while you were mad with desire. What offense do you incur? It is like one who harms his mother while intoxicated and feels remorse once sober.

Nor is there any karmic retribution. Your Majesty is now intoxicated by craving; this was not done with your original intention. Since it was not done with your original intention, how can you incur guilt?
Men and women created by illusion, the echoes of mountains and valleys, the reflection of a face in a mirror, and the pleasures of the five desires in a dream—fools deem these real.
Wisdom knows that things are illusory; killing is likewise so. Ordinary people regard it as real, but the Buddha knows it is not true.

Great King, the nature of killing, the karma of killing, the causes of killing, the fruits of killing, and liberation from them—I know all these, yet I am without fault. Although you, O King, know killing, how could there be any fault?
It is like a person who knows wine and does not drink it, thus remaining sober; or again, like one who knows fire [but does not touch it].
It is burning with fire. Although the King knows that he has ordered the killing, how can he be guilty? Furthermore, it is like a person who commits various crimes when the sun and moon are shining;
although these crimes occur because of the sun and moon, they are not guilty. Although the killing occurs because of the King, the King is truly without guilt.

For example, within the royal palace, he constantly issues orders to slaughter sheep without the slightest fear in his heart. Although humans and animals differ, their precious lives are no different. How then [can he be guilty] toward his father?
"O Great King, one who lives alone gives rise to a fearful mind. People in this world are slaves to craving;

they lack self-mastery and carry out acts of killing under the驱使 (driven) of craving. Even if there were a karmic retribution, it would be the fault of craving. Since the King lacks self-mastery, what fault could there be?
O Great King, sentient beings are named for their inhalation and exhalation; because one cuts off these inhalations and exhalations, it is called 'killing'."
The Buddhas, following worldly convention, also speak of "killing. Great King, form is impermanent. Since form arises from impermanent causes, how could it be permanent?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Because they are impermanent, they are suffering; because they are suffering, they are empty.
Because it is empty, it is impermanent. As for suffering, emptiness, and non-self—what is there to be killed? By killing impermanence, one attains the eternal bliss of nirvana;
by killing suffering, one attains happiness; by killing emptiness, one attains reality; and by killing non-self, one attains the true self. Great King!
If you kill that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, then you are the same as I.
I too kill that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, yet I do not enter hell; why then do you enter?
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, following the instructions of the Buddha, contemplated form and so forth up to consciousness. Having performed this contemplation, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that form is impermanent, and so forth up to consciousness, which is impermanent.

World-Honored One, had I known this previously, I would not have committed these acts. World-Honored One, I have heard in the past that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always [teach] for the sake of the multitudes..."
"Since birth, I have been their parents. Although I had heard these words before, I was not yet certain; now I know for sure.

Furthermore, I have heard that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is composed of four treasures (gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal), and that wherever flocks of birds gather, they take on the same color as the mountain.
Now that I have come to this Mount Sumeru of the Buddha, I have become the same color as it. To be of the same color means to realize that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty.
There is no self. Had I not encountered the World-Honored One, I would have been undergoing immeasurable suffering in the great hells for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Now that I have seen the Buddha, the merit I have obtained shall destroy all afflictions and evil minds of sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "If one can act in this way, then one will always remain in Avīci hell to undergo suffering for the sake of sentient beings, yet not consider it to be suffering.
At that time, immeasurable people of the Magadha kingdom resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they had thus given rise to such great resolve, King Ajātaśatru’s grave offenses were immediately rendered light. The king, his queen, and the palace ladies all attained this together.
He resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The King said to Jīvaka: "I have not yet died, yet I have already attained a celestial body;
I have cast off a short life and obtained a long life, and I have cast off an impermanent body and obtained an eternal body.

To cause all sentient beings to resolve their minds upon *bodhicitta* is itself the attainment of a celestial body, a long life, and an eternal body. He then made offerings of various kinds of fragrant flowers and necklaces, and spoke thus.

The verse praised the Buddha, and the Buddha praised King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You are able to give rise to this mind, thereby adorning the great assembly. You should always diligently cultivate the bodhicitta;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, you shall attain the eradication of immeasurable evils. Thus spoke [the Buddha] to the king and the people of the nation.

Taking leave of the Buddha, he returned to his palace and respectfully addressed the assembly gathered at the present site of practice who were sincerely repenting: "King Ajātaśatru first repented and reproached himself before he was able to see the Tathāgata.

The Buddha taught that all phenomena are empty and that all conditioned factors lack intrinsic nature. King Ajātaśatru deeply regrets his delusions and perversions, which led him to falsely create the causes for evil."

Therefore, we have resolved to attain great Bodhicitta and realize the true, eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Since immeasurable kalpas past, we have not been free from the causes and conditions of evil and rebellion;

for many days now we have personally repented and eliminated them. We have also heard that King Ajātaśatru previously repented, and now we further hear this wondrous scripture of the *Nirvāṇa*, in which the Buddha himself explains the root source of repentance.
Since the root source is fundamentally empty and non-existent, how could one remain complacent?
Deluded attachment; when there is neither delusion nor attachment, one is no longer a slave to craving and love.
Since one no longer serves greed or anger, the causal conditions for creating transgressions are forever severed. Body and mind become pure, as clear as lapis lazuli.
All actions and deeds are then the true nature itself. This is ultimate, authentic repentance.
Having finished the repentance, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.

With a sincere heart, make this vow (based on the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-gāthā*): "Now that this ritual arena has concluded, I finally offer this vow from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which remains unfulfilled, praying to attain perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree."
May I always remain far removed from evil associates, Forever free from all adverse conditions;
May I swiftly behold the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light, And fully realize the most supreme vows of Samantabhadra.
At this time, may I well obtain an excellent lifespan, Attaining mastery and being born among humans with ease.
Before long, the Bodhisattva shall achieve accomplishment, Just like those practices for enlightenment of Samantabhadra.
In the past, due to the power of my lack of wisdom, I committed extremely evil causes leading to the Avīci hell;
Now, by means of the Great King of Vows of Samantabhadra, They are all swiftly extinguished in a single thought-moment.
The lineage, caste, and physical appearance, as well as the marks and wisdom, are all perfectly complete;
neither celestial Māras nor external paths can defeat him. He is worthy of being honored by the three periods of time;
he swiftly approaches the king of Bodhi trees, and having sat down, he subdues all Māras and enemies.
Having attained perfect enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma, you universally benefit all sentient beings.
Having made this vow, with a sincere heart, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
[Addressing the assembly: Listen as I recite the verses on impermanence from within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter Five).
Kings who have attained mastery, Whose power is without equal— All these are subject to change;
life is likewise so. The wheel of manifold suffering is boundless, Circling without a moment’s rest.
The three realms are all impermanent; In all states of existence there is no joy; Such is the fundamental nature of the Way.
All things are empty and non-existent; The flow of phenomena is subject to destruction; There is always sorrow, affliction, and the like.
(Each recites a verse on impermanence.
From the Extensive Text of the Ritual of Repentance for Cultivation and Realization at the Maṇḍala of Perfect Enlightenment, Volume Sixteen.
The Extensive Text on the Cultivation and Realization of Chan Contemplation in the *Enlightened Awareness* (Yuánjué) Retreat Site, Scroll Seventeen.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.

Section Eight: The Methods for Seated Meditation (Five gates herein: 1. General Overview; 2. Harmonizing the Body and Mind; 3. Preparatory Expedients; 4. Discerning Demonic Hindrances; 5. Treating Illness).

Part One: General Introduction Now, in this age of the semblance Dharma, people lack the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When the Dharma is preached, it is like playing music for the deaf; when dwelling in seclusion, they are like elephants without a hook.
They do not strive to cultivate the mind, but merely boast of their wild wisdom (*prajñā*). If they intend to create the realm of the Buddha, upon what can they rely? Furthermore—
Now, those who practice the Way but cannot awaken to the principle and cling only to phenomena do so because their minds are largely subject to sinking and agitation;
they grasp at worldly arts and indulge in the flavors of sensual pleasure. Therefore, wisdom without concentration is like water being stirred or a lamp in the wind.

It is often associated with restlessness and distraction; how, then, can one realize the truth? To have concentration (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*) is like wishing to travel at night while having feet but no eyes.
Furthermore, to lack both concentration and wisdom is to be either mad or foolish. To practice one door exclusively leads to ignorance and false views.

Only when these two are practiced in tandem does one become a "Two-Legged Honored One" (*dvipada-agrya*). Therefore, the Tiantai school’s cultivation relies primarily upon *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). How much more so [in this case]?

Because this Bodhisattva relies upon this [method], they now enter the contemplation of the principle of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). It is necessary to rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) to still the mind and quiet the heart before one can attain resonance with it;
it is like still, clear water that only then reflects the myriad forms. Since this is the essential method for entering the Way, he exhorts diligent cultivation.

Furthermore, among the four postures (*īryāpatha*), sitting is the most excellent. As it distances one from both dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), it is praised by the Sages. Therefore, the treatise [states]:
It is said: "When one sees even a painted image sitting in the full lotus posture, the Māra-kings are still struck with awe and fear; how much more so for one who has entered the Way?
With body upright and unmoving. 2. Harmonizing.
What is meant by "harmonization"? It refers to five methods: first, harmonizing food and drink;
second, harmonizing sleep; third, harmonizing the body; fourth, harmonizing the breath; and fifth, harmonizing the mind. Why is this so?
To illustrate this principle through a proximate analogy: it is like a worldly potter who, wishing to fashion various vessels, must first skillfully temper the clay.

One must ensure that [the instrument] is neither too tight nor too loose before it can be placed upon the frame and wheel. It is just like playing the lute: one must first tune the strings so that they are neither too slack nor too taut;
only then can one enter the performance and produce various exquisite melodies. When a practitioner cultivates the mind, it is likewise so:
if the five factors are well-adjusted and the mind is made harmonious and appropriate, then samādhi will easily arise. If there is anything that is not adjusted, [samādhi] will mostly...
Regarding various obstacles and difficulties: it is difficult for roots of goodness to arise.
As for the foremost method of regulating food: the purpose of eating is fundamentally to sustain the body and advance on the Path; if one eats to excess, [the roots of goodness will not arise].
Then the breath will become labored and the body will feel full; the hundred vessels will be obstructed, causing the mind to be constricted and one’s seated contemplation to be restless.

If one eats too little, the body becomes emaciated and the mind feels suspended, such that one’s mental faculties are not firm. These two states are both not the way to attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, if one eats impure or turbid things, they cause the human consciousness to become clouded and deluded. If one eats things unsuitable for the body, it causes agitation.

Chronic illnesses cause the four great elements to fall into disharmony; this is the primary concern when beginning the cultivation of meditative concentration, and one must exercise profound caution regarding it.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "When the body is at ease, the Way flourishes; know moderation in eating and drinking; always delight in dwelling in seclusion; with a tranquil mind, delight in diligent effort—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas."
Second, regarding the regulation of sleep: Sleep is shrouded by the obscurations of ignorance and delusion; it must not be indulged in.
If one sleeps or remains in bed for too long, not only will the cultivation of the noble Dharma be neglected, but one’s diligent efforts will also be lost.
It causes the mind and consciousness to become darkened and the roots of virtue to sink away. One should awaken to impermanence, subdue sleep, and clarify the spirit and faculties.
Pure and clear; with a mind of mindfulness that is luminous and pure, one may thus settle the mind upon the sacred realm, and samādhi will manifest before one.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Do not let the first watch of the night or the last watch go to waste. Do not, on account of sleep, cause this entire life to pass in vain without attainment.
One should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek early deliverance for yourself and do not sleep."

The third is the regulation of the body; the fourth is the regulation of the breath; the fifth is the regulation of the mind. These should be regulated in combination and must not be explained separately.
There are only differences in the methods for the beginning, middle, and end, as there are distinct characteristics for entering, abiding in, and emerging from [samādhi].

Regarding the first, regulating the three matters upon entering dhyāna: when the practitioner wishes to enter samādhi, this is the appropriate way to regulate the body while still outside of meditative concentration.
Whether walking, standing, advancing, or halting, whether moving, being still, or acting, one must always exercise thorough discernment.

If one’s actions are coarse and violent, the breath will follow suit and become coarse; because the breath is coarse, the mind becomes distracted and difficult to collect. Furthermore, while sitting, one will feel restless and agitated, and the mind will not be at ease.
Therefore, even when outside of formal meditation, one must apply the mind and practice preparatory skillful means. When subsequently entering dhyāna, one must...

One should settle the body well so that it finds its proper place. Upon first reaching the rope-couch (rajjupīṭha), one must immediately sit down securely in the pre-arranged seat, ensuring it remains stable for a long time without causing disturbance.
Next, one should remove the robes, loosening the belts and adjusting them so they are perfectly aligned; this ensures they do not slip off while sitting.

Then, one should properly position the feet. If sitting in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), place the left foot upon the right foot, drawing it close to the body so that the toes of the left foot [are positioned correctly].
Align it with the right thigh. Align the toes of the right foot with the left thigh.

If you wish to perform the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), then place the right foot upon the left. Next, you should position the hands: place the left palm upon the right hand and rest them both upon the left leg, with the palms near the heart.
Next, you should straighten the body; first, extend and adjust the torso. And...
Massage all the joints seven or eight times according to the method of massage, taking care not to cause any injury to the hands or feet.

When finished, straighten the body upright so that the shoulder blades face each other; do not slouch, nor do you arch the back. Next, align the head and neck so that the nose is directly opposite the navel;
keep it neither biased nor tilted, neither lowered nor raised, remaining level and upright. Finally, exhale through the mouth with the sound "ha."
This expels the foul vapors from within the chest. As for the method of *tuo* and *he*: open the mouth and exhale the breath, releasing the air outward.

Visualize all places within the body where the hundred vessels are obstructed, and imagine that they are all completely expelled along with the breath. Close the mouth and inhale pure air through the nose.
In this manner, repeat up to three times. If the body and breath are harmonized, one repetition alone is sufficient.

Next, one should close the mouth, with the lips and teeth just barely touching, and the tongue directed toward the upper palate. Next, one should close the eyes, just enough to cut off external light.
One should sit upright with the body straightened like a stone pillar, ensuring that the head, torso, and four limbs do not deviate from their proper alignment.

One must not move or shake at all; this is the method for adjusting the body when first entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). To state the essential point: it should be neither too loose nor too tight.
This is the method for harmonizing the body.

Second, regarding the initial method for harmonizing the breath when entering dhyāna: there are four characteristics of the breath: first, wind; second, panting; third, gasping; [and fourth, respiration].
There are four types of breathing. The first three are signs of lack of regulation; the last one is the sign of regulation. What is the sign of wind?
When sitting, the breath entering and exiting through the nostrils is constantly audible. What is the sign of panting?

When sitting, although the breath is silent, its entry and exit are obstructed and不畅 (unclear/stagnant); this is the sign of panting. What is the sign of gasping? When sitting, although it is silent, nor... [text continues]

It is without obstruction, yet its entry and exit are not subtle; this is called the characteristic of the breath (*āśvāsa*). As for the characteristic of the respiration (*praśvāsa*): it is without sound, without obstruction, and without coarseness;
its entry and exit are continuous, as if existing and yet as if non-existent. It sustains the spirit with tranquility, and the mind is filled with joy; these are its characteristics.

If one dwells upon the wind [element], it will disperse; if one dwells upon the panting, it will become knotted; if one dwells upon the vital energy (*prāṇa*), it will lead to exhaustion; if one dwells upon the breath, it becomes settled.

Furthermore, while sitting, there are three signs such as wind and so forth which constitute lack of regulation; for one who applies the mind [to these], they will later become a source of affliction, and the mind will likewise be difficult to settle.
If one wishes to regulate them, one should rely on three methods: first, placing the mind in a low position; second, relaxing and letting go.
Third, one visualizes the breath circulating through all the pores, entering and exiting freely and without obstruction.
If one concentrates the mind, causing the breath to become subtle, then as the breath becomes regulated, various afflictions will not arise and the mind will easily attain stability.

This is called the method for regulating the breath when a practitioner first enters meditative absorption. To state the essentials: being neither constricted nor slippery is the sign that the breath is regulated.
Third, regarding the initial settling of the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are two points. First, to subdue distracted thoughts so that they do not arise.
Second, to ensure that sinking (*laya*) and floating (*auddhatya*), as well as laxity and tension, are brought into their proper balance. What constitutes the sign of sinking?

If, while sitting, the mind is dull and obscure with nothing being registered, and the head tends to droop low, this is the sign of sinking. At that time, one should fix the attention on the tip of the nose to bring it back.
The mind dwells within its object, ensuring that no distracted thoughts arise; this can be remedied through settling. What are the signs of mental agitation?
If, while sitting, the mind is prone to wandering and the body is likewise restless, and one attends to external, disparate objects, these are the signs of agitation.

At such a time, one should appropriately settle the mind by directing it downward, binding it to the navel, and restraining all discursive thoughts; thus the mind will become stably established. The mind...
Be quiet. To state the essentials: neither sinking nor floating is the sign of a balanced mind. Question:
Can the mind also have signs of being too loose or too tight? Answer: Indeed it can. Regarding the sign of a mind that is too tense during concentration:

because one grasps the mind with effort while sitting and thereby enters meditative absorption, the breath rises and there is sharp pain in the ribs and chest. One should relax the mind and imagine [the breath flowing freely].

The vital energy will all flow downward, and the ailment will immediately subside. If the pain persists despite a relaxed mind, one should perceive the mind and will wandering freely and the body becoming expansive;
or perhaps saliva flows from the mouth, or at times there is a sense of darkness. At such times, one should contract the body and urgently cause it to abide within the object of focus.
The body and its features are in harmony. This serves as the remedy for the mind’s states of roughness or smoothness; it can be understood through inference.

This is the method for regulating the mind when first entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since the primary intent is to enter concentration, one proceeds from the coarse toward the subtle, causing the mind to become tranquil.
This is the initial expedient for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the second point, regulating the three matters while seated: during the time one sits—whether the duration be long or short—one should collect the mind and apply focused attention.
Within this, one must clearly discern the signs of whether the body, breath, and mind are properly regulated or not. When sitting, if one...

Although one has regulated the body and mind, if one perceives that the body is either too loose or too tense, or is uneven, slanted, or tilted such that it is not upright, one should correct it as soon as this is noticed.
One should ensure that within a state of constant composure, the body is everywhere neither loose nor tense, but remains level, straight, and correctly positioned.
Furthermore, during a single sitting, although the body may be harmonized, the breath may still be unregulated. As for the characteristics of this lack of regulation, they are as follows:

Regarding what was explained above: if one experiences panting or labored breathing, or if the body feels distended and full, one should employ the aforementioned method to treat it accordingly, ensuring that the flow of the breath remains constant, as if both present and yet absent.

Furthermore, while sitting, even if the breath within the body is regulated, the mind may sometimes sink or become agitated, such that relaxation and tension do not coexist. At such times, if one becomes aware of this, one should employ the aforementioned [method].
Dharma-Adjustment: This involves making these three matters—body, breath, and mind—equally balanced throughout, without priority or sequence.
One adjusts them according to whichever is unadjusted, so that within a single sitting, body, breath, and mind are all harmonized and do not conflict with one another.
If they are fused into non-duality, then every pore will be permeated and chronic ailments will be eliminated. By practicing concentration in this manner, one may escape from the path [of suffering].
Third, when the time for seated meditation is nearly over and one wishes to emerge from *samādhi*, one should first release the mind toward external objects.
Open the mouth and exhale the breath, imagining it dispersing freely through the hundred vessels. Then, move the body very slightly;
next, move the thighs, followed by the hands, head, and neck. Next, one should move both feet until they are entirely warm and supple. Thereafter, rub all parts of the body thoroughly with the hands.
Next, rub the hands together to warm them. Close both eyes and then open them. Wait until the heat and impurities of the body have subsided;
only then may one enter or exit at will. If one does not do so, when sitting, the mind may suddenly emerge and ascend prematurely.
Consequently, the meditative state (*samādhi*) has not yet dissipated, remaining within the body, causing pain in the neck and stiffness in the hundred joints, as if—
If, while sitting later on, one becomes restless and uneasy due to wind-disorder (*vāta*), the mind will desire to emerge from meditative absorption. One must always remain mindful of this;

this constitutes the method for emerging from absorption by regulating the body and calming the mind. Because one proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, it is called "skillfully entering, emerging, and abiding. As the verse says:
Advancing and halting follow a sequence; the coarse and the subtle do not conflict. It is like a well-trained horse that wishes to go when it wishes to stay. 3.

The Preparatory Expedients (The preceding three gates—preliminaries, equipment, and so forth—are merely the requisites for practicing dhyāna and the techniques for quelling delusion. The aforementioned harmonization still pertains to physical posture and is not yet called the method of dhyāna. Although it is said to "tune the mind," [it is not yet the true cultivation].)

This is explained in terms of the body; therefore, it is the remote preparation (*dūre-prayoga*). These five factors are all the direct volitions (*cetanā*) that lead toward meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, they are called the proximate preparation (*āsanne-prayoga*).
What is called "the practice of skillful means to discipline the five dharmas"? As for the names of these five dharmas: first, desire; second, diligence;
third, mindfulness; fourth, skillful wisdom; and fifth, single-mindedness. Regarding the first, desire:

it is the distancing from all worldly delusions and inversions, because one desires to attain the dharma-gate of pure wisdom. It is also called resolve, and it is also called aspiration. It is also called...
It is for the sake of joy. Because this person’s aspiration is to delight in all dharma-gates, it is called desire (*chanda*). As the Buddha said:
"All wholesome dharmas have desire as their root. Second, diligence (*vīrya*) consists of firmly upholding the practice of the precepts and abandoning the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
During the first and last watches of the night, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence without ceasing; it is like drilling for fire—one must never rest until heat is generated.
This is called vigor. As the Buddha told Ānanda: "Because all Buddhas were single-mindedly diligent and vigorous, they attained *sambodhi*."

How much more so for other dharmas of the wholesome paths. Regarding the three recollections: one recollects that the world is deceptive and contemptible, while meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are honorable and precious.

If one attains meditative concentration, one is then able to fully develop all the powers of the untainted (*anāsrava*) supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), achieve equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and extensively deliver sentient beings; this is what is meant by being "precious. Therefore, it is called "recollection."

Regarding the four types of skillful wisdom (*kauśalya-prajñā*): they involve weighing the gains and losses, and the lightness and heaviness, between the pleasure of worldly meditative concentration and the pleasure of supramundane wisdom.
Why is this so? Worldly pleasure involves little joy and much suffering; it is deceptive and unreal, thus it is a loss and something light.

The pleasure of meditative concentration and wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), tranquil, and serene; it is forever free from birth and death, and eternally separated from suffering.

To attain this weightiness and to discern it in such a manner is called skillful wisdom (*kauśalya*). Furthermore, when a practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they skillfully employ them as explained below by alternating their cultivation;
thus, the mind becomes settled and one attains realization. Because of this, one necessarily enters the gateway of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*), and for this reason it is called skillful wisdom.
Regarding the fifth, "one-pointedness of mind": mindfulness and wisdom are clear and distinct, and one clearly perceives the world as something to be dreaded.

How loathsome! The merits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are noble and worthy of respect. At that time, one should practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with single-minded resolve.
With a mind like a diamond (*vajra*), one cannot be destroyed by celestial Māras or non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).

Even if one gains nothing from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one shall never regress or deviate. Even if one were to die because of this, it would still be superior to the karma accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
At the end of life, this is called "single-mindedness. Furthermore, it is like a person traveling: first one must know the characteristics of the path’s passability and obstructions;
only then can one resolutely advance along the road with single-minded focus. Therefore, it is said that skillful wisdom and single-mindedness go together.
Thus, it is stated: "Without wisdom there is no dhyāna; without dhyāna there is no wisdom. The meaning lies precisely here.
IV. Discerning the Deeds of Māra.
*Māra* is translated into Chinese as "the Killer. Because he robs practitioners of their wealth and kills the life-force of wisdom, how is it that these are called the deeds of Māra?
For example, the Buddha takes as his task the liberation of sentient beings through merit and wisdom, and entering into *nirvāṇa*; [this is what Māra opposes].
It is also like this. They constantly take it as their business to destroy the roots of goodness in sentient beings and cause them to wander through birth and death.

If one can settle the mind within the gateway of the Way, because the Way is high, the demons will be numerous; therefore, one must skillfully recognize the works of demons. There are, however, four kinds of demons.

First, the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*); second, the demon of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana-māra*); third, the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*); and fourth, the demon of ghosts and spirits (*bhūta-graha-māra*).

Regarding the characteristics of the demon of ghosts and spirits, one should know that they are to be understood in this context; now they shall be briefly explained. The *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) states:

"If one practices the higher [stages], one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with right mindfulness (and so forth, up to...)... Or there may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness, and thus fall under the influence of various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).

One may be deluded and disturbed by ghosts and spirits. If, while sitting in meditation, they manifest forms to terrify you, or appear in the likeness of handsome men and the like, you should contemplate that these are but the mind;
then the objective realm will vanish and they will ultimately not cause you distress. Or they may manifest as celestial beings or bodhisattvas.
He also manifests as an image of the Tathāgata, complete with all the primary and secondary marks. He may preach dhāraṇīs;
or he may preach generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

or he may speak of equality, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of enmity and the absence of kinship, the absence of cause and the absence of effect, ultimate emptiness and quiescence—this being true nirvāṇa; or he may cause people to know their past lives.
He knows the affairs of the past and also knows the affairs of the future. He attains the knowledge of others' minds and possesses unimpeded eloquence.

He can cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit. Furthermore, he causes people to frequently become angry and frequently rejoice, their natures lacking any constant standard.
They may become excessively compassionate, or suffer from excessive sleep and illness; their minds may become indolent, or they may suddenly exert great diligence, only to subsequently...
It is abandoned and discarded. It arises from a lack of faith, characterized by much doubt and excessive deliberation.

One may either abandon fundamental, superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous karmas, or become attached to worldly affairs, becoming entangled in various ways; these can also cause a person to attain a small portion that resembles the various samādhis.
Yet all such states are merely those attained by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and are not true samādhi. Or again, it may cause a person, for one day, or two days, or...
For three days, or even up to seven days, one remains in meditative concentration and obtains naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink. Body and mind are at ease and joyful;

one is neither hungry nor thirsty, causing others to feel affectionate attachment. Or it may cause people to eat without moderation, sometimes much and sometimes little, so that their physical appearance changes.
For this reason, the practitioner should always observe with wisdom and not allow this [to occur].
When the mind falls into the net of error, one should diligently apply right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging; thus one can distance oneself from these various karmic obstructions.
One should know that all samādhis of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not transcend the mind of views, craving, and self-conceit, for they are greedily attached to worldly fame, profit, and honor.
(The following section on "Inspiring Faith" was newly added by me.)
There are three kinds of spirits, demons, and māras: first, the *piśācas*; second, the *bhūtas*; and third, the *māras*.
As for the *piśācas*, they are transformations of beasts of the twelve hours, assuming various forms and colors—appearing as young men, young women, or the forms of elderly elders.

Even unto fearsome bodily forms and so forth, which are not of a single kind, they afflict the practitioner. These various seductive spirits, wishing to disturb the practitioner, each arrive at their respective times.
One must skillfully direct the consciousness: if many appear during the hour of the Tiger (3–5 a.m.), they are certainly tigers, rhinoceroses, and the like;
if many appear during the hour of the Rabbit (5–7 a.m.), they are certainly hares, stags, deer, and the like. If many appear during...

Those that arrive during the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. must be dragons, tortoises, and the like. If many arrive during the hour of the Snake (9–11 a.m.), they must be snakes, pythons, and the like.

If many arrive during the hour of the Horse (11 a.m.–1 p.m.), they must be horses, donkeys, camels, and the like. If many arrive during the hour of the Sheep (1–3 p.m.), they must be sheep and the like.
If many arrive during the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m.), they must be monkeys, langurs, and the like. If many [arrive during the hour of the Rooster...]
Those that appear during the hour of You (15:00–17:00) must be birds such as the *jīji* and so forth. If many appear during the hour of Xu (19:00–21:00), they must be dogs, wolves, and the like.
If many appear during the hour of Hai (21:00–23:00), they must be pigs and swine. If many appear during the hour of Zi (23:00–01:00), they must be rats and the like.
If many appear during the hour of Chou (01:00–03:00), they must be oxen and the like. Should the practitioner see these...
They always arrive at this time. Recognizing them as the spirits of beasts who employ seductive charms, one should speak their names and rebuke them;
they will then immediately apologize and vanish. As for the *dvārapālaka* (gate-guarding) spirits, they also manifest in various ways to harass travelers:

sometimes they crawl like insects upon a person’s head and face, pricking and stinging incessantly; sometimes they strike and poke under both armpits; sometimes they suddenly embrace a person; or again...

If there are those who come to disturb the practitioner with clamorous speech and sounds, or by assuming the forms of various beasts with manifold strange appearances, he should immediately become aware of this.
With single-minded focus, he should close his eyes and secretly revile them, saying: "I now recognize you!
You are a *lāmgulī* demon of false views from this Jambudvīpa, who feeds on fire and smells fragrances. He should say this with delight.
They break the precepts and afflict me in various ways. Now that I uphold the precepts, I shall never fear you. If one is a renunciant, one should recite the Preface to the Precepts;
if a layperson, one should recite the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. Then the ghosts and spirits will retreat, crawling out on their bellies.
Thus, regarding the various signs of creating obstacles and afflicting people, as well as other methods for removing them, it is all as follows:
This is explained in detail in the *Dhyāna-sūtras*. Regarding the three *māras* who cause affliction and distraction:

these *māras* frequently manifest the appearances of the three kinds of objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*) to destroy a person’s wholesome mind. First, they create circumstances that are contrary to one's feelings;

that is, they produce the five sensory objects that are terrifying, causing the mind to feel dread. Second, they create circumstances that are agreeable to one's feelings; that is, they produce the five sensory objects that are desirable, causing...

The human mind is attached. The three types of actions—neither contrary nor compliant—are those that engage with the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) in a neutral manner, thereby agitating and disturbing the practitioner.
For this reason, Māra is called the "Slayer" and also the "Killing Arrow," because he shoots at the five faculties (*pañca-indriya*).

Furthermore, within each individual form (*rūpa*), he creates three kinds of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) to delude and confuse the practitioner: he may manifest forms that accord with one's desires, or he may manifest as one's father, mother, or elder brother.
"Disciple, the images of the Buddhas, handsome men and women, and other lovely objects cause the mind to become attached to forms.
Those who create adverse conditions may appear in the forms of tigers, wolves, lions, or rākṣasas—various terrifying figures that come to frighten the practitioner.
These are not merely adverse or favorable conditions; rather, they manifest as neutral forms to agitate the human mind and cause one to lose meditative concentration."
Because it obstructs meditative concentration, it is called "Māra. It produces various pleasant and unpleasant sounds; it produces various fragrant and foul odors;
it produces various pleasant and unpleasant tastes; and it produces various realms of suffering and pleasure that come to contact the human body—all of these are the deeds of Māra.
Their manifestations are numerous and cannot be fully described. To state them in brief: if they manifest as various objects of the five sensory dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*).
They harass and disturb people, causing them to lose wholesome dharmas and giving rise to various afflictions; these are all the armies of Māra.
Because they can destroy the impartial Buddha-dharma, they cause people to give rise to greed, desire, sorrow, anger, sleep, and other factors that obstruct the Path.
As a verse in the Sūtra says:
Desire is your first [army], Sorrow is the second, Hunger and thirst are the third army,
Contact with craving is the fourth, Sleep is the fifth army, And fear is the sixth.
Doubt and regret are the seventh army; anger and hatred are the eighth; gain and honor are the ninth, and self-exaltation is the tenth.
Against such hosts of armies as these, which overwhelm and submerge renunciants, I shall, by the power of my wisdom, destroy all your forces and attain the Way of the Buddha.
When a practitioner who liberates all beings is able to recognize the activities of Māra, Māra shall immediately be eliminated and destroyed. There are two methods for this:
first, one eliminates them by practicing *śamatha*. Whenever one perceives any external demonic objects—whether pleasant or unpleasant—one knows them all to be empty and deceptive.
Do not feel attachment or fear; neither grasp nor reject. When the discriminating mind ceases, it becomes naturally quiescent, and those [disturbances] will extinguish of their own accord.

Second, counteract them by practicing *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). If you see various demonic realms as described above and they do not depart through the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding), you should instead turn back and contemplate the mind that perceives them.
Since no location for them can be found, what is there to cause affliction? When contemplating in this way, immediately...
They shall then perish. If they do not depart immediately, you should simply maintain right mindfulness and not give rise to thoughts of fear.
Do not cherish nor cling to your body or life; keep your mind upright and unmoving. Know that the suchness of Māra’s realm is identical to the suchness of the Buddha’s realm.

Since the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are one and the same without duality, there is nothing to be abandoned in Māra’s realm and nothing to be grasped in the Buddha’s realm. Thus, the Buddha-dharma manifests of itself.
When it manifests before you, the realm of Māra will be extinguished. Furthermore, if you see the realm of Māra and it does not subside, do not worry;

if you see it subside, do not rejoice. Why is this? Never has anyone been seen who was devoured by a person transformed by Māra into a tiger, nor has anyone been seen who became a husband and wife with a person transformed by Māra into a man or woman; one already knows that all these are illusions.

When a deluded person is startled and terrified by these transformations, they instead give rise to craving and attachment. Because of this, their mind becomes distracted and they lose meditative concentration;
they become agitated by external objects and fall into affliction. All such afflictions are caused by the practitioner’s own lack of wisdom, not by the deeds of Māra.

Furthermore, if various demonic realms cause disturbance and do not depart even after months or years have passed, one should simply maintain an upright mind and firm, correct mindfulness, without cherishing the body.
"O Life-Span! Do not harbor fear or dread. You should recite the various Mahāyāna Vaipulya mantras for subduing Māra; recite them silently while maintaining mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Even when emerging from meditative concentration, you must likewise recite the mantras to protect yourself. Practice repentance and shame, and recite the Prātimokṣa.
If the false does not yield to the correct, the body will eventually perish after a long time, and the activities of Māra will be too numerous to describe."
[This] is exhaustive. One must recognize this well. For this reason, a practitioner at the initial stage of the path must personally attend upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

This is because of such difficulties as these: when Māra enters a person's mind, their spirit becomes deranged; they may suffer from illness or experience excessive joy, and due to this, they may fall ill and die.
Or, [Māra] may cause them to attain various false meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and *dhāraṇīs*. Thus it is said.

The Dharma transforms and teaches, and all people believe and submit to it. Later, however, it will be greatly ruined, destroying the wholesome deeds of people in the world and thereby subverting the True Dharma.

Such various anomalies are not limited to one; they cannot be fully described. Now, I shall briefly indicate their essentials so that practitioners, while in seated meditation, do not mistakenly grasp at various objective realms.
To state the crux: if one wishes to dispel the heterodox and return to the orthodox, [one must proceed as follows].

One should contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and skillfully cultivate tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). In this way, there will be no evil that remains unbroken. Therefore, the *Śāstra* says:
"With the exception of the true reality of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra. As a verse states:
If one discriminates and recollects through conceptual thought, this is the net of Māra;
to be unmoving and non-discriminating—this is the Dharma-seal (5).
[This is] the healing of illness.

The practitioner settles the mind to cultivate the Way. Sometimes, due to an underlying ailment of the four great elements, the mind now exerts itself with such intensity that it agitates those original ailments.
Or, at times, one is unable to properly harmonize the three matters of body, breath, and mind; because of internal and external transgressions, illness arises.
Now, as for the method of sitting meditation, for one who can skillfully apply the mind, even the four hundred and four diseases [will not arise].
The illness will naturally be cured. However, if one’s mental focus is misplaced, it will stir up four hundred ailments.

Therefore, whether practicing for oneself or transforming others, one should understand the source of illness through its meaning and skillfully know the methods for treating internal illnesses while seated.
If one does not know these methods for treating illness, it is inappropriate to stir them; this will not only create obstacles to the practice of the Way, but one’s life itself may be at risk. Now...

Within the *Meiji-hō* (The Dharma of the Ming Dynasty), there are two primary intentions: first, to clarify the manifestations of the onset of illness; second, to clarify the methods for treating illness.

Regarding the manifestations of the onset of illness, although there are many pathways, they can be summarized briefly into no more than two types: first, illnesses arising from the increase or decrease of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

second, illnesses arising from the five viscera (*pañca-dhātu*). As for the onset of illness among the four great elements: if the earth element increases, then there is swelling, hardening, and sinking.
Heavy; the body becomes withered and emaciated. In this way, one hundred and one ailments arise.

If the water element increases, then there is rapid swelling and distension, indigestion, abdominal diseases, diarrhea, and so forth—one hundred and one ailments arise. If the fire element increases...
Then, cold-natured heat increases, the limbs and joints all ache, the mouth loses its relish, and the large and small intestines lose their function; thus, one hundred and one ailments arise.

If the wind element increases excessively, then the body feels empty and suspended, it trembles and aches, there is a sense of oppression and swelling with urgent vomiting, coughing, and labored breathing;
thus, one hundred and one ailments arise. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one of the three elements is out of harmony, one hundred..."
First, regarding the affliction of illness: when the four great elements are out of harmony, the four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously.

As each of the four great elements manifests its own specific symptoms, one should observe them while sitting in meditation or within dreams. Next, the signs of disease arising from the five viscera will be explained.
Those illnesses arising from the mind are mostly characterized by physical coldness and heat, as well as dryness of the mouth and so forth; for the mind governs the mouth.

Those illnesses arising from the lungs are mostly characterized by distension and fullness of the body, distressing pain in the four limbs, mental oppression, and coldness of the nose; for the lungs govern the nose.
Those illnesses arising from the liver are mostly characterized by suffering from sorrow, anxiety, and lack of joy, as well as grief, excessive joy, anger, headache, and eye pain.

Blindness of the eyes and so forth, because the liver governs the eyes. For those who suffer from conditions arising from the spleen, there is a wandering wind throughout the body and face, characterized by pricking, itching, numbness, pain, and loss of taste in food;
this is because the spleen governs the tongue. For those who suffer from conditions arising from the kidneys...
One may suffer from ailments such as throat obstruction, abdominal distension, and fullness in the ears;

for the kidneys govern the ears, and thus many afflictions arise within the five viscera, each having its own specific characteristics. These should be observed during seated meditation and in dreams so that they may be known.

Such pains and afflictions of the four elements and five viscera arise from manifold causes, and their symptoms are so numerous that they cannot be fully described. If a practitioner wishes to practice...

Regarding the dharma-gate of śamatha and vipaśyanā, if afflictions should arise, one must skillfully understand their causal origin. These two types of illness manifest through both internal and external factors.

If the illness arises from both sources due to external factors such as the imbalance of yin and yang, cold and heat, or a lack of care in diet, one should know that it is triggered by external causes.
If, however, it arises from an unbalanced state of mind, or from errors and deviations in the practice of contemplation, or...

Because at the time of giving rise [to a thought], one does not know how to take or give, this illness is brought about. Second, when afflictions arise from discursive thought, this is an illness arising from internal factors.

Furthermore, there are three different causes and conditions for contracting illness: first, illness is contracted through the increase or decrease of the four great elements and the five viscera, as previously explained;
second, illness is contracted because of the actions of ghosts and spirits; third, illness is contracted due to karmic retribution.
Regarding illnesses: such diseases as these are very easy to cure if treated immediately upon onset. However, if they persist for a long time, the illness will become severe;
when the body is emaciated and the disease has become chronic, it is difficult to heal.

Second, a brief explanation of the methods for treating illness. Once one has gained a profound understanding of how the source of the illness arises, one should apply the appropriate methods to treat it.

There are many approaches to the treatment of illness; however, to state the essentials, they do not exceed the two types of skillful means mentioned above: [the internal] contemplation and [the external] application.

What is the characteristic of using *śamatha* (calm abiding) to treat illness? A master says: "If one places both [the mind and the object] upon the location of the illness within the mind, then one can cure it.
Why is this so? Because the mind is the sovereign of the retributive fruit of a single lifetime; it is like a king who goes wherever he wishes."
Thereupon, the bandits dispersed. Next, another teacher said: "One inch below the navel is called the *udāna*, which here is translated as the 'dantian' (elixir field).
If one can settle the mind there and maintain it without distraction, after a long time, one will achieve mastery over [the body]. Another teacher said:
"Always settle the mind beneath the feet, regardless of whether one is walking, standing, sleeping, or reclining; thus one can cure all illnesses. Why is this? Because people—

Because the four great elements are out of harmony, many illnesses arise. This is due to the mind-consciousness taking external objects as its focus, which causes the four great elements to become unbalanced.
If one settles the mind upon the soles of the feet, the four great elements will naturally become harmonious and all ailments will be eliminated.
A master said: "Simply know that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; do not grasp at the characteristics of illness, but remain in tranquil stillness. Thus, there is much benefit.
It is treated. Why is this? Because the four great elements are stirred up by the mind’s recollections and imaginings, illness arises;
when the mind is stilled and harmonized with joy, all illnesses are immediately cured. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* asks: "What is the root of illness?

It is called 'clinging to objects' (*ālambana*). How does one still this clinging? It means that the mind has nothing to be attained. Such various explanations describe the characteristics of using the mind to treat illness. This is not [the case here].
1. Therefore, one should know that if one cultivates the method of *śamatha* (calm abiding), it can cure various ailments. Next, to clarify curing illness through *vipaśyanā* (insight):
there is a teacher who says that one cures illness by visualizing the mind and employing six kinds of breath. This means that visualization itself can cure illness.

What are these six kinds of breath? First, blowing (*cī*); second, exhaling (*hū*); third, *he*; fourth, *hā*; fifth, sighing (*xū*); sixth, sneezing (*tì*). These six types of respiration all involve the lips and mouth.

Within this [practice], one employs the mental application of visualization while turning the body from side to side. If practicing while seated, one should blow when it is cold and exhale (hu) when it is hot.
If used for treating illness, blowing removes cold, exhaling (hu) removes heat, and the sound "xi" removes disease;
it also treats wind disorders. "He" removes vexation and further descends the qi; "xu" treats the liver, "he" treats the lungs, and "xi" treats the spleen.
Sneezing is used to treat the kidneys. Next, there is the Master’s statement: "If one can skillfully employ visualization and practice the twelve types of breath, one can cure all manner of ailments.
These are: first, the upward-moving breath; second, the downward-moving breath; third, the filling breath; fourth, the burning breath; fifth, the increasing breath;
sixth, the dissolving breath; seventh, the warming breath; eighth, the cooling breath; ninth, the piercing breath; tenth, the sustaining breath; eleventh, the harmonizing breath..."

Breathing. The twelve types of breathing. These twelve breaths all arise from the mind of contemplative visualization. Herein, I shall briefly clarify the visualizations for the remediation of these twelve breaths:
upward breathing remedies heaviness; downward breathing remedies a sense of emptiness or suspension; full breathing remedies emaciation; parching breathing remedies excessive drowsiness;
increasing breathing remedies physical decline; destructive breathing remedies an increase in cold; and warming breathing remedies chill.
The cold breath (*śīta-prāṇa*) treats heat. The penetrating breath (*āveśa-prāṇa*) treats congestion and obstruction. The breath held during obstruction (*nirodha-prāṇa*) treats trembling.

The harmonizing breath (*sāmya-prāṇa*) universally treats the disharmony of the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*). The nourishing breath (*puṣṭi-prāṇa*) provides sustenance for the four great elements.

By skillfully employing these breaths, one can treat all manner of ailments; yet if they are applied incorrectly, they will instead give rise to further ailments—this can be inferred through reasoning. Thus, a master said: "Skillful..."

By employing imaginative visualization (*parikalpa-bhāvanā*), one can cure various ailments. For example, if a person suffers from a cold disorder that arises because the fire-element within their entire body has been suppressed, this visualization can immediately cure the cold.
This is explained in detail among the seventy-two secret methods for curing meditative illnesses found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
However, because the faculties (*indriya*) of people today are dull, such visualizations are often not successful; therefore, they have not been transmitted in the world. Next...

There are masters who say: "By employing only *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to examine the mind and subdue the body, the diseases of the four elements cannot be found, and the diseases within the mind cannot be found;
thus all illnesses naturally subside. Such various explanations regarding the use of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to treat illness possess sound reasoning.
One should know that as for the two dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if a person grasps their essential meaning, there is no illness that they cannot cure. If...
This is a disease caused by spirits; one should employ powerful mantras along with incantations to assist in its treatment.

If it is a disease resulting from karma, one must cultivate merit and perform repentance, and the affliction will then be extinguished. Regarding these two methods for treating illness, if a practitioner can properly attain single-mindedness, they will benefit both themselves and others;
how much more so if they possess complete mastery! If one knows nothing at all, then the illness—

If one is born [into such conditions], there will be no one to provide governance; it will not only result in the neglect of the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, but I fear it may even endanger one’s life.

How could one possibly practice this for oneself or teach it to others? Therefore, those who wish to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must thoroughly understand the methods for treating the illnesses of the internal mind.
Although these methods for treating internal illnesses are numerous, how could they all be fully transmitted in writing? If you wish to study them, you should...

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent criticisms: what has been presented above is precisely intended to demonstrate the general meaning. If one relies upon this for practice, I fear it may not yet be sufficient for formal adoption.

Question: When applying the mind during seated meditation, will there necessarily be efficacy in treating illnesses? Answer: If one possesses the ten dharmas, there is nothing that will not be effective.
It is beneficial. The ten factors are: first, faith; second, application; third, diligence; fourth, constant abiding within conditions;

fifth, discerning the causes of illness as they arise; sixth, skillful means; seventh, long-term practice; eighth, knowing what to adopt and what to abandon; ninth, skillfully protecting [the patient]; and tenth, recognizing hindrances. What is meant by faith?
It means having faith that this dharma will certainly be able to cure the disease. What is meant by application? It means using it at all times.
What is meant by diligence? It refers to being single-mindedly energetic and uninterrupted, taking the attainment of practice as its measure. What is meant by constantly abiding within conditions?
It refers to a subtle mind that, moment after moment, relies upon the Dharma without shifting to other objects. What is meant by specific ailments? They arise from specific causes.

This has already been explained above. What is meant by "skillful means" (*upāya*)? It refers to the mastery in the skillful application of exhaling, inhaling, and directing the mind through visualization, such that one does not lose what is appropriate.
What is meant by "long-term practice"? It means that if its application does not immediately yield benefit, one does not calculate the days spent, but constantly practices without changing course.
What is meant by "knowing how to adopt and abandon"? One diligently applies it when it is beneficial and abandons it when it causes harm, thereby transforming the mind.
To apply the remedy. What is meant by "knowing how to protect"? It means being well-aware of the transgressions incurred through external conditions.

What is meant by "recognizing obstacles"? It means that when one gains benefit, one does not speak of it outwardly; and when one has not suffered harm, one does not harbor doubts or slander. If one relies on these ten dharmas, the remedies applied will certainly be effective;
there is no need for concern.
The Extensive Text on the Cultivation and Realization of Chan Contemplation in the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) Practice Hall, Scroll Seventeen;
The Liturgical Text for Cultivation and Realization in the *Complete Enlightenment* Practice Hall, Scroll Eighteen, Concluded.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Zhōngnán Mountain.

VI. Regarding the two types of cultivation for the higher contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) in correct practice: first, cultivation while seated; second, cultivation by traversing conditions and confronting objects.

As for the first, cultivation of the higher contemplation while seated: among the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), it is through all of them that one attains the study of the Path, yet sitting is the most essential.

It is superior. Therefore, first, regarding sitting, I shall clarify the superior contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Briefly stated, there are five different intentions: First, practicing the superior contemplation to counteract the coarse distraction of a beginner’s mind.
Second, practicing the superior contemplation to counteract the afflictions of mental sinking and excitation. Third, practicing the superior contemplation according to what is most suitable.
Fourth, practicing the superior contemplation as an antidote for the subtle mind that perceives meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as a fixed view. Fifth, for the purpose of achieving equilibrium.

Cultivating the superior contemplation through concentration and wisdom is the first [method]. What is meant by "counteracting and breaking the coarse distraction of the initial mind while cultivating the superior contemplation"?
It means that when a practitioner first sits in meditation, because the distracted mind is coarse, they should cultivate the superior [contemplation] in order to eliminate and break it.

If cessation (*śamatha*) is not yet broken through, one should then cultivate insight (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it is said that one cultivates insight by confronting and breaking the coarse distractions of the initial mind.

Now, to clarify the cultivation of the superior insight, there are two points: first, clarifying the cultivation of the superior; second, clarifying the cultivation of insight. Cessation is of two kinds:

first, cessation of phenomena (*vastu-śamatha*); second, cessation of principle (*tattva-śamatha*). Cessation of phenomena refers to guarding the object and restraining the mind, and so forth. If one binds the mind...
Not allowing the mind to be attached to the five locations, such as the tip of the nose or the navel, is called "stopping by guarding the object. Therefore, a sutra says:
"Bind the mind so it is not negligent, like a monkey placed in a cage.

As for "stopping by restraining the mind," this means that whenever the mind arises [toward an object], one immediately restrains it so that it does not wander or scatter. A sutra says: "Of these five faculties, the mind is their master. Therefore, you..."
And so forth. One should properly restrain the mind. Such forms of cessation are all cessations by means of phenomena (*vastu-śamatha*); they will not be analyzed here.

As for cessation by principle (*tattva-śamatha*), this is precisely cessation by realizing the true nature (*tattvārtha-śamatha*). That is to say, according to whatever phenomena the mind contemplates, one thoroughly knows that they all arise from causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the mind does not grasp or cling. When the mind does not grasp or cling, deluded thoughts cease.
Therefore, it is called "stopping. As it is said in a sutra:
"Among all dharmas, causes and conditions are empty and without a master; The mind at rest reaches the fundamental source, and for this reason one is called a śramaṇa."
Now, as for the practitioner who, when first beginning to practice seated meditation, wishes to cultivate the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
they should first give rise to a great vow to deliver all sentient beings and resolve to seek the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood with a firm and steadfast mind.
It is like a vajra; with courageous and fierce diligence, one does not begrudge body or life. If all Buddha-dharmas are not accomplished, one shall never retreat.

Why is this? If there is no vow, then even if one contemplates emptiness and cultivates the path, one will mostly fall into the stages of the [lesser] vehicles, and thus all Buddha-dharmas will ultimately never manifest before one. Therefore, at all times, the practitioner...
With great compassion and vows, never let them depart from your mind. Then, while sitting upright, contemplate with right mindfulness the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is called "the teachings of all Buddhas" refers to the explanation of all the causal phenomena of the three realms in terms of the mind.
The causes of the three realms consist of all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.
All such things as greed, hatred, and delusion are the fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*).

As for the fruits of the three realms, they refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*)—as well as all phenomena pertaining to birth and death. All such phenomena exist because of the mind. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:

"There are no separate phenomena within the three realms; they are produced solely by this one mind. If a practitioner realizes that the mind has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could there be [any such phenomena]?
The reality of all phenomena, such as the wholesome and unwholesome: if phenomena were not real, they would be deceptive. If one knows them to be deceptive, they are empty and without a master.
If they are empty and without a master, there is no grasping or attachment. If there is no grasping or attachment, then the mind of false conceptualization ceases.
If the mind of false conceptualization ceases, then the fetters and bonds are forever severed. If the fetters and bonds are forever severed, then...

Silent mindfulness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). That which is unconditioned is the fundamental source of all phenomena (*dharmas*). If one penetrates this source, then defiled attachment does not arise.
If defiled attachment does not arise, then the vehicle of all birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is destroyed.

If the vehicle of birth-and-death is destroyed, then there will be no bitter fruits of suffering in future lives. If there are no bitter fruits of suffering in future lives, that is ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Huan. Thus the Sūtra says:
"The mind does not know the mind; the mind does not see the mind. When the mind gives rise to conceptualization, it is delusion;
when there is no conceptualization, it is Nirvāṇa."
If a practitioner is able to cultivate the true cessation of essence in this manner, it should be known that this person’s mind has attained *nirvāṇa* and is called a great *śramaṇa*.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of cultivating the true cessation of essence.

Second, what is meant by "cultivating contemplation"? There are two kinds of contemplation: first, contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*); second, contemplation of principle (*tattva-vipaśyanā*).

Contemplation of phenomena refers to the contemplation that serves as an antidote and aids the path. Contemplation of principle refers to the correct contemplation that enters the path. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Contemplation is of two kinds: first, contemplation through practice and understanding (*xingjie*); second, contemplation of reality (*shiguan*). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"Practice is of two kinds: first, the practice of practice; second, the practice of wisdom. Such terms as these are all alternative names for the two types of contemplation: that of phenomena (*shi*) and that of principle (*li*).
I shall not explain this in detail here. What is meant by "contemplation of phenomena" (*vastu-vipaśyanā*)?

It refers to the contemplations of the five gates of counteractive practice (*pratipakṣa*), such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to remedy lustful desire, and the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) to remedy malice. Thus it is called the contemplation of phenomena; I shall not analyze it further here.

Second, the "contemplation of principle" (*tattva-vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā*), also called the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is the wisdom that contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Thus it is.

There are various such alternative names, as explained in the *Sutra of the Necklace* (*Ārya-śrī-mālā-sūtra*). There are three kinds of contemplation: first, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional;
second, the contemplation of emerging into the conventional from emptiness; and third, the correct contemplation of the Middle Way. That sutra states:

"Entering emptiness from the conventional is called the contemplation of the two truths; emerging into the conventional from emptiness is called the contemplation of equality. These two contemplations serve as the skillful means."

By means of these two contemplations on emptiness, one attains entry into the Middle Way contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Simultaneously illuminating the two truths, each moment of mind is quiescent;
one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience). This is called the Middle Way contemplation of the ultimate truth.

When the three contemplations manifest before one, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*). What is meant by practicing the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional? As a verse in the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra* says:
All phenomena are not solid; one should always remain established in mindfulness.

Having understood and seen that they are empty, the practitioner who is free from all conceptualization, at the time of first sitting in meditation, observes that all phenomena, according to whatever the mind takes as its object, do not abide for even a single moment. Although...

While employing the aforementioned cessation that realizes reality, if deluded thoughts do not cease, at that time you should, according to whatever the mind takes as its object—whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, ignorance, craving, anger, or any other thought of grasping—immediately turn back and observe the mind that has arisen.
You should examine whether such a mind exists or does not exist. If it does not exist...
