If [the mind] does not exist, then there is no mind; how, then, could there be mindfulness? If you claim that the mind exists, does it exist in the past, the future, or the present?
If it is in the past, the past has already ceased. That which has already ceased is non-existent. How can a non-existent dharma be the mind?
If it is in the future, the future has not yet arrived. That which has not yet arrived is non-existent...
Regarding characteristics: how could a dharma that lacks characteristics constitute the mind? If it were present, then a present dharma does not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
A dharma that does not abide cannot be apprehended; a dharma that cannot be apprehended has no mind.
Because there is no mind, all dharmas are empty. Furthermore, if a practitioner thinks that although the present mind does not abide, yet...
It is not that there is no momentary cognition or awareness to serve as the mind; rather, one should examine and investigate this by means of the three kinds of existence.
What are these three? They are explained at length in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: first, existence through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-bhava*).
Second is existence as continuity; third is existence as mutual dependence. How does one contemplate existence through causes and conditions?

The arising of the present mind cannot be apprehended. For example, when there are the six internal sense bases internally and the six external objects externally, consciousness arises through the mutual dependence of the sense bases and their objects.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Conditioned by eye-contact, craving arises; and so on, up to: conditioned by mind-contact, craving arises."

Because the faculties (*indriya*) are internal, they act as causes; because the objects (*viṣaya*) are external, they act as conditions. Therefore, it is said that "internal and external conditions give rise to sensation (*vedanā*).
Sensation is precisely the arising of the mind. Among these five faculties, the mind is their master; therefore, one should first clearly contemplate the present mind:

does it arise from the internal faculty of the mind (*manas*), or does it arise from the external object of mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*), or does it arise from the conjunction of the faculty and the object? Or...
Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) do not coincide, consciousness arises from them together; it does not arise apart from the sense faculties and their objects.

If one were to claim that mind definitely arises from within the mental faculty (*manas*), this would constitute arising from self-nature (*svabhāva*). If there were arising from self-nature, then it would follow that it is a real arising.
Then, within the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), multiple minds would have to arise simultaneously; however, this is not actually the case.
Furthermore, if the internal faculty could arise by itself, it should also be able to arise by itself before it has encountered external objects; yet this is not actually the case.
Therefore, it does not arise through its own nature within the internal faculty. If it is claimed that it definitely arises from external mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*), [the following applies].

This is precisely arising from other-nature (parabhāva). Why is this so? If the sense-faculties (indriya) depend upon objects (viṣaya) for their own nature, then when one regards the objects in relation to the faculties, are they not indeed [their] nature?
If the mind arises from other-nature, then if that other-nature were the mind, [how could it arise from itself?]
Thus, the mind arises from the mind itself; there is no separate mental factor that arises from another nature. If it were not the mind, how could that which is not the mind give rise to the mind?
Since that which is not the mind cannot produce the mind, how could it be that the mind arises solely due to external objects?
Therefore, because it is not external objects, it does not arise from the other-nature of external objects. If one claims that the internal faculties and external objects unite—
Therefore, regarding that which has a mind arising: if it were to arise through co-arising, then it would have arising by way of both self-nature and other-nature. However, in reality this is not so.
If there were arising within each of self and other individually, then it would arise without depending on co-arising. If it were co-arising, then there would be two arisings simultaneously.
If there is no arising within self and other individually, then even when combined they cannot produce arising. Therefore, the sense faculties and their objects do not possess intrinsic nature.

Arising occurs through the conjunction of other-natures (*parabhāva*). If the mind were to arise in order to separate from internal faculties and external objects, then it would be arising without causes or conditions.
Since it is already impossible for the mind to arise from the causes and conditions of faculties and objects, how much more so could it arise without causes or conditions?

If that were the case, there would be no sin in doing evil and no merit in doing good; even though one has left the household life, one’s cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) would be in vain.

[The practitioner] practices. Because they have already fallen into the constant cessation within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not encounter internal faculties or external objects, and thus no [new] birth occurs.

The practitioner contemplates the causes and conditions of internal faculties and external objects through the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). They find that the arising of the present mind is ultimately unobtainable.

Because it is unobtainable, the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is not perceived. Since the characteristic of arising does not exist, then all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*)— [...are likewise unarisen.]

All things are without arising. To speak of arising where there is no arising is because worldly beings, through their inversions and lack of understanding, give rise to false conceptualizations regarding phenomena such as self and other.
This birth born of false conceptualization is not truly birth;
it is like a dream, an illusion, an echo, a transformation, or a reflection in a mirror—merely provisional names. Since the birth of a name is not called "birth," the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:

It is said: "Dharmas do not belong to causes, nor do they abide in conditions. Within this context, one should extensively apply the four preceding propositions to all dharma-gates concerning both delusion and awakening—such as the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās—to distinguish the characteristics of how [phenomena] arise.
These matters are numerous and cannot be fully recounted here. Once the practitioner has thus contemplated arising, their contemplation of cessation is likewise the same.
If the mind is without arising or ceasing and exists merely as a provisional designation, then all phenomena are likewise without arising or ceasing and exist merely as provisional designations.
Since these phenomena of names and words are not, in fact, phenomena, if a practitioner realizes that all phenomena are not phenomena, then even "name" is not a name.
If the mind under observation employs the eight contemplations to examine the eight propositions, it investigates the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

Regarding that which is ultimately unobtainable: the wisdom capable of observing it likewise employs the eight observations to examine the characteristics of arising and ceasing across the eight propositions;

that these too are ultimately unobtainable is also like this. Thus, within the context of causes and conditions, there are sixteen types of observation—combining the observing subject and the observed object—which, by traversing the sixteen propositions, examine the characteristics of the mind’s arising and ceasing, finding them to be ultimately unobtainable.

If one does not perceive arising and ceasing, yet gives rise to attachment and dwelling within that which is neither arising nor ceasing, one should then return to the sixteen contemplations within the context of causes and conditions.
One should examine each of the sixteen phrases; the investigation of the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing is likewise.
If one does not perceive either arising-and-ceasing or non-arising-and-non-ceasing, yet relies upon that which is neither non-arising-and-non-ceasing nor arising-and-ceasing, then...

When returning to the existence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one employs the sixteen contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*) to traverse the sixteen propositions, examining that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
The mind that is neither arising nor ceasing is likewise so. Thus, within the existence of dependent origination, one should employ sixty-four contemplations to traverse sixty-four propositions;
seeking the mind, it is ultimately not to be found. Since the mind produced by causes cannot be found, the cause itself is thereby destroyed.

This accomplishes the refutation of the delusion of continuity. If one falsely conceives of a mind within the continuum, one should likewise employ the sixty-four contemplations to examine the mind through the sixty-four propositions;
that it cannot be found is also thus. Although the contemplation of the mental faculty (*manas*) is the same, its specific application differs.
Since the mind of continuity cannot be found, the delusion of the continuity-construct is thereby destroyed. If, regarding...
Among the [three types of] dependence, those who falsely conceive of a mind as existing should likewise employ the sixty-four contemplations to examine the mind through the sixty-four phrases;
that it is entirely unobtainable is also like this. Although the contemplation of the *manas* (mental faculty) is the same, its corresponding application differs.
Since the dependent mind cannot be found, the delusion of dependent designation is thereby shattered. Thus, regarding the three designations (*tri-prajñapti*), they should be applied in combination.
Through one hundred and ninety-two contemplations, traversing one hundred and ninety-two propositions, one seeks the mind but ultimately finds it unobtainable.
If it is unobtainable, then the mind has nothing upon which to rely. If the mind has nothing upon which to rely, then the mind has no place of abiding.
If the mind dwells nowhere, then there is no discrimination. If there is no discrimination, then there is neither right nor wrong.

If there is neither right nor wrong, then there is no grasping or rejecting. If there is no grasping or rejecting, then the mind of contention subsides. If the mind of contention subsides, then there is neither craving nor aversion.

If there is neither craving nor aversion, then one does not give rise to applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*), nor to the lifting up of conditions. If one does not give rise to applied and sustained thought...
By means of these conditions, the three karmas become tranquil and unmoving. This tranquility and immovability of the three karmas is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

If one attains right concentration, then one suddenly awakens to great enlightenment, and the mind becomes like empty space. When the mind is like empty space, the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) arises.
This wisdom of the true mark is the realization of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Realizing all-knowledge, one understands the nature of spontaneity; this is the teacherless wisdom (*asatya-jñāna*).
One awakens by oneself and attains the purity of the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

If one realizes the purity of the eye of all-encompassing wisdom, one will forever be free from the karmic fetters of birth and death within the triple world (*tridhātu*), penetrate the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the mind will be without obstruction.
This is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā-praveśa-bhāvanā*). Thus, a verse in praise of Prajñā in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Prajñāpāramitā is the true Dharma, free from inversion; having eliminated conceptualization and observation, all verbal dharmas are extinguished.
Having removed immeasurable multitudes of sins, with a pure mind always remaining as one—such a venerable and wondrous person is then able to see Prajñā.
If one cultivates the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, there are one hundred and ninety-two reversals;
because it ceases based on contemplation, there are likewise one hundred and ninety-two reversals. Why is this so?

Within the one hundred and ninety-two phrases of contemplative illumination, the mind that grasps and is deluded and the dharmas it calculates are all non-existent; this is termed "contemplation. One hundred and ninety...
The twelve kinds of inverted conceptualizations and discursive thoughts are stilled; therefore, this is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).

When *vipaśyanā* (insight) and *śamatha* are combined in their enumeration, there are three hundred and eighty-four repetitions. Those who cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* should skillfully investigate them for themselves; their number is distinct and complete, each having its own specific character.
If a practitioner skillfully grasps their essential meaning, how could it be only *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? Each [of the two] individually possesses one hundred and ninety-two [repetitions].
The Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Pāramitās, and all dharma-gates for resolving delusion and awakening are clarified by means of successive permutations;

each of these likewise possesses one hundred and ninety-two permutations. If one were to analyze them through their mutual negation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their reciprocal identity (*tādātmya*), the words and phrases would be infinite.
All of this is for the sake of those sentient beings who have not yet attained realization, as a correspondence between medicine and illness.

Diligently making this distinction: if within the awakened mind there were anything at all, it would be like empty space, where not even a single phrase of a teaching could exist, let alone an immeasurable amount.
This is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional through the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);

it is not shared with the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional through the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which involves the analytical disintegration of phenomena.

This has been a brief clarification of the characteristics of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) to counteract the coarse distractions of a beginner’s initial mind;

this has already been transmitted to those newly learning. If one were to analyze these extensively, the three sets of three would be difficult to exhaust, and those who have not yet attained understanding might instead increase their web of doubts.
Therefore, they have not been set forth in full. This concludes the brief explanation of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to counteract the coarse distractions of a beginner’s mind.
Second, regarding the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as remedies for the mental ailments of sinking and agitation:

when a practitioner is engaged in seated meditation, their mind may become darkened and obstructed, characterized by a state of neutral dullness (*avyākṛta*) or torpor, or they may frequently fall asleep. At such times, one should practice *vipaśyanā* to bring about clear comprehension. If, during...
While sitting, if the mind is floating, restless, and uneasy, one should then practice *śamatha* (calm abiding) to settle it.

This is a brief explanation of the methods for distinguishing and applying *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (insight) as remedies for the ailments of mental sinking and floating; these are identical to what was stated previously.
However, one must skillfully recognize the correspondence between the medicine and the ailment when applying them, so as not to fall into the error of misapplying the remedy.
Third, regarding the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā according to what is appropriate:

when a practitioner is practicing seated meditation, although they cultivate vipaśyanā as an antidote for mental sinking, if the mind remains unclear and unpurified, there will likewise be no benefit from the Dharma. At such a time, one should experimentally cultivate śamatha to settle the mind.
If, during the practice of śamatha, one perceives that body and mind become tranquil, peaceful, clear, and pure, one should know that it is appropriate to continue with śamatha.

One should immediately apply "calming the mind" through *śamatha*. If, while practicing seated meditation, the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* to remedy mental agitation yet the mind does not settle and there is no benefit from the Dharma, they should attempt to practice *vipaśyanā*.

If, during *vipaśyanā*, they perceive the mind and spirit to be luminous, pure, tranquil, and serene, they should know that it is appropriate for *vipaśyanā*; they should then apply *vipaśyanā* to settle the mind. This is a brief explanation.

Cultivate the characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* according to what is appropriate. The methods for distinguishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are no different from those previously explained; one need only skillfully apply them according to what is convenient.
Thus, the mind and spirit will become peaceful and secure, the afflictions and ailments will cease, and the various Dharma-gates will be brought forth.

The fourth pair refutes those who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā with a subtle mind while maintaining fixed views. This means that the practitioner first uses the mind to observe and counteract coarse mental distraction.
Once the distracted mind has ceased, one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Because the mind in absorption is subtle, one perceives the body as empty and quiescent, experiencing bliss.
Alternatively, a sharp and expedient mind may arise, whereby one uses this subtle mind to grasp at partial or deviant principles.
If one does not know that what is seen in concentration is false and deceptive, one will inevitably give rise to craving and attachment, grasping at it as real.
If one realizes through direct experience that it is false, deceptive, and unreal, then the two afflictions of craving and views will not arise; this is called the cultivation of *śamatha*.

If the mind remains deluded and attached to craving and views, such that the bonds of karma do not cease, then at that time one should cultivate *vipaśyanā*, observing the subtle [nature] within that which was seen in concentration.

Regarding the mind: if one does not perceive the fixed view within the subtle mind, one will not cling to that fixed view. If one does not cling to the fixed view, then craving and views will not arise;
these, along with the afflictions, fetters, and karma, should all be investigated and extinguished. This is called the distinct cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

This has been a brief explanation of the characteristics of cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the subtle mind of fixed views, as well as the methods for distinguishing the techniques of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. And...
It is the same as before; the only difference is that it addresses the subtle fault of breaking through fixed views.
Fifth, regarding those who cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by balancing concentration and wisdom:

if, during seated meditation, a practitioner extinguishes [afflictions] by cultivating *śamatha* and enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by cultivating *vipaśyanā*, yet although they have attained absorption, their wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) remains weak and inferior, then—
One cannot give rise to true wisdom, sever the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), or manifest the various Dharma-gates.

At that time, one should practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to break through and dismantle [delusion], specifically the gate of analytical observation, as fully explained previously. If, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom is developed, then concentration and wisdom will be balanced;
one can then sever the fetters and realize the various Dharma-gates. If a practitioner, while practicing seated meditation, due to the cultivation of contemplation...
Therefore, sometimes through the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding), the mind may suddenly open up and understand clearly, and wisdom becomes distinct;
yet, because the concentrated mind is slight, the mind then becomes restless and scattered, like a lamp in the wind that does not illuminate objects clearly. As the *Śāstra* says:
"If there is no concentrated mind, although one possesses the wisdom of contemplating emptiness, signlessness, and so forth, this is inverted wisdom; it is a mad wisdom."
Wisdom alone cannot transcend birth and death or illuminate all things. At that time, one should practice *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The methods for this are fully explained as previously stated. By practicing *śamatha*, one immediately attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Because one attains profound meditative concentration, wisdom and the concentrated mind become equal, like a lamp in a sealed room which can dispel darkness and illuminate objects with clarity. This is the method for practicing *śamatha*.
The Dharma is as fully explained above. It is for the purpose of balancing the two dharmas of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

If a practitioner can thus skillfully employ the meaning of these five stages of cultivation for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while sitting upright with the body straightened, neither adopting nor rejecting inappropriately, it should be known that this person is skillfully cultivating the Buddha-dharma.
Because they are skillfully cultivating the Buddha-dharma, they will necessarily cultivate...
Throughout one's life, one shall not commit transgressions.
Next, to clarify the second method—cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while traversing conditions and confronting objects—one should always sit upright with the body;

this is the superior expedient for entering the Way. However, as a body subject to conditioning, one must inevitably engage with worldly affairs and conditions. If, when encountering conditions and facing objects, one...

If one practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with intervals, then the fetters and karmic activities will arise at every point of contact; how then could one quickly become in accord with the Buddha-dharma?
If, at all times, one practices the skillful means of meditative concentration and wisdom, you should know that such a person will certainly be able to penetrate all the Buddha-dharmas.
How does one practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while traversing conditions? As for what is called "conditions," it refers to...
There are six kinds of conditions: first, walking; second, standing; third, sitting; fourth, lying down; fifth, working; and sixth, speaking.
What is meant by "cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā in relation to objects"? As for "objects," they refer to the six sense-objects: first, the eye facing forms; second, the ear facing sounds.
Third, the nose encounters odors; fourth, the tongue encounters flavors; fifth, the body encounters tangibles; sixth, the mind encounters mental objects (*dharmas*).

Because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in relation to these twelve matters, it is called "cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by traversing conditions and confronting objects.
When the practitioner is walking, they should reflect: "For what purpose do I wish to walk now? Is it for the sake of affliction..."
One is driven by afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as unwholesome and neutral states; this is what constitutes "walking. How does one cultivate tranquility (*śamatha*) while walking?

If, while walking, one understands that because of walking there arise all phenomena—whether afflictive, wholesome, or neutral—and realizes that both the mind that walks and the walker, as well as all phenomena, are ultimately unapprehendable, then deluded thoughts cease. This is called "walking."

Cultivate *śamatha* within walking meditation. The extensive explanation of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as before; in all instances of walking, employ it according to what is appropriate for the occasion.
How does one cultivate *vipaśyanā* while walking? One should reflect thus: "Because the mind arises and the body moves, there is forward progression, which is called 'walking.
Due to this walking, there arise all phenomena, such as afflictions, wholesome states, and unwholesome states. Thereupon, one should immediately turn back to observe them.
Regarding the mind in movement: one does not perceive its characteristics. One should know that both the practitioner and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent;

this is called cultivating contemplation within movement. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of contemplation is as previously explained. Within movement, one should apply it according to what is appropriate.
The practice within movement is also as described above, categorized into five successive stages for the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, when it is time to abide, one should reflect: "For what purpose do I wish to abide now?
If it is for the sake of afflictions, unwholesome states, or neutral matters, then one should not abide. If it is for the sake of wholesome and beneficial matters, then one should abide.
What is called the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) while abiding? It is when, during the time of abiding, one recognizes that it is precisely because of abiding [that this state arises].
Then, regarding all phenomena—whether afflictions, virtues, or non-virtues—one realizes that both the abiding mind and all phenomena abiding therein are unapprehendable.

When deluded thoughts thus subside, this is called the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) while abiding in the middle. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as previously described;
one should employ this while abiding in the middle according to its specific application. How does one cultivate *vipaśyanā* (insight) while abiding in the middle? One should act as follows:

This mindfulness fixes the mind upon a single point; therefore, it is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Because of this abiding, one should then reflect back upon the abiding mind regarding all phenomena—whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome—and see no defining characteristics (*nimitta*).
One should know that both the one who abides and all phenomena within that state of abiding are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) within the state of abiding. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this insight is as follows:

First: while dwelling in the middle [state], one employs it according to whatever application is required. Dwelling in the middle also has five types of categories, which are the repeated cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
their meaning is as explained above. Furthermore, if while sitting one should form this thought: "For what purpose do I now wish to sit?
If I am sitting for the sake of the various afflictions (*kleśas*), unwholesome states, or neutral matters (*avyākṛta*), then [it is not right]."
One should sit. If it is for the sake of wholesome and beneficial matters, one should indeed sit. How does one cultivate *śamatha* while sitting?

At the time of sitting, because one knows the cause of sitting, all afflictions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise—and the mind that sits, as well as all afflictions and wholesome or unwholesome phenomena within that sitting, are realized to be unapprehendable. Thus, [delusion]...
The mind’s mindfulness rests; this is called the cultivation of *śamatha*. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as previously explained.
One should apply it during seated meditation according to its practical requirements. How does one cultivate *vipaśyanā* while seated? One should reflect as follows:

"It is by means of the mind that mindfulness is produced. To cross the legs and settle the body is called 'sitting. Because of this sitting, there arise all phenomena, including afflictions, the wholesome, and the unwholesome."

The practitioner should then reflect back upon the mind that is sitting. If no signs or characteristics are perceived, one should know that both the sitter and all phenomena within the state of sitting are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called cultivating contemplation while seated. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained.

While sitting, one should employ [the practice] according to what is appropriate for the occasion. Within the sitting posture, there are also five successive stages for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which are similar to what was explained above.
Furthermore, when lying down to sleep, one should form this thought:
"For what purpose do I now wish to lie down? Is it for the sake of various afflictions (*kleśa*), unwholesome states, or unrighteous negligence?"
One should not lie down [indiscriminately]. If one lies down for the purpose of harmonizing the four great elements, one should lie in the manner of a lion king.
How does one cultivate *śamatha* while lying down? At the time of resting, one clearly understands that because of sleep, all phenomena—whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome—arise.
One clearly understands the sleeper and all the afflictions, wholesome and unwholesome, within sleep.

When all phenomena (*dharma*) are found to be ungraspable, the deluded mind subsides; this is called practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding) while asleep. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as previously explained;
it should be applied according to its specific utility while one is sleeping. How does one practice *vipaśyanā* (insight) while lying down? One should form this thought:
"If the mind is exhausted by exertion, it will immediately become dark and dull. If one allows the six consciousnesses to function in a state of indulgence, then..."
Regarding all phenomena, whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome, the practitioner should immediately turn back and observe the mind as it lies down.
Seeing no marks or characteristics, one should know that the one who lies down and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent. This is called the cultivation of contemplation while lying down.

The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained; it should be applied according to its practical utility during sleep. The state while lying down is likewise analogous [to other states].
The fifth point, regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, is as explained above. Furthermore, at the time of acting, one should reflect:
"For what purpose do I wish to act? Is it for the sake of the afflictions (*kleśa*), or for unwholesome and indeterminate matters?"
One should not perform it; however, if it is for the sake of a wholesome and beneficial matter, one should perform it. What is meant by "cultivating *śamatha* during activity"?
It is when, while performing an action, one knows that because of that very activity, all phenomena—whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome—arise.
When one realizes that the agent, the act, and all phenomena such as afflictions, good, and evil are entirely unapprehendable, then the mind of deluded thought ceases;
this is called practicing *śamatha* through action. How does one practice *vipaśyanā* while acting? One should reflect thus:
"It is by the movement of the mind that the hands and body perform various tasks; because these actions are performed, there arise all phenomena such as good and evil."

One should immediately turn back and observe the mind that performs the action; when no characteristics are perceived, one should know that the agent and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called cultivating contemplation within the act. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained.

Within the act, one employs it according to whatever application is required. Furthermore, there are five types of alternating cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the act, which are the same as those described above.
Furthermore, when about to speak, one should reflect: "For what purpose do I wish to speak now?
If it is driven by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and one speaks with the intent to discuss unwholesome or indeterminate matters, then one should not speak.
If it is for the sake of a wholesome and beneficial matter, one should speak. What is meant by "cultivating *śamatha* within speech"?
When it is time to speak, one realizes that because of this speech, all phenomena—whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome—arise.

One thoroughly understands that both the speaker and all the afflictions, wholesome, and unwholesome factors within the speech are ultimately unapprehendable; thus, the mind of discursive thought [is stilled].
Breathing. This is called the cultivation of *śamatha* within speech. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as previously explained;
it is to be applied according to its specific utility within speech. How does one cultivate *vipaśyanā* within speech? One should form this thought:
"It is through the mind’s *vitarka* and *vicāra* that the vital breath is stirred, striking the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, and palate to produce sounds and speech. Because of this speech, then..."
Regarding all phenomena, whether they be afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome, one should immediately turn back and contemplate speech and mind.
When no characteristics are perceived, one should know that speech and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent; this is called the cultivation of contemplation within speech.

The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained. Within speech, there are likewise five successive stages for the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, identical to what was stated above.
Furthermore, what is meant by practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding) when seeing forms with the eye?
It is when, upon seeing a form, one immediately knows it to be like a reflection in a mirror, the moon in water, or a city of the Gandharvas—though it is seen, it lacks any fixed reality.

Thus, when seeing a form that accords with one's desires, one does not give rise to craving; when seeing a form that contradicts one's desires, one does not give rise to anger or affliction; and when seeing a form that is neither contrary nor accordant, one remains equanimous.
One does not give rise to ignorance or various distracted thoughts; this is called the cultivation of *śamatha*. The characteristics of *śamatha* are analyzed in detail as previously described.
When the eye sees forms, one employs it according to its appropriate function.

How is it that when the eye sees forms, one should cultivate *vipaśyanā*? One should form this thought: whatever is seen is, in itself, devoid of the characteristic of seeing. Why is this so? Because...
Those faculties, objects, and names are empty. Within this emptiness and clarity, each lacks seeing and there is no discrimination.
Through the causal conditions of their conjunction, eye-consciousness arises. With eye-consciousness as a causal condition, mental consciousness is produced.

When mental consciousness arises, it is able to discriminate various forms. Because of this, all dharmas—such as afflictions, goodness, and evil—come into being. One should then turn back [from them].
Contemplate the mind that perceives form; when no characteristics are seen, one should know that the seer and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The detailed analysis of the characteristics of contemplation is as previously explained.

When the eye sees form, it should be employed according to its practical application. Within the seeing of form, there are likewise five types of alternating cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as described above.
It is said: Furthermore, when one practices *śamatha* while hearing sounds with the ear, one immediately recognizes whatever sound is heard as being like an echo.

If one hears a sound that is agreeable to the mind, one does not give rise to a mind of attachment; if one hears a sound that is disagreeable to the mind, one does not give rise to a mind of aversion;

if one hears a sound that is neither disagreeable nor agreeable, one does not give rise to a mind of discursive discrimination. This is called practicing *śamatha*. The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as follows: [text continues].
First, regarding hearing sounds: one should employ them according to their respective applications. How does one cultivate contemplation? One should reflect as follows:

whatever sounds are heard are empty and non-existent; they merely arise from the conjunction of the sense organ and the object, producing auditory consciousness, which is followed by the arising of mental consciousness that forcibly gives rise to discrimination.
Because of this, all phenomena—whether afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome—come to exist. Thus...
One should turn back and contemplate the mind that hears sounds; seeing no marks or characteristics, one should know that the hearer and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.

This is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The detailed analysis of the characteristics of contemplation is as previously explained. Regarding sounds, one should employ this according to what is applicable.
The practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within hearing sounds is likewise analogous to the fivefold sequence, as described above.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) when smelling odors with the nose: as soon as one perceives an odor, one should understand it to be like a flame within fire, like vapor within water, or like fragrance within empty space.

If one smells an odor that accords with one's desires, one does not give rise to a mind of attachment; if one smells a foul odor that contradicts one's desires, one does not give rise to signs of aversion;
and regarding odors that are neither contrary nor agreeable, one does not produce distracted thoughts. This is called the cultivation of *śamatha*. *Śamatha*.
The detailed analysis of the characteristics is as previously explained. Regarding the smelling of odors, one should employ it according to its practical application.
How does one cultivate contemplation? One should form this thought: "The grasping of the perception of fragrance is deceptive and lacks reality. Why is this so?

Because the sense organ and the object meet, olfactory consciousness arises; subsequently, mental consciousness arises and forcibly discriminates, falsely giving rise to the notion of fragrance. On account of this..."
Regarding all phenomena, whether they be afflictions, wholesome, or unwholesome, one should immediately turn back and contemplate the mind that perceives the fragrance.

When no characteristics are perceived, one should know that the one who perceives the fragrance and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent; this is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained. Within the perception of fragrance, one should employ it according to its specific application. Regarding the perception of fragrance:
There are likewise five types of cultivation for the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as explained above.

Furthermore, when the tongue experiences flavors while practicing *śamatha*, one follows whatever flavor is experienced and immediately knows it to be like obtaining a taste within a dream or an illusion. If a delicious flavor that accords with one's desires is obtained, one does not give rise to attachment;
if a disagreeable, foul flavor is obtained, one does not give rise to anger; and regarding a flavor that is neither disagreeable nor agreeable, one does not...
To give rise to conceptual thoughts is called the cultivation of *śamatha*. The characteristics of *śamatha* are as extensively analyzed previously.
When experiencing the flavor of food, one should employ it according to its practical application. What is meant by cultivating *vipaśyanā* when the tongue experiences flavor?
One should form this thought: "The flavor currently being experienced is truly unattainable. Why is this? Because the nature of the six external flavors is without conceptual differentiation.
The fundamental nature of the internal tongue is likewise without cognition. When internal and external causes and conditions combine, tongue-consciousness arises;
subsequently, mental consciousness arises and forcibly grasps the characteristics of taste. Because of this, all dharmas—such as afflictions, good, and evil—come to be.
If one turns back to examine the consciousness that perceives taste, no characteristics are seen. One should know that the experiencer of taste and all dharmas are ultimately empty.

Quiescence (*śamatha*) is called the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*). The detailed analysis of the characteristics of insight is as previously explained. Regarding the savoring of flavors, one should employ it according to what is appropriate.
Within the tongue’s experience of flavors, there are likewise five types of alternating cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, following the same principles as those described above.

Furthermore, when the body experiences contact, one who cultivates *śamatha* should recognize, in accordance with whatever contact is perceived, that it is a mere reflection or transformation and lacks reality.

If, when experiencing a pleasant contact that accords with one's inclinations, one does not give rise to craving and attachment; when experiencing an unpleasant contact that contradicts one's inclinations, one does not give rise to aversion or delusion;
and when experiencing a contact that is neither unpleasant nor pleasant, one does not give rise to discursive thought or conceptualization—this is called the cultivation of *śamatha*.

The detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* is as previously explained. Regarding feelings and contacts, one should employ them according to what is appropriate for the application. What is bodily feeling and contact?
At the time of practicing meditation, one should form this thought: "Lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, roughness, smoothness, and so forth are called 'contact' (spraṣṭavya).
The six parts, such as the head and so on, are called the 'body' (kāya). The nature of contact is false and illusory; the body, too, is not real. Who is it that can feel contact?

Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) arises, followed by mental consciousness (manovijñāna), which recollects, imagines, and discriminates the characteristics of suffering, pleasure, and so forth. Therefore, it is called [consciousness]."

Regarding contact (*sparśa*): one should immediately turn back and contemplate the mind that conditions contact; not perceiving any marks or characteristics, one should know that the experiencer of contact and all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
This is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The detailed analysis of the characteristics of this contemplation is as previously explained.

Within the experience of contact, it should be applied according to its specific utility. Regarding the experience of bodily contact, there are likewise five types of sequential cultivation by analogy.

The meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is as explained above. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), this was clarified previously in the section on seated meditation;
the fivefold sequence of the intent for practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* has been extensively analyzed therein, so it will not be explained again here.

If a practitioner can cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in all circumstances—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or during seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—it should be known that this person is practicing the true Mahāyāna. As the Buddha told Subhūti in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"If a bodhisattva knows he is walking when walking, and knows he is sitting when sitting, even when putting on his saṃghāṭī robe or looking at a target..."
With a single mind, they know all that enters and exits meditative concentration; therefore, they are called Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Because the Mahāyāna is ungraspable, furthermore, if a person thus practices the Mahāyāna amidst all such states, that person, within the world...
The Most Victorious One is without equal. As stated in a verse within the *Śāstra*:
Sitting serenely beneath the forest trees, Tranquil and having extinguished all afflictions, With a mind attained in profound stillness— This joy is true peace and happiness.
People seek worldly profit, Fame, fine garments, and comfortable beds.
This pleasure is not secure; seeking profit brings no satiety. Wearing the patched robe and wandering for alms, his mind is always unified in every movement.
With the eye of wisdom, he observes and knows the reality of all phenomena.
Amidst the manifold variety of dharmas, he enters them all through equal contemplation; his liberating wisdom is stilled and tranquil.
7. Peerless in the Three Realms:
If a practitioner who has generated the roots of goodness can thus skillfully cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā within the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, then...
While seated, the mind and body become clear and pure. At that time, various roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) will manifest; this should be recognized.
To briefly clarify the signs of the manifestation of these roots of goodness, there are two distinct types. The first is the sign of the manifestation of external roots of goodness.

What are called generosity, observing the precepts, being filial and obedient toward parents and elders, making offerings to the Three Jewels, as well as reciting, studying, and listening to the teachings—these are the signs of the arising of external roots of goodness. These belong to the realm of Māra and are not analyzed here.
Second are the signs of the arising of internal roots of goodness, which refers to the development of roots of goodness through various dhyāna-dharmas. This constitutes three [categories].

[The following] clarifies the meaning: first, the correct explanation of the signs of the arising of the roots of goodness; second, the discrimination between the genuine and the false; third, the cultivation of the roots of goodness through the application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the first, the internal signs of the arising of the roots of goodness, there are five types of distinct characteristics for the arising of the roots of goodness: first, the arising of the roots of goodness of the path of breath (*ānāpāna*).
1. The sign of the arising of the roots of goodness through the contemplation of impurity; 2. The sign of the arising of the roots of goodness through the contemplation of loving-kindness; 3.

The sign of the arising of the roots of goodness through the contemplation of causes and conditions; 4. The sign of the arising of the roots of goodness through the recollection of the Buddha. Regarding the first, the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness through the path of breath:

because the practitioner has skillfully cultivated *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, body and mind become harmonious and well-adjusted, and discursive thoughts subside. Consequently, one becomes self-aware of the mind.
Gradually entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the body and mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) become utterly empty and quiescent.
The concentrated mind becomes stable; within this concentration, one perceives no characteristics whatsoever of body or mind.
Thereafter, whether for one sitting, two sittings, or even for one day, two days, one month, or two months, if one maintains proper rest and care, one will not regress nor lose [the attainment].
Then, while in meditative concentration, one suddenly perceives the movement of body and mind, giving rise to the eight tactile sensations (*aṣṭaspraṣṭavya*).

These eight tactile sensations refer to the perception of bodily movement, itching, cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, roughness, and smoothness. At the moment these sensations arise, body and mind become tranquil, subtle, and joyful;
there is a blissful, cool clarity that is beyond comparison. This is the emergence of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) within the fundamental dhyāna-concentration of counting the breaths.
Characteristics.

Furthermore, the practitioner, perhaps within the "not-yet-arrived" stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) of the desire realm, suddenly becomes aware of the length of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, and knows that all the pores of the body are entirely porous and hollow.
He then perceives with the mind’s eye the thirty-six internal substances, as if...
It is like opening a granary and seeing various sesame seeds, beans, and the like; the mind is filled with great joy and surprise, becoming tranquil, peaceful, and refreshed.

This is the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness for the *viśeṣa* (special) practice of mindfulness of breathing. Second, the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness for the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*):

If the practitioner attains the concentration of the threshold stage (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm, their body and mind become empty and still. Suddenly, they see the bodies of other men and women, which, after death, have become bloated and putrid.
When one sees pus and worms oozing out and white bones scattered in disarray, the mind experiences both sorrow and joy, developing a weary detachment from what is cherished;
this is the sign that the roots of goodness of the nine meditations on repulsiveness have arisen.

Alternatively, while in a state of tranquil concentration, one may suddenly see the impurity of one's own body and external bodies as bloated and scattered in disarray, seeing the white bones of one's own body from head to foot, with each joint supporting the next; upon seeing these things...
When the concentrated mind is peaceful and secure, one awakens to impermanence, feels weary of the five desires, and does not cling to the notions of self or person;

this is the sign that the roots of goodness for renunciation have arisen. Alternatively, within the state of meditative concentration, one perceives all internal and external bodies—whether flying birds or running beasts, clothing, food and drink, houses, mountains, or forests—as entirely impure; this is known as the "Great Impurity."
The signs of the arising of roots of goodness: third, the sign of the arising of the roots of goodness of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they attain the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the desire realm, within this concentration they suddenly give rise to the thought of compassionately regarding sentient beings.
Alternatively, by taking as their object the aspect of people obtaining happiness, they immediately enter deep concentration; their inner mind becomes joyful and pure beyond compare.
It is likewise for those who harbor resentment toward others, even including sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the five realms of existence.

Upon arising from meditative concentration, their minds are joyful and their countenance remains ever harmonious toward whomever they encounter; this is the sign of the manifestation of the roots of goodness of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they attain the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the desire realm, their body and mind become tranquil and settled.

Suddenly, awakening arises in the mind, and as they investigate the various causal conditions—such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—throughout the three periods of time, they do not perceive a self or a person.

Thus, one immediately departs from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, shatters all false attachments, attains stable composure, and develops liberating wisdom. Joy in the Dharma arises in the mind, and one no longer dwells upon worldly affairs.
This applies likewise to the analysis of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the signs arising through causes and conditions, these are the signs of the arising of the five roots of goodness associated with mindfulness of the Buddha. Because the practitioner cultivates *śamatha*, if they attain [the stage of] the desire realm...

In the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the concentration of the stage not yet reached), the body and mind are empty and tranquil. Suddenly, one recollects that the merits, marks, and signs of all Buddhas are inconceivable;
that all their ten powers (*daśabala*), four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), unique dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), samādhis, and liberations are inconceivable;
and that their supernatural transformations, unimpeded preaching of the Dharma, and vast benefit for sentient beings are inconceivable. Such as these...
The immeasurable merits are inconceivable. When one contemplates in this way, a heart of reverence and love immediately arises;

samādhi is manifested, and body and mind experience bliss, purity, and tranquility, free from all evil signs. Upon arising from meditative concentration, the body becomes light and agile, and one personally realizes that one's merits are sublime.
One enters into the state of being revered and loved; this is called the arousal of the roots of goodness of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi.
[The] signs.

Furthermore, as the practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they may attain physical and mental tranquility, or give rise to [the contemplations of] impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, [perceiving] the world as something to be loathed and afflicted.
[They may contemplate] the impurity of food, the thought of its inexhaustibility despite its consumption, and the mindfulness of the Buddha’s Dharma.

The monastic precepts, the relinquishment of the heavens, the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the supernormal powers and transformations, and so forth—the manifestations of all these dharma-gates should be extensively analyzed herein. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To regulate them."
In one place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.

Regarding the second [section], the discernment of the true from the false, it consists of two parts: first, clarifying the characteristics of the deviant; second, distinguishing the characteristics of the authentic and true.

Regarding false signs: when one gives rise to the various meditative absorptions mentioned above, they manifest according to their respective causes as phenomena such as the agitation of the hands and body, or at times the body feeling heavy as if weighed down by objects, or at times the body feeling light as if about to fly, or the body feeling as if it were bound.

At times they may escape while still immature; at times they may be chilled by the heat of the cauldron; at times they may experience sensations of heat; or they may see various strange and diverse objects.
At times their minds may be shrouded in darkness; at times they may give rise to evil thoughts; at times their goodness may be distracted by external things;
at times they may be joyful and restless; at times they may be sorrowful and filled with grief; and at times they may be touched by unpleasant sensations, and their bodies...
The body hairs stand on end, and at times one becomes intoxicated by great pleasure. Such various false dharmas arise simultaneously with dhyāna and are termed "perverse and counterfeit.
If a person becomes attached to this perverse concentration, they will correspond with the ninety-six kinds of ghost-spirit methods;
they will mostly lose their minds and become insane, or at times various ghosts and spirits will know that the person’s thoughts are fixated upon them.
He then exerts his power to cause [the practitioner] to produce various profound, heterodox concentrations, wisdom, eloquence, and supernormal powers, thereby moving the people of the world.

Those who see him claim he has attained the fruits of the Path, and all come to believe in and submit to him. Yet, in his inner mind, he remains inverted, single-mindedly practicing and contemplating these [heterodox] dharmas.
When such a person’s life ends, they will never encounter a Buddha again, but will fall back into the realm of ghosts and spirits. If, during their lifetime, they...
By practicing unwholesome dharmas, one immediately falls into hell. If you wish to know the causes and conditions for this, you should seek out the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths;

then you will clearly perceive this matter. When a practitioner cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if they realize such meditative states (*dhyāna*) and these various false and deceptive signs arise, they should immediately reject them.
If they recognize them as empty and deceptive, maintaining a correct mind without attachment, they shall then vanish and cease to exist.
If they do not cease, one should apply *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; through contemplation and analysis, they will be destroyed and extinguished. Second, clarifying the signs of the arising of dhyāna:

if, while sitting, various states of dhyāna arise, even though the aforementioned dharmas are absent, at the moment the dhyāna arises, one immediately perceives a correspondence with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It is empty, luminous, and pure; the inner mind is joyful, tranquil, and blissful, free from obscuration.
In brief: when the wholesome mind is awakened, faith and reverence increase, wisdom and discernment become clear, and the body and mind grow supple.
One becomes subtle, profound, and tranquil; weary of the world, one becomes unconditioned and desireless, attaining mastery over entering and emerging from meditation.

This is the sign of the manifestation of right dhyāna. It is like working with an evil person who constantly causes irritation; yet if one works with such a person for a long time, they eventually come to see their true nature.
Its excellence lies in its differentiation between the two types of characteristics: the deviant and the correct; it is also like this.

Third, to clarify the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to nourish the faculties: when various roots of goodness arise while seated, one should employ the two methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to cultivate them so that they increase.
How does one cultivate them? If it is appropriate to apply *śamatha*, then by means of...
Cultivate it through stillness (*śamatha*). If it is appropriate to employ insight (*vipaśyanā*), then one may employ insight. A brief indication of the general meaning follows.
VIII. Signs of Realization:
When a practitioner cultivates stillness and insight in this manner, they are able to understand that all phenomena arise solely from the mind.
Birth is empty because its causes and conditions are false and unreal. Because one knows this emptiness, one cannot apprehend the names or characteristics of any phenomena;
this is "stopping by realizing the true nature" (*tattva-vipaśyanā*). At that time, one perceives neither a Buddha-fruit to be sought above nor sentient beings to be delivered below.

This is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā-praveśa-vipaśyanā*), also called the contemplation of the two truths (*dvi-satya-vipaśyanā*), and also called...
The eye of wisdom is also called omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). If one dwells in this contemplation, one falls into the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the śrāvakas and others lamented, saying:

"If we were to hear of purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings, we would not give rise to joy or delight. Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent. There is no...
It is unborn and unceasing; it is neither great nor small; it is untainted and unconditioned. When one contemplates in this way, no joy or pleasure arises.

You should know that if one perceives the unconditioned and enters the stage of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), such a person will ultimately be unable to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is because their power of meditative concentration is excessive, and thus they do not see the Buddha-nature. If a bodhisattva, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, achieves...

Because all Buddha-dharmas are [unconditioned], one should not grasp at or cling to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). At that time, one should cultivate the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñapti-avatāra-vipaśyanā*).
One should then observe with clarity: although the nature of the mind is empty, when it encounters conditions, it is also able to give rise to all dharmas.
It is like a magical illusion: although it lacks any fixed reality, it nevertheless possesses the characteristics of being seen, heard, sensed, and known, with various distinct differences.
When the practitioner contemplates in this way, although they know that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, they are able, within that emptiness, to...
Cultivating and planting practices is like planting trees in the air; it also enables one to discern the various faculties and natures of sentient beings.
Because these are immeasurable, the Dharma taught is likewise immeasurable. If one can achieve immeasurable eloquence, one is then able to benefit the suffering beings of the six realms.
This is called "cultivating cessation according with conditions through skillful means," which is precisely the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), also known as...
The contemplation of equality is also called the Dharma-eye and is also called the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
Abiding within this contemplation, although the power of wisdom is great, one perceives the Buddha-nature yet does not do so with clarity.

Although a bodhisattva may achieve these two contemplations, they remain merely gates of skillful means (*upāya*) and are not yet *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "The preceding two kinds are the path of skillful means."
These two contemplations on emptiness lead to the entry into the Middle Way contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein one simultaneously illuminates the two truths.
With each thought-moment extinguished in stillness, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

If a bodhisattva wishes to be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas within a single thought-moment, they should cultivate the cessation of dualistic discrimination and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way. How does one cultivate this correct contemplation?

If one can realize that the nature of the mind is neither real nor false, and thus brings to rest the conditions of both reality and falsity—this mind that brings to rest the conditions of reality and falsity is called *śamatha*.

To contemplate clearly that the nature of the mind is neither empty nor false, yet without destroying the dharmas of emptiness and falsity—if one can thus illuminate and understand, one will penetrate the Middle Way within the nature of the mind and perfectly illumine the two truths. If one can, within...
Within one's own mind, one perceives the Middle Way and the Two Truths; that is, one perceives all dharmas as the Middle Way and the Two Truths.

Yet, one does not even grasp at the Middle Way and the Two Truths, because a determinate nature cannot be found. This is called the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, as stated in the verses of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I say that these are empty; they are also designated by provisional names, and this is the meaning of the Middle Way.
Contemplating the intent of this verse, it not only fully possesses the characteristics of correct discernment and contemplation, but also simultaneously clarifies the two preceding [truths].
The middle-way right contemplation within the various gates of expedient observation is itself the Buddha-eye; it is itself the knowledge of all modes.
If one abides in this contemplation, then the powers of samādhi and prajñā are equal, and one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature, thereby dwelling securely in the Mahāyāna.
His gait is level and upright, and his speed is like the wind. If his movement is as swift as the wind, he naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
If he flows into the ocean of all-knowledge, he is practicing the conduct of a Tathāgata. If he practices the conduct of a Tathāgata...
This is precisely entering the Tathāgata’s chamber. If one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber, one dons the Tathāgata’s robe.
If one dons the Tathāgata’s robe, one sits upon the Tathāgata’s seat. If one sits upon the Tathāgata’s seat, one adorns oneself with the adornments of the Tathāgata.
If one adorns oneself with the adornments of the Tathāgata, one thereby attains the purity of the six sense faculties.
Purity. If one attains the purification of the six sense faculties, this is entry into the realm of the Buddhas.
If one enters the realm of the Buddhas, one is then unstained by and unattached to all phenomena.
If one is unstained by and unattached to all phenomena, then all Buddhas appear before one. If all Buddhas appear before one, this is the accomplishment of mindfulness.
The Buddha’s samādhi: if one achieves the buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), this is precisely abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

If one abides in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, one attains the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body Samādhi (sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi). One is then able to universally enter the lands of the ten directions to transform and guide sentient beings.
If one universally enters the lands of the ten directions to transform and guide sentient beings, this is itself the purification and adornment [of those lands].
All Buddha-fields. If one adorns and purifies all Buddha-fields, this is itself the making of offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is the ability to receive and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
If one can receive and uphold the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, one will be able to fulfill all practices and all pāramitās. If one fulfills all pāramitās...
One immediately enters the stage of a Great Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment and becomes an equal companion to Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
If one is an equal companion to Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, one abides within the Dharmatā-kāya. If one constantly abides within the Dharmatā-kāya, [one realizes non-duality].
He is immediately praised and granted a prophecy by the Buddhas of the ten directions. To be praised and granted a prophecy is itself the adornment of the Tuṣita heaven.
To adorn the Tuṣita heaven is to be able to manifest the descent of one’s body into a mother’s womb.
If he manifests descending into his mother’s womb, he is immediately able to manifest leaving the household life and proceeding to the tree of enlightenment.
If he manifests proceeding to the tree of enlightenment, he is immediately able to manifest subduing the powerful Māra, the enemy.

If he manifests subduing the enemy Māra, he is immediately able to manifest attaining equal and perfect enlightenment. If he manifests attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, he is immediately able to manifest...
To turn the wheel of the true Dharma; if one manifests the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma, one is then able to manifest entry into parinirvāṇa.
If one manifests entry into nirvāṇa, this is the ultimate fulfillment of all Buddha-works throughout the lands of the ten directions.
If one fulfills all Buddha-works, this is the perfection of the two bodies—the true body and the responsive body. If one perfects these two bodies, this is the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
This refers to one who dwells as a bodhisattva. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening;
one thoroughly realizes the true nature of all phenomena, and this wisdom-mind is not realized through another. It is also called the "bodhisattva who has first generated the mind."
One attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is immeasurable bodies. It is also said that a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind is fully endowed with the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
It is further said that a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening is himself a Buddha. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things;
between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also says: "Subhūti, there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."
O Bodhisattva, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, you turn the wheel of the true Dharma even while seated at the site of awakening.

You should know that such a bodhisattva is like a Buddha. As evidenced by the pearl offered by the dragon girl in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these and other scriptures all clarify that the initial resolve is fully endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas.
If one is endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas at the initial resolve, that is precisely the Great [Vehicle].
The *A* syllable dharma-gate in this chapter of the sutra is identical to that in the *Lotus Sutra*, which aims to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
it is also identical to that in the *Nirvana Sutra*, whereby one perceives the Buddha-nature and abides in Great Nirvana.

This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the fruit realized by a beginner bodhisattva through the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Next, the characteristics of the fruit realized by the final mind will be clarified. Hereafter—

The realm realized by the mind is ultimately unknowable. Now, when we infer what is clarified by the teachings, it never departs from the two dharmas of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Why is this so? As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the wisdom of the Buddhas is earnestly praised—this is precisely the meaning of *vipaśyanā*.

This is an elucidation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) by way of *vipaśyanā*. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is an extensive explanation of the "one hundred phrases of liberation."
"Deliverance. To explain *Mahāparinirvāṇa* in this way is to clarify the fruit by means of *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Therefore, it is said: "Mahāparinirvāṇa is also called the Samādhi of Eternal Quiescence (*nityapraśāntasamādhi*). Here, "samādhi" carries the meaning of *śamatha*. Although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the fruit by means of *vipaśyanā* (insight-wisdom), it nonetheless subsumes *śamatha*;
thus it says: "...down to ultimate *parinirvāṇa*, the mark of eternal quiescence ultimately returns to..."

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Although *nirvāṇa* is explained here in terms of cessation (*śamatha*) as the fruit, it also encompasses contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, the three virtues constitute Great *Nirvāṇa*.

Although these two great sutras differ in the appearance and disappearance of their phrasing and meaning, there is not one that does not analyze the lack of ultimate attainment through the two gates of cessation and contemplation, nor one that clarifies the supreme fruit by relying on the two dharmas of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). A practitioner should know that if, at the beginning...
The middle and subsequent fruits are all inconceivable. The *New Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata of the past limit is inconceivable;
the Tathāgata of the middle limit is adorned with various ornaments; the Tathāgata of the future limit is eternally indestructible.

Thus, these are all explained in terms of the fruits realized through the two mental states of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Therefore, a verse in the *Pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra* says:
All Buddhas attain liberation through the mind; The mind is pure and called stainless.
The five paths are pristine and do not receive form; He who understands this is praised as having attained the Great Way of Perfect Enlightenment.
Composed by Pei Xiu, Jinzi Guanglu Dafu, Acting Minister of the Secretariat, concurrently Minister of the Ministry of Revenue,
Participant in Deliberations of the Zhongshu Menxia, and Grand Scholar of the Jixian Hall:
"The myriad virtues of all sentient beings and Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are equally contained within the Great Canon of Radiant Light."
The awakened mind is equal and pervasive throughout the ten directions; deluded people are inverted and give rise to discrimination.
The Dharma King possesses a teaching named Perfect Enlightenment, from which flow forth True Suchness and Nirvana.
Ignorance has no substance, like flowers in the sky; once the awakened mind is revealed, ignorance is extinguished.
When the external environment is tranquil, the body and mind are pure; First, one must form the vast vow for Bodhi.
One must rely on universal illumination to clear away the dust of the emotions;
Only then is this the original ground of the Tathāgata. Therefore, you all should know: Follow the Dharma of Mañjuśrī’s stage of practice.
The illusory realms of all sentient beings All arise within the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment.
Just as flowers in the sky are never truly born, They exist from emptiness and thus cease back into emptiness.
When the cataract is removed, the flowers vanish and emptiness is primordially pure; Knowing this manifestation, the dust of delusion is extinguished and awakening is perfected.
The illusory mind arises solely from the awakened mind; do not seek liberation from illusion outside of awakening.
When the sun’s orb is at its zenith, all shadows vanish; now that the essence of awakening is manifest, the multitude of illusions is eliminated.
With illusion removed, awakening is fulfilled; awakening is not empty. Do not doubt this is illusion and return to cultivating illusion.
Therefore, you and all others should know: In accordance with Samantabhadra, cultivate the illusory dharma;
The Tathāgata’s pure awakening is free from defilement. To seek realization, first rely on the gates of precepts and concentration;
The false body has no substance, and the false mind is empty. Because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects cease.
When the mirror’s tarnish is polished away, its blue and yellow colors appear; when wisdom illuminates, emotions empty and self and others merge.
There is only the perfectly luminous mind of Great Awakening, wherein the sense organs, objects, and the physical world are all pure and clear.
When the sun sets behind Mount Yuquan, the mountain valleys fall into darkness; when the spiritual treasury is clouded, the mind is muddled by the toil of dreams and illusions.
Profoundly contemplate that both person and phenomena are empty; Realize that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas.
Therefore, you and all others should know: By practicing in reliance upon this, you shall avoid delusion and distress.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous, enlightened, and perfect body— Afflictions and suchness are fundamentally not divided.
From beginning to end, arising and ceasing revolve like a cycle; all these are seen within the delusions of saṃsāra.
The shore shifts and the moon moves, both returning again and again; though the ore is exhausted and gold is formed, the ore does not cease to exist.
With a floating mind, one employs clever views and clings to doubt; ultimately, such a person cannot journey across the ocean of quiescent extinction.
In the morning, purify your thoughts of the realm of the Tathāgata; first sever the root of the mind that transmigrates in saṃsāra.
If you contemplate within delusion regarding Perfect Enlightenment, your awakening will follow the delusions—how then can you distinguish the truth?
Therefore, all of you must know this: do not give rise to the three doubts regarding Perfect Enlightenment.
All sentient beings, from the beginningless past, Have all received various bodies due to lustful desire.
Knowing that they have wandered in saṃsāra for many kalpas, It is solely because of craving and attachment that serves as the root.
Amidst the chaotic realms of desire, with much opposition and compliance, They wander lost on a dark path, weary of birth and death.
If one eliminates craving and severs the cycle of rebirth, one will then be able to awaken to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Though the sunlight may be intense, it is obscured by drifting clouds; though the nature of awakening is ever-perfect, it is clouded by the two types of delusion.
If you wish to find peace within the City of Wondrous Enlightenment, rely on your vows to practice and sever all obstacles.
Therefore, you all should know this: always take the sun of wisdom as the mirror of the mind.
The Great Enlightenment is perfectly luminous and free from all marks; there is neither saṃsāra nor the distinction between the holy and the ordinary.
Both sentient beings and bodhisattvas are empty; it is only within delusion that functional differences are manifested.
With a pure mind, one gives rise to understanding and faith within the ordinary;
