From the essence of awakening, the mind is born, and the sage and the external worthy illuminate and realize, forgetting both; When truth and delusion are fully integrated, one first becomes a Buddha.
In the twilight, when objects and phenomena are all empty and still, This is precisely the time to withdraw the mind and abide in contemplation.
If you aspire to realize Bodhi through contemplation of the world, And remain free from delusion amidst all objects of perception, Then you, O assembly, should know this:
Swiftly transcend the ordinary stages and become perfected true wisdom.
*The Text for Cultivation, Realization, and Repentance at the Perfect Enlightenment Dharma-Assembly*, Fascicle 18.
Verses on the Twelve Chapters of the Ritual for Cultivating and Realizing Perfect Enlightenment by Guifeng,
Compiled as Individual Verses by Jing’an, Śramaṇa Xingting.
The Introduction explains that for the ritual of Perfect Enlightenment, one must first understand the ritual; it differs from the impure lands where ordinary capacities are intermingled.
Here, the Bhagavān’s sovereign body is fully manifest, a marvel within the Great Radiant Treasury.
A hundred thousand great beings are gathered in this assembly;
when the twelve *ṛṣis* wish to inquire, within the non-dual realm, they are like reflections in a perfect mirror—how different from a radiant, pure lapis lazuli!
This is the verse for Mañjuśrī.
Wondrous Virtue first inquires into the causes of the original source: He has long known that by departing from illness one may cultivate the *dhāraṇī* gate that pervades the Dharma-realm;
The great ocean of Perfect Enlightenment is devoid of shores or fords, yet within the dream of ignorance one is deluded by the shadows of conditions;
Like flowers seen by a cataract-afflicted eye, one falsely clings to a self within them.
Suddenly waking from the dream, the obscuring flowers vanish; When has the person of original nature ever been moved?
This verse on Samantabhadra follows the chapter on Samantabhadra.
Next, he asks about the gradual cultivation of the truth, Comprehensively explaining the gateway of practice for the three capacities.
Illusions are not the awakened mind; objects do not exist outside the mind. Flowers are not the nature of emptiness; they abide within that very nature.
When the awakened mind is unmoving, delusory flowers subside. Since delusive objects have no arising, what wisdom could there be to discuss them?
When illusion is exhausted and awakening is perfected, the true body manifests. Like ashes flying and smoke vanishing, the fire has no cause.
Verse on the Universal Eye:
The Universal Eye is the perfect fusion of cause and effect; The substance of body and mind is a reflection that follows delusion.
First, one realizes the gate of purity through the two kinds of emptiness; Next, one cultivates the practice of the three contemplations, which are perfect and sudden.
Subject and object are both delusions; the sentiments of ordinary and sage—how could likes and dislikes possibly be discussed as distinct?
Having once known the originally present *maṇi* jewel, how can its five colors—blue, yellow, and the rest—be described?
This is the verse for the Chapter on Vajragarbha.
The Vajra-holding One’s body is difficult for both sages and ordinary beings to grasp; fundamentally awakened, how could there be a cause for delusion?
These three questions form a continuous chain of discernment. Through various gates, the metaphors reveal that the nature is originally empty;
the arising and ceasing of flowers are fundamentally due to delusion. When the gold ore is smelted away, it is forever severed from dust.
If one wishes to measure the ocean of perfect enlightenment, Entering the stage of contemplation will only lead to deeper immersion.
In this verse on Maitreya, Maitreya investigates the root of saṃsāra: "If one cuts off craving and love, birth and death will end."
The fault of craving as a cause is already profound; the condition of craving for life as a fruit is difficult to eliminate.
As the two obstacles are categorized according to the five natures, the four modes of birth subsequently form the aggregates of the six realms.
If one associates with virtuous friends, views of attachment will perish, and one will naturally awaken to and enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In this chapter on Pure Wisdom, those who have realized the truth are categorized into four distinct stages: the natural, the ordinary, the sage, and the fruit.
Although these differ according to their states of awakening or delusion, and their defilement or purity, with whom does the essence of wisdom truly align?
First, clarifying the sequential traversal of the various natures according to their stages; next, distinguishing the causes for the sudden realization through the forgetting of the mind.

When the single wisdom clearly transcends the realm of detachment, existence and non-existence are exhausted and the sprout of awakening flourishes like spring—this is the "Chapter on the Praise of Majestic Virtue."
The majestic power requests the opening of the three types of contemplation; For those of middling capacity, this begins the division into four sections.
Wherever the gates are opened, they come as appropriate; When the three classes practice, there is no confusion.
The still mirror is perfectly bright and fully manifest; The illusory sprouts grow without bound.
The crossbar within a vessel may serve as a metaphor for *dhyāna*; The three dharmas can bring one to the shore beyond birth and death.
In the "Chapter on Discerning Sound," Bianyin again asked: "How many kinds of wheels are there? By practicing how many methods can one realize the Truth?"
Although the gates of the single, manifold, and perfect circles differ, one must distinguish between stillness, illusion, and tranquil contemplation;
establish each according to its designated mark. If you wish to investigate the knots, first yearn for compassion and repent of the roots of transgression.
The twenty-five wheels rely upon illusory awakening; where there is no place for cultivation, they reveal the causes of practice.
Chapter on Purifying Karma:
Purifying karma involves severing the grasping at self and person. Both take the four marks as their object;
the habit-energy of delusion and ignorance takes the sovereign as the root of the self. When the mind harbors a sense of a "realizer," there the person is established.
The life-span, karma, and wisdom continue to exist in hidden succession; they are beyond the reach of sentient beings, the self, and the person.
From these arise aversion and attachment, afflictions, birth, and death; how can those who are obscured regarding this enter the City of Awakening?
This concludes the verse on the Chapter of Universal Awakening.
Universally awaken to freedom from illness by relying upon a teacher and kin;
one should follow those of upright knowledge and vision, without calculating the traces of walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.

Through the non-arising of the causes of illness—neither self nor other—the illness is eliminated without eliminating phenomena. One should serve through offerings of wealth and the relinquishment of the body.
Hatred and love must be rendered seedless; Only then can one cultivate the truth within Perfect Enlightenment.
In the Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment, it is said:
Within the Sanctuary of Perfect Enlightenment, one realizes perfect awakening; Those of inferior capacity thereby open the true path.

The three periods and limits may be adjusted as appropriate; because the fourfold assembly observes the rains retreat free from external conditions, they take Great Perfect Enlightenment as their monastery.
Seated upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, they fulfill their practices and vows to deliver others;
having previously known and realized entry [into the Way], this encompasses all that preceded. All Buddhas rely together upon such a dwelling.
The Chapter on the Praise of the Worthy and Virtuous Leader:
The Propagation of the Dharma Gate by the Virtuous Leader; Its five names are thus distinguished as the true definitive meaning of the twelve divisions of the sutras;
Discussed together by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.
The realm and ground of the Buddha have already been expounded; now those of sudden capacity may hear them.
If one understands that the hundred rivers all return to the great ocean, what prevents a single dharma from benefiting many faculties?
(This verse serves as a judgment on the inclusion.)
Guishan attained enlightenment and immediately propagated [the teaching], relying upon Xianshou to expand the school’s tenets.
He explored the four commentaries to clarify their distinctions and exhaustively investigated various exegeses to determine the existence or emptiness [of phenomena].
The Sudden Teaching was subsumed within the sutras as judged by the Buddha himself; the Perfect Gate encompasses both aspects, and its principles are worthy of following.

If one were to categorize the sūtras, śāstras, and teachings according to their characteristics, they would be fully subsumed within the Perfect, Sudden, and Middle [teachings] by grasping their essential substance.
